method: Notes saved to /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-priyanshu-Sex-Ed/f50ea7ee-0855-46a2-8572-0aa08df5b855/scratchpad/characters/method.md. The evidence pictures are drift-sheet.png and forehead-check.png in the same folder, and the raw text of every source page is in its src/ folder. The repo was read only; nothing was painted.

1. Write the person before drawing them. Comics and TV start from a bible entry: what they want, what they fear, one contradiction, a little history, and how they talk. The draft cast table gives each person one temperament line (Papa is 'exact and dry'). That makes them types. Section 4 of the notes has a seven-question test for 'memorable, not a type': a want this year and a want from you; one contradiction that shows the same way every time; one thing you could draw in five strokes; one line people quote back or one speech habit; one friction and one tenderness with another household member; a change across the year; and one of the six players saying 'I know this person'.

2. Write a voice file for each person: pet words, one speech habit (a habit survives three languages and the 10-word cap better than a slogan), a 'never says' list a script can check, gender-free ways of addressing you (rule 66), polite forms to elders, three sample lines and three sample messages, each in Hinglish, Hindi and English. Typing is part of the character: in one study a full stop at the end of a text read as less sincere, so punctuation shows who someone is.

3. Give each person an identity stack, strongest anchor first: silhouette and height on a cast line-up, hair as a shape, one face accessory or facial hair, one garment with a pattern and a light or dark value, one prop with a story and a named hand, and one posture. Gate: no two people share an anchor in the top four; the cast can be told apart as black shapes at phone size and in two inks (Station's look); the round, square and triangle shapes are not sorted by gender; an Indian reader checks every sheet against rule 3.
4. Add painter's glossary rows for every garment and prop word with more than one meaning, and plan a reference picture for each prop.

5. Paint one master model sheet per person in the present-day style: front, three-quarter, profile, back, full figure, usual posture, and four to six expressions written as what the whole body does. Use three seeds and pick by eye against the anchor checklist, a close-up of forehead and skin, a count of hands, and a check for stray lettering. The owner approves the pictured parts sheet before any panel is painted.
6. From the picked master, make one reference picture for each world a person appears in, using the edit model to restyle it. Chapter voices need two references each; the household may need six.

7. Paint by scene with cutscenes.py paint-refs. Put at most two people from references in a panel (klein takes 4 reference pictures in all), describe people by role and never by name, and put props in the scene with the hand that holds them. Check every panel against each person's checklist, repaint failures with a new seed, and record the pass rate for each person.
8. Only if one person keeps failing: first add more reference views of them; then, and only then, run a one-person LoRA test through heavyq.

9. Voice read-through: read the strip with the names covered, and a reader should be able to name the speaker of most lines from the words alone. Run it beside rule 24's 'What was this about?' playtest.
10. Keep the bible live: a change to a look or a voice reaches the person's entry, the glossary and the reference files the same day.

Indian comics, as the sources describe them: Chacha Chaudhary has a fixed outfit (red turban, stick, waistcoat, pocket watch), a saying other people repeat about him, and a small body with a big mind. Pran's brief was a type made specific: 'Each family has its own wise old man'. That is a design brief for Nani. The turban that makes him instantly readable is exactly what rule 3 forbids, so our anchors must be secular: spectacles, a shawl, a cardigan, a watch, a cane, a scorebook.

Suppandi's head was drawn flat because he has no brains, his editor says he takes everything literally, and the same family drew him for decades. Shikari Shambu's creators dropped his gun after a few episodes but kept the hat over his eyes, and he is a coward the world thinks brave. Nagraj was drawn by several artists in turn, and his parallel versions are told apart by costume and hair. Tinkle calls itself completely secular, with names like Aisha and Kabir. I found no source on how Amar Chitra Katha kept faces the same across its artists.

Voice examples: Sarabhai vs Sarabhai tells each family member apart by one want, one irritation aimed at another member, and one speech habit or catchphrase. Forster says flat characters are recognisable and memorable, so a chapter voice (Mausi, Masterji) can be flat by design while the household must be rounded. McKee is quoted as saying a character's depth is a contradiction held consistently, and that the protagonist shapes the rest of the cast. Since you, the protagonist, are never drawn, define each person partly by what they want from you.

Side finding: six of eight reused library faces I checked close up carry a painted forehead dot, including a man (jadugar-salim). None of them is in portraits.py's DOTS list. They are not this cast, but any face brought back needs the close-up check first.

Questions for the owner: is a plain cap with no badge allowed for Captain sahab (the bible's list says 'cap')? May several people wear spectacles if the frames differ? Should each person get their own bubble style (Todd Klein's Sandman way) or only name tags? Should we run a one-person LoRA test if reference editing fails?
template: The full fillable template is in section 7 of method.md, one file per person. It opens with a short frontmatter block (type: character, title, description, plane_issues).

0. At a glance: what you call them (English, Hindi, and the first-time English label rule 65 needs); age, relation to you, where they live and what fills their day; the type in five words; the one contradiction, said as 'X, but Y'; what they want this year; what they want from you; what they fear; the line people quote back or their speech habit (10 words at most, in all three languages); which of the six players would say 'I know this person'; flat or round.

1. Inner life: two or three facts from the past that still show in a panel or a line; how they show care; what makes them cross and what makes them laugh; what they would never do (including never doubting a report of harassment or a dowry demand, and never being on a card); their year, from January to December, and which chapter turns it.
2. Relationships: one friction and one tenderness with each of Nani, Mummy, Papa, Mama ji, Tinku, you, and the chapter voice they share a chapter with.

3. Voice (spoken): register and pace; 3 to 5 pet words as Hinglish, Hindi and English; one speech habit; how they address you (rule 66 forms: commands, 'who should' asks, lines where you are not the doer; no gendered word); how they address elders and younger people; how they argue, praise and say sorry; their humour, or none (the chapter's asker is never the comic one, rule 37); a 'never says' list a script can check; 3 sample lines in all three languages, read aloud by a Hindi-first reader.

4. Typing: script (Devanagari, Hinglish in Latin letters, or English); length; full stops or none; capitals; emoji; voice notes; forwards; when they message and how fast they reply; typos; 3 sample messages as live text on the painted blank phone.

5. Look, as an identity stack with the strongest anchor first: (1) silhouette, height rank and build; (2) hair as a shape, in one sentence the painter cannot misread; (3) face accessory or facial hair, never shared with another person; (4) everyday clothes as garment, pattern, value and fit, plus clothes for the wedding week; (5) a colour key table naming the signature garment's ink in each look (now, Lugdi, Station, Jadugar, Cricket, Rukavat); (6) a signature prop, its story and the hand that holds it, with its glossary row and its own reference picture; (7) posture at rest, the gesture they repeat, and what their hands do when idle; (8) skin words that resist whitening, face shape and signs of age. Then the rule 3 read by an Indian reader, and a note on how this person's shape sits against the cast's gender spread.
6. Expressions, written as what the body does: neutral, pleased, worried, cross, laughing, tired, moved.

7. Painter sheet: the role word (never the name); the fixed present-day look words; additions for each look; what must never go in the fixed look (props go in the scene); glossary rows needed; files (master sheet, reference for each look, seeds tried, seed picked); the audit checklist for every panel; known painter traps (forehead dot, whitening in soft looks, swapping with another person when painted together).
8. Where they appear: chapters, looks, panels, lines per chapter, and asker or voice in which chapter.

9. Rule checks: never on a card; not comic if an asker; Hindi passes rule 66; polite forms to elders; no rule 3 marker in words or on the sheet; within the line caps; British spelling with no em or en dashes.

Short version for circle (card) people: first name, age, a job most people can do, how they stand to the household, one want and one habit shown only in story panels, and hair shape plus one anchor for the portrait. The measure judge checks that these traits stay off the cards, fall as often on women as on men, and never follow gender across a pair (rules 17, 19, 20).

Cast line-up sheet (section 8): one row for each person who speaks or is drawn, with columns for height rank, build, hair shape, face accessory, garment pattern, value, prop, posture, base shape and gender. A repeated value is a clash to fix. The checks: black shapes at phone size, two inks, base shapes not sorted by gender, and varied skin tones.

Section 9 has a short worked example on Papa, as an illustration only and not a cast decision. His contradiction: exact about time, unable to say what he feels, so booking you the lower berth is how he says he missed you. He ends every text with a full stop, which the family reads as cross. His stack: tallest and thin, side-parted grey-sided hair, no spectacles (left free for someone else), a light shirt with thin vertical stripes, and the travel list in its sleeve held in his left hand.
ai_consistency: Evidence from our own pictures: four library people painted in all five worlds from the same words kept their hair shape (4 of 4), their spectacles, stubble and beard (3 of 3), Kamla's checked pattern (even in two-ink Station) and white clothes in every look. Face shape, apparent age, skin tone and the colour of their clothes changed. See drift-sheet.png.

Why panels drift: a 2025 comic-generation paper (arXiv 2506.18900) says painting each panel on its own carries no identity between panels, so hair, clothing colour and face structure drift. Its fix is a list of each character's fixed traits, an audit of every panel against it, and repair, which is our trunk checklist made general. Attribute swapping is a known failure too (SynGen, arXiv 2306.08877: a pink sunflower and a yellow flamingo come back swapped). So two people in one panel need contrasting top anchors, both from references, and both checked.

Reference editing is the main tool. Black Forest Labs says FLUX.2 keeps a character through multi-reference editing and can put a person from one picture into another picture's style. FLUX.2 klein takes at most 4 reference pictures, so a panel can carry at most two people from references plus a prop and a place. cutscenes.py already does this for the trunk (paint-ref, pick-ref, paint-refs with Flux2KleinEdit, 8-bit, 4 steps, 1024x768, seeds 7100, 7203 and 7319). REFS holds only the trunk today.

One master sheet per person in the present-day style, then one reference per world look derived from it and picked by eye, so the painter is never asked to change style and keep a face in the same step. Not yet tested: whether klein can paint a multi-view sheet in one picture, and whether a present-day reference pulls its own style into a Lugdi or Station panel.

Seeds fix one picture for one prompt. They do not hold a face across different prompts. A repaint with the same seed and slightly changed words comes back nearly the same, so repaints need a new seed (SEED_BUMP).

Prompt anchors: the same LOOKS words every time; a role, never a name (names get painted as lettering); props in the scene with the hand that holds them (the three-hands lesson); glossary definitions say what to paint, never what not to paint; 'South Asian features and warm brown skin' fixed the whitening in soft looks. Prompts do not stop forehead dots, so check faces close up and paint dots out.

Per-character LoRA: the installed mflux 0.19.1 can train one, but only on the FLUX.2 klein base models (4B or 9B), and it supports edit-pair training. Only the distilled klein-4B is on the Mac (15 GB in the cache). Base 4B is a separate download of the same size on Hugging Face, under Apache 2.0 and not gated. 9B is non-commercial. Memory and time on 24 GB: no source gives a figure. Painting alone fills most of memory, and two FLUX models crashed the Mac on 22 Oct. Not tested: whether a base-trained LoRA works with the 4-step distilled model, and whether two LoRAs work in one panel. A LoRA also needs a consistent set of pictures, which reference editing has to make first. So it is phase two: one person, alone, through heavyq, measuring peak memory, time and audit pass rate.

Anchors that survive a change of style, strongest first: (1) hair and head shape (our sheet; Groening; Sinha and Poggio found people lean on head shape and hair more than on inner features); (2) spectacles and facial hair; (3) body silhouette, height and posture (the comics standard, untested on our painter because our sheet shows head and shoulders only); (4) garment pattern; (5) light or dark value; (6) a prop painted from its own reference, which still needs a checklist; (7) garment colour (Station has two inks, and Lugdi's lamp light recolours everything); (8) the face, which is the least stable and is carried only by the reference picture.

Colour key for each look, from the STYLE strings: Now (clean outlines, warm lamplight against cool blues); Lugdi (violet and indigo, vermilion and marigold); Station (enamel blue or black on cream); Jadugar (vermilion, magenta, indigo, emerald, old gold; cards in crimson, midnight blue, old gold and cream); Cricket (outfield green, chalk white, cherry red); Rukavat (teak brown, faded teal, cream, one signal orange). So a person's key is a value, a pattern and one named ink per look.
Voice is the one channel the painter cannot spoil: speech bubbles and typing are live text. Let words, name tags and face chips carry identity alongside the pictures.

How age changes the mix [1]: in a Dehradun recording of six women, the older speakers (54 to 63) built 68% of clauses on Hindi and dropped in single English words, 69% to 84% of them nouns. The younger speakers (24 to 35) built 75% on English and switched whole clauses. Both used 'English verb + kar/ho' ('start kar diya'). The sample is small and upper middle class, so a small-town shop family will use less English, but in the same direction.

Setting moves the language as much as age does. Domain, status, intimacy and topic decide which language and how much switching [2]. A retired teacher went into English on the topic of school [1]. So Mummy talks shop in English nouns (stock, bill, delivery, shutter), Captain sahab talks cricket in English calls, Papa uses English for times, numbers and 'confirm ho gaya', and Nani speaks Hindi with only doctor, BP, ward and ticket in English.

The three Hindi 'you's. आप is the highest respect, for seniors, parents and elder siblings [3][4]. तुम is for relatives and close friends [3]. तू is intimate, or rude, and is used to small children [3]. 'Ji' and 'haan ji' mark respect [4]. तू is heard as warm in Mumbai's Hindi (from Marathi) but rude in much of the north [5], so it means different things in different cities.

Keep respect equal inside the household. An essayist describes a common pattern: honorific to the father, familiar to the mother, copied by the children, in Tamil, Kannada, Telugu and Hindi [6]. It is one essay with no data. Have the player use आप/-इए to Mummy and Papa alike, and have Mummy and Papa use the same form to each other (both तुम), so the game's own family does not encode that hierarchy.

Kinship words go after the name, separate the mother's side from the father's and older from younger, and are used for non-relatives as respect ('Kamala mausi') [8]. For names with no community lean: Mummy and Mama ji call Nani 'Maa' or 'Amma', Papa calls her 'Mummy ji', and Mama ji calls Mummy 'Didi'. Avoid Ammi, Khala, Mamu and Mataji. No source was found for these leanings, so readers should confirm.

Each voice, as team judgement built on [1][2]. Nani: short orders, head-counts, 'Arre/Bas/Chalo', तुम to all younger people. Mummy: lists, times, prices, आप to customers. Papa: exact and dry, whole sentences. Mama ji: fast, whole English clauses. Tinku: teasing, English clauses with Hindi tags, but plain polite Hindi with Nani (Gen Z talk with parents is 'completely different' [9]). Mausi: warm, talks over people. Mausa ji: 'Ho jayega.' Masterji: views about cloth, fit and punctuality. Captain sahab: one-line cricket verdicts. Mami: numbered, firm.

How the player can speak without showing a gender. Hindi verbs and adjectives agree with what they refer to [4]. These shapes stay gender-free: polite requests (लिस्ट दिखाइए); offers in the subjunctive (मैं देखूँ?); the transitive past with an explicit मैंने, where the verb agrees with the object (मैंने टिकट बुक कर दिया) [7]; possessives, which agree with the thing owned (तुम्हारा फ़ैसला) [4]; English verbs in Hinglish (Reached, Coming, Done); and impersonal हो जाएगा. Rule 66's checker will flag some of these (कर दिया at a sentence end, रेडी हूँ), and a native reader clears them.

Tinku's address to the player. Real younger siblings say didi or bhaiya, which rule 8 forbids. Use no address word, or 'oye' and 'sun'. Do not use 'bro' or 'bhai': Gen Z uses 'bhai' for anyone [9], but most players will hear a boy.

Regional speakers show where they are from through one real word a reader from that region approves, never through spelled accents. No line from the household or a chapter voice doubts a report of harassment or a dowry demand, or calls it a misunderstanding (rule 22). This binds Mausi's talk-over-everyone energy most.
typing: Script: informal Hindi online is mostly in Roman letters. On public Facebook pages in 2014, Roman far outnumbered Devanagari, except on a Hindi news page, and romanised spelling varies freely [10]. No source was found on script choice in private chat by age.

Many people do not type. A 2025 long read describes a 'non-typing majority' in smaller towns and villages who talk to their phones and find Indic keyboards clunky [16]. A 2025 trade piece opens with a mother whose stiff fingers and the foreign alphabet keep her on voice notes [15]. This is journalism; no survey of voice notes by age was found.

Older adults message every day. 17 of 19 urban adults aged 55 and over used WhatsApp daily, with YouTube and motivational or spiritual videos. One needed his son's help to set up a call, and one woman said failing eyesight shuts the very old out [17].

What older relatives send: motivational quotes, prayer emoji, home remedies, and good-morning, good-afternoon and good-evening greetings with babies and roses [11]. Good-morning messages start before sunrise and peak before 8 am, with flowers, toddlers and birds; one in three Indian smartphone users ran out of storage daily [13]. Families swap glittery good-morning roses; one father sends only stickers of an old film singer [14]. The family group is where news of illness and babies travels, and older members expect deference there [12].

How a 21-year-old types: all caps reads as shouting, proper punctuation as uptight, lowercase as relaxed. Stretched letters ('loool', 'brooo') soften a message, and abbreviations keep replies quick [9].

Limits the game sets: there is no group chat (23 Oct), only single messages on a painted blank phone or a message card. Show no app name, app look or 'forwarded' label, and no stickers of real singers or actors (rule 3). Good-morning images are flowers, a sunrise, tea or a bird, never gods. A forward is a small loving habit, never misinformation or politics. The folded-hands emoji is real and common [11] but sits close to 'prayer', so it is the owner's call; until then, use it only after a thank-you.

Each person, as team judgement. Nani barely types: calls and voice notes, and her opening message reads best as a voice note shown as live text. Mummy: short Roman Hinglish, photos of bills, voice notes when her hands are busy, 'ok', 👍. Papa: full sentences with full stops, the train number, coach and berth each on a line, 'Reached?', a daily good-morning flower, one slow finger. Mama ji: English, several messages in a row, '!!'. Tinku: lowercase, no full stops, stickers with friends, plain short Hinglish to Nani. Mausi: long voice notes, 'Reached??'. Mausa ji: 'Ok.' Masterji: photos of measurements. Captain sahab: '9 am sharp. Lane ground.' Mami: numbered lists with ✅.

How the player types to each. To Nani: a call or voice note. To Mummy: 'Done', 'Reached', a photo, 👍. To Papa: 'Ji Papa. Maine PNR bhej diya.' To Mama ji: 'Mama ji, sorted. Don't worry.' To Tinku: lowercase, a sticker, 'lol'. To the chapter voices: polite and short with 'ji'. The player's emoji are faces and objects only; a person emoji carries a gender and a skin tone.
dress: Saris and suits. The Nivi drape is the commonest [23]. A pallu worn over the front (sidha pallu) reads as Bihar, UP, Gujarat or Rajasthan [23]. The salwar kameez is now worn by women all over India [24]. Urban women mostly keep the sari for formal or occasion wear; fewer than a fifth of 270 surveyed women, most aged 41 to 55, called it daily wear [25]. A 2005 Delhi report found city women moving to jeans or the easier salwar kameez while rural women of all classes still wore saris daily [26].

Home wear. In Kerala the nightie is daily home wear for women of every age; one woman's mother took to it at 88 [27]. Kerala men live in the lungi at home [29]. In Odisha, West Bengal, Bihar and Haryana the lungi is home or night wear, and Hindu men avoid it on the street [28], so outdoors there it reads as a community marker. Use these only indoors, and only if the story places the family in that region.

Winter: Chennai buys mufflers, shawls and monkey caps for its mild 'winter' [31], and in Bengal the monkey cap is both a staple and a film joke [30]. The safari suit belongs to the 1970s to 1990s office [32], so it is wrong for today. Chappals are the most typical footwear across all religions [34], and the hawai chappal has its own national standard [33]. 48% of adults aged 45 and over report vision impairment [35], so many of this cast wear glasses, some only for reading.

Pan-India defaults (team judgement). Women: Nivi-draped saris or salwar suits and kurtas, with the dupatta on the shoulders and never over the head. Men: shirt and trousers, kurta, T-shirt, track pants at home. Young people: T-shirt and jeans, hoodie, kurti over jeans. Everyone: chappals, sandals or plain sports shoes. Everything plain or simply printed, with no letters or logos (FLUX paints logos onto T-shirts). Mixed, muted colours: not all-white on an older woman, not saffron with green, not black head to foot.

Nani: a printed cotton sari in a soft colour (dusty blue, mustard, grey-green), Nivi drape, reading glasses, a cloth purse, her cane with a rubber foot; a deeper silk-look sari and shawl for occasions; a cardigan or shawl in winter. Do not dress her in white: with the forced bare forehead it reads as a Hindu widow [21], which is how the painter code already marks Badi Amma. Whether Nana is alive is the owner's question.

Mummy: at the shop, a printed cotton salwar suit with the dupatta pinned across one shoulder, clear of the stool; reading glasses pushed into her hair; a wristwatch; flat sandals; a cardigan in winter; a silk-look sari for the wedding. Papa: a tucked half-sleeve shirt, belt, leather sandals, watch, pen in the pocket, reading glasses; at home a kurta-pyjama or T-shirt and track pants; a sleeveless sweater and muffler in winter; a plain kurta with a Nehru-collar jacket for occasions.

Mama ji: a polo or untucked shirt, jeans or chinos, plain sports shoes, the black umbrella; a kurta with a Nehru-collar jacket for the wedding, never a safa. Tinku: a plain T-shirt, jeans or track pants, an open overshirt or hoodie, a claw clip or ponytail, earphones; a kurti over jeans for occasions. Mausi: a printed synthetic sari or suit, a cardigan for the AC coach, a big handbag. Mausa ji: a cotton shirt worn out over trousers, a handkerchief. Masterji: a half-sleeve shirt and spectacles, with the measuring tape round his neck as his recurring object. Captain sahab: a pale polo, white trousers, a plain floppy sun hat. Mami: a cotton kurta with straight trousers, glasses and her list; a silk-look sari or long kurta set for the last night.

Off screen and out of prompts, from Pew's 2019 to 2020 survey [19]: the bindi (84% of Hindu women), the head covering (North and Central Hindu women 82 to 84%, South 22%), religious pendants (about half of adults), the tilak and janeu (caste-linked), the kara (84% of Sikhs; any plain steel bangle reads Sikh [22]), the skullcap, the turban, and long beards or beards with a shaved upper lip. Marital markers [20][21]: sindoor, toe rings, glass bangles, chooda, shell-and-coral bangles, the mangalsutra or thali. From team knowledge, with no source: wrist threads, ankle threads, rudraksha or tulsi beads, mehendi, the wedding safa.

Safe accessories (team judgement): one wristwatch, spectacles on a cord or not, small plain studs or hoops for women, a thin chain with no pendant [19], hair clips and claw clips, cardigan, shawl, muffler, handkerchief, cloth purse, sling bag, umbrella, a pen in the pocket. No earrings on men. No bangles on the married women, because almost every bangle carries marital meaning somewhere [20].

Clothing words to define in the painter's glossary before painting: suit (salwar or Western), vest (undershirt or waistcoat), cap (sun hat or skullcap), glasses (spectacles or tumblers), chain, tape, jumper and sweater, where the shawl and dupatta lie, chappal, track pants. Give each person one fixed look line, word for word every time, as LOOKS in cutscenes.py does. Keep props out of the fixed look and say which hand holds what.
posture: The head bobble most often means yes or 'I understand', and can mean thanks or hello [38]. Use it sparingly, as one small nod-tilt, because it is also the stock caricature of Indians.

Older bodies. Squatting and floor sitting are named as possible knee-arthritis risks in older women [37], so Nani sits in an armchair, never on the floor, and rises in stages with a hand on her knee. Self-reported vision impairment is 48% at 45 and over [35], and failing eyesight gets in the way of phones [17], so elders hold the phone at arm's length or on speaker and look over or under their glasses.

A tailor's body: among 100 sewing-machine operators, 70% had muscle or joint problems, low back pain was the commonest, and the neck carried very high exposure [36]. Masterji leans his neck forward over the machine, rubs his lower back when he stands, and looks over his glasses at the needle.
Keep folded hands and touching feet out of the panels. A primer files both as Hindu greetings [4], and in a painting folded hands read as prayer (rule 3).

Each person, as team judgement (no source found for shopkeeper, coach or youth gestures). Nani: upright, cane against the chair arm, counts heads with one finger, the one who points. Mummy: on her feet behind a glass counter, one hand flat on it, phone wedged at her shoulder while she writes a bill, glasses down to read and up to look at you. Papa: straight-backed at the coach door, checks his watch, holds the list in its clear sleeve, reads with glasses low on his nose. Mama ji: always moving with the phone to his ear, big open arms, umbrella under his arm.

Tinku: cross-legged on a plastic chair, scorebook on her knee, pen in her teeth, up on her feet at a wicket. Mausi: leans in and touches your arm, holds out the berth chart, carries too many bags. Mausa ji: still, forearms on his knees, stands when the doctor passes. Captain sahab: side-on with his weight on his good leg, arms folded at the boundary, shadows a stroke, points with two fingers. Mami: list in one hand and pen in the other, counts on her fingers, phone on speaker held flat to her chest.

Painter craft (painter-glossary-rule): say which hand holds what and count hands in every pick, or the painter adds a third. Paint recurring objects from one reference with paint-refs: the list sleeve, cane, key ring, scorebook and umbrella, plus Masterji's tape and Mami's list. The player is never painted, so people hold things out towards 'you' with screens and papers painted blank.
caricature_traps: Spelled accents and the funny-shopkeeper voice. The Apu documentary traced how a put-on Indian shopkeeper accent fed the bullying of children, and actors were asked to perform it [39]. Never spell anyone's Hindi or English to sound foreign or comic.
The north-south joke. Hindi cinema has long mocked south Indians' dress, food and speech, starting with the 1960s 'madrasi' comic [40]. No 'Aiyyo', no idli or coconut-oil gags, no lungi as a joke.

Community stock characters. A secondary report of an IIM Ahmedabad study of 1960 to 2010 films (figures unverified) says corrupt businessmen were mostly trader-caste, Sikh characters mostly comic relief, and Christian women often cast as loose [41]. The slur of the greedy trader caste is old [42]. So Mummy's shop has a glass counter and fair prices: no floor cushion, ledger, pot belly or haggling for laughs. No Sikh-coded comic coach.

Soap-opera women: the veiled daughter-in-law in heavy shiny clothes and jewellery from morning, feeding everyone before herself, the controlling mother-in-law, and women set against women [43]. Mummy and Mami are never veiled or loaded with jewellery. Nani's authority is wit and warmth, not control over the women. Mausi and Mami are allies. Men pour the tea too.

Older people as props. Older people appear in fewer than 4% of Indian ads, as background filler, the silent patriarch, the dutiful grandmother as a symbol of tradition, the unfit uncle, the couple who cannot work technology, or the moral compass [44]. Mausa ji's few words must be kind and active, not silent-patriarch. Nani runs things rather than symbolising them. Papa's phone habits are his own way, not a joke about age. Mama ji's worry is not a pot-belly gag. Nobody preaches.

The 'aunty' and the 'WhatsApp uncle'. Middle-aged women get boxed into aunty tropes [45], loyal users get called 'WhatsApp aunties' [11], and all caps reads as 'aggro WhatsApp uncle energy' [9]. Mausi's talking over people is care, never gossip about people's characters. Masterji's views are about cloth, cut and punctuality, never women's morals or dress. Papa's good-morning flower is affection, not spam. No one forwards politics or false news.
Tinku as a slang machine or a phone addict. Her quickness is scoring and teasing. She drops into plain Hindi with Nani [9]. She is never the comic one (rule 37).

Visual tells that mark religion, caste or marriage (Pew [19], marital markers [20][21], kara [22]). An older woman all in white with a bare forehead reads as a widow [21]. A lungi or long beard out of doors in the north or east reads as a community [28][19]. The monkey cap is a film joke [30]: use it once, on someone dignified, or not at all. A safari suit is the wrong era [32].

The painter's own caricatures (memory flux-portrait-biases). FLUX.2 klein paints a bindi on nearly every Indian woman whatever the prompt says, so check every face close up and paint it out by hand (DOTS). It lightens brown skin in soft styles, so the Rukavat look needs 'South Asian features and warm brown skin'. A repaint needs a new seed (SEED_BUMP). Skin tones should vary across the family, and the painter runs only through heavyq. Nothing was painted for these notes.

Story-level traps from the rulebook. No household member or chapter voice doubts a harassment report or a dowry demand (rule 22). The household is never the one doing the wrong (rule 27). No famous-face stickers or brands (rule 3). No outsider trade jargon (rule 2).

characters.name: Nani (नानी), turning 80
characters.essence: The lane's old grocer (44 years behind a counter in her front room, 1972 to 2016), who still runs her family and her lane from the cane chair that stands where her counter used to be. Label: 'Nani, Mummy's mother'. Round.
characters.want: This year: everyone under her roof at once for her eightieth, every head counted. From you: the plain truth, unsoftened, and someone to hold her list when she cannot.
characters.fear: Being moved out of her own house into a child's flat, a guest in someone else's kitchen. The May fall makes it real.
characters.contradiction: She runs everyone's life, but will not let anyone run hers: every time she is helped, she turns the help into an order she gave ('Use them'). Year: Jan orders 'Everyone comes'; May runs the ward night from the bed to prove she is fine; Dec sits in the front row of her own house and lets the cake be carried to her. Habit: counts heads aloud with one finger ('Ek, do, teen... sab?'). Line: 'Sab aayein.' | 'सब आएँ।' | 'Everyone comes.' Players who know her: Mr Natarajan, Sunita.
relations: Mummy: Mummy learned to count change at Nani's counter at eight and swore never to run one; Nani lent her the shop's first stock money in 1999 and still tells her how to price fuses. Friction: unasked advice. Tenderness: their nine o'clock phone call every night.

Papa: the son-in-law from the railway colonies who had no home town until he married in; she made him hers, teases his formality, and is the only one who lets him finish a sentence. He calls her 'Mummy ji', books her ticket first; she pours his tea first.

Mama ji: her youngest, who left at twenty and phones at eight every morning to worry. Friction: after the fall he wants her in his city flat ('My own bed'). Tenderness: she keeps his school cricket bat behind her door.

Tinku: Nani taught her to keep accounts on the grocery's old ledger; Tinku keeps Nani's carrom scores and medicine times and drops every English word for her. Nani calls her 'scorer', never 'the youngest'.
Mausi: her eldest, who married first and brings the food; Nani relies on Mummy for decisions and on Mausi for dinner, and Mausi minds. Tenderness: Mausi is the one Nani phones when she cannot sleep.
Mausa ji: the quiet son-in-law who has fixed her wiring for thirty years unasked; she trusts him with her spare key. He calls her 'Amma ji'.
Masterji: when Mummy's shop opened beside his in 1999, Nani inspected the street and haggled with him for an hour over one hem; mutual respect since, and he asks after her by name.
Captain sahab: met at Mummy's housewarming and argued cricket for an hour; each still believes they won.

Mami: the city daughter-in-law who logs the BP readings Nani speaks into her phone and sends the doctor a numbered list each month. Friction: whose kitchen it is during the wedding. Nani trusts her lists and pretends not to.

You: you have read her bills and letters aloud since you could read; you are her plain-truth person, the one she wants holding her list. She says तुम; you say 'Nani' and आप. Proposed album payoff: she counts heads and counts you last, 'Aur tum.' | 'और तुम।'
characters.grid: Silhouette: a small seated triangle, cane planted upright at her right side like a pole; rises in stages, hand on knee. Height/build: rank 10 of 10, tiny, upright, almost always seated. Base shape: triangle. Hair: white, pulled straight back into one thin plait down her back. Face: big round spectacles, thick dark frames, always on (shared kind only with Masterji, never in one chapter). Colour key: sage green sari with a tiny dark leaf print + oatmeal shawl (never white: with the bare forehead it reads as a widow). Station two inks: mid-tone fine all-over print, light shawl. Prop: wooden cane with a rubber foot, bought for her knee; she points with it more than she leans on it; right hand; counts heads with her left forefinger. Skin: deep brown, finely wrinkled; thick straight brows (now white) shared with her line. Voice: low, slow, final; verbless fragments; counts aloud. Says to you: तुम, short commands. Mix: Hindi; English only single nouns (doctor, BP, ward, ticket, cake). Never says: 'please' to family, 'I'm fine' (says 'Bas'), a pet name, any doubt of a report. Typing: speaks into the phone and lets it type Devanagari, so messages come out as fragments with full stops where she paused; no greeting, no emoji; or a voice note: 'अस्सीवाँ। मई। सब आएँ।'

characters.name: Mummy (मम्मी), 52
characters.essence: The electrical-shop owner (station road, facing the platform, since 1999) who runs the family like her shop: everything has a time, a price and a place, and she knows all three. Round.
characters.want: This year: the shutter up at nine every Saturday, flood or no flood, without asking anyone for help. From you: to take half the phone calls, which she will never ask for outright; holding out the red pen is how she asks.
characters.fear: The shutter staying down: losing the shop that Nani's money started.
characters.contradiction: She swore she would never sit behind a counter like her mother, but runs hers exactly like her, down to the head-count with one finger. Year: Jan hangs the shop's calendar and holds out the pen; July the flood makes her hire strangers and take the lane's help; Dec sits down beside Nani at the wedding for once and lets others serve. Habit: answers any question with a time or a price. Line: 'Nau baje. Shutter up.' | 'नौ बजे। शटर ऊपर।' | 'Nine o'clock. Shutter up.' Player who knows her: Ravi.
relations: Nani: learned to count change at Nani's counter at eight and swore never to run one; Nani lent the first stock money in 1999 (repaid in instalments, last receipt kept) and still advises on fuse prices. Their nine o'clock call every night.

Papa: married 1997, both say तुम (equal respect); her shutter faces his parcel office and he waves when it goes up at nine. Friction: he times everything, she prices everything. Tenderness: when his phone dies on the night train she reads him the time off her father's watch.
Mama ji: the younger brother she half raised while Nani ran the counter; he calls her 'Didi' and sends money she did not ask for. Friction: he solves with money, she with time.
Tinku: works her Saturday counter and keeps the stock tally on her phone; Mummy is hardest on her because Tinku is most like her.
Mausi: sisters three years apart; Mausi the elder, Mummy the one Nani calls; rivalry dressed as concern and a daily call both look forward to.
Mausa ji: the lineman gave her her first wholesaler's name when the shop opened; his is the only wiring advice she takes without arguing.
Masterji: neighbours sharing one wall for 27 years; he opens at ten and calls her nine 'showing off'; every monsoon they lift each other's shutters.
Captain sahab: a lane neighbour who buys every fuse from her and haggles for sport; she sells him the lane cup's floodlight bulbs at cost.
Mami: sisters-in-law who both run things; Mummy trusts her lists and doubts her city prices; at the wedding they split kitchen and guests without a word.
You: she taught you to count change; in January she holds out the red pen ('Everyone calls you anyway'). She says तुम; you say आप, exactly as to Papa.
characters.grid: Silhouette: square-set and standing, one hand flat on the glass counter, a light diagonal band across her chest. Height/build: rank 7, medium-short, sturdy, feet planted apart. Base shape: square. Hair: black greying at the temples, a big low bun at the nape (her anchor from behind). Body detail: her father's man-sized wristwatch loose on her left wrist (always 'a wristwatch with a round white face on a steel strap', or the painter may make a plain steel band that reads as a kara). Colour key: maroon plain salwar suit + cream dupatta pinned across one shoulder; wedding: maroon silk-look sari, Nivi drape, never over the head. Station: solid dark kameez with one light diagonal band. Prop: the shop key ring with a plain brass tag, the first shutter key cut in 1999; hooked on her right forefinger. Skin: warm medium brown; the family's thick straight brows. Voice: brisk, mid-fast, lists in threes; every answer a time or a price. Says to you: तुम. Mix: Hindi frame with trade nouns and English verbs with kar/ho (stock, bill, delivery, shutter, 'check karo'). Never says: 'don't worry', a vague time. Typing: short Roman Hinglish, lowercase, no full stops; photos of bills; voice notes when her hands are busy; replies within a minute in shop hours, never after 9 pm: 'stock aa gaya 👍'. Caricature guard: glass counter, fair prices, no haggling for laughs.

characters.name: Papa (पापा), 56
characters.essence: The railway parcel clerk (son of a railway guard, raised in railway colonies across several states, four years from retiring) who loves in timetables: he cannot say he missed you, so he books you the lower berth. Round.
characters.want: This year: all of them at Nani's door at 6:00 for her eightieth, and to be counted as one of hers. From you: to be the one who never needs reminding.
characters.fear: Being late when it matters; and under it, that in the family he married into he is only as welcome as he is useful.
characters.contradiction: Exact to the minute about time, but cannot say one plain thing he feels; every feeling comes out as a number. Year: Jan 'Trains: booked'; May his phone dies on the night train and he hands you his list, the first he has ever let go of, and never takes it back. Habit: corrects any time to the minute. Line: '9:40. 9:45 nahin.' | '9:40, 9:45 नहीं।' | '9:40, not 9:45.' Player who knows him: Mr Natarajan.
relations: Nani: she made the man with no home town hers; teases his formality and is the only one who lets him finish a sentence. He calls her 'Mummy ji', books her ticket first; she pours his tea first.
Mummy: married 1997, both तुम; he waves from the parcel office when her shutter goes up at nine. He times, she prices. When his phone dies she reads him the time off her father's watch.
Mama ji: brothers-in-law with opposite clocks: Papa books in January, Mama ji the night before and phones Papa to fix it; he calls Papa 'Jija ji' and means 'the family's railway'.
Tinku: the only one who makes him laugh, by scoring his corrections ('That's four not-9:45s today'); he taught her timetables, she taught him scorebooks.
Mausi: she brought his marriage proposal in 1996 and overrules his berth chart every trip; he books her a lower berth for her knee before she asks and never says so.
Mausa ji: the two who married in sit side by side at every function, contentedly silent; Papa talks trains, Mausa ji says 'Hmm'.
Masterji: stitched Papa's one good jacket and says his posture ruins it; Papa arrives at fittings to the minute, which Masterji finds suspicious.
Captain sahab: lane neighbours and two clocks: Captain sahab calls the cup for nine, Papa says 8:55; they walk at six every morning and never discuss it.
Mami: the other list-keeper; he sends her the guests' train times, she replies with a numbered list, the happiest exchange of his year.
You: in May he hands you his list on the train; he texts 'Reached?' and means 'I missed you'. He says तुम; you say 'Ji Papa'.
characters.grid: Silhouette: the tallest, thinnest line in the cast, leaning forward as if walking to a train, a flat clear sleeve held to his chest. Height/build: rank 1, tall, thin, long-necked. Base shape: line (tall vertical). Hair: short, side-parted, combed flat, black on top, grey at the sides. Face: none, clean-shaven, the only bare face among the five older men. Colour key: pale sky-blue shirt with thin white vertical stripes, tucked, belt + charcoal trousers; wedding: sky-blue kurta, charcoal Nehru-collar jacket. Station: light top in fine vertical lines, dark trousers, belt line. Prop: the travel list, one sheet of ruled paper in a clear plastic document pocket, painted blank, a fresh one every trip since his first job; left hand, flat to his chest. Skin: dark brown. Voice: measured, even, whole careful sentences (the railway colonies' Hindi); dry; corrects by minutes. Says to you: तुम. Mix: Hindi, English for numbers, times and railway words (PNR, coach, berth, 'confirm ho gaya'). Never says: 'I missed you', 'about', 'roughly'. Typing: full English sentences each ending in a full stop (read as cross; it is not); train, coach and berth each on its own line; one slow finger; a good-morning flower picture at 6:10 daily: 'Coach B2. / Berth 34. / Reached?'. Caricature guard: his phone habits are his own way, never an age joke.

characters.name: Mama ji (मामा जी), 47
characters.essence: The youngest, who left Nani's town for the city at twenty (sells water pumps to builders) and loves his family by phone: generous, worried, always making the number bigger. Label: 'Mama ji, Mummy's brother' (rule 65). Round.
characters.want: This year: his daughter married from Nani's house with the whole family there, bigger than anyone expects. From you: to hear 'Sorted, Mama ji' so he can stop worrying; you are his eyes in Nani's town.
characters.fear: That Nani grew old while he was on the phone in the city; that he is the son who was not there (in May, he is not).
characters.contradiction: Worries about everything, but plans nothing: he makes every number bigger and leaves the how to others. Year: Jan types Nani's words back ('Everyone comes'); May hears of the fall in the city and wants Nani moved to his flat, and she refuses; Dec brings the whole wedding to her house instead: he comes to her. Habit: raises every number by ten. Line: 'Saath? Sattar kar do!' | 'साठ? सत्तर कर दो!' | 'Sixty? Make it seventy!' Player who knows him: Shruti.
relations: Nani: her youngest, phoning at eight every morning to worry; after the fall he wants her in his flat and she says 'My own bed'. She keeps his school bat behind her door.
Mummy: 'Didi', who half raised him; he sends her money she did not ask for and stock leads; he solves with money, she with time.
Papa: opposite clocks; he books the night before and phones 'Jija ji' to fix it, and means 'the family's railway'.
Tinku: the uncle with gifts too expensive to use; she scores his promises ('You said March. Nil for one.').
Mausi: the eldest who half raised him too and still scolds him for the city; he pays for the benches in her tuition room.
Mausa ji: taught him to ride a scooter at fifteen; Mama ji now earns the most and Mausa ji still pays for the tea first.
Masterji: measured him for his first interview shirt the summer Mummy's shop opened; now he orders his wedding kurta by phone and argues over photos of cloth.
Captain sahab: little history; Captain sahab still brings up a catch he dropped in a family match years ago.
Mami: married 2001 in the city; he promises, she plans; he says seventy, she counts sixty; they bicker in public and decide everything in private. He is the worrier, she is the calm one.
You: he calls you, not his sister, when something must be done in Nani's town. He says तुम; you say 'Mama ji, sorted.'
characters.grid: Silhouette: a broad figure mid-stride, phone at his ear, a long black umbrella hooked over his forearm. Height/build: rank 5, medium, broad-chested, solid (never a pot-belly gag). Base shape: round (round face, round open arms). Hair: thick jet-black hair in a wave brushed up at the front, short at the sides. Face: a thick black moustache (the only moustache, unless Captain sahab's fallback is used). Colour key: tan-and-chocolate large check shirt, untucked + chocolate chinos; wedding: tan kurta, chocolate Nehru-collar jacket, never a safa. Station: big two-tone check. Prop: a big black umbrella bought his first city monsoon when he arrived without one, carried every day since, rain or not; hooked over his left forearm, phone in his right hand. Skin: warm light brown, always with 'South Asian features and warm brown skin' (whitening risk); the family brows. Voice: fast, loud-warm, run-on; stacked questions; numbers grow. Says to you: तुम. Mix: whole English clauses at speed, then Hindi ('Don't worry, main dekh lunga', said of himself). Never says: 'no' to a guest, a number smaller than the last. Typing: English in bursts of four or five messages, double exclamation marks, then a call before you can reply: 'Didi!! / nani ok?? / calling / pick up'.

characters.name: Tinku (टिंकू), 21
characters.essence: The family's scorer (final-year commerce student, Saturday shop counter, the lane team's scorer since twelve), who keeps the tally of everything, runs, promises, who said what in which year, and is quietly scoring her way out. Label: 'Tinku, your sister' | 'टिंकू, आपकी बहन'. Round; an asker, so never the comic one.
characters.want: This year: to be more than 'the youngest': a place on the district cricket association's scorers' course. From you: to be treated as an equal; on cup day she hands you the decisions to see what you do with them.
characters.fear: Being 'the youngest' for ever, left in the junction town while everyone calls you.
characters.contradiction: She keeps exact score of everyone else's game, but never writes down her own. Year: Jan 'Lane cup. I'm scoring'; Aug runs the cup's book and Captain sahab says the district should see it; Dec the course letter has come (painted blank, live text). Habit: turns everything into a tally. Line: 'Teesri baar. Teen-zero.' | 'तीसरी बार। तीन-शून्य।' | 'Third time. Three-nil.' Player who knows her: Meena.
relations: Nani: Nani taught her accounts on the grocery's old ledger; she keeps Nani's carrom scores and medicine times and speaks only plain polite Hindi to her. Nani calls her 'scorer'.
Mummy: works her Saturday counter and keeps the stock tally; Mummy is hardest on her because they are most alike.
Papa: makes him laugh by scoring his corrections; he taught her timetables, she taught him scorebooks.
Mama ji: scores his promises ('You said March. Nil for one.') and never uses his expensive gifts.
Mausi: did her Class 3 sums in Mausi's tuition class; Mausi still checks them and tells everyone her marks.
Mausa ji: they watch matches side by side without talking; she scores, he says 'Hmm' at every wicket; the only adult who never calls her 'the youngest'.
Masterji: he stitched her first school uniform and says she is too thin for any pattern; she brings his eleven o'clock tea on Saturdays.
Captain sahab: taught her to keep the lane cup's book at twelve and now says the district should see it; she teases him about 1979; the successor he has not named.
Mami: thinks Tinku should do a proper accounts course and says so at every function; Tinku keeps a tally.
You: her older sibling and her rival for being the one everyone calls. No address word, or 'oye', 'sun' (never bhai or bro); you say तुम to her.
characters.grid: Silhouette: high ponytail, knees up on a plastic chair, a book on her knee, headphones round her neck. Height/build: rank 6, medium, slight and wiry, all elbows and knees. Base shape: triangle (angles). Hair: a high ponytail that swings. Detail: plain matte black over-ear headphones with no markings, round her neck (radio commentary while she scores). Colour key: teal T-shirt with black raglan sleeves + blue jeans; wedding: teal kurti over jeans. Station: mid-tone body, solid dark sleeves. Prop: the scorebook with a plain cover, a new one each season since she was twelve; under her left arm or on her knee, pencil in her right hand. Skin: dark brown, like Papa; the family brows. Voice: quick, light, teasing; tallies; 'your call'. Mix: English clauses with Hindi tags with you; plain polite Hindi with Nani, every word in full. Never says: slang to Nani; any gendered word to you. Typing: all lowercase, no full stops, stretched letters, short forms; stickers with friends (never a famous face); short plain Hindi to Nani: 'nani bp fine dw / 3-0 lol'. Caricature guard: not a slang machine, not a phone addict.

characters.name: Mausi (मौसी), about 55, chapter 1 voice
characters.essence: Mummy's elder sister, who has run a tuition class for Classes 1 to 5 from her front room for thirty years and talks to every room as if it were Class 3. Label: 'Mausi, Mummy's elder sister'. Flat by design, with one contradiction.
characters.want: This year: to feed all fourteen on the night train from her basket and be the first one Nani thanks. From you: your news first-hand, not through Mummy.
characters.fear: That she, the eldest, is the daughter Nani tolerates, while Mummy is the one Nani relies on.
characters.contradiction: She never lets you finish a sentence, but remembers every word of it a year later. Her chapter: boards loud at 9:40 pm with too many bags, feeds everyone, quotes back what you told her last year. Habit: says everything three times. Line: 'Suno, suno, suno!' | 'सुनो, सुनो, सुनो!' | 'Listen, listen, listen!' Her talking over people is care, never gossip about character; she is the first to believe a report (rule 22). Player who knows her: Sunita.
relations: Nani: the eldest, who married first and brings the food; Nani relies on Mummy for decisions and on her for dinner, and she minds; but she is the one Nani phones when she cannot sleep.
Mummy: three years older and the one Nani calls less; rivalry dressed as concern, and a daily call both look forward to.
Papa: she brought his marriage proposal in 1996 and says so at every wedding; she overrules his berth chart, and he quietly books her a lower berth for her knee.
Mama ji: she half raised the youngest and still scolds him for the city; he pays for her tuition room's benches.
Tinku: taught her Class 3 sums and still checks them, and tells everyone her marks.

Mausa ji: married 34 years: she talks, he says 'Hmm', she finishes his sentences and he lets her; on night trains they hold hands when the coach is asleep. Friction: she tells everyone his blood pressure.
Masterji: his customer for decades; complains about every fitting and comes back every time.
Captain sahab: once sent him a two-minute voice note on the cup's timings; he replied '9 am'.
Mami: thinks city people waste money, while Mami thinks she feeds people too much; at the wedding her basket feeds Mami's list and they are allies.
You: has heard your life only through Mummy and wants it first-hand; talks over your answer, quotes it back word for word a year later. She says तुम; you say आप.
characters.grid: Silhouette: the widest figure, arms out, hair puffed wide, a woven basket on one forearm. Height/build: rank 4, tall-medium and broad. Base shape: round. Hair: shoulder-length, dyed copper-red, worn open and puffed out wide (never 'henna' in a prompt, or the painter may add mehendi on her hands). Detail: big plain gold hoop earrings (replaces the glasses on a cord she shared with Mausa ji; an Indian reader confirms big hoops, since small ones are the safe default). Colour key: magenta sari with big bold flowers (Nivi drape) + gold; wedding: magenta silk-look sari. Station: large flowers on a light ground. Prop: a woven plastic-wire basket bag with two handles, overfull with food for fourteen (replaces the steel tiffin, which sat close to Nirmala's tiffin note); right forearm, left hand waving in circles as she talks (she never touches 'your' arm: the player is never painted). Skin: warm medium-deep brown; the family brows. Voice: the loudest and fastest; overlaps; everything three times; rhetorical questions. Says to you: तुम. Mix: Hindi with travel and home nouns (AC, coach, berth, tiffin). Never says: anything about a person's character beyond habits; any doubt of a report. Typing: two- to three-minute voice notes; typed, double question marks and smileys: 'Reached?? Khana khaya??'

characters.name: Mausa ji (मौसा जी), about 58, chapter 2 voice
characters.essence: Mausi's husband, a lineman retired after 34 years with the electricity board, with big scarred hands, who says two blunt words and does twenty kind things. Label: 'Mausa ji, Mausi's husband'. Flat by design. Changed from the draft's 'slow, kind, few words' so his four harsh chapter 2 remarks fit (continuity read).
characters.want: This year: a quiet first year of retirement, useful and unthanked. From you: that you sleep while he sits up.
characters.fear: That his tongue undoes what his hands do, so he keeps it to two words.
characters.contradiction: Blunt in words, but soft in deeds: he calls a man lazy, then peels an orange and hands you half. His chapter: sits the whole ward night by the door, peels oranges for everyone, stands when the doctor passes. Habit: one word, then an action. Line: 'Hmm. Ho jayega.' | 'हम्म। हो जाएगा।' | 'Hmm. It'll get done.' Never the silent patriarch. Player who knows him: Farida.
relations: Nani: has fixed her house's wiring for thirty years unasked; she trusts him with her spare key; he calls her 'Amma ji' and says आप to her.
Mummy: gave her her first wholesaler's name when the shop opened in 1999; the only wiring advice she takes without arguing.
Papa: the two who married in sit side by side at every function, contentedly silent; Papa talks trains, he says 'Hmm'.
Mama ji: taught him to ride a scooter at fifteen; still pays for the tea first though Mama ji earns the most.
Tinku: they watch matches side by side without talking; he says 'Hmm' at every wicket and never calls her 'the youngest'.
Mausi: married 34 years; she talks and finishes his sentences, he lets her; they hold hands on night trains when the coach is asleep.
Masterji: rewired Masterji's shop for nothing in 2001; Masterji has stitched his shirts at cost ever since; neither mentions it.
Captain sahab: two men of few words who once watched a whole lane final side by side and said four words between them.
Mami: first to arrive and last to leave at her daughter's wedding, carrying chairs; she puts him on no list because he does everything that is not on it.
You: takes the night chair outside the ward so you can sleep and never mentions it; hands you half of every orange he peels. He says तुम, rarely.
characters.grid: Silhouette: a solid block seated forward, forearms on his knees, peeling an orange. Height/build: rank 8, medium-short, thick-set, still. Base shape: square. Hair: thick white hair cut short, standing up like a brush. Face: a short, close-trimmed white beard (replaces the glasses on a cord he shared with Mausi). Colour key: dove-grey shirt worn out over trousers + olive shawl over both shoulders; wedding: grey kurta, olive shawl. Station: flat mid-tone shirt, a darker block of shawl across the shoulders. Prop: an orange he is peeling, from the bag of fruit hospital visitors bring; both hands; in Rukavat it is the one signal orange. Glossary row needed: orange is also a colour. Skin: deep brown, weathered from years outdoors; check close up for whitening in the Rukavat style, which lacks the skin words. Voice: the slowest and softest; one or two words, then silence; blunt. Says to you: तुम, rarely. Mix: Hindi, almost no English. Never says: more than five words; 'I'. Typing: 'Ok.' an hour later, capital and full stop; or a thumbs-up. His judging notes: two-word work verdicts, landing as often on men as women.

characters.name: Masterji (मास्टरजी), about 60, chapter 3 voice
characters.essence: The tailor next door on the station road (apprenticed at 14, own shop since 1988, sharing Mummy's wall since 1999), who measures everything, cloth, mud, people, weather, and has an opinion on every inch. Label: 'Masterji, the tailor next door' (South Indian reader checks it, as मास्टरजी often means a teacher). Flat by design.
characters.want: This year: the drain mended before another monsoon ruins a bolt of cloth. From you: a listener who does not walk off.
characters.fear: That the station road forgets him: ready-made shops, and a drain that floods his cloth every July.
characters.contradiction: Precise to an eighth of an inch, but never on time for anything, his own shutter included; he opens at ten and calls Mummy's nine 'showing off'. His chapter: stands in his flooded doorway with an opinion on the mud and ends by handing the drain to the cup ('Let the lane cup decide'). Habit: speaks in measurements. Line: 'Do inch ka farq.' | 'दो इंच का फ़र्क़।' | 'Two inches out.' His views are on cloth, cut, weather and time, never a woman's dress or morals. Player who knows him: Sunita, herself a tailor, so he is dignified, never a joke.
relations: Nani: she inspected the street when Mummy's shop opened and haggled with him for an hour over one hem; mutual respect ever since; he asks after her by name.
Mummy: neighbours sharing a wall for 27 years; his ten against her nine; they lift each other's shutters every monsoon.
Papa: stitched Papa's one good jacket and says his posture ruins it; finds Papa's to-the-minute arrival at fittings suspicious.
Mama ji: measured him for his first interview shirt the summer the shop opened; now argues with him over photos of cloth for the wedding kurta.
Tinku: stitched her first school uniform, says she is too thin for any pattern; she brings his eleven o'clock tea.
Mausi: his customer for decades, complaining about every fitting and coming back every time.
Mausa ji: rewired his shop for nothing in 2001; he has stitched Mausa ji's shirts at cost ever since.
Captain sahab: the two old men of the drain, arguing since 1994 about whose drain floods the station road; 'Let the lane cup decide' hands thirty years of argument to a match.
Mami: never met; she sends Mama ji's measurements by message, numbered, and he says she is the only customer in thirty years who measures correctly.
You: has known you since you were small and talks cloth and weather while you hold his tea; you are the listener who stays. He says तुम.
characters.grid: Silhouette: short and craned forward like a question mark, a tape hanging both sides of his neck. Height/build: rank 9, short, narrow, neck forward from years at the machine. Base shape: curve (the stoop). Hair: bald on top, a neat grey horseshoe round the sides and back. Face: half-moon reading glasses low on the nose; he looks over them. Colour key: lavender half-sleeve shirt + black trousers. Station: plain light shirt, dark trousers, one thin dark line of tape round the neck. Prop: a plain cloth measuring tape with no markings, from his first employer, living round his neck (worn, never also held; audit every panel for painted numbers); his right hand rubs his lower back when he stands. Skin: medium brown. Voice: slow and chatty; digresses into cloth and weather; 'Dekhiye'. Says to you: तुम. Mix: Hindi with tailoring English (fitting, inch, alter, size, finish). Never says: a word on a woman's dress or morals. Typing: Roman Hindi with numbers and short forms; photos of the measurement slip, painted blank: 'kurta ready h 5 baje'. His judging notes: fit, finish and punctuality, evenly on men and women.

characters.name: Captain sahab (कप्तान साहब), about 65, chapter 4 voice
characters.essence: The lane's old club captain (captained the town side through the 1990s; 36 years a mechanic at the state bus depot; one state trial in 1979, aged 18), who still stands side-on as if waiting for the next ball. Label: 'Captain sahab, the lane's old captain'. Flat by design. Title kept; Tinku's 'captain' stage dropped from the batting-order card (rule 36 clash; the making judge already says it cannot be built).
characters.want: This year: one more lane cup, and someone to hand the lane's scorebook and team to. From you: a straight bat and a fair pick.
characters.fear: That the lane cup dies with him and the lane ground becomes parking.
characters.contradiction: The strictest umpire in the lane, but still sore about one decision against him in 1979. His chapter: sets the stakes (the losing lane mends the drain), umpires strictly, and sees Tinku's book. Habit: one-line verdicts in cricket calls. Line: 'Seedha bat. Front foot.' | 'सीधा बैट। फ़्रंट फ़ुट।' | 'Straight bat. Front foot.' Player who knows him: Ravi.
relations: Nani: met at Mummy's housewarming and argued cricket for an hour; each still believes they won.
Mummy: buys every fuse from her and haggles for sport; she sells him the cup's floodlight bulbs at cost.
Papa: lane neighbours and two clocks (his nine, Papa's 8:55); they walk at six every morning and never discuss it.
Mama ji: still brings up a catch Mama ji dropped in a family match years ago.
Tinku: taught her to keep the cup's book at twelve and says the district should see it; she teases him about 1979; his unnamed successor.
Mausi: received her two-minute voice note on the cup's timings and replied '9 am'.
Mausa ji: two men of few words who once watched a whole final side by side and said four words between them.
Masterji: the two old men of the drain, arguing since 1994; the lane cup now decides it.
Mami: no history; strangers who would agree on everything and discuss nothing.

You: taught you, like every child in the lane, to hold the bat straight; still says 'Front foot' when you pass; on cup day he watches whether you pick a side as he would. He says तुम; you say आप (the player's 'पहले सब पानी पियो' must become 'पहले सब पानी पी लें').
characters.grid: Silhouette: side-on, weight on his left leg, a floppy hat brim, tossing a ball. Height/build: rank 3, tall, lean, wiry, broad in the shoulder. Base shape: inverted triangle. Hair: close-cropped white under the hat; clean-shaven, deep sun creases. Detail: a plain white floppy cotton sun hat with no badge (owner's question; fallback a thick white moustache, which would echo Mama ji's black one two chapters away). Colour key: cherry-red polo with a white collar + chalk-white trousers (the only red on the Cricket look's green; never rust or saffron, which with white and green would read as the flag). Station: solid dark polo, light collar, light trousers and hat. Prop: an old red leather cricket ball worn pink on one side, from his last club match; right hand tossing and catching it, left hand on his hip; the stump stays a scene object. Skin: deep sun-darkened brown; check the apparent age (painted ages read young). Voice: clipped, commentary cadence, one-line verdicts. Says to you: तुम. Mix: Hindi with English cricket calls (over, front foot, 'well left'). Never says: a speech; never raises his voice. Typing: telegram English, time first, no punctuation, the same message to everyone: '9 am lane ground bring water'. His judging notes: game words, evenly on men and women ('drama queen' flagged sexist on sight, so it goes).

characters.name: Mami (मामी), about 45, chapter 5 voice
characters.essence: Mama ji's wife and the bride's mother, manager of a city hospital's billing desk (her mother's family is Bengali), who runs her daughter's wedding off a clipboard, item by numbered item. Label: 'Mami, Mama ji's wife' (South Indian reader checks whether 'maami' marks caste for a Tamil player). Flat by design.
characters.want: This year: a wedding with no surprises: every envelope, key and plate accounted for. From you: a second pair of hands she need not explain things to twice.
characters.fear: Something going wrong in her husband's family's house, in front of everyone, when she is the one from outside.
characters.contradiction: Plans every minute, but cries only at the one thing that was not on her list (Nani's cake). Her chapter: holds the clipboard out to you ('Then you run my list'), runs the week, and is the only one who cries at the cake. Habit: numbers her sentences. Line: 'Pehla, chaabiyan. Doosra, lifafe.' | 'पहला, चाबियाँ। दूसरा, लिफ़ाफ़े।' | 'One, keys. Two, envelopes.' She and Mausi are allies, never women set against women. Players who know her: Farida, Shruti.
relations: Nani: logs the BP readings Nani speaks into her phone and sends the doctor a numbered list each month; friction over whose kitchen it is during the wedding; Nani trusts her lists and pretends not to.
Mummy: sisters-in-law who both run things; Mummy trusts her lists and doubts her city prices; at the wedding they split kitchen and guests without a word.
Papa: the other list-keeper; he sends her the guests' train times and she replies with a numbered list.
Mama ji: married 2001; he promises, she plans; he says seventy, she counts sixty; they bicker in public and decide in private. She is the calm one.
Tinku: tells her at every function to do a proper accounts course; Tinku keeps a tally.
Mausi: thinks Mausi feeds people too much, while Mausi thinks city people waste money; at the wedding Mausi's basket feeds her list and they are allies.
Mausa ji: puts him on no list because he does everything that is not on it, first to arrive and last to leave, carrying chairs.
Masterji: never met; sends Mama ji's measurements numbered, and he calls her the only customer in thirty years who measures correctly.
Captain sahab: no history; strangers who would agree on everything and discuss nothing.

You: has watched you at every function doing the job nobody gave you; in December she holds the clipboard out to you, eyes on you with Mama ji behind her, so 'Then you run my list' is plainly said to you (the players' judge could not tell). She says तुम.
characters.grid: Silhouette: bolt upright, a strap across her body, a clipboard flat to her chest. Height/build: rank 2, tall, straight-backed, narrow-shouldered (taller than Mama ji). Base shape: line (tall vertical). Hair: a straight jaw-length bob tucked behind her ears, a few grey strands. Detail: a plain canvas sling bag, strap from right shoulder to left hip. Colour key: indigo block-print kurta with a small white motif + white straight trousers; last night: indigo silk-look sari with a thin white border. Station: dark top with light printed motifs, light trousers. In Jadugar her indigo must be lamp-lit and keep its white print, or she sinks into the indigo sky. Prop: a plain brown clipboard holding her numbered job list on a cream card with a crimson border; left arm flat to her chest, pen in her right hand. Skin: warm light-medium brown, with the skin words; close-up check of forehead, hair parting and neck. Voice: crisp and even; numbered points; firm with vendors, polite with elders. Says to you: तुम. Mix: switches whole clauses; lists, money and timings in English; one Bengali word only if a Bengali reader signs it off. Never says: 'maybe', 'whatever'. Typing: a numbered list with ticks at eleven at night, edited and resent: '1 tent ✅ 2 cook ⏳ 3 keys ?'. Her judging notes: time and phones, evenly on men and women.

characters.name: You (the player, a voice only)
characters.essence: The grown-up child of the house, 22 to 30, whom everyone phones: the family's switchboard, who speaks to each of them in their own language. Never painted (no face, hand, sleeve or shadow, rule 7); no name, gender, caste or religion (rule 8). Label: 'You' | 'आप'.
characters.want: The story's want for you: get everyone through the year without leaving anyone off the list. What the player wants for themselves stays their own.
characters.fear: The story's fear for you: the one person left off the list.
characters.contradiction: Everyone calls you, but nobody asks how you are, until the album, where Nani counts heads round the table and counts you last: 'Aur tum.' | 'और तुम।' | 'And you.' (proposed, gender-free). Your object: the red pen Mummy holds out in January, painted on the calendar or held out by someone whose face is in frame, never in your hand. Habit: you ask to see the list first: 'Dikhaiye.' | 'दिखाइए।' | 'Let's see.' Works for all six players (the review).
relations: Nani: you have read her bills aloud since you could read; her plain-truth person and the one she wants holding her list; you say 'Nani' and आप, she says तुम; you call or send a voice note, never text.
Mummy: she taught you to count change and holds out the red pen in January; you say आप and -इए to her exactly as to Papa; you text 'Done' and 👍.
Papa: he hands you his list on the night train; you text 'Ji Papa. Maine PNR bhej diya.' (with मैंने the verb agrees with the ticket, so no gender).
Mama ji: you are his eyes in Nani's town; 'Mama ji, sorted. Don't worry.'
Tinku: your younger sister and rival for being the one everyone calls; she hands you the decisions on cup day; you say तुम and trade lowercase messages and stickers.
Mausi: she talks over your answer and remembers it word for word; you let her.
Mausa ji: he sits up so you can sleep; you share his oranges and his silence.
Masterji: you hold his tea and listen to his weather; the listener who stays.
Captain sahab: he taught you to hold the bat straight; you say 'Captain sahab' and आप.
Mami: she trusts you with her clipboard without explaining twice; you answer 'Dikhaiye, Mami.'
characters.grid: Silhouette, hair, height, build, colour: none (never painted); your bubble is never yellow, tail off the bottom edge, tag 'You' | 'आप' (rule 38). Prop: the red pen on the calendar. Voice: short, practical, polite to elders, a little dry; never comments on a person, never names a card person, never agrees with a remark (rule 38). Says: आप and -इए to every elder, Mummy and Papa alike; तुम to Tinku. Mix: mirrors each listener's language. Never says: मैं कर लूँगा/लूँगी, आ गया/गई, थका/थकी, or 'me'/'my' if the line goes on a button (rulebook Q8). Typing: mirrors each recipient (a call or voice note to Nani; 'Done' 👍 to Mummy; 'Ji Papa.' with full stops to Papa; 'sorted' to Mama ji; lowercase and a sticker to Tinku; short and polite with 'ji' to the voices). Emoji: faces and objects only, since a person emoji carries a gender and a skin tone.

notes: Written to /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-priyanshu-Sex-Ed/f50ea7ee-0855-46a2-8572-0aa08df5b855/scratchpad/characters/cast-map.md (399 lines, with frontmatter). It has the family tree, the eleven profiles, all 55 pairs, grid A (how they look) and grid B (how they sound and type), the spread, a clash check, painter notes and owner questions. Nothing was painted and the repo was only read.

CHANGES FROM THE DRAFT, AND WHY. (1) Mausa ji changes from 'slow, kind, few words' to blunt in words and kind in deeds, so his four harsh chapter 2 remarks fit (continuity read). (2) Mausi loses the glasses on a cord, which she shared with Mausa ji, and the steel tiffin, which sat close to Nirmala's tiffin note. She gets big gold hoops and a woven basket bag. (3) Captain sahab keeps his title, and Tinku's captain stage is dropped (the rule 36 clash; the making judge says that stage cannot be built). His signature becomes an old ball, because 'stump' has two meanings in chapter 4. (4) Nani was the lane's grocer for 44 years, which is why her lane comes to the ward, and it gives Mummy her trade. (5) Papa is a railway parcel clerk raised in railway colonies. That explains the trains, his careful Hindi and why his side never appears. (6) Mami's mother is Bengali, and chapter 5's circle becomes Mami's side (the continuity fix). That gives Mitali, Shampa and Tapan a home in the family's story.

HEADCOUNT FLAG. Nani's three children (Mausi, Mummy and Mama ji) cannot give ten cousins aged 27 to 37. Chapter 1's travellers need Nani's siblings' grandchildren, whom any Indian family calls cousins. Writers fix the number.

SPREAD. Ten speak: five women and five men. The household is 3 women and 2 men; the voices are 2 women and 3 men. Each chapter's asker and voice are a woman and a man (rule 22), and the askers are 3 women and 2 men (rule 37). Each temperament is held by one woman and one man: loud and warm (Mausi, Mama ji), brisk (Mummy, Captain sahab), exact and dry (Mami, Papa), few words and deep care (Nani, Mausa ji), quick and teasing (Tinku, Masterji). Base shapes are not sorted by gender: triangle (Nani, Tinku, Captain sahab), square (Mummy, Mausa ji), round (Mausi, Mama ji), line (Papa, Mami), curve (Masterji). Ages run 21, 22 to 30, 45, 47, 52, 55, 56, 58, 60, 65 and 80. Nobody who speaks is aged 31 to 44; Mausi's elder child (about 32) could fill that band. Region: no state is named (rule 3). Nani's town, the mixed railway junction town and Mama ji's city carry the year. The pan-India card circles all have a reason to be there: Nani's grocery served her whole lane, and the junction is a railway town.

THE FAMILY READS AS ONE FAMILY through a shared painted feature: thick, straight, dark eyebrows on Nani's line (Nani, Mausi, Mummy, Mama ji and Tinku); the three who married in lack it. Skin tones are varied, and every look line carries skin words against whitening.

CLASH CHECK. Silhouette hook, hair shape, height rank, first colour, prop, voice tempo and typing style are each different for all ten. Near-misses, kept on purpose: (a) spectacles on Nani (round) and Masterji (half-moon), who never share a chapter; (b) three paper props (a clear sleeve, a bound scorebook, a rigid clipboard), since each asker's list of targets takes their own form; (c) the same value stack for Papa and Masterji, and for Captain sahab and Mami, told apart by pattern and height and never in one chapter; (d) a moustache on Mama ji only, unless Captain sahab's fallback is used. Pairs who share panels have opposite top anchors, which guards against the painter swapping attributes between them.

RULE 3 AND THE PAINTER. Nothing listed is a religious, caste or marital marker. An Indian reader should confirm Mausi's big hoops and her copper-dyed hair. Never write 'henna' in a prompt, or the painter may add mehendi. Always describe Mummy's watch as 'a wristwatch with a round white face on a steel strap', so it is not painted as a plain steel band that reads as a kara. Glossary rows are needed for orange (fruit and colour), sun hat (which clashes with the old 'cap' row), clipboard, sling bag, basket bag, headphones, tape, ball, travel list or document pocket, and where the shawl and dupatta lie. The proposed roles never use names; 'the grandmother' clashes with the old take's Dadi in ROLE.

EACH VOICE'S JUDGING NOTES STAY IN ITS OWN IDIOM: Papa on travel, Mausi on home, Mausa ji in two-word work verdicts, Masterji on fit and punctuality, Captain sahab in game words, Mami on time and phones. A voice read-through can then identify the speaker, and each speaker's notes land as often on men as on women. The continuity read found 'argues', 'gives orders' and 'bossy' only ever on women.

OWNER QUESTIONS: (1) Is Nana alive? The map assumes he died some years ago, off screen, and is never a plot device. (2) Captain sahab's plain sun hat, or none? (3) Spectacles on two people? (4) Do the pasts suit the family: Nani the grocer, Papa from the railway colonies, Mami's Bengali mother? (5) Tinku's want, the district scorers' course? (6) The album beat 'Aur tum.'? (7) Readers must confirm the address words: 'Mummy ji' (Papa), 'Amma ji' (Mausa ji), 'Didi' and 'Jija ji' (Mama ji).
