FIX: keep Nani's torn-up credit book on screen and let Mummy give credit to her regulars. Papa (railway), Mausi (teaching) and Mausa ji (lineman) already widen the family's work. Use them.

The competence is lopsided by gender. The women run everything: Nani the ward, Mummy the shop, Mami the wedding, Tinku the book. The men are late (Masterji), grudging (Captain sahab), mute (Mausa ji, Papa on feelings) or plan nothing (Mama ji). This turns one script over and lands on another, and Ravi, plus the screenshotter in the anti-personas, will read it as one-sided. FIX: every man gets one competence on screen that the plot needs (Mama ji's phone book brings the vendors, Papa's lists work, Mausa ji's wiring saves the flood), and every capable woman gets one real cost (Mummy's pride, Mami's list missing the human thing, Nani's refusal risking her health).

People the six players will look for are missing, and the owner has lifted the cap on characters. Farida will look for the night sister and the ward boy on a district ward. The wedding needs its cook (halwai) and the tent man as people, not lines. Nani's lane and the station road need women neighbours and men neighbours from more than one community in ordinary speaking roles (rule 21's mix, beyond the cards). FIX: add a ward night nurse as a minor voice, never on a card and never a joke, and at least two named neighbours per place.

Hinglish romanisation of numbers collides with common words: 'saath' is both 60 and 'with' (Mama ji's catchphrase, Mami's tease). FIX: figures in Hinglish bubbles, as every character's typing already uses.

Most of the cast's Hindi to and from the player passes rule 66: commands, 'who should' asks, ने pasts and verbless lines throughout, and every line the checker flags is cleared in its own file. Two real failures: Captain sahab's 'गली में रहते हो? खेलो।' (gendered if said to the player), and Nani's 'डॉक्टर बोले', which gives the ward doctor a gender. Fixes are in their entries. A native reader still clears the whole set.

Two titles mean something else in some regions: 'Captain sahab' is most often a retired army man, and 'Masterji' is a schoolteacher in the east. FIX: keep both first-use labels exactly ('the lane's old cricketer', 'the tailor next door', in Hindi 'टेलर मास्टर') and show the ball and the tape in each man's first panel.

Hot-season dress: shawls in May, July and August (Mausa ji's fixed look, Nani's stole) fight the Hindi-belt heat that every player knows. FIX: a cotton towel over the shoulder for Mausa ji. Nani's thin stole can stay, since old women do keep their shoulders covered. Wool appears only in January and December.

per_character.name: Nani (नानी), turning 80
problems: BACK-VIEW ANCHOR HAS NO CONTRAST. look.hair: 'From behind she reads as a white line down a light shawl: her back-view anchor'; colour_key RUKAVAT: 'shawl cream'. A white plait on an oatmeal or cream shawl is light on light. In Rukavat, her own chapter, where the draft paints her from behind (2.02, 2.24, 2.33), the plait will vanish. FIX: let the plait fall over a dark band (a teak or mid-dark shawl in Rukavat), or lead the back view with the upright stick and the small seated triangle and treat the plait as secondary.

THE PANEL RULE CONTRADICTS ITSELF IN THE WARD. colour_key PANEL RULE: 'the wall behind her is paler than her sari and darker than her shawl ... the pale-green ward wall becomes pale cream'. But Rukavat makes the shawl 'cream', and outfits adds 'a plain white hospital blanket'. A cream wall, cream shawl, white blanket and white hair dissolve her figure, and a pale mass on a widowed 80-year-old is the white-sari reading her own avoid list rules out. FIX: make the ward wall a mid faded teal or teak, keep the shawl oatmeal (never cream), and make the blanket a mid grey-blue.

SHE POINTS AT CARD PEOPLE. best_scenes: 'counting her lane at the door with one finger' (also draft 2.03, 'counting heads at the door'); year_arc: at dawn 'counting the arrivals with one finger'. The lane is chapter 2's circle and the arriving cousins are chapter 1's. Painted, they break rule 32. Pointed at before a decision, they break rule 36 and her own never_does ('Never points at ... anyone on the coming cards'). FIX: save the count for the household and the album; in chapter 2 have her count an empty doorway or the household's tea glasses; keep 1.37's 'No people'.

THE CODE WILL PAINT HER INTO PEOPLE-FREE PANELS. Once she has a LOOKS entry, cutscenes.py looks() adds her whole look to any description that names her, possessives included. I tested it: 'dusk, Nani's back step, wet ... No people.' came back as '... No people. The grandmother is a very small, thin Indian woman of eighty ...'. That paints her at 1.40, where 'Nani is never shown falling', and at 1.37, 2.33 and every 'Nani's house' fix (fix 7). FIX: write people-free panels without her name ('the back step of the pale yellow house'), or change looks() to read a list of the people in each panel.

A SCENE WORD TRIGGERS AN OLD GLOSSARY ROW. The scene words 'her feet flat on a low wooden stool' match the old 'flat' row, which appends 'The flat is a home in a small Indian apartment building.' (my probe, using the code's own terms()). FIX: write 'her feet resting on a low wooden stool'.

HER GLOSSARY ROWS USE WORDS OTHER PEOPLE SHARE. model_sheet proposes rows 'spectacles: big round spectacles with thick dark-brown frames', 'shawl: an oatmeal-coloured shawl', 'studs', 'plait' and 'chappals'. terms() appends a row to any panel description that uses the word, whoever wears the thing. Masterji's 'spectacles' would get her round frames, Mausa ji's shawl would turn oatmeal, and Mausi's file proposes a different 'chappals' row. FIX: keep her clothes and worn things in her LOOKS entry only; give glossary rows only to her objects, under keys nobody else uses ('walking stick', 'cloth purse', 'box of birthday candles').

SKIN WORDS ARE NOT THE TESTED ONES. painter_prompt: 'South Asian features and deep brown skin'. The words that fixed whitening in the soft styles on 22 Oct were 'South Asian features and warm brown skin' (flux-portrait-biases). FIX: write 'South Asian features and warm deep brown skin' in every look, Rukavat above all.

THE WARD INVITES SYMBOLS AND LABELS. Her ward props ('buff hospital file', wheelchair, drip, X-ray corridor) sit in a hospital scene, where painters habitually add a red cross and printed labels. A cross can read as a religious symbol (rule 3), and labels break rule 30. FIX: add 'red cross' and 'label' to the close-up check for every chapter 2 pick, and give the file and the drip bag their own glossary rows that describe them as plain.

LOW: AN OVERSTATED CODE CHECK. role: 'the old take's Dadi entry in ROLE and LOOKS retires first, or clash() refuses it'. clash() only refuses two names that share one role in the same panel, so it will never stop Nani. Retire Dadi anyway, so that 'the grandmother' means one person.

per_character.name: Mummy (मम्मी), 52
problems: A PROP IN THE FIXED LOOK, THE VIKRAM LESSON AGAIN. painter_prompt FIXED LOOK: 'a red ballpoint pen pushed through the bun'. At 1.05 she holds the red pen out, and in her usual pose her right hand writes bills. That makes two pens, an invitation to a third hand, and a muddle over which red pen is the player's. painter-glossary-rule says props stay out of the fixed look. FIX: take the pen out of the fixed look; if it is wanted as a back-view anchor, add it only to back-view scene words, and only when no pen is in her hand.

THE WATCH WORDS ARE A HAND-COUNT TRAP. painter_prompt: 'a man's wristwatch with a plain round white face and two hands on a steel link strap'. 'Two hands' is the multi-meaning word the hand count catches, and 'a man's' can bring a man into the panel. Separately, the old glossary row 'watch: a plain steel wristwatch on a steel strap' is appended to any description that says 'watch'. My probe of 'shows him the time on the watch' appended it, which is exactly the steel band her file avoids. FIX: write 'a large wristwatch with a plain round white face with no marks, on a steel link strap', and replace the old 'watch' row before chapter 1.

A POSE IN THE FIXED LOOK. The fixed look ends 'standing with her feet planted apart', word for word every time. That fights her seated scenes: the nine o'clock call on a chair edge, sitting back in the December front row, the album. FIX: move stance and sitting into the scene words.

SCENE WORDS TRIGGER OLD ROWS. In the chapter 3 sample, 'The shop owner stands behind ...' appends 'The stands are rows of wooden spectator benches beside a small cricket field', and 'her left palm flat on the glass' appends the apartment-building row (probe). The plural 'plain brown cardboard boxes' slips past the need-list check (unclear() matches only the singular 'box'). FIX: write 'is behind the counter' and 'her left palm pressed on the glass', and add a 'cardboard box' row.

A PROPER NOUN IN THE PROMPT. WEDDING VARIANT: 'in the Nivi drape'. The painter does not know the word, and the glossary rule says prompt words name nothing readable. FIX: describe the drape: 'pleated at the front, the end pinned over her left shoulder'.

HER OCCASION SARI WILL TURN RED IN JADUGAR. WEDDING VARIANT: 'a deep wine-dark maroon silk-look sari with a thin cream border'. chapter-5.json's look line allows only 'flat crimson, gold and black', and the code STYLE pushes 'saturated vermilion and magenta', so maroon will print crimson. A red silk sari with a light border reads as the bride or as a marital marker (rule 3), which her own avoid list rules out. 'Border' also fights STORY_NO's 'no border, no frame'. FIX: choose an occasion colour the chapter 5 inks can hold that is not red (for example black with a cream edge), write 'edge', and check every pick by eye.

CALENDAR AND CASH CARRY PICTURES THE PAINTER KNOWS. year_arc: 'the shop's free one-sheet calendar'; model_sheet pose 7: 'counting a bundle of blank notes'. Shop calendars typically carry deity art (Nani's own avoid list names a calendar as a religious-picture risk), and Indian banknotes carry a famous face and numerals (rules 3 and 30). FIX: describe the calendar as 'a plain white paper sheet ruled into a grid of empty squares, with no picture'; keep cash off the panel or folded inside a closed pouch.

'RING' HAS TWO MEANINGS. Scene words: 'a plain steel key ring ... hooked on her right forefinger'. On a finger, 'ring' can come back as a finger ring, which her avoid list bans. FIX: write 'a plain steel split key ring with three keys hanging from her right forefinger', and key its glossary row as 'shop key ring' only.

HIRED HANDS ARE CARD PEOPLE. relationships: 'Hired hands are paid daily in cash, counted twice in front of them.' The hired hands are chapter 3's circle, so any panel of her paying them paints card people (rule 32). FIX: keep the wage counting off the panel or after the chapter's cards.

ADDRESS WORDS DISAGREE BETWEEN FILES. This file: 'NANI (she says Maa, माँ)' and 'MAUSI (Didi and आप)'. Nani's file: 'Mummy, Mausi and Mama ji say अम्मा'. Mausi's file: 'Mummy says Didi and तुम'. FIX: settle one word and one pronoun for each pair before the readers check them (rule 65).

per_character.name: Papa (पापा), 56
problems: A HOUSEHOLD HAND REACHES OUT, AGAINST THE BIBLE AND THE DRAFT. year_arc: 'proposed 1.10: ... face in frame, the list held out in his left hand'; the model sheet repeats it ('holding the list out at arm's length'). Bible section 4: 'Household hands never reach towards you.' Draft 1.10: the list 'lies on the lower berth ... Nobody holds anything out.' Mummy's file also counts her 1.05 pen as the only household hand. FIX: keep the draft's hand-over with no hands (the list on the berth, turned to the viewer), or put 1.10 to the owner as a second marked exception.

THE ROLE WORD MAY ADD A PERSON. role: 'Painter's role word: the father'. Mummy's file dropped 'the mother' because it might add a child, and 'the father' carries the same risk. In English, 'Father' is also a priest's title (rule 3). FIX: use a neutral look noun that names no relation and no title (untested; check the first sheet for an extra child or clerical clothes).

THE PAINT CHECK WILL REFUSE HIS LIST, AND THE LINES INVITE WRITING. Scene words: 'one sheet of plain blank ruled paper inside a clear plastic document pocket'. 'Sheet' is on the glossary's need list with no row of its own (only 'team sheets'), so paint() would refuse the panel (probe). Ruled lines also invite painted digits and script (rule 30). FIX: write 'a plain blank page with no lines', and give the 'travel list' its own row.

A POSE IN THE FIXED LOOK. FIXED LOOK: 'he stands very straight with a slight forward lean, feet close together'. That fights the berth, ward-bench, walking and sleeping-back scenes. If writers copy 'stands' into a description, the old 'stands' row also appends spectator benches. FIX: move stance into the scene words, and write 'is standing'.

A BROW LINE THAT CAN BECOME A TILAK. painter_prompt: 'thin eyebrows lifted at their inner ends with one crease between them'. A vertical line between the brows has the shape of a tilak, and painted forehead marks appear on men too (method note: jadugar-salim). Mama ji's file dropped forehead lines for this reason. FIX: drop the crease from the prompt; carry his age in the eye lines and hollow cheeks; check every forehead close up.

NAME THE GOOD-MORNING FLOWER. typing: 'a picture of a flower at 6:10' (if a message card ever shows it). The painter may choose a lotus, which is a party symbol (rule 3), or a marigold, which leans towards ritual. FIX: name a flower with no such meaning, such as a sunflower, or use the cup of tea.

LOW: THE CLEAR POCKET CAN SHINE. 'a clear plastic document pocket' under Lugdi's single hard lamp can turn into a mirror (the player's file treats reflections as a rule 7 risk). FIX: write 'matte clear plastic'.

per_character.name: Mama ji (मामा जी), 47
problems: A PLACE WORD IN THE ROLE. role: 'Painter role word: the city uncle'. The role replaces his name in every sentence, and naming a thing draws it (glossary rule), so his chapter 5 panels in Nani's small-town lane may grow a city skyline. FIX: use a role word with no place in it, such as 'the round uncle'.

'WEDDING' INVITES RITUAL. Sample prompt: 'Under a striped wedding canopy at dusk'. The word invites ritual imagery: a fire altar, a bride in red, marigold garlands (rule 3; the old glossary 'garland' row is already marigolds). FIX: write 'a striped canvas canopy', and keep 'wedding' out of every chapter 5 prompt.

HIS WORDS MATCH AN EXISTING LIBRARY FACE. FIXED LOOK: 'a thick black moustache ... a large tan and chocolate-brown checked pattern ... sleeves rolled'. portraits.py FAMILY Ramesh is 'a thick black moustache, a checked shirt with the sleeves rolled', and LOOKS has Ramesh too. The file bans reuse, but near-identical words will make Ramesh again, and reviewers may wave through a lookalike. FIX: keep the old Ramesh files out of the reference folder, and compare every pick against Ramesh so an accidental likeness is caught.

THE FOUR-REFERENCE BUDGET IS FULL BEFORE THE PLACE. model_sheet: 'the set is him, Mami, the umbrella and Mami's clipboard, which leaves no slot for the place'. 5.03 is at Nani's blue gate, a recurring place. cutscenes.py paint_refs() passes every matched reference and never checks the four-picture limit. FIX: paint the umbrella into his master so it rides with him (as the file proposes), paint the gate from words, and add a cap of four to paint_refs.
KNOCK-ON EFFECT ON MAMI. His skin moved to 'warm medium-brown', which leaves Mami as the lightest person in the cast; see Mami.

HIS PHONE CLASHES WITH MAMI'S NOTES. never: 'phone before 5.07 (Lalit's note)'. He is painted phone to ear in every chapter 5 panel, and his voice is calls ('calling', 'call me', 'ok ok call karo'), while Mami's file now makes phones her whole note idiom. Rule 36's note-word check would then refuse his phone lines before several decisions, and the panels prime the phone note. FIX: see Mami; one of the two files has to give up phones.

per_character.name: Tinku (टिंकू), 21
problems: SCENE WORDS TRIGGER TWO OLD ROWS. painter_prompt scene: 'her feet on the front edge of the seat' appends 'The driver's seat is the bench seat in a lorry's cab, seen through the open door', and 'with a plain ochre cover' appends 'The painted cover is the front of the pulp novel' (probe). FIX: write 'the front edge of the chair' and 'a plain ochre cloth binding', and key the scorebook row as 'scorebook' only.

THE ALBUM POSE TRIGGERS A ROW AND A BLESSING GESTURE. posture.sitting: 'On the floor beside Nani's armchair with her back against its leg, where Nani can reach her head'. 'Floor' appends 'The room is a bedroom in the family's Nashik flat in 2026 ... a window streaked with rain' (probe). An elder's hand on a younger person's head also reads as a blessing gesture (rule 3; the cast already bans folded hands and touching feet for the same reason). FIX: write 'sitting low on a durrie beside the armchair', and keep Nani's hands on her stick and purse.

A BRAND WORD AND A LOGO WINDOW. typing: 'a mid-price Android in a clear back case'. 'Android' is a brand if it reaches a prompt (rule 3), and a clear case shows the back of the phone, where logos sit (rule 30). FIX: write 'a plain phone in a plain dark case'.

HER TEAL MAY MELT INTO THE CHAPTER 4 GROUND. colour_key CRICKET: 'the teal must stay bluer than the outfield green'. That assumes the code STYLE. chapter-4.json's look line instead paints 'flat slate-green and chalk-white grounds', and teal sits right next to slate green. A mid-tone body is also the kind of value the drift sheet lost. FIX: settle the Cricket style string first; then let the solid black sleeves and the ponytail lead, and keep her against the whitewashed wall, as the file says.
A YEAR ON SCREEN. relationships CAPTAIN SAHAB: '1979 again, Captain sahab?'. Rule 2: 'no year on screen'. FIX: 'Your one trial again, Captain sahab?'

POLITE FORMS CONTRADICT. never_does: 'says तुम to any elder', but address: 'In Hindi she says तुम to you', and you are her elder sibling (22 to 30). FIX: define 'elder' as a generation up, or have her say आप to you; settle it with the Hindi-first readers.

per_character.name: Mausi (मौसी), about 55, chapter 1 voice
problems: SINDOOR'S OWN COLOUR AT HER HAIRLINE. colour_key LUGDI: 'the hair glows copper-vermilion'. Vermilion is sindoor's colour, placed at her hairline, in the look whose STYLE already pours 'hot vermilion' lamp light, and red at the hairline is the first risk on her own avoid list. FIX: write 'dark copper-brown hair catching marigold light', and check the hairline close up in every Lugdi pick.

A FAMOUS FILM TITLE. samples COMFORTING: 'Arre, arre, arre. Main hoon na. Aao, baitho.' Mama ji's and the player's files both ban 'Main hoon na' as a famous film's title (their reading of rule 3). FIX: 'Arre, arre, arre. Yahin hoon. Aao, baitho.' (यहीं हूँ is about herself).
A YEAR ON SCREEN. samples TEASING: '1996 mein rishta main laayi thi. Berth bhi main laaun?' Rule 2: 'no year on screen'. FIX: 'Rishta main laayi thi. Berth bhi main laaun?'

'COACH' AGAINST PAPA'S RULE. painter_prompt PANEL 1.09: 'an Indian sleeper-class railway coach' and 'The plain coach wall'. Papa's file rules 'use sleeper carriage, never coach' (a coach can be painted as a sports coach; the old ROLE holds 'the coach'). FIX: 'sleeper carriage' in both places, plus a 'sleeper carriage' glossary row.

THE MASTER-SHEET PROMPT FIGHTS ITSELF. 'A character model sheet ... painted five times in a row ... on a plain warm off-white ground ... (Then the code's STORY_NO.)'. 'Ground' and 'sheet' are on the glossary need list (cricket ground, team sheets); my probe flags both, and the reference path does no check at all. STORY_NO then tells the painter 'One illustration panel, full-bleed', which fights five views. FIX: write 'on a plain warm off-white background' and 'five views side by side', and give references their own ending without 'one illustration panel'.

'BORDER' AGAINST STORY_NO. look.outfits: 'a solid magenta border', 'a broad old-gold border'. STORY_NO says 'no border, no frame', so the painter may drop the sari border or frame the panel. FIX: write 'edge' (Mami's file already does).

HER JADUGAR SARI WILL READ AS BRIDAL. OCCASION: 'a magenta silk-look sari with a broad old-gold border'. Nani's key reserves 'vermilion or magenta (the stage's colours)', and chapter 5's look line ('flat crimson, gold and black') will print magenta as crimson. A red silk sari with a broad gold edge is the bridal look her own avoid list rules out. FIX: choose a colour the chapter 5 inks hold that is not red, or keep her out of chapter 5's panels until question 11 is answered.

SHE FEEDS THE CARD PEOPLE. samples ORDER: 'Chalo, chalo, chalo! Ek-ek karke.' (to the whole bay); gestures: 'a foil parcel held out at full stretch to whoever is nearest'. The bay is chapter 1's cousins, its card people, so painting them breaks rule 32. FIX: offer only to the viewer (face in frame), to Papa or to Mausa ji; the bay stays out of frame.

LABEL TRAPS IN THE BASKET BAG. prop: 'a squat clear glass jar of ... lime pickle with a plain white screw lid', 'a small plain white box of birthday candles'. Painters put printed labels on jars and candle packets (rule 30). FIX: add both to the stray-letter check; the candle box also has three owners across the files (see cast-wide).

per_character.name: Mausa ji (मौसा जी), about 58, chapter 2's voice
problems: HIS WARD WORDS TRIGGER THREE OLD ROWS. best_scenes: 'the steel bench outside the ward', 'Rising in one movement as the doctor's round passes'. My probe of 'sits on the steel bench outside the ward door as the doctor passes; he watches the door' appended the railway pass row ('a tiny black-and-white passport photo of a young woman with a plait'), the steel wristwatch row, and 'a wooden bench at a small table beside the cricket field'. FIX: retire or re-key the old take's rows before chapter 2, and write 'goes by' and 'looks at'.

THE ORANGE ROW CANNOT MATCH. prop: GLOSSARY ROW 'orange (the fruit): ...'. _phrase() matches the key literally, parentheses included, so 'an orange' in a description finds nothing. A bare 'orange' key would instead fire on every orange colour word (marigolds, the signal orange). FIX: key the row 'peeled orange, orange fruit' and use those exact words in scenes.

RUKAVAT'S 'ONE SIGNAL ORANGE' LANDS WHERE THE PAINTER LIKES. STYLE['rukavat'] (wides 'sunday') asks for 'one signal orange' in every panel, but his orange fruit is in one or two. In the other chapter 2 panels the painter picks its own orange thing, and a saffron cloth or thread is the worst case (rule 3). FIX: name one fixed, plain orange object in every chapter 2 panel (an orange plastic water jug on the locker), or drop 'one signal orange' from the story-panel style.

cast.name: Nani (नानी), turning 80
cast.role: The household's eldest: Mummy's mother, grandmother of you and Tinku, mother of Mausi, Mummy and Mama ji. Chapter 2's asker (all eight decisions of the ward night, Rukavat look). She sends the game's first message (January, present day) and has the year's last line (the album, present day). Silent presence in chapters 1 and 5; heard once in chapter 3 (the nine o'clock call, off panel); absent from chapter 4. First-use label 'Nani, Mummy's mother' | 'नानी, मम्मी की माँ' (rule 65). Painter role 'the tiny white-haired woman', taken from her look and never from a relation (one policy for the cast: a relation word such as 'the grandmother' can paint the relation, a grandchild, into the panel). Retire the old take's Dadi from ROLE and LOOKS anyway, so no old role lingers; clash() only refuses two names that share one role in one panel, so it would never have stopped her. Round, not flat. Never on a card, and never the comic one in her own chapter (rules 10, 37).
cast.essence: The lane's old grocer. For 44 years she weighed out rice and dal in her own front room and never once put a thumb on the scale; now she weighs everyone's plans from the wicker armchair that stands where her counter used to be. She runs everyone's life and lets no one run hers, and what she fears most is becoming a head that somebody else counts. She is not always right: she cheats at carrom, she is the only person alive who says the 1979 umpire was right, and her pride put her on a wet step in the wrong shoes. The type in five words: the grocer who weighs everyone.
cast.backstory: Born in 1946, the eldest of four, in the older small town one night by train from the household's junction. She has lived there all her life. She studied to Class 5: she reads Hindi slowly in big print and does sums in her head faster than anyone with a phone. From 1972 to 2016 she ran a grocery from the front room of her house. Her one rule at the counter was the grocer's oldest, 'डंडी मत मारना' (no thumb on the scale), and the lane trusted her weights for 44 years. She also carried half the lane on credit in an account book. In 2016 her bad left knee closed the counter, and that day she tore up the credit book in front of the lane. That is why the whole lane still calls her Nani, and why it comes to the ward in May. The counter is gone. Her wicker armchair stands where it stood, facing the lane door; the shop's old brass pan scale hangs on a nail on the wall, never used; Mama ji's school cricket bat leans behind her door. Her children: Mausi (b. 1971), Mummy (b. 1974) and Mama ji (b. 1979). Nana is the owner's question. The default: he died before the story begins, off screen. He is never a plot device and nothing on screen marks it (no white sari, no garlanded photograph). His wristwatch is on Mummy's wrist, so Nani wears none and tells the time by the lane. A younger sister and a younger brother live in other towns; their grandchildren are among the cousins on the night train. The headcount is the writers' to fix (Papa's file has sixteen people and twelve berths, the draft bible fourteen), so none of Nani's lines carries the number. Her day now: up at five and tea at her window by half past, while the lane passes and reports in. Mama ji phones at eight. A neighbour's grandson fetches the milk and the medicines. In the afternoons the lane still sits in her front room and she settles its arguments; on Sundays she loses at carrom to Tinku and disputes the score. At nine she calls Mummy: BP, the day's takings at Mummy's shop, then a silence neither of them ends, until Nani hangs up first. Lights out at ten. Health: a bad left knee, so a walking stick since 2016; BP tablets; cataract operations on both eyes in 2019, hence the big round spectacles. In March Mummy brought her strapped sandals with a ridged sole; Nani called them 'the doctor's shoes', left them in their box under the bed and kept her smooth old chappals, and in May she slipped in those on the wet back step. Nobody ever says so; the shoes say it. Her phone is a large-screen one Mama ji gave her, and Tinku set it up for voice typing so she never has to ask anyone to read or write for her. All of this is team judgement built on the cast map, for the owner to approve. None of it appears as a caption; it surfaces only in lines, objects and rooms.
cast.want_fear_contradiction: WANT this year: everyone under her roof at once for her eightieth, every head counted by her own finger. WANT from you: the plain truth, unsoftened, and someone to hold her list when she cannot. You have read her bills aloud since you could read. FEAR: being moved out of her own house into a child's city flat, a guest in someone else's kitchen; underneath that, becoming a head that somebody else counts. The fall in May makes the fear real, and Mama ji's 8 am call says it out loud. CONTRADICTION: she runs everyone's life, but will not let anyone run hers. It shows the same way every time: when someone helps her, she turns the help into an order she gave ('The doctor said one night. I said yes.'; 'My whole lane's here. Put them to work.'; 'Someone holds it.'). She can ask for help only in the third person ('Who rides home with Nani?'). THE COST, so that she can be wrong: the refusal is never free. She refused the doctor's shoes and fell; on the ward night, too proud to sleep, she sends Tinku a voice note disputing a carrom board she lost, and Tinku's book is right. WHO WOULD SAY 'I KNOW THIS PERSON': Mr Natarajan (his own mother); Sunita (the woman behind the counter in her own lane, since Sunita's husband runs a small grocery, and she will know 'dandi mat maarna' at once); Farida (every ward she has worked on has one patient who runs it from the bed).
relationships: MUMMY (Nani uses no word for her, or teases her 'दुकानवाली' | 'Shopkeeper' when Mummy talks prices at home; Mummy calls her अम्मा and says आप, as Mausi and Mama ji do: Mummy's file has 'Maa', and three siblings need one word for their mother, settled in the cast's address table). Mummy learned to count change at Nani's counter at eight and swore she would never sit behind one; in 1999 she opened her own with stock money Nani lent her. Mummy repaid it in instalments and keeps the last receipt. Nani says she never kept that account, but she knows the sum to the rupee. Friction: fuse prices, advised by phone, unasked. Tenderness: the nine o'clock call every night, Nani talking, Mummy winding the watch, then a silence neither of them ends, until Nani hangs up first. After the fall Mummy takes her side against Mama ji's flat without being asked (Mummy's file). On the ward night Nani sends Mummy to the house full of guests ('Your Mummy's with the guests. I sent her.'), because the daughter who runs a shop is the one who can run a house full of people.

PAPA (she says आप to him; he calls her मम्मी जी). The son-in-law from the railway colonies, a man with no home town until he married in. On his first visit in 1996 she made him hers by giving him the chair by her window. Everyone who married into her family gets आप from her, the way her customers did, and Papa has asked for तुम for 29 years. She teases his timetables ('Does the sun rise by your timetable too?'; he wears no watch, his file) and is the only person who lets him finish a sentence. He books her ticket first; she pours his tea first. Before the train her worry is Mausi's knee; Papa booked Mausi the lower berth in January without telling anyone (his file). Proposed December beat: her first तुम, to the three who married in at once ('तुम सब भी बैठो।'), with an English-mode form that carries it (see MAMI).

MAMA JI (she calls him छोटे, 'the youngest', at 47; he calls her अम्मा and says आप, his file). Her youngest, who left for the city at twenty and has phoned at eight every morning since, to worry. She answers 'बस, सब ठीक' and hangs up first. Friction: after the fall he wants her in his city flat, and she refuses ('Your flat is yours. My bed is mine.'). Tenderness: she keeps his school cricket bat behind her door. In December the wedding at her house is his answer: since she will not go to him, he comes to her. When he arrives he bends down to her chair and she lays her palm on his head, the greeting that stands in for touching her feet.

TINKU (she calls her 'स्कोरर', 'scorer', never 'the youngest'; Tinku calls her नानी). Nani taught her accounts on the grocery's old ledger. Tinku keeps Nani's carrom scores and medicine times, and with Nani she drops every English word. Friction, seen on screen: Nani cheats at carrom and Tinku writes it down (Tinku's file); on the ward night Nani's one message after ten is a voice note disputing last Sunday's board, and the scorebook is right. Tenderness: being called 'scorer' is the only place in the family where Tinku is not 'the youngest'; Nani greets her with a hand on the shoulder.

MAUSI (she calls her बड़ी, 'the eldest'; Mausi calls her अम्मा and says आप). Her eldest, who married first and brings the food. Nani relies on Mummy for decisions and on Mausi for dinner, and Mausi minds. Friction: 'बड़ी, धीरे।' ('Slower.') every time Mausi starts talking. Tenderness: Mausi is the one Nani phones when she cannot sleep (Mausi's 2:20 am message on the ward night). The box of birthday candles is Mausi's (one owner, proposed for the cast table): she bought it the morning the January message came, though Nani had typed 'No cake. Halwa.'; it sits shut on Nani's stool at 2.33 and goes back into the basket bag; in December it comes out of the bag in Mausi's own panel.

MAUSA JI (she says आप; he calls her अम्मा जी). The quiet son-in-law who has fixed her wiring unasked for thirty years. He has held her house's spare key all that time, and every winter he fits a new rubber foot on her walking stick. She still orders him about as if he were 24 ('Ladder. Now.', his file) and will not let him spend a rupee in her house. She never thanks him, and he would be embarrassed if she did. On the ward night she sends him to sleep at 2 am; he does not go, and she does not ask again. Painted together, two white-haired elders: never side by side at one depth (one in front, the other behind or in the doorway), each from a reference picture plus a short tag, and their strip anchors kept apart (her small seated triangle, white swept-back head, dark round rims, light shawl, upright stick; his square block, white brush cut, short white beard, dark band across the shoulders).

MASTERJI (she says आप; he calls her नानी जी, as the whole lane does). In 1999 she came to inspect the street where Mummy's shop would open, and haggled with him for an hour over the price of one hem; he lost, and they have respected each other since. She still says his hems are a hair uneven, and after 44 years behind a counter she may be right, so he re-measures every hem she touches and edges her shawls free (his file). He asks after her by name whenever Mummy's shutter goes up.

CAPTAIN SAHAB (she says आप and 'Captain sahab'; he calls her नानी जी). They met at Mummy's housewarming and argued cricket for an hour (she follows the radio commentary), and each still believes they won. She is the only person alive who says the 1979 umpire was right ('Pad first, bat after.', his file), her contrary streak, and he has not forgiven her. After her fall he asks Papa one word about her on the six o'clock walk every morning (his file).

MAMI (she says आप; Mami calls her मम्मी जी). The city daughter-in-law who logs the BP readings Nani speaks into her phone and sends the doctor a numbered list each month. Nani trusts the lists and pretends not to ('मेरा BP मुझे पता है।'). Friction: whose kitchen it is during the wedding week. The आप to a daughter-in-law of 25 years is rare in a small-town home and could read as coldness, so it is made a trait people see: Mami remarks on it once (proposed for Mami's writer), and December's first तुम includes her as well as Papa and Mausa ji, honouring women and men who married in alike. In English mode her words to the three in-laws are 'Do sit.' all year and 'All of you too. Sit with us.' in December, so the change reaches English players too. At the cake Nani hands Mami the first slice in Mami's own panel (one payoff a panel).

YOU (she says तुम with commands, 'who should' asks and lines where you are not the doer, and no family word, whatever rulebook Q7 decides; you say 'Nani' and आप, and you call or send a voice note, never a text). You have read her bills and letters aloud since you could read, so you are her plain-truth person, the one she wants holding her list. Friction: she hands you the list and then tells you how to run it. The setup: in May at her door she counts the household with one finger and stops, because you are never painted and so never counted. The payoff: in the album she counts heads round the table and counts you last ('And you.'), and you answer (your file has 'Main bhi, Nani.').

HER LANE (chapter 2's circle). She ran their grocery for 44 years and gave half of them credit, and the day she shut the counter she tore up the credit book in front of them. They are card people: never painted in her panels (rule 32), never counted, pointed at, named or described before a decision (rule 36). The torn credit book is told once on screen by a household voice on the ward night (proposed for Tinku's tally voice, 'पूरी गली का उधार। एक दिन में शून्य।' | 'The whole lane's credit. Wiped in one day.', or Mausa ji's), so the grocery reads as generous and never as the stingy-trader stereotype. Her judging notes on them are about tempers ('moody', 'snappy'), in her own idiom, and land as often on men as on women.

THE NIGHT NURSE (proposed new minor voice on the ward, never on a card and never a joke). The one person on the ward who does not take Nani's orders, and by 4 am Nani respects her for it. Nani says आप and uses whatever job title the writers and readers settle (the usual Indian 'Sister' marks a gender, so the readers choose).
NANA, off screen (owner's question). The default: he died before the story, is never a plot device, and is never marked by a white sari or a garlanded photograph. His wristwatch is on Mummy's wrist.
HER YOUNGER SISTER AND BROTHER, off screen. Their grandchildren are among the travelling cousins on the night train (the writers fix the count).
cast.year_arc: JANUARY, the opening (present day): her voice-typed message is the first thing in the game ('My eightieth. May. Everyone comes.'). Her portrait sits on the household screen with the walking stick upright beside her. The order is her want. APRIL (opening pages, proposed): 'No cake. Halwa. That's that.', and the doctor's shoes stay in their box. MAY, chapter 1 (Lugdi): she is where the night train is going. 1.37 stays people-free (the blue door and gate, no name in the description). Proposed: after the chapter's last pick, a household-only panel: at dawn she stands small and face-on in her lit blue doorway, a dark shape against the lamp, and counts the household through the gate with one finger, silently (no line while rulebook Q11 is open; no cousins in the frame, since they are the chapter's card circle). She counts the painted ones and stops; you are never painted, so you are not counted. That evening the wet back step is shown, with no name in the description and no people, never the fall (1.40). MAY, chapter 2 (Rukavat), her chapter: from a district hospital bed, face-on (owner answer 6), she asks all eight decisions and runs the ward night to prove she is fine, turning every help into her own order. She counts the steel tumblers on the locker to see who has come, never the lane at the door. Past midnight comes the one message she ever sends after ten: a voice note to Tinku disputing last Sunday's carrom board, which she lost (her petty fault, seen). The turn comes at 7:30 am outside X-ray. In a wheelchair, the walking stick upright in her hand, she has to say 'My purse stays out. Someone holds it.', the first time she cannot hold her own (a close-up insert of the purse). Mama ji's 8 am call brings her fear (his flat) into the room. By morning she is home in her wicker armchair and cancels the party ('No party. When everyone comes again.'). Mausi's shut box of birthday candles sits on the stool, then goes back into the basket bag. From now on she wears the doctor's shoes, without a word. JULY, chapter 3: one beat only, the nine o'clock call heard on Mummy's phone at her shoulder (off panel); the draft's pencil circle on the calendar goes, since one object stand-in a person is shorthand and more rebuilds the empty rooms. AUGUST, chapter 4: not in the strip. DECEMBER, chapter 5 (Jadugar): the wedding comes to her house because she would not go to Mama ji's flat. Face-on and silent, she sits in the front row; she lays her palm on Mama ji's head when he arrives; proposed, she tells the three who married in to sit, her first तुम to them ('All of you too. Sit with us.'). For the first time she lets things be carried to her: the cake with one candle from Mausi's May box (5.28, her panel and her payoff only; Mausi's box coming out, Mummy sitting back and Mami's first slice each take a panel of their own, numbered by the writers). THE ALBUM (present day), face-on, two lines in all: Nani's count, 'One, two, three... everyone came. And you.', the one time she counts aloud, and your reply (your file). Built as a planned group shot in passes, or as split panels, with two reference faces up front. THE CHANGE: from an order ('Everyone comes') to a count ('everyone came') to asking after the one who did the counting ('And you'). She still counts; she has learned to be counted. DRAFT FIXES SHE NEEDS: (1) 2.04 'Tonight, you're in charge.' becomes 'My lane, your list.', since Papa said the first line the night before. (2) 2.09 'My spare key' becomes 'My locker key', since Mausa ji has held her house key for thirty years, and the draft's key 'on a red thread' goes on a plain steel ring (a red thread can read as a religious thread). (3) 2.03 is said face-on to you in the readers' wording ('My whole lane's here. Put them to work.'), and she counts no heads at the door (rules 32, 36). (4) Mummy's absence from the ward: 'Your Mummy's with the guests. I sent her.' (5) The slip is told in words early in chapter 2 ('I didn't fall. I sat down. Hard.'), if the owner allows a dry line from an asker (rulebook Q5). (6) The cake box at 2.33 becomes Mausi's shut box of birthday candles, paid off by the one lit candle at 5.28. (7) Her house is one house: a low blue iron gate in a plastered front wall, a blue wooden front door, a grey stone back step (fixes 1.37, 2.30 and 5.01), always written 'the pale yellow house' with no name, because looks() adds a person's whole look whenever their name appears, possessives included. (8) The 1.01 Hindi takes the form her phone produces, 'अस्सीवां। मई। सब आएं।'. (9) In every painting, 'cane' becomes 'walking stick' and 'cane chair' becomes 'wicker armchair', with no aliases left. (10) Owner answer 6 (characters drawn from model sheets) makes her face-on in Rukavat possible, and rule 33's text needs rewriting to match. (11) Outside X-ray the stick is upright in her right hand, never across her knees; in the ward bed it hangs upright from the head rail. (12) 2.02: the ward wall a mid faded teal, the blanket and pillow a mid grey-blue, so a white head on a white pillow cannot vanish. (13) 2.02's line reads 'डॉक्टर ने कहा', never 'डॉक्टर बोले', which makes the doctor a man. WAITS ON THE OWNER: Is Nana alive? Spectacles on two people (her and Masterji)? The words बड़ी, छोटे and the tease दुकानवाली? The first तुम to the three in-laws? A dry line from an asker (rulebook Q5)? The torn credit book and the brass scale as her past? The doctor's shoes as the cause of the fall? The carrom voice note? Mausi as the candle box's one owner? The album's 'And you.'?

voice.register: Low, slow and final. She talks in two gears, and the gear is the tell. Orders and jobs come in closed fragments, one to three words each, one to three to a bubble, each shut with a full stop the way she ruled off each line of a bill ('Bori upar. Chappal upar. Bachche andar.'). Comfort, news and asides come in short whole sentences that keep their हूँ and है ('Main yahin hoon. Kahin nahin jaa rahi.'), because an old woman soothing someone does not talk in telegrams. On the phone she runs on: a voice note is four to six short sentences of lane news, 'Haan,' first and 'Bas.' last. Never a comma list (that is Mummy's shape); a saying or an 'X, not Y' keeps its one comma ('Beemar hoon, behri nahin.'). At most one real saying a scene, from the counter, never a coined one. Never hurried and never raised, except one 'Bas!' a year. Her questions are 'who should' asks or sly questions handed back to the speaker. Help still turns into her own order ('Doctor ki salaah thi. Maine haan kar di.'), but warmth is now said out loud: she blesses ('Khush raho.'), owns a mistake in plain words ('Main galat.') and asks for the call home. Sly, with a straight face, and never the comic one in her own chapter. She tells time by the lane (after the milk, when the lamps come on, after Mummy's call), never by a clock, and says no figure at all, apart from the album count.
voice.mix: The most Hindi in the cast: the everyday spoken Hindi of a small Hindi-speaking town, full of the counter's idioms, with the town's ordinary Urdu-rooted words in it as in anyone's mouth (ज़रूर, यक़ीन, फ़िक्र). English comes only as the nouns the world handed her: doctor, BP, ward, X-ray, ticket, berth, cake, party, flat, list, phone, torch, timetable. Where her lane puts kar or ho after one of those nouns, so does she ('phone karna', 'BP high ho gaya'), but she takes up no English verb of her own ('check karo', 'adjust karo' and 'miss kiya' are other people's habit) and no English clause or tag. The young people's English things she waves off with the everyday echo word ('cake-vake', 'thank you-vank you'), at most once a scene. Her images come from the scale and the sacks, never the account book or a price: तौल, डंडी, तराज़ू, बोरी, छुट्टा, and the goods she weighed out (गुड़, नमक, आटा, घी, राई, जीरा, चीनी); dal and chillies stay Papa's and Mummy's images. In English mode her orders keep the fragments and the stops, her comfort is whole plain English sentences, each saying becomes the English saying people know ('A mountain out of a molehill.', 'Little drops make an ocean.', 'Weigh your words.'), and 'Baap re.' stays as it is, the way Mami's 'Ish.' does.
tics: TWO GEARS. Orders and jobs: closed fragments, one to three words each, one to three to a bubble ('Seedhi. Jaldi.', 'Meri gali. Tumhari list.'). Comfort, news and asides: short whole sentences that keep हूँ, है or था ('Paani hi toh hai.', 'Mujhe gussa aa gaya tha.'). A reader can tell which she is doing from the shape alone.

THE BARE LINE stays for orders and for her cross moments ('Badi. Chhote. Bas.'). Verbs come in orders ('Kaam pe lagao.'), 'who should' asks ('Nani ke saath ghar kaun jaaye?'), facts about herself ('Giri nahin. Baith gayi.') and every comfort line.
ORDERS start with the thing, then the verb or nothing: 'Bori upar.', 'Seedhi. Jaldi.'

JOBS go to 'कोई' with the plain plural command, the way a real house gives them, never to a name: 'Koi torch lao.', 'Arre, koi kapda lao.', 'Koi sambhalo.' The command marks no gender (rule 66). The 'should' form stays only where Hindi itself uses it: her 'kaun' asks ('kaun jaaye?'), her want ('Sab aayein.', 'Sab phir aayein, tab.') and the typed 'Koi na aaye.'
POSSESSIVES carry her orders and her no: मेरी गली, मेरा बिस्तर, मेरा बटुआ; and 'तुम्हारी लिस्ट' when she hands something over.

ONE SAYING a scene at most, and only a real one a Hindi-first reader knows: 'डंडी मत मारना।', 'राई का पहाड़।', 'बूँद-बूँद से घड़ा भरता है।', 'जितना गुड़, उतना मीठा।', 'आटे में नमक।', 'ऊँट के मुँह में जीरा।', 'दूध का दूध, पानी का पानी।', 'तोल-मोल के बोलो।', 'काम खरा उतरा।'. She never coins one.
SLY TURNS: a question handed back to the speaker, often with no verb ('Chai mein cheeni? Ya cheeni mein chai?'), sometimes with one ('Suraj bhi aapke timetable se nikalta hai?').
THIRD PERSON: she calls herself 'Nani' only when she needs help, because she cannot ask for it in the first person ('Nani ke saath ghar kaun jaaye?').

'BAS.' is her closer and her answer to 'how are you', and the question always goes straight back ('Bas. Apni sunao.'). The open palm presses down once, then her eyes go to the lane door, where her counter faced (the window is Mausa ji's look when he is moved). One raised 'Bas!' a year.

COMMON WORDS are anyone's, hers too: arre, achha, haan, chalo, dekho, suno and theek hai come and go mid-line as in any house ('Arre, koi kapda lao.', 'Achha? Agle hafte?'). What is hers is the shape, not a word. Other people's set phrases stay theirs ('Arre waah', 'Had hai!', 'Suno, suno, suno!', Mausa ji's one-word 'Theek.', Mummy's thanks-received 'Arre, isme kya.' and her platform 'Pahunchkar phone karna').
ECHO WORDS: the young people's English things get the everyday echo word when she waves them off ('cake-vake', 'thank you-vank you'), at most once a scene, never about a person.
ON THE PHONE SHE RAMBLES: she asks your news ('Apni sunao.') and then tells hers, short sentences about the lane, the milk, the rain and Mummy's call, before 'Bas.' ends it.
COUNTS SILENTLY: her left forefinger taps the air once a person, lips moving, no sound. Only the household, never card people. Aloud once in the game, in the album.
TIME BY THE LANE: 'doodh ke baad' (after the milk), 'batti jale' (when the lamps come on), 'phone ke baad' (after Mummy's call). Never a clock time.

ADDRESS BY BIRTH ORDER to their faces: बड़ी (Mausi) and छोटे (Mama ji) in Hindi and Hinglish; 'दुकानवाली' as a tease for Mummy; Tinku by her name. To you she names them plainly ('तुम्हारी मौसी', 'तुम्हारी मम्मी'), so you know who is meant.

TOLD FROM MAUSA JI, the other very short Hindi speaker: she owns things (मेरी, तुम्हारी), says मैं, hands jobs to 'koi', quotes the counter, blesses out loud and runs on in voice notes. He leaves himself out, speaks one verdict on the work ('Mazboot.', 'Dheela.') and lets his hands do the rest.
catchphrases: 'डंडी मत मारना।' | 'Dandi mat maarna.' | 'No thumb on the scale.' The grocer's own idiom (डंडी मारना, to short-weigh), known across the north: do the job honestly and in full. Said before a job she hands over.
'बस।' | 'Bas.' | 'Enough.' when it stops someone; 'Enough about me.' when it answers 'how are you'. Her closer, with the palm pressed down once.
'सब आएँ।' | 'Sab aayein.' | 'Everyone, come.' Her want, put as an order, and the game's first message (the phone types it 'सब आएं।'). In the album it turns into 'सब आए।' | 'Everyone came.'

'ख़ुश रहो।' | 'Khush raho.' | 'Stay happy.' (by sense in English mode: 'Well done.' for good news). Her good wish, with no religious word in it: for good news, at a goodbye with her palm on the bent head, and as her thank-you. The owner and the Hindi-first readers confirm it passes rule 3.
voice.exclamation: 'Baap re.' | 'बाप रे।' | English mode keeps 'Baap re.', as Mami keeps 'Ish.', because 'Well I never.' turned her into an English grandmother. For real astonishment only: news that truly surprises her. Said low and closed with a full stop, never an exclamation mark, so it is the one exclamation in the cast that is not raised. No religious meaning: literally 'O father', an everyday cry of surprise across the Hindi belt. Never followed by a name, and always in this one form ('Baap re baap' is not used). A power cut or a late guest does not earn it.
voice.sorry_thanks_love: SORRY: plain words in her own मैं, then the tea. When she is wrong: 'मैं ग़लत।' | 'Main galat.' | 'I was wrong.'; after she snaps: 'मुझे ग़ुस्सा आ गया था।' | 'Mujhe gussa aa gaya tha.' | 'I lost my temper.'; then 'चाय पियो।' | 'Chai piyo.' | 'Drink your tea.', the steel tumbler pushed across. The tea follows the words and never stands in for them, and tea means sorry and nothing else. THANKS: the good wish 'ख़ुश रहो।' | 'Khush raho.' | 'Stay happy.'; her old way, the next job ('अब ये भी।' | 'Ab ye bhi.' | 'Now this one too.', the stick pointing at it), comes after the good wish at most once a chapter. THANKED HERSELF: she brushes it off with the everyday echo word, 'रहने दो ये थैंक यू-वैंक यू।' | 'Rehne do ye thank you-vank you.' | 'None of your thank-yous.', and to the in-laws with आप, 'थैंक यू-वैंक यू रहने दीजिए।' | 'Thank you-vank you rehne dijiye.' ('Arre, isme kya.' is Mummy's, not hers). LOVE: said in comfort with its verb ('मैं यहीं हूँ। कहीं नहीं जा रही।' | 'I'm right here. Not going anywhere.'), in the goodbye wish with her palm on a bent head ('ख़ुश रहो। पहुँचते ही फ़ोन।', the call home put as an order), in a hand on Tinku's shoulder, and in words once, the album's 'और तुम।' | 'Aur tum.' | 'And you.' Never the English 'sorry', 'thank you' or 'I love you' to family.
uses: सब (everyone)
गली (the lane)
तौल, तौलो (weight, weigh); तोल-मोल के बोलो (weigh your words)
डंडी (the scale's beam; डंडी मारना, to short-weigh)
तराज़ू (scales), बोरी (a grain sack), छुट्टा (change)
गुड़, नमक, आटा, घी, राई, जीरा, चीनी (the goods she weighed, as images)
खरा (true to the mark): काम खरा उतरा, her praise
पूरा (full), of an honest measure: घी पूरा डालिए
उधार (credit), only about the credit book she tore up
बस (enough; her closer; her answer to 'how are you')
बाप रे (astonishment)
ख़ुश रहो (her good wish and her thank-you)
मैं ग़लत (I was wrong); ग़ुस्सा आ गया था (I lost my temper)
कोई (someone), with the plain plural command: कोई लाओ, कोई सँभालो
मेरा, मेरी, तुम्हारा, तुम्हारी (my, your)
चाय (tea), for sorry only, after the words
रहने दो, रहने दीजिए (leave it), with the echo word, to brush off thanks
अपनी सुनाओ (tell me your news)
धीरे (slowly); the town words ज़रूर, यक़ीन, फ़िक्र are open to her, never as a formula
हूँ, है, था in comfort and news ('Main yahin hoon.', 'Paani hi toh hai.')
the fillers anyone uses: अरे, अच्छा, हाँ, चलो, देखो, सुनो, ठीक है
echo words for the young people's English things: केक-वेक, थैंक यू-वैंक यू
बड़ी, छोटे (two of her children by birth order, to their faces); दुकानवाली (her tease for Mummy); 'स्कोरर' once, when Tinku's book settles a point
English nouns only, some with the lane's kar or ho: doctor, BP, ward, X-ray, ticket, berth, cake, party, flat, list, phone (phone ho gaye), torch, timetable
never: प्लीज़ / please, to family
the English 'sorry' or 'thank you', or शुक्रिया or धन्यवाद, in her own voice (she says 'मैं ग़लत।' and 'ख़ुश रहो।'); 'thank you' appears only when she throws someone's thanks back with its echo word
'मैं ठीक हूँ' or 'सब ठीक' about herself: she says 'Bas.' and hands the question back (an everyday 'ठीक है' as agreement is fine)
any figure in speech: a clock time, a price, a score, a head-count, berth arithmetic, an ordinal (पहली included), an age in years. The album count is the one exception
बेटा, बेटी, बच्चा, भैया, दीदी or any gendered or pet word for you, and no verb that gives you a gender (rules 8, 66)
an English verb of her own choosing, an English clause or an English tag ('check karo', 'miss kiya', 'don't worry', 'okay?')
a comma list (Mummy's shape)

another person's set phrase, or an exclamation as her habitual cry: 'Arre waah', 'Had hai!', 'Kamaal hai', 'Oho!', 'Haaye!', 'Hain?', 'Uff', 'Ish', 'Gazab!', 'Badhiya', Mausa ji's one-word 'Theek.' and 'Lo.', Mausi's 'Suno, suno, suno!', Mummy's thanks-received 'अरे, इसमें क्या।' and her platform 'पहुँचकर फ़ोन करना'. The common words inside them stay free, and so does a cry said now and then
account and bill words as images (हिसाब, बिल, खाता), and a trade code for sorry or thanks: the next-job thanks comes at most once a chapter, after the good wish
हुक्म or हाज़िर (court and feudal Hindi, the wrong class and region for a small-town grocer)

habits: DEVICE: the large-screen phone Mama ji gave her (no brand ever named or shown), lying on her lap on speaker. Tinku set up the microphone key and she taught herself the rest, so no one has to read or write for her (her contradiction, on a phone).

SCRIPT: Devanagari only, because she dictates in Hindi, written the way the phone actually produces it: anusvara forms (अस्सीवां, आएं), English nouns in Devanagari letters (डॉक्टर, बीपी), and echo words without their hyphen (केक वेक). A Hindi-first reader checks every typed sample against a real phone's voice typing.

SHAPE: the same two gears as her speech. Orders go as fragments of one to three words; news goes as short whole sentences. Each is closed with one firm tap on the full stop (।), the way she ruled off each line of a bill. Voice typing adds no danda by itself, so the stops are hers. No commas, because the stop is the only key she taps.

NUMBERS: none. The one figure she ever sends is the occasion in the opening message, which the phone writes as it hears it (अस्सीवां or 80वां, checked on a real phone). No time, no price, no BP reading (Mami logs those).
NEVER: a greeting or sign-off, anyone's name, emoji, the folded hands, stickers, forwards or good-morning pictures.

VOICE NOTES: anything longer than three short pieces becomes a voice note, and that is where she runs on: four to six short sentences of lane news (the milk, the rain, the sacks, Mummy's call), each bubble at most 10 words. It starts with 'हाँ,' as if you had rung her and ends with 'बस।'. Shown as live text on the painted blank phone; the caption is her speech, in standard spelling like her bubbles.
REPLIES: she never answers a text with a text. She phones back, usually within the hour.
WHEN: before seven in the morning and just after the nine o'clock call with Mummy; never after ten, except once, the ward night, which is how Tinku knows she is not sleeping.

THE FAMILY GROUP: Mama ji added her. She reads it on her lap and posts only to stop news she does not want (the fall). The owner ruled out a group chat on screen on 23 Oct, so it exists for the writers only.
HOW YOU TYPE TO HER: you don't. You call, or send a voice note.
