look.build: Smallest height band, alone in it (the cast's four bands: tall, middle, short, smallest): the smallest figure in any frame she is in, a head shorter than Mummy ('shorter than my counter', she says). Thin, narrow-shouldered and light as a bird, with an upright back she is proud of. Large knuckly hands from 44 years of weighing and lifting sacks. Her left knee is the bad one, so the walking stick goes in her right hand, the usual way (side is a preference to check, never what tells her apart). Almost always seated. Base shape: a triangle (a wide seated base, the point at her white head).
look.face: A small round face with high cheekbones, a straight narrow nose and a small firm mouth that sets in a straight line when she decides. STRIP ANCHOR: big round spectacles with thick dark-brown rims, which read even at phone size as a dark ring on a white head. CLOSE-UP DETAILS (inserts and the face chip only): thick straight white eyebrows (the family's brows, which her children and Tinku share in black); long earlobes with small plain gold studs. Her age is carried in the eyes, the mouth and the neck, never between the brows, because upright lines there can be painted as a forehead mark: two deep lines from nose to mouth, crow's feet behind the lenses, loose skin at the throat, thin wrists.
look.skin: Deep brown with a warm undertone, finely wrinkled. Age spots only on the backs of her hands, never on the face (a mark on the face can turn into a painted dot). Every prompt carries the tested words 'South Asian features and warm brown skin' unchanged, with her depth after them ('deep in tone'), in every look, the present day and Rukavat above all (flux-portrait-biases: that exact phrase is what stopped the whitening). Every pick is compared with the skin swatch on her master sheet, because the lamp light of Lugdi and Jadugar recolours skin too.
look.hair: Thin white hair combed straight back from the forehead with no parting, into one thin plait to the shoulder blades, its end tied with a plain black elastic. Seated, as she is in most panels, the plait is brought forward over her left shoulder so it is seen from the front; only standing back views let it hang down her back. The plait is a second anchor, not a first: white on an oatmeal shawl has little contrast, so her back view leads with the upright stick and the small seated triangle. STRIP ANCHOR: a white head swept back, with a dark ring of rims (Mummy's swept-back hair is black with a big low bun, so value carries the difference). Prompt words: 'thin white hair combed straight back from the forehead into one thin plait'.
look.glasses_jewellery: Big round spectacles with thick dark-brown rims, always on, since her cataract operations in 2019 (round is hers; Masterji's are half-moons, and they never share a chapter). Small plain round gold studs in long earlobes. Nothing else: no watch (Nana's is on Mummy's wrist; she tells time by the lane), no chain, no nose stud, no rings, no bangles (almost every bangle carries a marital meaning somewhere).
outfits: SIGNATURE, every day: a sage-green cotton sari (a soft grey-green of middle depth, never pale enough to read as white) with a tiny dark-green leaf print all over (a close-up detail: at strip size it reads as one mid tone), Nivi drape, the end over her left shoulder and down her back, never over her head; a plain dark-green half-sleeve blouse; an oatmeal-coloured shawl over both shoulders, ends hanging down the front. It is wool only in January and December; from February to November it is a thin cotton stole of the same colour, because old women keep their shoulders covered in the heat.

THE WARD (May): the same sari and the thin oatmeal stole (the ward fan is cold at night); a mid grey-blue hospital blanket over her knees in bed, never white, since a white blanket, white hair and a pale wall dissolve her and read as a widow's white. At a district hospital she stays in her own sari.
HOME, evening: an older, softer sage sari from the same family of prints, the stole folded on the chair arm, a folded handkerchief tucked at her waist.
DECEMBER, winter: the signature sari, the oatmeal wool shawl, and dark grey socks with her sandals.

WEDDING WEEK AND OCCASIONS (comics keep the costume): the same sage green and the same tiny leaf print at the same scale, in a finer silk-look cloth, with the oatmeal wool shawl and the same studs. No gold edge (old gold is already crowded on others in Jadugar), no new jewellery, no red, no white. She wears it in the front row, at the cake and in the album photograph.
look.colour_key: SIGNATURE: sage-green sari with a tiny dark-green leaf print (mid tone); an oatmeal shawl (light); a dark-green blouse; white hair; dark-brown rims; a dark-brown walking stick; a dark-blue purse. VALUE STACK, strongest first (white and dark hold across looks, mid tones drift): a white head with a dark ring of rims, a thin dark vertical stick, a light band of shawl, then the mid-tone sari. PROVISIONAL: the chapter JSON look lines and the code STYLE disagree (for example Jadugar is 'flat crimson, gold and black' in the JSON and vermilion, magenta, indigo, emerald and old gold in the code), so every line below assumes the code STYLE and is re-checked on the cast's look strips once one string per look is settled. BY LOOK: NOW, as above under warm lamplight. LUGDI (violet, indigo, vermilion, marigold): inverted, because several others claim the brightest lamp-lit shape: in her lit doorway she is a small dark shape, the sari a deep teal going indigo, the white head and the shawl's edge rim-lit marigold, the rims black; never vermilion. RUKAVAT (teak, faded teal, cream, one signal orange): the sari a deep faded teal; the shawl oatmeal as a light warm teak tint, never cream; the stick a dark teak close to black; the ward wall a mid faded teal; the blanket and pillow a mid grey-blue; never the signal orange, which is Mausa ji's. STATION and CRICKET: she is in neither chapter; if a later take paints her, Station is a mid halftone sari, cream shawl and hair, black rims and stick, and Cricket a darker green than the outfield with a chalk-white shawl, never cherry red. JADUGAR (vermilion, magenta, indigo night, emerald, old gold): the sari emerald with the leaf print and no gold edge; the shawl lamp-lit cream-gold; her face lit warm by the one candle at 5.28; never vermilion or magenta (the stage's colours); her emerald must not sit against Tinku's teal (Tinku's writer moves Tinku's Jadugar ink). PANEL RULE: the wall behind her is darker than her shawl and lighter than her sari, so neither sinks; never a pale cream wall behind her.
look.prop: SIGNATURE: her walking stick, a plain straight dark-brown wooden walking stick with a short T-shaped handle and a black rubber foot, reaching her hip. She bought it in 2016, the year her knee closed the counter, and Mausa ji fits a new rubber foot every winter. She points with it more than she leans on it, until May. THE UPRIGHT RULE: in every room the stick is a vertical line beside a small white head: upright beside her right knee in the armchair; hung upright by its T-handle from the steel head rail beside her right shoulder in the ward bed; held upright in her right hand, foot on the footrest, in the wheelchair; never lying across her knees, where it reads as a bar. It is told apart from Mama ji's umbrella by posture, not handle: hers stands planted and vertical, his hangs from a forearm (at phone width a T against a crook handle is two or three pixels, so the handle is a close-up detail). Her master is painted with the stick in her hand, so she and the stick take one reference slot. SECOND: a small thin dark-blue cotton purse, the size of a hand, closed with a brass clasp of two little metal balls that twist shut. It was the grocery's last cash purse, and she still keeps exact change in it, always shut (coins and notes carry numerals and faces). It lies in her lap under her left hand. Its beats at 2.21 and 2.22 are close-up inserts, because the clasp vanishes at strip size. ROOM THINGS (scene, not her look): the wicker armchair by the window, the steel tumbler of tea, the brass pan scale on the wall, Mama ji's old school cricket bat behind her door, the buff hospital file, the locker key on its plain steel ring. The box of birthday candles is Mausi's (one owner), seen beside Nani only at 2.33.
look.silhouette: STRIP: a small seated triangle with a thin dark stick upright beside it, a white head with a dark ring of rims, a light band of shawl. It holds in the armchair, in the ward bed (stick hung upright from the head rail) and in the wheelchair (stick upright in her hand). Standing, she is the shortest figure in any line-up, a straight back on a short frame, the stick out to her right. In profile: a straight back, chin up, the stick vertical. FAR SPEC, for when she is small and painted from words without her reference: the triangle, the white dot of her head, the light shawl band and the thin dark vertical stick, nothing finer. As a black shape at phone size, the upright stick beside a small seated figure is hers alone.
look.shoes: January to May: plain dark-brown slip-on chappals with a single strap, rubber soles worn smooth. In March Mummy brought her dark-brown sandals with a back strap and a ridged sole; Nani called them 'the doctor's shoes' and left them in their box under the bed, and in May she slipped on the wet back step in the smooth chappals. After the fall she wears the sandals without a word, in front of anyone, and nobody ever says why. December: the same sandals with dark grey socks. At home she leaves them at the door and sits with her feet resting on a low wooden stool, because her feet do not reach the ground from the armchair.

posture.stance: When she stands, which is rarely: small and upright, feet together, her right hand on the stick's T-handle with the stick a little forward and out to her right, her left hand free, its forefinger ready to count. She never leans on a wall or a person. She does not walk and talk at once: to say something she stops and plants the stick first.
posture.sitting: Upright and right back in her wicker armchair, her straight spine against its back, the wide chair round her small frame like a throne, feet resting on a low wooden stool, the stick upright at her right knee, the purse in her lap under her left hand, the chair facing the door so she sees who comes in. She is the one person in the cast who sits back: the front-edge perch is shared by eight files and is Mummy's December beat (sitting back at last), so Nani claims the opposite. When she laughs she rocks forward and slaps her knee, the only time she leaves the chair back. She rises in stages: left hand on her bad knee, right hand on the stick, then up, refusing help. In a hospital bed she sits up against the head rail rather than lie down whenever anyone is in the ward. Never on the ground (floor sitting and squatting are knee risks at her age).
posture.walk: Slow, short, even steps, the stick going first, never hurried, chin up. She stops to look at whoever she is passing. After the fall she is slower and the stick takes real weight for the first time, which she hates. By December she walks again, slowly, and points with the stick once more.
gestures: COUNTING, hers alone in the cast: her left forefinger taps the air once for each head, lips moving, no sound, eyes going from face to face. She counts only the household (and the steel tumblers on the ward locker), never a card person, and counts you only in the album.

POINTING WITH THE STICK: from the chair she lifts the walking stick level and points it at the thing she means (the file, the door, the cot), never at a person, and never at anyone on the coming cards (rule 36). She directs; she does not hand over.
'BAS': an open palm pressed down once in the air to end an argument, then she turns her face to the window.

GREETING, the gesture that stands in for touching her feet (used by families of many communities): her palm laid on the bent head of a grown child who arrives (Mama ji in December), a hand on the shoulder for the younger ones (Tinku). Only between painted people, since the player is never painted.
IDLE HANDS: her right thumb rubs the T-handle of the stick; her left hand smooths the edge of her sari end on her knee, the way she smoothed banknotes at the counter.
YES: one slow downward nod with the eyes closed for a moment (never the side-to-side head bobble, a stock caricature).
expressions: NEUTRAL: upright, mouth in a firm straight line, eyes steady behind the lenses, one hand on the stick, one on the purse, both still.
PLEASED: the chin lifts, a small closed-mouth smile deepens every line, one slow nod.
WORRIED: she counts again, faster, lips moving silently; she sits even straighter, because worry makes her more upright, not less.

CROSS: one tap of the stick's rubber foot, the 'bas' palm, then she turns her face to the window and will not look at the person. Her anger is a tap and a turned face, not stillness or volume; in chapter 2 Mausa ji's tell is going still and standing up, so the two never share one.
LAUGHING: a sudden wide open laugh, rocking forward out of the chair back, shoulders shaking under the shawl, one hand slapping her knee.
TIRED (only on the ward night, after the X-ray): the shoulders drop under the shawl, both hands stacked on the T-handle, chin down on her hands, eyes shut; the one time her posture is small too.

MOVED: she cannot say it. She looks hard at the thing (the cake, the full table), pushes her spectacles up with one finger, then busies her hands smoothing her sari end and counts heads again. Her eyes are wet behind the lenses.

across_looks: STRIP ANCHORS, the audit for every full-figure pick, checked in this order, strongest first: (1) the smallest figure in the frame, usually seated; (2) a white swept-back head with a dark ring of big round rims; (3) the thin dark walking stick upright beside her; (4) a light shawl band over a mid-tone sari; (5) warm deep brown skin and a face that reads eighty; (6) an upright back; (7) bare of every marker, checked close up at the forehead, the hairline, the neck, the wrists, the nose and the feet; (8) two hands, each with a known job; (9) no letters or symbols anywhere. CLOSE-UP DETAILS, checked only in inserts and the face chip: the T-handle, the purse clasp, the gold studs, the leaf print, the white brows, the plait and its elastic.

NOW (present day, the master): STYLE['now'] plus her master text. The style's fixed 'cool rainy-evening blues' fights a January morning and the December album, so her present-day pages need the agreed present-day style string first.

RUKAVAT (chapter 2, her chapter, the most panels): her reference picture plus the panel tag, 'present-day clothes' and the tested skin words, because period styles paint period dress. The ward wall a mid faded teal, the blanket and pillow a mid grey-blue, the stick hung upright from the head rail. With Mausa ji: never side by side at one depth (one sits in front, the other is behind or in the doorway); each from a reference picture and a short tag, never both long texts in one prompt, because two white-haired elders in shawls are exactly where the painter swaps traits (method notes).

JADUGAR (chapter 5, silent presence and the cake): the occasion sari in emerald with no gold edge, the shawl lit cream-gold by the tent lamps, her face lit warm by the one candle at 5.28, which is her panel and her payoff only. She must be lamp-lit or she sinks into the indigo night. With Mama ji in a panel: her stick planted upright, his umbrella hanging from his forearm.

LUGDI (chapter 1, the proposed household-only doorway after the last pick): a small dark shape in her lit blue doorway, rim-lit marigold, rims black. Pulp faces drift most (the drift sheet showed a bindi appearing on Kusum in pulp), so this reference needs the strictest close-up check.
STATION and CRICKET: she is not in chapters 3 and 4. Make these references only if a later take paints her there; the anchor is value and shape.

HER HOUSE IS ONE HOUSE in every look: a narrow two-storey plastered house painted pale yellow, a low blue iron gate in the front wall, a blue wooden front door, a grey stone back step. Inside: the wicker armchair by the window facing the door, the brass pan scale on a nail, a low wooden stool. Every people-free panel of it is written without her name ('the pale yellow house', 'the grey stone back step of the pale yellow house'), because looks() adds a person's whole look whenever the name appears, possessives included; or looks() is changed to read an explicit list of the people in each panel.

REFERENCES AND THE FOUR-PICTURE LIMIT: the present-day master is painted with the stick in her hand, so a panel spends one reference slot on her and her stick; then one reference each for Rukavat, Jadugar and Lugdi, derived from the master with the edit model, so the painter never has to change style and keep a face in one step (method step 6). A panel carries at most two people from references; crowds put two reference faces up front and everyone else small, side-on or from behind, from their far specs; the album is a planned group shot built in passes, or split panels. paint_refs() does not check klein's limit of four reference pictures today, so the pipeline must refuse a fifth.

PIPELINE GAPS to close before any face-on panel of her (read in cutscenes.py; not this file's to change): LOOKS and ROLE are keyed by year and ERA maps years to looks, so per-look ink words have nowhere to live; story_panels() reads first-take-script.md, not the chapter JSONs; REFS holds objects only; the panel painter has only SEEDS 7100, 7203 and 7319, with no SEED_BUMP and no DOTS paint-out (both exist only in portraits.py). Needed: per-panel seed bumps and an eye-confirmed dot paint-out; Station's halftone would fool an automatic dot finder, so a person reads every forehead.
cast.painter_prompt: TWO TIERS. MASTER TEXT, used only to paint her master sheet (her LOOKS entry, word for word, with the role and never the name; ROLE 'the tiny white-haired woman'): 'a very small, thin Indian woman of eighty with South Asian features and warm brown skin, deep in tone and finely wrinkled, a small round face with high cheekbones and a straight narrow nose, lined at the eyes, the mouth and the neck, thick straight white eyebrows, big round spectacles with thick dark-brown rims, thin white hair combed straight back from the forehead into one thin plait, small plain round gold stud earrings, a sage-green cotton sari with a tiny dark-green leaf print, its end over her left shoulder and down her back, a plain dark-green half-sleeve blouse, and an oatmeal-coloured shawl laid over both shoulders, in present-day clothes'. PANEL TAG, used in panels together with her reference picture (about 30 words): 'a small Indian woman of eighty with South Asian features and warm brown skin, deep in tone, white hair combed back, big round dark-rimmed spectacles, an oatmeal shawl over a sage-green sari'. SCENE WORDS, never in the fixed look, each hand named. AT HOME: 'She sits upright and right back in a low wicker armchair by a window, her feet resting on a low wooden stool, her white plait brought forward over her left shoulder. Her right hand rests on the T-shaped handle of a plain dark-brown wooden walking stick with a black rubber foot, held upright beside her right knee. Her left hand rests on a small dark-blue cloth purse in her lap.' WARD BED: 'She sits up in a hospital bed against its steel head rail, a mid grey-blue blanket over her knees, the ward wall behind her a mid faded teal. The walking stick hangs upright by its T-shaped handle from the head rail beside her right shoulder. Her left hand rests on the cloth purse in her lap.' WHEELCHAIR: 'She sits in a plain steel hospital wheelchair, holding the walking stick upright in her right hand, its rubber foot on the footrest, the cloth purse in her lap under her left hand.' Then STYLE for the look, then STORY_NO. Probed read-only with cutscenes.py's own terms() and unclear(): across all of this only the existing stool row fires, and no need-list word is left undefined. Words kept out of all her painter text because old glossary rows fire on them: flat, stands, floor, seat, bench, room, watch, cover, match; 'frame' and 'border' are kept out because STORY_NO says 'no border, no frame' (so her spectacles have rims, the armchair has legs and the sari has an edge).
painter_avoid: A forehead dot (bindi) or any forehead mark. The prompt does not stop it: check every face close up, paint confirmed marks out by eye and repaint with a new seed. The panel painter has neither DOTS nor SEED_BUMP yet (only portraits.py does), so both are added before any face-on panel of her.
Upright lines or a crease between the brows (they can be painted as a tilak).
Sindoor or red in the hairline (her hair is combed back with no parting; check anyway).
A chain or black-bead necklace at the neck (mangalsutra), any pendant.
Bangles of any kind, wrist threads, a steel band (it reads as a kara), rings.
Toe rings, ankle threads (check the feet in May; socks in December).
A nose stud or nose ring.
Prayer beads, rudraksha or tulsi beads, folded hands, a namaste, anything held as if in prayer.
The sari end drawn over her head.
A white, cream or very pale sari, and a white blanket or pillow behind her head: with a bare forehead pale masses read as a widow (the painter code already paints Badi Amma that way).
Lightened skin or European features, worst in the soft present-day and Rukavat styles; repaint, never accept.
A face that reads sixty (painted ages read young; the old Dadi had to be repainted at 78).
A bun instead of the plait (Mummy's anchor), or loose hair.
Half-moon spectacles (Masterji's) or changing rim shapes; the rims stay big and round.
A crook-handled stick (it reads as Mama ji's umbrella), a rattan cane, a second stick, or the stick lying across her knees.
A third hand; count hands in every pick.
Letters, numbers or logos anywhere: on the sari edge, the purse, the hospital file, the drip bag, the locker, the bed, the phone, the candle box, the cake; an open purse showing coins or notes.
A red cross anywhere on the ward (it can read as a religious symbol, rule 3) and printed labels (rule 30): added to the close-up check for every chapter 2 pick.
A red thread on the locker key or anywhere else.
A religious picture, calendar or shrine on her walls, or a garlanded photograph of Nana.
Sitting on the ground or squatting.
Being swapped with Mausa ji or Mama ji when painted with them (check every strip anchor against each person's list), or painted into a people-free panel because her name was in the description.
model_sheet: ORDER OF WORK, which is not hers alone: first the cast line-up (all ten as black shapes at phone width, in the four height bands) and the six look strips, then the cast's trait-table dedupe; the owner approves the pictured line-up before her sheet is painted.

MASTER TURNAROUND, standing with the stick in her hand, present day: front, three-quarter, profile and back (the plait down her back and the stick at her right), full figure beside a height line in the smallest band.

SEATED TURNAROUND, right back in the wicker armchair, her usual posture: front, three-quarter, profile and back (from behind, the anchor is the upright stick and the small triangle), stick upright at her right knee, plait forward over her left shoulder, purse in her lap, feet resting on the low stool.
RISING IN STAGES: three poses (left hand on her knee; right hand on the stick; up).
WALKING: three frames, the stick going first; and one 'stopped to speak' pose with the stick planted.

THE WARD (Rukavat): sitting up in a hospital bed from the front and from behind the steel head rail, the stick hung upright from the rail beside her right shoulder; in a plain steel hospital wheelchair from the side and from behind, the stick upright in her right hand, the purse in her lap.
EXPRESSIONS, the whole body, not just the face: neutral, pleased, worried, cross, laughing (rocking forward), tired, moved.
GESTURES: the silent count with the left forefinger; pointing level with the stick; the open 'bas' palm; the palm on a bent head (with Mama ji); smoothing the sari end on her knee; the slow nod.
HANDS: the counting hand; the right hand on the T-handle; both hands stacked on the handle (tired).

HEAD CLOSE-UPS for the audit: front and profile, showing the forehead, the hairline, the ears with their studs, the neck, plus close-ups of the wrists and the feet in chappals and in the strapped sandals.
FAR SPEC: her figure at phone size in each look as silhouette and two value blocks only, the reference for crowds and for panels where she is small and painted from words.

OUTFITS: the signature sari with the wool shawl; the cotton stole for February to November; the ward with the grey-blue blanket; home without the shawl; December with socks; the wedding-week sari in the same sage and print, in finer cloth.

PROPS SHEET, each painted alone as its own reference: the walking stick (T-handle, black rubber foot, hip height on her), the dark-blue purse with its brass ball clasp, shut, the spectacles, the wicker armchair, the steel tumbler, the brass pan scale, the locker key on its steel ring, the school cricket bat, the smooth chappals and the strapped sandals. The box of birthday candles is on Mausi's sheet.

GLOSSARY ROWS, objects only and under keys nobody else uses (her clothes and worn things live only in her LOOKS entry, so 'spectacles', 'shawl', 'plait', 'studs' and 'chappals' get no rows); each says what to paint, never what not to paint: 'walking stick: a plain straight dark-brown wooden walking stick with a short T-shaped handle and a black rubber foot'; 'wicker armchair: a low armchair woven from pale brown wicker on curved wooden legs, with a faded cushion'; 'cloth purse: a small thin dark-blue cotton purse the size of a hand, closed with a brass clasp of two small metal balls'; 'steel tumbler: a plain stainless-steel cup with no handle, a little wider at the top' (a shared object, one definition for everyone); 'locker key: one small brass key on a plain steel ring'; 'hospital file: a plain buff cardboard folder'; 'drip bag: a plain clear plastic bag of clear liquid hanging from a plain steel stand'; 'back step: one wide step of plain grey stone outside a back door'; 'pan scale: an old brass balance with two shallow round pans hanging from a bar, hung on a nail on the wall'; 'wheelchair: a plain steel hospital wheelchair with a black canvas back'; 'pale yellow house: a narrow two-storey plastered house painted pale yellow with a low blue iron gate and a blue wooden front door' (no name in the key); 'school cricket bat: an old worn wooden cricket bat with a faded grip, leaning behind a door' ('bat' is on the need list). The 'box of birthday candles' and 'birthday candle' rows are shared with Mausi's file and merged into one definition each. The existing 'stool' row (a low wooden stool) already fits. Writers also keep 'bench' (the X-ray corridor) and 'front room' out of her panel descriptions, or give them rows, since 'bench' fires the old scorer's-bench row and 'room' is on the need list.

COLOUR KEY SWATCHES: one strip per look (now, Lugdi, Rukavat, Station, Cricket, Jadugar), with the sari, shawl, rims, stick and skin each named in that look's ink, and her master's skin swatch for comparison.

PAIR TEST, before any panel is written further: one two-person test sheet, Nani with Mausa ji (each from reference plus tag, at two depths), recording the pass rate for each strip anchor and the swap rate; and a line-up beside Mama ji as black shapes at phone size.

HOW TO PAINT IT: only after this workflow and any browser checks have stopped (mac-memory-limit), through ~/.claude/heavy-queue/heavyq only, one job on the Mac at a time. Three seeds (7100, 7203, 7319). Pick by eye against the strip anchors, a forehead and skin close-up, a hand count and a check for stray letters and symbols. Whether klein can paint a multi-view sheet in one picture is untested: if it cannot, paint one view per picture from the same words. The owner approves the pictured sheet before any panel. Then derive the Rukavat, Jadugar and Lugdi references with the edit model, and record the seeds tried and the seed picked for each. Only if she keeps failing: first more reference views, and only then a one-person LoRA test through heavyq.
best_scenes: The ward night (chapter 2): running a district hospital ward from the bed, face-on, sitting up against the head rail, the stick hung upright beside her, counting the steel tumblers on the locker to see who came. Her whole contradiction in one room.
Past midnight on the ward: her one message ever sent after ten, a voice note disputing a carrom board she lost. Petty, wrong and entirely her.
7:30 am outside X-ray: small in a steel wheelchair, the stick upright in her hand, the purse in her lap, having to let 'someone' hold it. The turn of her year, told by her hands in a close-up insert.
The opening's first message: three voice-typed fragments that set the whole year going.
Home in her wicker armchair the morning after, tea in a steel tumbler, cancelling her own party, Mausi's shut box of candles on the stool and the doctor's shoes on her feet.
Her lit doorway at dawn in May, a small dark shape counting the household through the gate and stopping before you.
The front row and the cake under the tent lights (chapter 5): face-on, silent, letting something be carried to her for once, lit by one candle; and before it, telling the three who married in to sit.
The album: face-on at last, counting heads round the table and counting you last.
Any scene where someone tries to help her, and she turns it into her own order.

Next take, voice bank: a bank or ration counter where she is the fastest at the sums; a power cut with Mausa ji on the ladder ('Ladder. Now.') and Nani giving orders from the chair; Sunday carrom with Tinku keeping score.
never_does: Never sits on a card or is one of the equal two (rule 10).
Never doubts a report of harassment or a dowry demand, never calls one a misunderstanding or a family matter, never asks anyone to keep it quiet; she is the first to believe (rule 22).
Never the comic one in her asking chapter (rule 37); her dry lines and the carrom dispute are character, and any joke waits on rulebook Q5 and lives in the album or a later take.
Never addresses you by a gendered or pet word (bhaiya, didi, beta, beti), never your name, and never in a Hindi form that marks your gender (rules 8, 66).
Never wears white, never covers her head, never wears a religious, caste or marital marker (rule 3).
Never moves into Mama ji's flat.
Never says please, sorry, thank you or 'I'm fine' to family.
Never lets anyone carry her purse unasked; the X-ray corridor is the one time.
Never sits on the ground, and never perches on the front edge of a chair (she sits right back).
Never forwards a message, sends an emoji or a sticker, or posts a good-morning picture.

Never tells anyone how to dress or whom to marry, never sets the women of the house against each other, never rules the house as a controlling mother-in-law, never preaches or says 'in our day' (caricature traps): her authority is wit, weighing and care.
Never mocks anyone's community, region, looks or way of speaking.
Never gives a clock time, argues a price or keeps a score (Papa's, Mummy's and Tinku's).

Never points at, counts, names or describes anyone on the coming cards before a decision (rule 36), and never reacts to a pick before the chapter's end (rule 39); her finger counts only the household and, in the album, you.
Never holds anything out towards you with her hand; she points to it with the stick, since a hand reaching out of frame can be read as yours (bible line 78).
Never right about everything: she cheats at carrom, sides with the 1979 umpire and refused the doctor's shoes, and the story never turns any of these into wisdom.

Rule checks on every line of hers: at most 10 words in each language; Hinglish, Hindi and English written fresh; British spelling; no em or en dashes; lines flagged by the rule 66 checker (यहीं हूँ, की हूँ, गिरी नहीं, मैंने भेजा, कौन जाए?) are about her or are 'who should' asks, and a native reader clears them.
revision_notes: COMICS, ward silhouette: the stick now has an upright rule in every room (hung from the head rail in bed, upright in her hand in the wheelchair, never across her knees); X-ray panel fixed (draft fix 11).

COMICS and RULES, back anchor: seated, the plait comes forward over her left shoulder; the back view leads with the stick and the triangle. I did not take the rules review's other option, a dark shawl in Rukavat, because it would make her a second dark-shawled white-haired elder beside Mausa ji in chapter 2, which is the swap the comics review warns about.

COMICS, the count: only Nani counts heads with a finger, now silently; it is spoken once, in the album. Mummy's one-finger pose and Tinku's chapter 1 count must go from their files. The INDIA review wanted no head-counts in her speech. I took that, but kept the silent gesture, because it is the album's payoff and her strongest visual signature.

COMICS and INDIA, words: she owns the weighing words (तौल, डंडी, तराज़ू) and हिसाब goes to Mummy; देखो (Masterji's) and अरे (Mausi's) are dropped; 'बाप रे' is her one exclamation. The made-up 'Poora tolo' becomes the real idiom 'डंडी मत मारना' (with the spelling तौल). 'Teen kaam' becomes 'Saare kaam', and 'Hisaab poora' becomes 'Poora taul'.

COMICS and INDIA, numbers: the worry line no longer does berth arithmetic and no line carries the headcount, so her file cannot disagree with Papa's sixteen and twelve. She names no clock times and tells time by the lane. The 'BP 140' text to Mummy is cut.

COMICS, type test: one visible petty fault in chapter 2, the carrom voice note after midnight. I took that over the nurse-and-BP option, because that one is numeric and would put a medical error in the asker's mouth. INDIA, every capable woman gets a real cost: her refusal of the doctor's shoes caused the fall. That goes to the owner as a proposal, and no one in the story ever says it.

COMICS, props too small: the stick is told from Mama ji's umbrella by posture, not by handle. The purse beats at 2.21 and 2.22 become close-up inserts. Anchors are split into strip anchors and close-up details, and the checklist leads with white and dark values (RULES: mid tones drift).

COMICS and RULES, prompt length: two tiers. The 109-word master text paints only the master sheet. Panels use her reference plus a tag of about 30 words, and the master is painted with the stick in her hand so she and the stick take one reference slot. A far spec is added, and a two-person pair test with Mausa ji (pass rate per anchor) comes before any panel. With Mausa ji she is never staged at one depth.

INDIA, Hindi: हाज़िर becomes 'मेरी पूरी गली आई है। काम पे लगाओ।', keeping her possessive tic on the readers' wording. हुक्म is dropped. 'डॉक्टर बोले' becomes 'डॉक्टर ने कहा', so the doctor has no gender. The Papa tease is about his timetable, since he wears no watch (his file). मँझली is dropped; Mummy gets no word, or the tease 'दुकानवाली' | 'Shopkeeper', which readers confirm.

cast.essence: She runs the electrical shop on the station road, across from the station's parcel gate, and she runs the family the same way: every question gets a price, every account is settled before nine at night, and she has stood behind her glass counter for 27 years so that nobody can say she sits behind one like her mother.
cast.backstory: Born 1974 in Nani's town, the middle of Nani's three children: Mausi is three years older, Mama ji five years younger. From the age of eight she counted change at the counter of Nani's front-room grocery, and she half raised her little brother while Nani served the lane. She swore she would never run a counter. What she wanted was a bank's glass window, where nobody haggles. She took a commerce degree at the town college, married Papa, a railway parcel clerk, in 1997, and moved to the junction town. In 1999 she opened an electrical shop on the station road, across from the station's parcel gate, because 'a fuse is never a luxury: when the lights go, people pay'. Nani lent her the first stock money. Mausa ji, then a lineman, gave her her first wholesaler's name. Masterji the tailor has shared her wall ever since. She built the counter of glass, fixed her prices, and paid Nani back in instalments; the last receipt is taped inside the lid of her cash drawer. She lends but never borrows: the town's electricians and contractors, her regulars, buy on credit and settle at the month's end in a plain blue exercise book she keeps in the drawer, and only strangers hear 'Udhaar? Kal.'. What she will not do is owe anyone herself, and that pride is the thing the flood costs her. She wears her late father's man-sized wristwatch (the default answer to the owner's question about Nana; if he is alive, it was his gift when the shop opened). It runs two minutes fast, she has never corrected it, and she winds it every night at nine while Nani's call runs. Her reading glasses live in the cash drawer; she will not wear spectacles like her mother's big round ones in front of the shop. Today: fans, wires, switches, bulbs and fuses in plain boxes. The shutter goes up at nine by that watch, six days a week, Saturday the busiest, and comes down at half past eight. Papa cooks on weekdays and she cooks on Sundays. On the shop roof she grows green chillies and tomatoes in a row of old unmarked tins, the one thing she does slowly, and every Sunday a handful goes to Nani. She taught both her children to count change at that counter at eight, the age she learned, and has not noticed. She knows everyone on the station road by how they stand at a counter, which is where her judging notes come from. When a wholesaler's man asks for the 'malik' (the owner, assumed a man), she has one answer and has given it for 27 years: 'Main hi hoon. Boliye.'
cast.want_fear_contradiction: WANTS THIS YEAR: the shutter up at nine every Saturday, flood or no flood, without owing anyone. WANTS FROM YOU: to take half the phone calls, which she will never ask for in words. Laying the red pen down for you in January is how she asks, and laying the spare shop key down for you in the album is how she asks for more. FEARS: the shutter staying down, and the shop that Nani's money started going under. Under that, owing anyone anything: the one time she needed help, in 1999, she paid it back to the last rupee and kept the receipt. She lends to her regulars every month; she will not let anyone lend to her. THE COST (the India review: every capable woman pays for something on the page): her pride. On the first flood night she sends Masterji back to his own doorstep and bails alone until two, and the bottom shelf's cartons of wire, which his offer would have saved, are lost. That loss is why she hands you the hiring list next morning. CONTRADICTION (X, but Y): she swore she would never sit behind a counter like her mother, but she runs hers exactly like her, down to counting heads with one raised forefinger. She squares it by never sitting down: she has stood behind her counter for 27 years. It shows the same way every time: offered a chair, she perches on its front edge, back off the chair back, keys in her lap. In December, beside Nani in the front row, she sits back for the first time. HABIT OF SPEECH: answers any feeling with a price ('How are you, Mummy?' 'Copper's up again.'). QUOTED LINE: 'Nau baje. Shutter up.' | 'नौ बजे। शटर ऊपर।' | 'Nine o'clock. Shutter up.' I KNOW THIS PERSON (predicted; readers confirm): Ravi, who runs his family's shop with his father (the shutter time, the Saturday rush, the bill book, a parent who answers in prices, the credit book for regulars); Meena, who handles her neighbours' cash (counting it twice, the quiet skill); Sunita, whose husband runs a small grocery (the counter at the front of the house). Round.
relationships: NANI (her mother; she says 'Amma' | 'अम्मा' and आप, the word Nani's, Mausi's and Mama ji's files use, heard as their own word in the north and the south). History: she counted change at Nani's counter from the age of eight, and Nani's stock money started the shop in 1999, repaid in instalments, the last receipt taped inside the drawer lid. Friction: Nani's unasked advice on fuse prices ('Amma, fuse ka rate mujhe pata hai.'), and Mummy's refusal to look like her: she will not wear spectacles in front of anyone, because big round spectacles are Nani's. Tenderness: Nani rings at nine every night, BP first, then the day's takings, then a silence neither of them ends; Mummy winds the watch and never hangs up first. When Mummy arrives at Nani's door, Nani lays her palm on her daughter's head, and Mummy, at 52, still bends for it. Every Sunday a handful of her roof chillies goes to Nani. After the May fall she quietly takes Nani's side against Mama ji: Nani stays in her own house, because a woman who ran a counter keeps her own counter.

PAPA (her husband since 1997; both say तुम, equal respect; she uses no address word for him and starts with the item, as he starts with the time, so the game's couple carries no honorific-to-husband pattern; of him, to you and Tinku, 'tumhare Papa'). His parcel office window looks across the station road at her shutter. Friction: he times everything and she prices everything; he says the shutter went up at 8:58, she says nine. Tenderness: every Saturday he stands at the parcel-office window at 8:58; she never turns round, but lifts her right arm with the keys above her head as the shutter goes up. When his phone dies on the May night train, she lifts her left wrist and shows him the time on her father's watch, two minutes fast (one close-up insert). He cooks on weekdays; she has never once said he cooks well, and she always takes seconds. When he comes home with vegetables, she prices them aloud.

MAMA JI (her younger brother, whom she half raised; she calls him 'Chhote' | 'छोटे' and तुम, readers to confirm the word, which Mausa ji also uses, as elders often share one pet name for the youngest; he calls her 'Didi'). Friction: he solves things with money and she with time; he sends money she did not ask for, and stock leads from the city she never follows up. When she is angry with him he becomes 'Chhote ji' and she switches to आप. Tenderness: she has never spent a rupee he sent; it sits in its own account, untouched. Proposal: in December it comes back as the two advance envelopes for the tent and the cook, his own money, closed and plain, and she says nothing about it (keep it off any panel near chapter 5's dowry card).

TINKU (her younger child, 21; 'Tinku' and तुम, 'Tinku ji' and आप when cross). Tinku works the Saturday counter and keeps the stock tally on her phone, and Mummy pays her a full day's rate, the same as any hand (Tinku's file). Friction: Mummy is hardest on her because Tinku is most like her, quick and exact, and she times Tinku's arrival at the counter on her father's watch. Tinku is the one who says what the rest of the station road thinks: 'Baith jaiye, Mummy. Stool kaatega nahin.' | 'बैठ जाइए, मम्मी। स्टूल काटेगा नहीं।' | 'Sit down, Mummy. The stool won't bite.' Tenderness: Tinku grew taller than her at fifteen and she pretends not to notice. On cup day she comes to the boundary and stands at the back with her left palm pressed on Tinku's scorer's table from the first ball, her counter gesture: this is mine, and I stand behind it. When the scorers' course letter comes in December, her whole answer is 'Fees kitni?' and, the next day, 'Bhar di.' (paid).

MAUSI (her elder sister, three years older; 'Didi' | 'दीदी' and आप, as the rulebook's polite form to an elder and as Mama ji speaks to both sisters; Mausi's file has तुम and asks for one form, so the cast's address table settles it). Mausi calls her 'Chhoti'. Rivalry dressed as concern: Mausi says Mummy works too hard and should hire someone and sit down; Mummy says Mausi feeds people so they cannot leave. Friction: Nani calls Mummy for decisions and Mausi for dinner, and both sisters know it. Tenderness: a daily call in the shop's slow hour after two, both pretending it is about prices. In the flood week Mausi's basket arrives on the first bus with food for the hired hands, and Mummy sends her home with a new emergency light off the shelf for the tuition room: 'Didi, ye rakhiye. Iska bill nahin.', which is how she says thank you. Never women set against women.

MAUSA JI (Mausi's husband, the retired lineman; 'Jija ji' | 'जीजा जी' and आप). In 1999 he gave her her first wholesaler's name. His is the only wiring advice she takes without arguing, and in July it is his call that saves the shop: the mains stay off until the floor is dry, she does not touch the switch, and every wire in the walls survives (a man's competence the plot needs). Tenderness: she keeps fuses aside for him at cost and never lets him pay, and he never asks why.

MASTERJI (the tailor who has shared her wall since 1999; 'Masterji' and आप; he calls her 'Bhabhi ji'; chapter 3's voice beside her). Friction: he opens at ten and calls her nine 'showing off'; she calls his ten 'the afternoon'; both have a view on everyone who passes and they rarely agree. Tenderness: every monsoon they lift each other's shutters. On the first flood night she sends him back to his own step and it costs her the bottom shelf; the next morning he lifts her shutter before his own, with water over his doorstep, and she lets him. When his back is bad she sends her own plastic stool round. In the panels they are opposite shapes: her dark square block and high bun against his light, bald, stooping curve.

CAPTAIN SAHAB (a lane neighbour, the old club captain; 'Captain sahab' and आप; he calls her 'Bhabhi ji'). He buys every fuse from her and haggles for sport; she never drops a price, and she sells him the cup's floodlight bulbs at cost. Friction: he calls her shop 'the bulb counter'. Tenderness: on the morning the shop reopens he is the first customer, buying one fuse he does not need, so that the first bill of the new week gets written.

MAMI (Mama ji's wife, the bride's mother; Mummy calls her 'Bhabhi' | 'भाभी' with तुम, as a husband's sister does whatever their ages, and as Mausi's and Mami's files have it; 'tumhari Mami' when speaking of her to you; Mami calls her 'Didi' and says आप). Two women who both run things. Friction: Mami prices the caterer at city rates, and Mummy re-prices every line. Tenderness: at the wedding they split it, kitchen to Mummy and guests to Mami, without a word, and at one in the morning they stand side by side counting plates, neither saying thank you. Allies, never set against each other.

YOU (her elder child, 22 to 30; she says तुम in commands, 'who should' asks and lines where you are not the doer; आप and 'ji' only when she is cross; never a pet name, never beta). She taught you to count change at the counter at eight, and you are the only person besides her who counts the drawer at closing. Friction: she never asks, she assigns, and she answers 'How are you?' with a price. Tenderness: the red pen she lays down for you in January is the shop's 'paid' pen, her way of asking you to take half the calls. When you count the drawer right she says 'Ek rupaya kam nahin.', the most she praises anyone. In the album she lays the spare shop key on the table, turned towards you, and says nothing (owner option: 'Shanivaar, nau baje. Chaabi tumhari.' | 'शनिवार, नौ बजे। चाबी तुम्हारी।' | 'Saturday, nine. The key's yours.'). You say आप and -इए to her exactly as to Papa (rule 66; the realism notes' equal respect), and you text her 'Done' and a thumbs-up.

THE STATION ROAD AND CHAPTER 3'S CIRCLE. She knows everyone on the road by how they stand at a counter, so her notes are counter habits ('Chatty at work', 'Never sits still', 'Daydreams a lot'), two on women and two on men, never the skill the job needs. Her notes never touch the chapter's hard fact, a complaint of bullying at a past job, and she never hints that someone who complained about a boss is trouble (rules 22, 36). Hired hands are paid daily in cash, counted twice in front of them, off the panel: the hands are the chapter's circle, so no panel shows her paying them (rule 32).
cast.year_arc: OPENING (January, present day; she speaks): in the household kitchen she presses the shop's free paper calendar onto a nail ('From the shop. Free.'), rings May, 15 August and December in red with the shop's 'paid' pen, then lays the pen at the near edge of the table, turned towards you, her face in the frame looking out ('And the rest? Everyone calls you anyway.'). Her hand comes back to her side, so the beat meets rule 7 (people hold things out towards the player) and the bible's line 78 (household hands never reach towards you) at once. CHAPTER 1 (May, Lugdi, the night train; silent): she travels with the household, painted small but face-on in the bay. When Papa's phone dies she lifts her left wrist and shows him the time on her father's watch, one close-up insert. CHAPTER 2 (May, Rukavat, the ward night; silent): the review asks where Nani's daughter is. The proposed answer, true to her and to Nani's file: Nani sends her to the house full of guests. She does not sit at bedsides; she keeps the shutter up, and that night the shutter is Nani's front door. At dawn she appears once in the ward doorway, face-on and silent, holding Nani's own pillow from home. Mausa ji's one line can place her: 'Your Mummy's with the guests. The lane's downstairs.' CHAPTER 3 (July, Station, the flood week; her chapter as asker): the shop floods, water over her sandals at the door and every carton on the bottom shelf in it, the worst in years. Her pride costs the first night: she sends Masterji back and bails alone till two, and the bottom shelf's wire is lost (a proposal for the writers, off the asks). Next morning she hires strangers from her notice, hands you the hiring list ('Hands for the week. The list is yours.'), lets Masterji and the lane lift her shutter, and takes Mausa ji's word on the mains, which saves the wiring. As a proposal for the writers, she opens the credit book to the whole flooded lane, strangers included, as Nani did for 44 years. At 3.11, on the roof in the first sun, the first thing she checks is her chilli tins. On Saturday the shutter goes up at 9:00, 9:30 or 10:15 by her father's watch, with Papa at his window across the station road. The turn: owing the lane is how a lane works. CHAPTER 4 (15 August, Cricket, the lane cup; silent): the one day in the year she keeps her shutter down by choice. She stands at the back of the boundary, never with folded arms (that is Captain sahab's pose), her left palm pressed on Tinku's scorer's table from the first ball, and when Captain sahab says the district should see Tinku's book, she does not lift it. CHAPTER 5 (December, Jadugar, the wedding; silent): she and Mami split the house, kitchen and guests, without a word. As a proposal for the writers, the advance envelopes hold the money Chhote has sent her for twenty years, closed and plain. The candle box is not hers (the cast table gives it one owner). Her one payoff is her own two-person panel after the cake, not at 5.28: beside Nani in the front row she sits back in her chair for the first time all year and lets others serve. ALBUM (present day): face-on beside Nani, sitting back; she lays the spare shop key on the table, turned towards you, and says nothing (the album keeps its lines for Nani's count and your reply; her words are an owner option). NEXT TAKE: she hangs next year's calendar and lays the pen down without a word.

voice.register: Brisk, mid-fast and level: the pace of a shop counter on a Saturday, warm underneath, never cold, never loud. MEDIUM length, the middle of the cast. She has two shapes, and the job of the line picks the shape. ORDERS, PLANS, A NO AND A SCHEDULE come as one comma list of people and jobs (or goods), five to ten words, closed by one full stop and usually with no verb: 'Tum bill, Tinku stock, main shutter.'. CARE AND COMFORT get their verb back: short whole sentences with hai or hoon in them ('Shutter hai, counter hai, haath hain.', 'Main glass laati hoon.', 'Sab bag mein hai.'), so she is not one more clipped voice in a house that already has five. A second thought is a second bubble, never a longer one. Her list is people and jobs; it is not Nani's closed one-to-three-word fragments, not Captain sahab's call and then a reason, not Mami's item-and-status readback, and not Papa's run of whole sentences. HUMOUR: none on purpose. She is the straight face; the family laughs at her shop voice at home ('Haan ji, boliye.' to her own children, 'Aur kuch?' at a goodbye) and she never hears the joke. FEELING is changed into shop news with no figure ('Copper phir mehenga.'); love is mostly a deed, and when it is spoken it is a packed list that keeps its hai. CROSS: very still, the voice drops, and politeness rises. The one slow subject is her roof chillies: there the list stops and she says whole, unhurried sentences.
voice.mix: A Hindi frame, the everyday Hindi of a small Hindi-speaking junction town, with English nouns from today's counter dropped in whole: shutter, stock, bill, counter, delivery, godown, customer, fuse, wire, switch, fan, bulb, copper, MCB, mains, extension. The English verb + kar/ho ('check karo', 'delivery ho gayi') is the commonest Hinglish pattern in India and the whole house shares it; what marks her is where she aims it. The shop's words come home with her, as they do in any electrician's house: a power cut at dinner is 'MCB check karo', the water at the door is 'mains off karo'. No whole English clauses (Mama ji and Mami switch clause by clause). The common Hindi fillers are hers as much as anyone's (achha, haan, haan ji, chalo, suno, dekho, bas, theek hai, arre inside a line), and so are the everyday Urdu-rooted town words (zaroor, waqt, zaroorat). What her English carries: goods. Hindi mode keeps the trade nouns in Devanagari as Hindi speakers say them (शटर, स्टॉक, बिल, चेक करो). Her credit book is 'khaata' | खाता in both scripts, as every small-town shop says it, and the word means only that book. English mode is Indian English as it is spoken, not a word-for-word copy: 'Haan ji, boliye.' is 'Yes, tell me.', 'Aur kuch?' is 'Anything else?', 'Had hai!' is 'This is too much!', and the rising 'ji' stays on names when she is cross (Tinku ji, Chhote ji). Her two marked figures are said in words in speech ('nau baje', 'nau bajkar das'), which collide with no other word (unlike 'saath'); in typing a figure is a digit.
tics: Answers every phone call with the shop greeting, 'Haan ji, boliye.' | 'हाँ जी, बोलिए।' | 'Yes, tell me.', to Nani and to you exactly as to a customer. When she knows the voice she drops to तुम with 'Achha, tum.' and carries on, so the reader hears the switch and never takes it for a slip. This is her first tell.

Orders, plans and a no come as one comma list of people and jobs, five to ten words, ticked off on the fingers of her left hand: 'Tum bill, Tinku stock, main shutter.'. Comfort keeps the list's bones but gets its verb: 'Shutter hai, counter hai, haath hain.'.

Closes a talk the way she closes a sale: 'Aur kuch?' | 'और कुछ?' | 'Anything else?', after a compliment, at a goodbye, when asked how she is. At most one bubble in four, because Mami's 'Correct?' holds the cast's other closing question.
Changes a feeling into shop news with no figure: 'How are you, Mummy?' 'Copper phir mehenga.' The dodge is hers alone; Papa and Tinku drop theirs (C10).

The shop's English comes home: the English verb + kar/ho that the whole house uses, carrying the trade words of an electrician's house: 'MCB check karo.', 'Mains off karo.'. Never a joke on the kitchen: a too-sweet tea is plain 'Cheeni kam, dobara banao.'.
When cross, politeness rises instead of volume: 'ji' goes onto names that never carry it ('Tinku ji', 'Chhote ji'), तुम becomes आप, commands become -इए and -लीजिए, and her hands clasp at her waist.
Gives the hour in whole hours by her father's watch, which runs two minutes fast ('nau baje'). Minutes only in an emergency ('Nau bajkar das.'), which is how the family knows it is one.
On the roof, with the chillies, the list stops: slow whole sentences with their verbs ('Mirchi bach gayi.'). It is the only time she speaks slowly.
Counts heads with one raised left forefinger, exactly as Nani does, in silence: the count is never said aloud (a head-count in speech is Nani's one album line).
catchphrases: 'Haan ji, boliye.' | 'हाँ जी, बोलिए।' | 'Yes, tell me.' (every phone call, every customer, and you)
'Nau baje. Shutter up.' | 'नौ बजे। शटर ऊपर।' | 'Nine o'clock. Shutter up.' (her one catchphrase with a number: the shutter hour, which her target allows)
'Aur kuch?' | 'और कुछ?' | 'Anything else?' (the counter's closer, which the family quotes back at her; it takes the place of 'Iska bill nahin.', now a rare line)
voice.exclamation: 'Had hai!' | 'हद है!' | English mode 'This is too much!', which is how Indian English says it. For exasperation only: the water at the door, the lights failing in an electrician's own house, a delivery gone wrong. Secular: it means 'this is the limit', it calls on no one, and it is never followed by any name. No one else in the cast uses it as an exclamation. She has no exclamation for joy: good news comes out as orders ('Tinku, mithai lao.').
voice.sorry_thanks_love: SORRY, plain first: 'Meri galti.' | 'मेरी ग़लती।' | 'My mistake.', with the name ('Meri galti, Tinku.'). When her mistake cost someone, she names what she did and owns it in plain words, to an elder as to anyone: 'Masterji, kal raat ki zid meri galti thi.' | 'मास्टरजी, कल रात की ज़िद मेरी ग़लती थी।' | 'Masterji, I was stubborn last night. My mistake.'. No idiom: 'mere khaate mein daal do' is the sulky 'go on, blame me then', and khaata is her credit book. THANKS, GIVEN: plain words first, then a deed. To elders, 'Didi, aapne bahut kiya.' | 'दीदी, आपने बहुत किया।' | 'Didi, you did so much.', with something off the shelf put into their hands. To the young, 'Bahut achha kiya.' | 'बहुत अच्छा किया।' | 'That was really good.', and then something done for them ('Aaj raat ka khana mera.' | 'Dinner tonight is on me.'). When family reaches for a wallet at her counter: 'Aapse paise? Rehne dijiye.' | 'आपसे पैसे? रहने दीजिए।' | 'Money, from you? Put it away.'. 'Iska bill nahin.' survives only as a rare line, once a chapter at most, when a gift goes over the counter. THANKS, RECEIVED: the brush-off every elder in the north uses, 'Arre, isme kya.' | 'अरे, इसमें क्या।' | 'Oh, it's nothing.', and she turns straight to an order for someone else ('Tinku, agle ka bill banao.'). LOVE: mostly a deed: the red 'paid' pen laid down for you in January and the spare shop key in the album, each turned towards you, her hand coming back to her side; a handful of roof chillies for Nani every Sunday. When love comes out in speech it is a packed list that keeps its verb ('Torch, charger, extension, sab bag mein hai.') and the line every mother says on a platform ('Pahunchkar phone karna.').

'chinta mat karo' | 'don't worry' (she distrusts the line, which is Mama ji's); 'help' or 'madad' about herself; 'thak gayi' | 'I'm tired'; a vague time ('lagbhag', 'thodi der mein', 'around ten'): these are her character, not a word list

address: To you: तुम in commands (देखो, लो, भेजो, लॉक करो, लेट जाओ), in 'who should' asks (किसे रखें?, कौन करे?, never कौन करेगा?) and in lines where you are not the doer (बाक़ी फ़ोन, सब तुम्हारे।); one line waits on the owner: 'Bahut achha kiya.', a past with ने where you are the doer and किया agrees with the thing done, cleared only if rule 66 gains that fourth shape or the native reader puts it on the build's cleared list; आप and -इए only when she is cross (आप ही गिन लीजिए।). No address word for you at all: never beta or a pet name, never बेटा, भैया or दीदी. On the phone her shop greeting reaches you too, and बोलिए marks no gender; once she knows the voice she drops to तुम with 'Achha, tum.', so the switch is heard.
To Nani: 'Amma' | 'अम्मा', with आप ('Amma, aap baithiye.'), the word all three of Nani's children use.
To Papa: no address word; she starts with the item ('Bhindi itni mehngi?'), or with a plain 'Suno,' on the phone, with तुम, equal respect. Of him, to you and Tinku: 'tumhare Papa'.
To Mama ji: 'Chhote' | 'छोटे', with तुम; 'Chhote ji' and आप when cross (and when he arrives late).
To Mausi: 'Didi' | 'दीदी', with आप.
To Mausa ji: 'Jija ji' | 'जीजा जी', with आप.
To Tinku: 'Tinku', with तुम; 'Tinku ji' and आप when cross, in speech and in typing.
To Mami: 'Bhabhi' | 'भाभी', with तुम; 'tumhari Mami' when she speaks of her to you.
To Masterji and Captain sahab: their titles, with आप; both call her 'Bhabhi ji'.
To customers, wholesalers and hired hands: 'ji' and आप, always, with no comma before the ji ('Le jaiye ji.', 'Zaroor ji.'), and no kin word, so 'Bhaiya ji' stays Mami's.

(closes January's sab tumhare on the same words; check 3 flags गल्ला, a noun, so a native reader clears it)

habits: Device: a plain black Android phone in a plain black case, the screen painted blank with every word laid on as live text (rule 30). It lives in the side pocket of her kameez and comes out wedged between her left ear and shoulder.

Script: Roman Hinglish (Hindi in Latin letters), all lowercase. Commas only: no full stops, no question marks, no exclamation marks, even when she asks ('khud kab aa rahe'). Her spelling drifts (chabi, chaabi); her trade nouns never do.

HER HABIT: she acknowledges with the shop's 'haan ji', typed alone as the whole reply, to her own children as to a customer. Never 'ok', never 'done', never a thumbs-up. Anyone in the house may type haan ji inside a message; a bare 'haan ji' as the whole answer, every time, is her.

Shape: the same comma list of people and jobs as her speech ('daal tum banao, shutter neeche, ghar aa rahi'), two to eight words, one message per thought, never a paragraph, never a greeting or a sign-off.
Thanks are typed in plain words with a deed or a care after them ('bahut achha kiya, ab ghar jao'), never in a code.

Figures: only when the fact itself is a figure and only in an emergency, so a digit from her is rare and means trouble (the flood night's '6 baje'). Prices stay on the photographed bills, painted blank.
When cross, her texts get polite too: 'ji' on the name and -इए on the verb ('tinku ji counter pe aaiye').
Photos: of bills and stock cartons, painted blank, each with the same caption, 'ye wala check karo' or 'ye wala'.
Voice notes when her hands are busy in the shop. They start with her shop greeting even though she is the one calling ('haan ji boliye, achha tum'), shown as live text.

Emoji: none, ever (the thumbs-up is Mausa ji's, and your own reply to her). No stickers, no good-morning pictures (those are Papa's). The one news she sends unasked is the power-cut times, retyped the moment she hears them, shown as a message card (no group chat appears in the game).

Speed: reads within a minute between nine in the morning and half past eight at night, and replies only when she has the answer. Nothing between the shutter coming down and the end of Nani's nine o'clock call, and never after nine, so a late message from her means trouble. The flood night is the one time all year.
She never texts Nani. Nani rings her at nine every night, and Mummy waits for it.
Types fast with her left thumb, phone in her left hand, because her right hand is holding the keys or the pen.

look.build: Height band: middle, with Mausi, Mama ji and Tinku (the comics review's four bands; the old ranks of ten were finer than the painter can hold). The only exact gaps that matter are with people who share her panels: Papa a full head taller; Mami taller by half a head; Masterji and Mausa ji shorter; Nani the smallest in any frame. Tinku's being a little taller is a story fact, not a painting check. Sturdy and square-set: broad shoulders, broad hips, a solid straight waist and strong forearms from lifting cartons. Solid, never plump, never a comic figure. Base shape: square, shared only with Mausa ji, a man, so square is not sorted by gender; she stands where he sits forward. She stands with her feet planted apart, as if the floor might move.
look.face: A square face with a strong jaw. Two features carry her: (1) Nani's line, thick, straight, dark eyebrows set level, which make her look stern at rest; (2) a firm, straight mouth: when she smiles only one corner lifts, and when she laughs, which is rare, her whole head goes back. A short straight nose, laugh lines at the eyes that show only when she laughs, a little softness under the jaw. No lines between the brows: the painter can turn vertical creases there into a forehead mark (the painter review), so her age sits in the eyes, mouth and neck. Faces drift between paintings (method notes), so these features are for the master sheet and the face chip; at strip size her identity rests on the strip anchors.
look.skin: Warm brown skin of medium depth with South Asian features, the same depth on her face, neck, forearms and hands. The painter words start with the one tested phrase, 'South Asian features and warm brown skin', and add the depth after it (the painter review: only that phrase is tested against whitening, flux-portrait-biases). Where she sits against the rest of the family is settled on a painted swatch strip of all ten, not in words, because the files' word scales have already drifted apart. Every look's prompt names her skin, because neither STYLE['now'] nor Rukavat's 'sunday' style carries skin words, and Lugdi's and Jadugar's lamp light recolour skin too.
look.hair: Black hair combed smoothly straight back from the forehead, no fringe and no parting, gathered into one big round bun high on the back of her head, set high enough to show above the line of her head from the front and in profile. Two broad white-grey streaks run back from both sides of her forehead into the bun: white holds better than mid tones (the drift sheet), and face-on the two streaks frame her face. Face-on, the round knob above the head and the white streaks tell her from Nani (white hair, big round spectacles, a plait) and from Tinku (a swinging ponytail; check the pair in the line-up). Nothing in the bun: no pen, no flowers. The painter's words say 'combed smoothly back from the forehead', so no parting shows for the painter to fill, and they avoid 'temples' and 'crown', which name other things.
look.glasses_jewellery: Spectacles: none on her face, ever. Her reading glasses live in the cash drawer; she will not wear spectacles like her mother's in front of the shop, which also keeps spectacles for Nani and Masterji only (the cast map's clash check). Jewellery: small plain round gold stud earrings, and nothing else. Her one worn object is her father's man-sized wristwatch, loose on her left wrist (side is a preference, not an identity check), painted as 'a large wristwatch with a plain round white face with no marks on a steel link strap': the words 'watch', 'man's' and 'two hands' stay out of the prompt, because 'watch' pulls in the old glossary row (a plain steel band, which reads as a kara), 'man's' can paint a man and 'hands' trips the hand count. No numerals on the face (rule 30). No bangles of any kind by default (almost every bangle carries a marital meaning somewhere, realism notes; the India review's question about plain thin gold bangles goes to the owner), no chain, no rings, no nose stud, no toe rings. At strip size the watch and studs are close-up details, not anchors.
outfits: SHOP, every day (her signature; the opening, chapter 3 and the album): a plain deep maroon cotton salwar suit. The kameez is straight-cut to the knee, with three-quarter sleeves pushed up to the elbow and one side pocket for the phone; the salwar is loose and gathered at the ankle. A plain cream cotton dupatta lies diagonally across her chest from one shoulder to the opposite hip (the left shoulder preferred; a mirrored panel is fine), pinned at that shoulder, its other end hanging down her back, so it clears the stool and the ladder. Value: a dark body with one broad light diagonal band. No print, no embroidery, no edging, no lettering.
WINTER (the January opening, December): the same suit with a plain maroon wool cardigan a shade darker, unbuttoned and sleeves pushed up, so the cream diagonal still shows.
FLOOD WEEK (chapter 3): the same suit, sleeves rolled above the elbow, the dupatta's loose end knotted at the hip, the salwar wet to the shin, the same sandals in the water.
HOME, evenings (present-day night pages only): an older, softer maroon suit faded to a dusty rose-brown with a tiny cream dot print, the dupatta off and hung over a chair back.

WEDDING WEEK (chapter 5) and the last night: her signature costume in a finer cloth, as comics keep a costume: a plain deep maroon silk-look salwar suit with a straight knee-length kameez and elbow sleeves, a plain cream silk-look dupatta laid diagonally in the same way, the maroon cardigan open over it after dark, the same studs, wristwatch and sandals. No sari: a red silk sari with a light edge reads as the bride or as a marital marker, and in Jadugar's inks maroon prints crimson (the painter review). In Jadugar the suit is painted solid black ink with a pale cream band.
look.colour_key: Her key is a VALUE and a PATTERN before it is a colour: the darkest plain garment in her panel, crossed by one broad light diagonal band from one shoulder to the opposite hip. The broad light diagonal is hers alone in the cast (Mausa ji's shawl wraps both shoulders and Mami's bag hangs on a short vertical strap, both proposed to their files), so left and right never have to tell anyone apart. Then one named ink per look, all to be checked once the cast settles one style string per look (the JSON look lines and the code STYLE disagree). NOW: deep maroon suit, cream dupatta, maroon cardigan in winter; check that STYLE['now']'s 'cool rainy-evening blues' do not turn the maroon purple. LUGDI (chapter 1, silent): deep violet-crimson in the indigo shadows; the cream band catches the marigold lamp (it does not claim to be the brightest shape in the coach; the look strip decides that). RUKAVAT (chapter 2, silent): an almost black deep teak brown with a cream band, darker than anyone else at the ward door, so she never reads as a second Mausa ji; never the one signal orange, which is Mausa ji's orange. STATION (chapter 3, hers): a solid kameez in black or enamel-blue ink, with the cream paper left bare as the diagonal band; told from Masterji (light shirt, one thin dark tape line) by value alone. CRICKET (chapter 4, silent): near-black, never red, with a chalk-white band; cherry red is Captain sahab's alone. JADUGAR (chapter 5, silent): solid black ink with a pale cream band, never vermilion, magenta or gold, because old gold is already on five people. For Ravi, who is red-green colour blind, nothing about her rests on hue: the dark block and the light band carry her in every look.
look.prop: THE SHOP KEY RING (close-up and hand-sized beats, not a strip anchor): a plain steel split ring holding three plain keys (the long shutter key cut in 1999, the shop's first key; the small cash-drawer key; the godown padlock key) and one thin oval brass tag worn smooth, with nothing on it. It hangs from her right forefinger. When she has decided something she closes her fist on it, a still the painter can hold; when she writes, it lies on the glass beside her hand. It never leaves her: the 6 am openings use the spare set from the nail by the door, and it is that spare key she lays down for you in the album. It is painted from its own reference picture, and her master is painted with it hanging from her finger, so person and prop share one reference slot. Painter words: 'a plain steel split key ring with three plain keys and one thin oval brass tag hanging from her right forefinger' (never 'ring on her finger', which can come back as a finger ring). Glossary row keyed 'shop key ring' only. SECOND PROPS: the red ballpoint pen, her 'paid' pen (she circles a paid bill in red, which is why the calendar's planned dates are red circles; the pen she lays down in January is the player's for the year, so no other red pen is ever painted on her); the carbon bill book, painted blank; the plain blue credit book for her regulars, painted blank and kept in the drawer; her father's wristwatch, worn; the phone, with a blank screen. HAND MAP (a preference to check, never what tells two people apart): the left hand has the watch, the palm laid on the counter, the head-count forefinger and the phone; the right hand has the keys and the pen.
look.silhouette: STRIP SIZE, in black at phone width (a standing figure about 200 screen pixels tall, the comics review's estimate): a square block of middle height standing with its feet apart; a round knob of bun above and behind the head, visible from the front, the side and the back; one broad light band across the dark body from shoulder to opposite hip; face-on, two white streaks framing the face. From behind: the round bun, the dupatta end down her back, the square stance. In shop scenes her usual pose adds the phone wedged between her raised left shoulder and tipped head, a face-on shape nobody else has (Mama ji holds his phone up on a raised elbow), but it is a pose, not part of her fixed look. FAR SPEC (a small figure painted from words, no reference): 'a short square dark figure with one cream diagonal band and a round bun high on the head'. Against the cast: square like Mausa ji, but she stands where he sits forward, and has a dark bun where he has a white brush-cut. The keys, the watch and the studs do not count at this size.
look.shoes: Tan leather sandals with no heel and a back strap (they stay on up a stool or a ladder), worn every day and into the flood water; her 'good' pair for the wedding is the same sandal, newer. At home, plain dark rubber flip-flops with no marks. Never heels. The painter must leave her toes bare: no toe rings. The painter's words say 'no heel', never 'flat', which pulls in the old glossary row for an apartment.

posture.stance: On her feet behind a glass-topped counter, feet planted apart, weight even, shoulders square to the customer. Her left palm lies on the glass; her right hand writes or holds the keys; while she writes a bill, the phone is wedged between her left ear and shoulder. She stands all day: the plastic stool behind her counter is for the hired hand, and the strip lets Tinku say so once ('Sit down, Mummy. The stool won't bite.'), so players see that the family has noticed. When she must read small print she turns her back to the shop, puts on the reading glasses from the drawer and takes them straight off (off the panel; the arm's-length squint goes to whoever the trait table gives it). gestures: THE PALM ON THE COUNTER: her left palm laid on a counter, a table or a carton, meaning 'this is settled, and I stand behind it'. At the lane cup it goes on Tinku's scorer's table, in place of the folded arms that are Captain sahab's. A strip-size gesture: the arm's angle reads in black.

expressions: NEUTRAL: square stance, brows level and low, mouth a straight line, eyes already on the next thing, one hand busy.
PLEASED: one short nod, the fist closed on the keys, one corner of her mouth lifting; she says a price.
WORRIED: she tidies. She squares a stack of cartons that is already square, counts the same shelf twice, checks her wrist twice in a minute, and starts talking in minutes instead of hours.

CROSS: very still and very polite: both hands come off the counter and clasp in front of her at the waist (never folded across the chest), chin up, eyebrows lifted, a 'ji' on every name; the voice drops and never rises.
LAUGHING: rare and sudden: her head goes back, her mouth opens wide, her left palm slaps the counter once, then she goes straight back to work.
TIRED: both palms on the counter and her head down between her shoulders for one breath; or, at nine, sitting on the edge of a chair winding the watch with her eyes shut while Nani talks.
MOVED: she looks away at the shelves and counts something under her breath, and her right hand covers her left wrist.

never_does: Sits behind her own counter. She stands; the stool is for the hired hand.
Asks for help in words. She assigns, or lays something down for you (the album line is the owner's call).
Says 'don't worry', gives a vague time, or says she is tired.
Haggles for laughs, cheats a customer, charges city prices, or plays the greedy trader.
Gives credit to strangers, until the flood week, when she gives it to the whole lane. Her regulars always have credit.
Borrows, or lets anyone pay for her.

Hands anyone her own key ring; the spare set from the nail is the one that travels, and the one she lays down for you in the album. She would hand a new hand the broom, the counter or the scooter, but the cash drawer and the 6 am shutter only if she cannot be there herself, and then the strip should show why. Raises her voice. She gets politer instead.
Folds her arms (Captain sahab's), wears red in Cricket (his), or claims the cast's last-night sit-back for anyone but herself.
Covers her head, wears bangles, a chain or a forehead mark, wears a sari, or wears spectacles in front of anyone.
Doubts a report of harassment or bullying, or a dowry demand, or calls one a misunderstanding; she never hints that someone who complained about a boss is trouble (rules 22, 27).
Judges anyone's character beyond counter habits, or says anything about women or men in general (rule 22).
Sits on a card, is one of the equal two, or is the comic one in her own chapter (rules 10, 37).
Touches the player, or reaches towards the viewer; she lays things down instead (rule 7, bible line 78); calls the player by a gendered word or a pet name (rule 8).
Sets herself against Mausi or Mami as women against women: the rivalry is concern, and the alliance is real.
Feeds everyone before herself as a soap-opera sacrifice. She eats standing at the counter at two, and Papa cooks on weekdays.
Messages anyone after nine at night, except on the flood night; texts Nani, ever; or uses an emoji.
