cast.essence: The railway parcel clerk who loves in timetables: he cannot say he missed you, so he books you the lower berth, texts 'Reached?' and, once this year, lays his list down for you. Every feeling he has comes out as a time, and every time is exact. The type in five words: the punctual railway dad. What makes him not the type, and it is on the page, not only in his past: he is a goods-train guard's son who waited at a railway-colony gate for his father's late train, and he still lifts a hand to the last van of every goods train that goes by; he still counts under his breath in Tamil, learned from the colony children he played with (proposal); and the one thing he never times is the dal he cooks every weekday, by taste.
cast.backstory: Born in 1970 in a railway colony, the son of a goods-train guard who was away every other night. As a boy he waited at the colony gate at the minute his father's train was due, and could not sleep when it was late; that boy is where 'Reached?' comes from. When the train came, his father lifted a hand from the last van and the boy waved back. The family moved every few years across several states, so he grew up with no home town, a new school each time, careful Hindi that belongs to no one town, and one constant: the timetable. From eight to twelve his father was posted to a Tamil-speaking division; he learned to count in hide-and-seek with the colony children and still counts under his breath in Tamil (proposal; a Tamil reader signs it off). His father also taught him the guard's 'steady' signal, a flat hand lowered palm down, and he still uses it. He joined the railway at 19 as a clerk and has worked the parcel office on the junction's platform since 1995: bicycles, crates of fruit, a wedding's sweets, each weighed, entered in the register against the minute and sent on time. Mausi brought his marriage proposal in 1996; he married Mummy in 1997, and Nani's town became the home town he never had. His parents have died; his one brother lives far away and rings on his birthday, so nobody from his side appears in the story. Today he is four years from retiring. He walks to work in eleven minutes, walks with Captain sahab at six every morning for half an hour, and at 6:35, back home, sends the family one good-morning picture. On weekdays he is home at six and Mummy at nine, so the weekday dal is his, cooked by taste and never the same twice; nobody in the house remarks on it. On Saturdays he looks across the platform at nine and lifts a hand as Mummy's shutter goes up, the same hand he lifts to a guard's van. He travels on his privilege pass with the family members its rules allow, and everyone else goes on tickets; one booking holds at most six people, so a family trip is always several PNRs, which he enjoys. The story never says whether you are on his pass: the pass rules treat a grown son and a grown daughter differently, so saying it would give you a gender (rule 8). He writes a fresh travel list for every trip, one plain page folded once lengthwise into a long pale-blue plastic folder, and keeps every old one since his first job in a cardboard file box under the bed. He never reads his list in front of anyone: he knows it by heart. He wears no watch, because the phone keeps railway time to the second, and no spectacles, because his eyes are good: he reads the platform clock from the far end of the junction.
cast.want_fear_contradiction: WANTS THIS YEAR: all sixteen of them at Nani's door at 6:00 on the morning of her eightieth, and, under it, to be counted as one of hers, not only as the family's railway. WANTS FROM YOU: to be the one who never needs reminding. FEARS: being late when it matters; and under that, that in the family he married into he is only as welcome as he is useful. CONTRADICTION, held the same way all year: exact to the minute about time, but unable to say one plain thing he feels; every feeling comes out as a time, a berth or a ticket (he books Mausi's lower berth for her knee and never says so; he texts 'Reached?' and means 'I missed you'). The one thing he does not time is the dal. HABIT OF SPEECH: whole, careful sentences that keep their verbs, like a platform announcement, with any time corrected to the minute. THE LINE PEOPLE QUOTE BACK: '9:40, not 9:45.' | '9:40, 9:45 नहीं।' | '9:40, 9:45 nahin.' (the players' judge already picked it as a line that sounds like people you know; it is his one verbless line, the correction he adds after a sentence that held a time). WHO SAYS 'I KNOW THIS PERSON': Mr Natarajan (P5), the retired bank officer in Coimbatore who walks, then does the crossword with his coffee at about 6:30, and forwards good-morning messages; he is this man, and he will hear the Tamil count. Ravi (P2) knows him as the uncle at the station. ROUND.
relationships: NANI ('Mummy ji', आप): she made the man with no home town hers. Friction: she will never give him a time ('Come when you come'), which is torture for him, and she calls his lists 'your railway'. Tenderness: she is the only one who lets him finish a sentence; at dawn after the night train his tea is already poured on her step before he reaches the gate, because she knows his arrival to the minute; when they meet she puts her hand on his forearm for a second and he tells her the time (a greeting between two painted people, so the arrival does not feel scrubbed; the India review). He books her ticket first and she pours his tea first.

MUMMY (no address word; he starts with the time; both say तुम, equal respect): married 1997. Friction: he times everything, she prices everything ('When did it come?' against 'What did it cost?'), and he counts the minutes she spends 'just closing up'. Tenderness: on the night train, when his phone dies, she lifts her wrist without a word and reads him the time off her father's watch; on Saturdays he looks across the platform at nine and lifts a hand when her shutter goes up. He is home at six and she at nine, so the weekday dal is his; nobody comments, and the story shows it once, at 1.04, with no remark (the India review: shown as a lesson it becomes the one-sided message Ravi quits over).

MAMA JI (Mummy's younger brother; he calls Papa 'Jija ji'): opposite clocks. Friction: Mama ji books the night before, makes every number bigger (seventy guests, not sixty) and phones Papa to fix it; Papa always fixes it and says nothing. Tenderness: Papa meets Mama ji's train himself at 5 am on every visit, and Mama ji is the only one who calls him 'the family's railway' with pride.

TINKU ('Tinku', तुम): the only one who can make him laugh, by scoring his corrections ('That's four not-9:45s today'). He taught her to read a timetable, she taught him to read a scorebook. Friction: he wants her to sit the railway's recruitment exam for a safe job, his world (Tinku's file says 'bank exams'; it should say the railway exam, the India review); she wants the district scorers' course. Tenderness: he times her overs on his phone's stopwatch at the lane cup without being asked, keeps her first scorebook in his box of old lists, and in December gives her a ticket to the course's first day before she has said she will go.

MAUSI, CHAPTER 1's VOICE ('Didi', आप; readers confirm the word for a wife's elder sister): she brought his marriage proposal in 1996 and says so at every wedding (never the year on screen, rule 2). Friction: she overrules his berth chart every trip; this year she added four names in April after the twelve berths were gone, which is why sixteen people have twelve berths. Tenderness: he books her a lower berth for her knee before she asks and never says so, and her basket feeds him first. On screen: she shouts, he answers with a berth number. 'Reached?' is his alone, so Mausi's after-trip message should be about food only ('Khana khaya??').

MAUSA JI ('Bhai sahab', आप; readers confirm): the two who married in sit side by side at every family function, contentedly silent; Papa talks trains, Mausa ji says 'Hmm'. Friction: Mausa ji's 'Ho jayega' with no time in it drives him quietly mad ('When?'). Tenderness: on the ward night Papa takes the next chair in the hospital corridor so Mausa ji is not alone, and neither speaks.

MASTERJI ('Masterji', आप): stitched Papa's one good jacket, the charcoal one he wears in winter and at the wedding, and says his forward lean ruins its line. Friction: Papa arrives at fittings to the minute, which Masterji finds suspicious; Masterji is never on time. Tenderness: Masterji lets the jacket out every year and never charges for it.

CAPTAIN SAHAB ('Captain sahab', आप): lane neighbours and two clocks. Friction: Captain sahab calls the cup for nine, Papa says 8:55. Tenderness: they walk at six every morning, say nothing for half an hour, and neither has missed a morning; Papa sends the good-morning picture only after he is home, at 6:35.

MAMI (no name; आप, his formal habit even to a younger in-law): the other list-keeper. Friction: she numbers, he times; she asks 'What is item 3?' and he answers with a time. Tenderness: he sends her every guest's train times and she replies with a numbered list, the happiest exchange of his year; at the wedding her clipboard's item 1 reads 'Papa: trains', his name at the top of someone else's list. They never share a silhouette: her rectangle is held flat to her chest, his folder hangs at his side.

YOU (तुम; you say 'Ji Papa' and आप): when you were small he let you hold the tickets on every trip, and you never lost one. Friction: he checks twice what you have already done (your PNR, your platform). Tenderness: he books you the lower berth; he texts 'Reached?' after every journey you make without him; and in May, with his phone dead, he lays his list on the berth for you, the first he has ever let go of. From then on he buys folders in pairs and leaves the second copy where you will find it. He never calls you beta or any word that fixes your gender (rule 8, rulebook Q7), and never says on screen whether you travel on his pass.
HIS OWN SIDE (off screen): parents died; one brother far away who rings on his birthday. It is why no one from Papa's side appears, and why being one of Nani's matters to him.
cast.year_arc: JANUARY (opening, present day, the kitchen): when Nani's message comes he works out the day booking opens, not the day of travel. Proposed line at 1.04: 'Booking for May opens in March. My alarm is set.' | 'मई की बुकिंग मार्च में खुलेगी। अलार्म लग गया है।' | 'May ki booking March mein khulegi. Alarm lag gaya hai.' This replaces 'May. Trains booked.': a news report of a Railway Board circular says advance reservation fell from 120 to 60 days from 1 Nov 2024 (IANS, 17 Oct 2024, read in full), so a January booking for a May train would be wrong, and Mr Natarajan would spot it. Check the window still holds before the line is fixed. Behind him a steel pot of dal sits on the stove, painted without comment. MARCH (off the strip): at the counter the minute the window opens: twelve berths, on his pass and two PNRs; Mausi adds four names in April when no berths are left. CHAPTER 1, MAY (Lugdi, his chapter, the asker, about 8 to 10 lines): painted face-on from his model sheet at a level camera (owner answer 6). As the train comes in he counts the coaches under his breath in Tamil and is already standing where S4 stops. He has refreshed the running time since noon, so by 10 pm his phone is dead: the man of time without the time. Mummy reads him the time off her father's watch, and at 1.10 he lays his list on the lower berth, turned to face you, taps it twice and takes his hand away, his face in the frame: 'My battery has died. Tonight, you are in charge.' No household hand reaches towards you (bible section 4, and the draft's own 1.10). At the 2:10 long halt, as the train starts again, he stands in the carriage doorway and lifts a hand to the red lamp of a goods train's last van going the other way, then keeps looking down the dark line a beat longer than he needs: the boy at the colony gate, on the page, with no words. Dawn at Nani's gate: his tea already poured on her step. That evening, the wet step. CHAPTER 2, MAY (Rukavat, silent): painted face-on on the joined steel chairs of the hospital corridor beside Mausa ji through the night, neither speaking; at 5 am he goes to the station to move everyone's return tickets; a second pale-blue folder waits on Nani's locker for you, his one object beat of the year. CHAPTER 3, JULY (Station, silent): small but face-on in the parcel-office doorway across the platform; at 9:00 on Saturday he looks up at the platform clock and lifts a hand as the shutter goes up, the same hand he lifts to a guard's van (never in one panel with Masterji). CHAPTER 4, AUGUST (Cricket, silent): first at the lane ground at 8:55 with a steel water bottle for the side; Captain sahab says nine; he times Tinku's overs; Tinku may score him in her own line ('That's four not-9:45s today'). CHAPTER 5, DECEMBER (Jadugar, silent): alone and face-on under the platform clock before the 6:10 and the 9:40 guest trains, with no guests in the panel (rules 32 and 36); Mami's item 1 is 'Papa: trains'; in a two-person beat of his own, after Tinku's letter panel, he gives Tinku a small folded blank ticket for the course's first day. He is not in 5.28: the cake panel already holds too many payoffs. ALBUM (present day, may speak, in its own panel, never in Nani's): his one plain thing, still said as a number: 'Four trains this year. Nobody had to remind you once.' | 'इस साल चार ट्रेनें हुईं। तुम्हें एक बार भी याद नहीं दिलाना पड़ा।' | 'Is saal chaar trainein huin. Tumhein ek baar bhi yaad nahin dilana pada.' (May there and back, December there and back; the Hindi is impersonal, so it marks no gender). THE CHANGE: January, a man who keeps every list to himself; from May, a man who buys folders in pairs and writes two copies. The turn is May, chapter 1, the dead phone. If rulebook Q11 lets the household speak in every chapter, he gets one line in each; until then the silent beats carry him.

voice.register: Measured, even and quiet; never raised and never an exclamation mark (chapter 1's one shout is Mausi's). He talks like a platform announcement: an ordered run of whole sentences, each three to eight words with its verb and its full stop, one fact to a sentence, across one to three bubbles, and the last one often names what comes next ('Ab TT aayega.'). That is his long shape, and it is unlike the other long talkers: Mama ji runs on with commas and 'aur haan', Mausi triples and overlaps, Masterji gives a verdict and wanders into cloth and weather; Papa closes each sentence before he starts the next. The everyday fillers of spoken Hindi come into his lines the way they come into anyone's, softly at the head of a sentence ('Suno,' to Mummy, 'Achha?' at a piece of news) or in the middle ('aap bas time bataiye', 'aayenge zaroor'), never as a tag at the end, so the closed announcement stays his. Slow and exact, but not a machine: a time stands where others put a feeling, in the words railway people really say ('do ghante der se', 'baarah minute late'), never a robot count, and good news goes straight to Nani ('Mummy ji ko abhi batata hoon.'). His only verbless lines are the logged ones, the time correction ('9:40, aaspaas nahin.') and the deed logged in his thanks to the young ('Raat bhar, list ke saath.'), the repeated word when cross ('Koi nahin.'), 'Thank you, ji.' to strangers, and the fixed replies he types. With Nani, who lets him finish, the run is longest (three bubbles); with everyone else it is usually two sentences. Numbers: one of the two people in the cast who lean on them (with Tinku), and only clock times, durations and the count before a noun; never prices, scores or ordinals. Budget: at most one figure a bubble, and at least one bubble in three with none (in the test set below, 3 lines of 12 carry a clock figure and one more says 'do ghante'). Humour is deadpan, about himself and clocks, in the same flat announcement voice.
voice.mix: Careful standard Hindi of the railway colonies, belonging to no one town: full verbs, आप and -इए to elders, no regional colour, and the town's common Hindustani used the way anyone uses it ('fikr mat kijiye', 'zaroor'; cast-wide 8: these words belong to the town, not to Masterji). English comes as single words: the railway nouns every Indian traveller knows (coach, berth, platform, PNR, chart, waiting list, booking, ticket, running status, TT, board; railway people say TT, and 'checker' is an outsider's word) and the everyday nouns of a colony boy grown up (time, battery, alarm, gate, colony, joining, walk); clock times stay figures in all three modes ('9:40'). His verbs are mostly Hindi, many of them the railway's own (gaadi lagna, chhootna, chalna, chart banna, berth milna). The everyday English verb with kar or ho now comes too, where it suits him, and what he turns into one is the booking counter's own work: 'book kiya', 'book kar deta hoon', 'confirm ho gaya', 'cancel karna' (cast-wide 2; Mummy's mark is home things in counter English, 'MCB check karo', so the two still sort apart). He switches by single words, as older speakers do in the Dehradun study the realism notes cite, never by whole English clauses (Mama ji and Mami do that). टिकट is masculine in his mouth ('का टिकट', the standard booking-counter form); if Mama ji's file keeps 'की टिकट' it is Mama ji's colloquial mark and both files say so, otherwise both say 'का'. His late father is 'mere pitaji' | 'मेरे पिताजी' in Hinglish and Hindi alike: plain everyday Hindi with no lean to any community, and what a railway-colony man of 56 says to his Hindi-first mother-in-law ('father' was an outsider's word to her). Hindi mode uses plain Hindi where a low-English reader would stall: 'गाड़ी कहाँ है' for 'running status', 'सैर' for 'walk'. Tamil only in the coach count under his breath, kept in Tamil in every mode (a Tamil reader signs off the words and the script). When cross the English goes altogether: 'late' becomes 'der', 'halt' goes, and only the time stays. 'Darj hai.' | 'Noted.' is his reply to a fact (a PNR, a platform, 'Reached') and, to the young, his thanks as the deed logged ('Raat bhar, list ke saath. Darj hai.'); never his thanks for a kindness done for him (Nani's tea gets praise of its timing). His typed messages are English (see typing).
tics: Announces in order: whole sentences, one fact each, each closed with a full stop, the last naming the next step with 'ab ... aayega' or 'ab ... jaayenge' | 'अब ... आएगा' | '... comes next' ('Ab TT aayega.' | 'The TT comes next.'). Only for things that do arrive or go on their own (a train, the TT, the bags going up); a thing he fetches he fetches himself ('Kapda main laata hoon.').
Corrects any vague time to the minute: '9:40, aaspaas nahin.' | '9:40, not "around".' He hears 'about', 'around' and 'lagbhag' as errors; quoting the word back is the only time he says it.
The count before the thing: 'Hum solah log hain.' | 'There are sixteen of us.' (Tinku and Mama ji drop number-first).
Names a train by its time: '9:40 wali', '8:15 wali' ('the 9:40'), as railway people do.

A time where others give a feeling, in the words railway people really use: 'do ghante der se', 'baarah minute late', the 9:40 wali; never a robot count ('120 minute') and never a minute stamp on a kindness. Good news is not logged; it goes to Nani at once ('Mummy ji ko abhi batata hoon.').

Opens a sentence with an everyday filler, softly, as anyone does: 'Suno,' to Mummy (the way Indian couples who use no first names talk), 'Achha?' at news, 'bas' and 'zaroor' in the middle of a request. Never a tag at the end of a line (Tinku's 'haan?', Mama ji's 'aur haan').

Deadpan jokes in the station loudspeaker's frame: 'Kripya dhyan dein.' | 'Attention, please.' then a home fact ('Dal platform number ek par aa chuki hai.', 'Ye chai nahin, sharbat hai.'). At most once a chapter, never while he asks (rule 37), all of it waiting on rulebook Q5.
Never describes a person's temperament; he says what they did.
Counts the coaches under his breath in Tamil as a train comes in: '...naalu, anju, aaru.' (a whisper bubble; proposal, a Tamil reader signs off).
Looks up for a clock before he speaks in any new place (a gesture in the panel, not a word).
When cross: the time left, then one word said twice ('Koi neeche na utre. Koi nahin.'), the guard's flat hand lowered palm down; quieter, never louder, and the English goes.

His judging notes on cards: one time stamp, then the act, in the Hindi transitive past so a note reads the same of a woman or a man; no ordinal and no second figure: '10:20. Asked the coach number again.' | '10:20। फिर से डिब्बे का नंबर पूछा।'; '11:55. Changed seats again.' | '11:55। फिर सीट बदली।'; '1:40. Woke everyone for tea.' | '1:40। चाय के लिए सबको जगाया।'; '12:10. Repacked the bag again.' | '12:10। फिर से बैग बाँधा।'; '9:50. Finished all the snacks.' | '9:50। सारा नाश्ता ख़त्म किया।'; '10:00. Hummed the same tune again.' | '10:00। फिर वही धुन गुनगुनाई।'. Never on a decision whose task the note bears on (rule 20), as often on women as on men, lengths kept even within a decision (story_take.length_faults).
catchphrases: '9:40, aaspaas nahin.' | '9:40, आसपास नहीं।' | '9:40, not "around".' (the correction; his one catchphrase with a number in it, said whenever anyone gives a time with 'around' or 'about' in it; it replaced '9:40, not 9:45.', which held two figures; the owner may keep the old line as a marked exception, since the players' judge picked it)
'Nahin. Chart ban chuka hai.' | 'नहीं। चार्ट बन चुका है।' | 'No. The chart has been prepared.' (his final no: once the railway chart is out, nothing changes)

'Aakhri dibbe tak main yahin hoon.' | 'आख़िरी डिब्बे तक मैं यहीं हूँ।' | 'I'm here till the last coach goes.' (the platform vigil, the colony-gate boy grown up; the readers marked it true, and Mausa ji's goodbye now leaves before the train moves, so the vigil is Papa's alone)

'Pata nahin, Tinku. / Dal andaaze se banti hai.' | 'पता नहीं, टिंकू। / दाल अंदाज़े से बनती है।' | 'No idea, Tinku. / Dal is done when it tastes right.' (when anyone asks how long the dal takes: the one question the man of minutes answers 'Pata nahin', with the plain words every home cook uses; it replaces the maxim 'Dal ghadi dekhkar nahin banti. Swaad se banti hai.', which read as a made-up saying)
voice.exclamation: 'Kamaal hai.' | 'कमाल है।' | English mode 'Remarkable.' Said flat, with a full stop and never an exclamation mark, a whole sentence that keeps its verb. Two uses: real surprise at good news, which he then carries straight to Nani ('Kamaal hai. Mummy ji ko abhi batata hoon.'), and dry irony, in two bubbles ('Kal ki gaadi ka ticket aaj raat book kiya? / Kamaal hai.'; the power cut that came on time). No religious meaning: 'kamaal' is an everyday word for a wonder or a feat. His alone as an exclamation (Mama ji's 'Kamaal!' went in the matrix, 2.15). The English rendering avoids every mild oath (Gosh, Goodness, Good grief).
voice.sorry_thanks_love: SORRY: plain, said as a fact against himself: what he said, that it was wrong, and where the right answer is: 'Maine 9:40 kaha tha. / Galat nikla. / Board par 9:25 hai.' | 'मैंने 9:40 कहा था। / ग़लत निकला। / बोर्ड पर 9:25 है।' | 'I said 9:40. / I was wrong. / The board says 9:25.' No stamp and no trade word: 'Maine ... kaha tha. Galat nikla.' is how anyone owns a wrong fact ('9:40 mera time tha' was heard as 'it was my turn'). His own past with ने, so nothing marks you. It sorts apart by shape from Mausa ji's subjectless 'Galti hui.', Tinku's 'Sorry, meri galti.' and Mausi's tripled 'sorry'. THANKS, plain and warm: to Nani and the elders, never a register word; he praises the timing of what they did, the highest praise he knows: 'Mummy ji, chai bilkul time par thi.' | 'मम्मी जी, चाय बिल्कुल टाइम पर थी।' | 'Mummy ji, the tea was right on time.'; to you and Tinku, his own shape, the deed logged with no verb about the one he thanks, then the hand-over: 'Raat bhar, list ke saath. Darj hai. / Wo list ab tumhari hai.' | 'रात भर, लिस्ट के साथ। दर्ज है। / वो लिस्ट अब तुम्हारी है।' | 'All night, with the list. Noted. / That list is yours now.' (the matrix's '6:00, gate par. Noted.'; 'Bahut achha kiya' is Mummy's); to strangers and the TT, 'Thank you, ji.' | 'थैंक यू, जी।' | 'Thank you, ji.', the plain words people say, his by the whole sentences around it ('Ji, S4 mein solah hain.') and apart from Mami's 'Thank you, Bhaiya ji.' by the bare 'ji' ('Dhanyavaad' is announcement Hindi and reads Sanskritised in a person's mouth). WHEN HE IS THANKED: the everyday brush-off, then the next job: 'Roz ka kaam hai. / Ab wapsi ka ticket dekhta hoon.' | 'रोज़ का काम है। / अब वापसी का टिकट देखता हूँ।' | 'It's nothing, I do it every day. / Now for the return tickets.' (no 'Arre': Mummy's thanks reply opens on it, and the matrix gives 'arre' to Captain sahab). By text: 'No need.' and the next job. 'Darj hai.' is never his thanks for a kindness done for him (Nani's tea gets praise of its timing); it logs a fact, or a duty you or Tinku carried, and is 'Noted.' in his typing. LOVE: never said in words. A deed done ahead of time, said as a plain fact ('Didi, neeche ki berth aapki hai. / March mein hi ho gayi thi.'); 'Reached?' typed after any journey you make without him (his alone); standing on the platform till the last coach has gone ('Aakhri dibbe tak main yahin hoon.'), the colony-gate boy grown up; good news carried first to Nani. The nearest he comes to pride is the album's count: 'Four trains this year. / Nobody ever had to remind you.'
uses: Clock times in figures, to the minute (9:40, 6:35, 8:55); durations in the words people say (do ghante, das minute, baarah minute late)

address: YOU: तुम only in lines that show no gender (rule 66): commands ('सो लो', 'देखो'), 'who should' asks in the subjunctive ('टीटी के लिए टिकट कौन रखे?'), and lines where you are not the doer ('आज रात इंचार्ज तुम हो।', 'तुम्हें कभी याद नहीं दिलाना पड़ा।'). His thanks to you has no verb about you ('रात भर, लिस्ट के साथ। दर्ज है।'). One line falls outside the three shapes: the album's 'इस साल चार बार गाड़ी पकड़ी।', a past with ने where you are the doer and the verb agrees with गाड़ी. It marks no gender, but rule 66 does not name that shape, so the owner either adds 'a past with ने, where the verb agrees with the thing' as a fourth shape or has the native reader clear the line onto the build's cleared list; no wording change if the owner agrees. Possessives agree with the thing, not you ('बर्थ 36 तुम्हारी है', 'वो लिस्ट अब तुम्हारी है'). No name, no beta, no family word; he often opens with the time instead of 'you'. You answer 'Ji Papa' and आप, exactly as you speak to Mummy.

NANI: 'Mummy ji', आप and -इए ('Mummy ji, aap fikr mat kijiye.'). She is the one he talks to most and longest, because she lets him finish, and the one he carries good news to first. Readers confirm the word carries no community lean.

MUMMY: no name and no title; he opens with 'Suno,' or with the time ('Suno, nau baj gaye.'), the way Indian couples who never use first names talk; both say तुम, so the game's own couple carries no honorific-to-husband pattern.
MAMA JI: to his face तुम and no name (the household has no first names); to you he is 'Mama ji'. Mama ji calls him 'Jija ji'.
TINKU: 'Tinku', तुम.
MAUSI: 'Didi', आप. MAUSA JI: 'Bhai sahab', आप. Both wait on the Hindi-first and South Indian readers (rule 65) and the one family address table.
MASTERJI and CAPTAIN SAHAB: by their titles, आप.
MAMI: no name, आप (his formality, even to a younger in-law).
A CHILD: commands only ('Gilaas seedha karo.'), so no gender.
STRANGERS AND CARD PEOPLE: आप and 'ji', always; to the TT the count comes first ('Ji, S4 mein solah hain.' | 'जी, S4 में सोलह हैं।') and the thanks is 'Thank you, ji.'
samples: GIVING AN ORDER (the lead-in to the 1.08 ask: the headcount, then the goal of the moment; rule 37, both halves of the twin in this same three-bubble shape): 'There are sixteen of us. / We have only twelve berths. / The train leaves at 9:40.' | 'Hum solah log hain. / Berth sirf baarah hain. / Gaadi chhootne ka time 9:40 hai.' | 'हम सोलह लोग हैं। / बर्थ सिर्फ़ बारह हैं। / गाड़ी छूटने का समय 9:40 है।' (Kept. One figure a bubble. Count before the noun. The third bubble is a station announcement's own shape. No filler and no joke: it is the ask's lead-in.)

ANNOUNCING WHAT COMES NEXT (the train pulls in at the junction): 'The train is in. / S4 is at the front. / Bags go up next.' | 'Gaadi lag gayi hai. / S4 aage hai. / Ab bag upar jaayenge.' | 'गाड़ी लग गई है। / S4 आगे है। / अब बैग ऊपर जाएँगे।' (Kept: the readers marked his whole-sentence announcing true. 'Gaadi lagna' is railway Hindi with a Hindi verb.)

GIVING AN ORDER (the bay at night): 'Bags go under the berths. / Lights go out at ten. / The TT comes next.' | 'Bag berth ke neeche jaayenge. / Batti das baje bujhegi. / Ab TT aayega.' | 'बैग बर्थ के नीचे जाएँगे। / बत्ती दस बजे बुझेगी। / अब टीटी आएगा।' (Kept, with 'TT' for 'checker': a railwayman says TT. 'Batti das baje bujhegi.' rings true. The futures agree with bags, lights and the TT.)

MOVED (1.10: he lays the list on the lower berth, turned to you, taps it twice and takes his hand away): 'My battery has died. / Tonight, you are in charge.' | 'Meri battery khatam hai. / Aaj raat in-charge tum ho.' | 'मेरी बैटरी ख़त्म है। / आज रात इंचार्ज तुम हो।' (Kept word for word. You are not the doer of 'इंचार्ज तुम हो'.)

WORRYING (to Mummy on the platform; the refreshing is what kills his battery by ten): 'Listen, the train is twelve minutes late. / Now it is fourteen. / I will check the running status again.' | 'Suno, gaadi baarah minute late hai. / Ab chaudah ho gaye. / Running status phir dekhta hoon.' | 'सुनो, गाड़ी बारह मिनट लेट है। / अब चौदह हो गए। / मैं फिर देखता हूँ, गाड़ी कहाँ है।' ('Suno,' is how he opens to his wife, now that the filler belongs to everyone. Minutes are right here: running status shows minutes. Hindi mode says 'गाड़ी कहाँ है' for a low-English reader. Said to Mummy, not you.)

TEASING (Mama ji on the phone, who has booked the night before again; 'Kamaal hai.' as dry irony): 'You booked tomorrow's train tonight? / Remarkable.' | 'Kal ki gaadi ka ticket aaj raat book kiya? / Kamaal hai.' | 'कल की गाड़ी का टिकट आज रात बुक किया? / कमाल है।' ('Book kiya' is back: the counter's English verb with kar suits a railway clerk (cast-wide 2). टिकट masculine, his standard form.)

TEASING (Captain sahab, at the lane ground on cup day): 'Captain sahab, you said nine o'clock. / I have been here since 8:55.' | 'Captain sahab, aapne nau baje kaha tha. / Main 8:55 se khada hoon.' | 'कप्तान साहब, आपने नौ बजे कहा था। / मैं 8:55 से खड़ा हूँ।' (Kept. One figure a bubble.)

PRAISING YOU (the album, in its own panel, never Nani's): 'Four trains this year. / Nobody ever had to remind you.' | 'Is saal chaar baar gaadi pakdi. / Tumhein kabhi yaad nahin dilana pada.' | 'इस साल चार बार गाड़ी पकड़ी। / तुम्हें कभी याद नहीं दिलाना पड़ा।' (The Hindi note's fix: nobody says 'four trains happened'. पकड़ी agrees with गाड़ी and पड़ा is impersonal, so nothing marks you. No wording change if the owner agrees.)

COMFORTING (you, after the long halt): 'Nani's house is four hours away. / Sleep for three of them.' | 'Nani ke ghar tak chaar ghante hain. / Teen ghante so lo.' | 'नानी के घर तक चार घंटे हैं। / तीन घंटे सो लो।' (A command to you: no gender.)

LOSING HIS TEMPER (a two-minute stop, not the long halt; the time left, one word twice, the guard's flat hand lowered palm down; the English goes): 'We have two minutes here. / Nobody gets down. / Nobody.' | 'Yahan sirf do minute hain. / Koi neeche na utre. / Koi nahin.' | 'यहाँ सिर्फ़ दो मिनट हैं। / कोई नीचे न उतरे। / कोई नहीं।' (Kept.)

A JOKE AT HOME (calling everyone to dinner; deadpan, like the station loudspeaker; never while he asks, rule 37; rulebook Q5): 'Attention, please. / Dal has arrived on platform number one.' | 'Kripya dhyan dein. / Dal platform number ek par aa chuki hai.' | 'कृपया ध्यान दें। / दाल प्लेटफ़ॉर्म नंबर एक पर आ चुकी है।' (Kept word for word: the readers say every player will laugh. At most once a chapter.)

A JOKE ABOUT HIMSELF: 'I was born at 6:10. / Right on time, my mother said.' | 'Main 6:10 par paida hua. / Maa kehti thin, bilkul time par.' | 'मैं 6:10 पर पैदा हुआ। / माँ कहती थीं, बिल्कुल टाइम पर।' (About himself, at nobody's cost. 'Bilkul' added, as a mother would say it.)

THE DAL (Tinku asks how long it takes; the one thing he never times): 'No idea, Tinku. / Dal is done when it tastes right.' | 'Pata nahin, Tinku. / Dal andaaze se banti hai.' | 'पता नहीं, टिंकू। / दाल अंदाज़े से बनती है।' (The man of minutes says 'Pata nahin' once, and 'andaaze se' is the word every home cook uses. It replaces the coined maxim about the clock and taste. Said plainly, never praised by anyone.)

CARE, WITH MAUSI (the 1.13 lead-in, after her 'Lower berth for me, obviously'; the deed done ahead, said as a fact): 'Didi, the lower berth is yours. / It was booked in March.' | 'Didi, neeche ki berth aapki hai. / March mein hi ho gayi thi.' | 'दीदी, नीचे की बर्थ आपकी है। / मार्च में ही हो गई थी।' (Kept. No figure.)

THANKING NANI (dawn at her gate, the tea already poured on her step; the readers' fix): 'Mummy ji, the tea was right on time. / How did you know?' | 'Mummy ji, chai bilkul time par thi. / Aapko kaise pata tha?' | 'मम्मी जी, चाय बिल्कुल टाइम पर थी। / आपको कैसे पता था?' (His thanks praises the timing, the highest praise he has, with no minute stamp and no 'Darj hai'. The second bubble is the timekeeper finding that someone kept time for him; it asks, it never says what he feels.)

WITH NANI, THE FRICTION (she will never give him a time, 'Come when you come'): 'Mummy ji, of course we will come. / Just tell me a time.' | 'Mummy ji, aayenge zaroor. / Aap bas time bataiye.' | 'मम्मी जी, आएँगे ज़रूर। / आप बस टाइम बताइए।' ('Zaroor' and a mid-line 'bas', as anyone says them (cast-wide 1 and 8). आएँगे is the family's plural.)

COMFORTING NANI (on the phone the night before the train): 'Mummy ji, there is nothing to worry about. / Everyone will be at your gate at 6:00.' | 'Mummy ji, aap fikr mat kijiye. / Subah 6:00 baje sab aapke gate par honge.' | 'मम्मी जी, आप फ़िक्र मत कीजिए। / सुबह 6:00 बजे सब आपके गेट पर होंगे।' (His want, said as a time. 'Fikr' shared with the town (cast-wide 8); English avoids 'Don't worry', Mama ji's line. होंगे agrees with 'sab'.)

No figure in three bubbles. He states what happened and never says how it felt. Optional: the owner may keep the boy wordless only.)

His own past with ने, so nothing marks you. Plain owning, no trade word. Apart from Mausa ji's 'Galti hui.' and Tinku's 'Sorry, meri galti.')

Darj hai. / Wo list ab tumhari hai.' | 'रात भर, लिस्ट के साथ। दर्ज है। / वो लिस्ट अब तुम्हारी है।' (His own thanks shape, the deed logged, as the matrix's '6:00, gate par. Noted.', then the hand-over: from May he writes two copies. No verb about you, so nothing marks you; तुम्हारी agrees with लिस्ट. The old 'You did well.' went, since Mummy and Mausa ji already thank you in those words. Proposed: the owner places it.)

COUNTING THE COACHES IN (a whisper to himself before 1.08; Tamil in every mode; a Tamil reader signs it off): '...naalu, anju, aaru.' | '...naalu, anju, aaru.' | '...नालु, अंजु, आरु।' (Tamil script நாலு, அஞ்சு, ஆறு (four, five, six); the readers confirm it is correct spoken Tamil. The one marked exception to one figure a bubble: a whisper with no listener, once in chapter 1.)

habits: DEVICE: a plain black smartphone in a plain black case, in his trouser pocket, charged every night at ten; normal text size, since his eyes are good. On the night train it dies by 10 pm because he has refreshed the running status since noon (the worry line's reason, shown plainly, never as an age joke).

SCRIPT: English in Latin letters for everything he types, in all three language modes, because that is how he types and because 'Reached?' marks no gender while 'पहुँच गए?' does (rule 66). Devanagari versions are given in case the owner applies rule 65 to typed messages too.

SHAPE: he types the way he speaks. Each line is one short whole English sentence with its verb, a capital and a full stop, one fact to a line, in order. Times in figures with a colon (9:40, never 9.40 or 'nine forty').

NUMBERS: the speech budget carried onto the screen: at most one figure a line, and at least one line in three with none ('Charge your phone tonight.'). No prices, no scores, no numbered lists (no '1.', no ticks: Mami's), no ordinals.

FOUR FIXED LINES, his only ones with no full sentence: 'Reached?' (after any journey you make without him; it means 'I missed you'; his alone in the cast), 'Noted.' (his reply to a fact you send, a PNR, a platform, 'Reached'; never to a thank-you), 'No need.' (his reply to a thank-you, followed by the next job), 'Good morning.' (under the 6:35 picture).

FULL STOPS: the family reads them as cross; they are not. The method notes cite NPR's report of a study where a one-word text ending in a full stop read as less sincere. The story can use the misreading once, with Tinku explaining it.
SPEED: one slow forefinger, the phone in his other palm; he rereads before sending; no typos; autocorrect off.

REPLIES: within a minute, always, distinct from Mausa ji's 'Ok.' an hour later. Distinct too from Captain sahab's telegram style with no punctuation, Mummy's and Tinku's lowercase, and Mama ji's and Mausi's doubled marks.
EMOJI AND STICKERS: none. VOICE NOTES: never sends one (he says they have no time in them); he listens to Mausi's in full and replies in text.

FORWARDS: none, except one good-morning picture to the family at 6:35, after the walk with Captain sahab (a sunflower, or a glass of tea on a sunny windowsill; never a lotus, which is a party symbol, never a marigold, which leans to ritual, never a god or a famous face, rule 3) with 'Good morning.' under it. Never politics, never false news, never a forward he has not read. The readers marked the 6:35 flower true.
CALLS: anything that matters is a call, made at the minute he said he would call. Nani gets calls, never texts, and good news reaches her by a call before anyone else.
TIMING: 'Reached?' goes out within ten minutes of your train's due time, by the running status, not the timetable.
ON SCREEN: single messages only, as live text on a painted blank phone or a message card (rules 30 and 40); no app look, no 'forwarded' label, no group chat (owner, 23 Oct).
samples: TO YOU, MARCH, BOOKING DAY: 'The booking is done. / We have 12 berths. / They are on my railway pass and 2 PNRs.' then, a month later, on its own: 'Mausi has added 4 names. / No berths are left.' | Devanagari if wanted: 'बुकिंग हो गई। / हमारे पास 12 बर्थ हैं। / मेरे रेलवे पास और 2 PNR पर हैं।' then 'मौसी ने 4 नाम और जोड़े। / अब कोई बर्थ नहीं बची।' (who is on the pass is never said, rule 8; 'railway pass' because 'मेरे पास' alone also means 'with me')

TO YOU, THE NIGHT BEFORE: 'We are in coach S4. / Berth 36 is yours, a lower berth. / The train comes on platform 3. / It leaves at 9:40. / Carry your own water bottle. / Charge your phone tonight.' | Devanagari if wanted: 'हम कोच S4 में हैं। / बर्थ 36 तुम्हारी है, नीचे की। / गाड़ी प्लेटफ़ॉर्म 3 पर आती है। / 9:40 पर छूटती है। / पानी की बोतल अपनी रखना। / आज रात बैटरी पूरी रखना।' (four lines with one figure, two with none; 36 is a real lower berth in the run 33 to 44, so Mausi keeps 33; the last line is the irony nobody remarks on: by ten that night his own phone is dead)
TO YOU, AFTER ANY JOURNEY WITHOUT HIM: 'Reached?' (one word, in English letters in every mode; the readers marked it true)
TO YOU, AFTER THE WARD NIGHT, 10:02 AM: 'Nani reached home at 10:00. / Sleep now.' | 'नानी 10:00 बजे घर पहुँच गईं। / अब सो लो।'
TO YOU, A WEEKDAY, WHEN YOU WILL BE HOME LATE (his one message with no number and nothing to arrange; the readers marked it true): 'The dal is on the stove.' | 'दाल गैस पर है।'
TO YOU, REPLYING TO A FACT YOU SENT (a PNR, a platform, 'Reached'): 'Noted.' | 'दर्ज है।' (the readers' 'perfect': the register word as a reply to a fact, never as thanks)
TO YOU, WHEN YOU THANK HIM BY TEXT: 'No need. / Your return ticket is booked.' | Devanagari if wanted: 'कोई ज़रूरत नहीं। / वापसी का टिकट बुक है।' (the brush-off, then the next job, as he speaks)

TO MAMI, DECEMBER: 'The guest train times are below. / The morning train is at 6:10. / The night train is at 9:40. / Both are confirmed. / I will be at the station for both.' | Devanagari if wanted: 'मेहमानों की गाड़ियों का समय नीचे है। / सुबह की गाड़ी 6:10 पर है। / रात की गाड़ी 9:40 पर है। / दोनों कन्फ़र्म हैं। / दोनों बार मैं स्टेशन पर रहूँगा।' (the Hindi note's fix for 'दोनों पर मैं रहूँगा'; रहूँगा is Papa's own future; she answers with her own list, and his name heads her item 1 'Papa: trains', in her shape, not his)

THE FAMILY, EVERY MORNING (mentioned, never shown as a group; if a message is ever shown it is one message card with no group name, app look or 'forwarded' label): a picture of a sunflower at 6:35, then 'Good morning.'

look.build: Tall band, with Mami and Captain sahab, and the tallest of the three (the comics review's four bands replace the ten ranks, which the painter cannot keep). The one gap that must show, because they share chapter 1 and chapter 3: a head taller than Mummy. Beside Mausa ji (short band) on the ward chairs the gap shows even seated. Narrow shoulders, a long neck, long arms and long hands. He stands clearly tipped forward from the ankles, like a man walking into a wind, even when still. In the sleeper carriage he ducks his head under the upper berth, which says tall at any camera angle. Never broad, never a belly.
look.face: One head feature exaggerated so it holds when the face drifts: big ears that stick out plainly from a narrow head, his alone in the cast (Masterji's and Mausa ji's files should drop 'ears that stand out a little', the comics review). In black at phone size his head is a narrow oval with two handles. Then, for close-ups only: a long narrow face with hollow cheeks and a long straight nose; thin eyebrows (he lacks the thick straight brows of Nani's line, as the three who married in do), with no crease or line between them (a vertical line there can be painted as a tilak, the rules review); clean-shaven, like Masterji and Captain sahab, so the shave is not his anchor; thin lips pressed straight; fine lines at the outer corners of the eyes, which carry his age. He should read 56, not 40 and not 70 (painted ages read young, the old Dadi lesson).
look.skin: Dark brown, even, with South Asian features; the same dark brown as Tinku, a shade darker than Mummy's warm medium brown. Every look line opens with the tested phrase 'South Asian features and warm brown skin' and adds the depth after it ('a deep dark brown'), since only that phrase is tested against whitening (flux-portrait-biases, the rules review). Every pick is compared with his master's skin swatch, above all in the present day and Rukavat, whose soft styles whiten skin, and under Lugdi's and Jadugar's lamps, which recolour it.
look.hair: Short black hair parted on his left and combed down smooth to the head, grey at the sides above the ears, a hairline a little high at the temples. No tuft, quiff or knot at the crown: a crown tuft can be painted as a shikha, a religious marker (rule 3). The big ears do the work a hairstyle would.
look.glasses_jewellery: None at all: no spectacles (his eyes are good; he reads the platform clock from the far end of the junction), no wristwatch (the watch is Mummy's anchor; he trusts the phone's railway time and the nearest clock; Nani's file should drop its tease about his watch, the India review), no ring, no chain, no thread. A plain black belt is his only fitting.
outfits: EVERYDAY (the signature, in every look): a pale sky-blue short-sleeved cotton shirt with broad navy vertical stripes, each about a thumb wide and five across his front, two buttons open at the collar, tucked into plain charcoal-grey trousers with a plain black belt; brown leather sandals. Nothing in the shirt pocket.
THE NIGHT TRAIN, MAY: the same shirt and trousers; the striped shirt never comes off.

HOME (rarely seen): the same striped shirt, untucked, over loose white cotton drawstring trousers; plain grey rubber slippers. The pyjama's definition lives here, in his look, not in the shared glossary.

WINTER (January opening, December): his one good jacket, a plain charcoal wool jacket with narrow lapels and two buttons, stitched by Masterji and let out every year, worn open over the striped shirt so the stripes run down his front; a plain grey wool scarf (never 'muffler' in a prompt); black slip-on leather shoes with grey socks. No sleeveless V-neck sweater: Mausa ji and Masterji wear one, and a trait gets one owner (the comics review).
MONSOON (July): no rain jacket and never an umbrella (the umbrella is Mama ji's). He walks as he always does and gets wet to the shoulders; the folder is plastic and the page inside stays dry.

OCCASION (the wedding week): a new full-sleeved shirt in finer cotton with the same broad navy stripes on the same pale sky blue, tucked, the good charcoal jacket open over it, polished black leather shoes: the costume kept at the signature scale, as comics keep it. Never a kurta under a sleeveless stand-up collar jacket (Mama ji's cut), never the word 'Nehru' in a prompt (a name is painted as lettering, and a famous person is out under rule 3), no safa, no wedding turban.
look.colour_key: Key: pale sky blue with broad navy vertical stripes over charcoal grey; value LIGHT TOP WITH DARK STRIPES OVER DARK TROUSERS; pattern BROAD VERTICAL STRIPES, about a thumb wide and five across his front, so they still read when he is about 200 screen pixels tall (the comics review: fine stripes print as a flat tint). His folder carries the sky blue too. Nobody else wears sky blue or a vertical stripe, and nobody else's top is striped in Station. Per look (PROVISIONAL: the chapter JSON look lines and the code's STYLE strings disagree, and every colour key waits on one string per look; the value stack and the stripes hold under either): NOW: pale sky blue, navy stripes, charcoal. LUGDI (ch1, his chapter): the pale shirt catches the marigold lamp on its lit side, the stripes stay deep indigo, the trousers deep indigo; which shape is brightest in the carriage is settled on the Lugdi strip, since Mummy's file claims it too. STATION (ch3, two inks): cream shirt with broad blue-black stripes, solid blue-black trousers, a dark belt line; Masterji's plain light shirt no longer matches it, but they still stay out of one panel. RUKAVAT (ch2): cream shirt with broad dark teak-brown stripes, dark teak-brown trousers (Nani is the faded teal there and Mausa ji a mid teak block; he stays the light striped figure). CRICKET (ch4): chalk-white shirt with broad dark green stripes, dark green-grey trousers, so the stripes do not sink into the outfield; never cherry red (Captain sahab's alone). JADUGAR (ch5): the shirt lit cream by the tent lamps with indigo-black stripes, the good jacket charcoal, lamp-lit along its edges and worn open, so the shirt is a bright vertical band against the indigo night; never old gold or brown, which are Mama ji's check there.
look.prop: THE TRAVEL LIST. Glossary row (new, in Saal Bhar's own glossary section, keys 'travel list' and 'blue folder'): 'The travel list is one plain blank page with no lines or writing, folded once lengthwise, inside a long narrow matte pale-blue plastic folder with a darker blue edge strip, as long as a forearm and as wide as a hand.' He carries it down at his side in one hand, swinging in step as he walks; it is never held flat to his chest (that rectangle is Mami's clipboard, and the two of them share chapter 5 and the album). Done: two taps on it with his forefinger. Never 'sleeve', 'sheet', 'ruled' or 'clear' in a prompt: his shirt shares 'sleeve', 'sheet' has no glossary row and stops paint(), ruled lines invite painted writing (rule 30), and clear plastic paints as nothing or as a mirror under one hard lamp. Its story: a fresh one for every trip since his first job at 19; the old ones live in a cardboard file box under the bed; he never reads it in public because he knows it by heart. From May he buys folders in pairs: his, and one he leaves where you will find it (the year's change). Painted from one reference picture (paint-refs), always blank (rule 30); 1.11 and 1.38 show the page unfolded, its fold down the middle, with the target lines as live text. SECOND OBJECT: a plain black phone in a plain black case, screen painted dark and blank, in his other hand or his trouser pocket. Scene objects, never in the fixed look: the steel cup of chai at Nani's gate, the two cloth cash pouches (laid on the folder in 1.22, never in his hands with it), the steel water bottle at the lane cup, Tinku's small folded blank ticket.
look.silhouette: The tallest vertical in any panel, tipped clearly forward like a man walking into a wind, a narrow head with two ears standing out like handles, and a short pale-blue baton (the folder) hanging at his side. In black at phone size: a tall leaning line with two knobs at the head and a stick at the hip. In two inks: a light top in broad dark stripes over dark trousers, one belt line. Base shape: the line, shared with Mami (a woman, so shapes are not sorted by gender), but told apart at a glance: she is plumb with a rectangle flat to her chest and a strap across her; he leans, has the ears, and carries his paper at his side.
look.shoes: Brown leather sandals with a back strap, polished, no socks (everyday, and on the train, so he can step down fast); plain grey rubber slippers at home; black slip-on leather shoes with grey socks in winter, and polished at the wedding. No logos on any of them.

posture.stance: Straight back, feet close together (Mummy's are planted apart), the whole body tipped clearly forward from the ankles, like a man walking into a wind, even standing still. The folder hangs in one hand at his side; the other hand hangs free or holds the phone low. Head up, chin a little lifted, eyes on the nearest clock or the far end of the platform. Under an upper berth he ducks his head and keeps his back straight. (Stance lives in the scene words, never in the fixed look: the rules review.)
posture.sitting: Sits angled towards the nearest door, on the aisle end of a berth or the end of a row of chairs, one foot already pointing at the door, back straight, the folder across his knees: always ready to stand for a train. Not 'the front edge of the seat', which eight files claim. He sits back only when tired (see expressions). Never forearms on knees (Mausa ji's shape).
posture.walk: Long, quick strides, a step ahead of everyone, upper body leaning forward, the folder swinging at his side in step; he turns his head back to check the group without breaking stride, and stops dead at the exact door or the exact coach. He never runs: he is never late enough to need to.
gestures: LOOKS UP FOR A CLOCK: entering any place, his chin lifts and his eyes find the wall or platform clock before he greets anyone; then the phone, then the clock again when he is worried.

TWO TAPS ON THE FOLDER: his forefinger taps it twice when a thing is done; it is his 'It's confirmed.' without words, and at 1.10 it is how he gives you the list. His alone in the cast (Mausa ji's and Tinku's double taps should go, the comics review).

THE GUARD'S 'STEADY': a hand raised flat at chest height, palm down, lowered slowly; his father's signal, it means 'wait, nobody move'. It is his alarm and anger tell, used at the carriage door and at the two-minute halt while he gives the minutes left.

THE GUARD'S WAVE: he lifts an open hand to the last van of every goods train that goes by, as he did to his father's, and to Mummy's shutter at nine on Saturdays; he does not know he does it. His one habit with no number in it.
COUNTS UNDER HIS BREATH: lips moving, eyes on the coaches, as a train comes in; in Tamil (proposal).
IDLE HANDS: his thumb runs along the folder's darker edge strip, or rests on the phone in his pocket.
expressions: NEUTRAL: upright, the clear forward lean, mouth a straight line, eyes on the nearest clock, the folder at his side.
PLEASED: one short nod and two taps on the folder; only one corner of his mouth lifts; he looks at the clock, not at the person he is pleased with.
WORRIED: shoulders lift a little, his eyes narrow at the clock, the lean goes further forward; phone, clock, phone again.
CROSS: very still and very upright, the 'steady' hand raised, voice dropped to the minutes left, jaw set; he holds the look and does not glance at any clock.
LAUGHING: silent; his shoulders shake, he looks down and to the side, a hand over his mouth for a second. Only Tinku gets this.
TIRED: the one time his back touches a seat back: he sits back, head tipped against the wall or berth, eyes shut, the folder lying on his chest.
MOVED: he looks up at the clock and keeps looking, swallows, then lays the folder down without a word, his face in the frame. He never holds anything out towards the viewer (bible section 4).

across_looks: STRIP ANCHORS (must survive in all five looks and the present day at phone size; full-figure picks are checked against these only, strongest first): (1) the tallest figure in the panel, with a clear forward lean; (2) a narrow head with two big ears sticking out; (3) a light shirt in broad dark vertical stripes, tucked, one belt line, dark trousers; (4) the long pale-blue folder in a hand at his side; (5) short black hair grey at the sides, clean-shaven. CLOSE-UP DETAILS (inserts and the face chip only): the hollow cheeks, the long nose, the eye lines, the left parting, the sandals' back strap, the depth of his skin against his master swatch. The face itself is the least stable part and is carried only by the reference picture; the drift sheet shows hair, spectacles and patterns surviving style changes while face shape, apparent age and skin tone drift. Which hand holds the folder is a preference to check, never what tells him from anyone: the painter does not reliably keep left and right, and layouts get mirrored.

LUGDI (ch1, his chapter, about 8 to 10 panels): painted face-on from his model sheet under owner answer 6, so the chapter look line's 'Papa is only ever seen from behind' and rule 33 need rewriting. His panels use a level camera at eye height: STYLE['lugdi'] ends in 'dramatic angle', which flattens relative height and hides the lean, and a steep angle also gives the viewer a height, which the player's file bans. When the upper berth is in frame he ducks under it. The 1970s pulp style pulls clothes and hair back to its era (wide collars, flared trousers, long sideburns, a safari suit): the fixed look's present-day words and the reference picture hold him in today's clothes.

RUKAVAT (ch2, silent, on the hospital corridor chairs beside Mausa ji): 1980s family-magazine gouache; the tested skin phrase goes into the prompt, since the panel style lacks the skin words portraits.py gained on 22 Oct. The pair: a tall striped line against a short block, flat black-and-grey hair with big ears against a white brush cut and beard.

STATION (ch3, silent, small but face-on in the parcel-office doorway): colour is gone, so the broad stripes, the height and the lean carry him; Masterji's plain light shirt no longer shares his look, but they still stay out of one panel.

CRICKET (ch4, silent, the boundary at 8:55): chalk-white shirt with broad dark green stripes; STYLE['cricket'] also ends in 'dramatic angle', so the level camera again; the Cricket portrait template washes faces out in halftone, so his height, ears and stripes carry him.

JADUGAR (ch5, silent, alone under the platform clock in the dark and early light): the good jacket open over the lit striped shirt; men got forehead dots in the playing-card style, so his forehead gets the close-up check here first. No moustache and no umbrella, so he never reads as the magician.

PRESENT DAY (opening 1.03 and 1.04, the face chip on every bubble and card note, the album): the master sheet. STYLE['now'] bakes in 'cool rainy-evening blues', which fights a January morning; the present-day entry needs its weather taken out before his master is painted.
cast.painter_prompt: MASTER TIER (used only to paint his master sheet, word for word each time, as LOOKS does; body and clothes only, no pose, no prop): the lanky man, a tall, thin 56-year-old Indian man with South Asian features and warm brown skin, a deep dark brown, a long narrow face with hollow cheeks and a long straight nose, big ears that stick out plainly from the sides of his head, thin eyebrows, fine lines at the outer corners of his eyes, clean-shaven, short black hair parted on his left and combed down smooth, grey at the sides above the ears, a long neck, in present-day clothes: a pale sky-blue short-sleeved cotton shirt with broad navy vertical stripes, five across his front, tucked into plain charcoal-grey trousers with a plain black belt, and brown leather sandals. PANEL TIER (30 words, in every panel where his reference picture is supplied, so two people's words stay short and do not swap; the rules review asks for a two-person test first): the lanky man: tall, big ears sticking out, clean-shaven, black hair with grey sides, pale blue shirt with broad navy stripes, charcoal trousers, South Asian features and warm brown skin. SCENE WORDS (never in the fixed look; count his hands in every pick): 'the lanky man is standing with a clear forward lean, like a man walking into a wind'; 'in one hand, down at his side, a long narrow matte pale-blue plastic folder with a darker blue edge, a plain blank page with no lines folded inside it'; the master is painted holding the folder, so he and his prop take one reference slot. In the sleeper carriage, with the upper berth in frame: 'he ducks his head under the upper berth'. CAMERA (his panels in Lugdi and Cricket, whose style strings end in 'dramatic angle'): 'seen at eye level from a level camera'; untested whether these words win over the style string, so the code may need a people-panel variant of the two styles. PER-LOOK INK WORDS appended after the look (provisional until one look string per look is settled): Lugdi 'his pale shirt lit marigold by the lamp, its broad stripes deep indigo, his trousers deep indigo'; Station 'his shirt cream with broad blue-black vertical stripes, his trousers solid blue-black'; Rukavat 'his shirt cream with broad dark teak-brown stripes, his trousers dark teak brown'; Cricket 'his shirt chalk white with broad dark green vertical stripes, his trousers dark green-grey'; Jadugar 'his shirt lit cream by the lamps, its broad stripes indigo-black, a plain charcoal jacket with narrow lapels worn open over it'. Then the look's STYLE string and STORY_NO. WORDS KEPT OUT of every description of him, each because it fires an old glossary row, stops paint() or draws the wrong thing (probe run on this text: no old row fires and no need-list word is left): his name, father, clerk, sleeve, sheet, ruled, clear, flat, stands, cover, pass and passes, watch, bench, seat, floor, flask, coach (write 'sleeper carriage', since 'the coach' is Shirin's ROLE), Nehru, muffler.
painter_avoid: Any forehead mark: a dot, a tilak, lines of ash; and any crease or line between his brows, which can be painted as a tilak (men got dots in the playing-card style; check his forehead close up in every panel, Jadugar first)
A tuft, quiff or knot of hair at the crown (it can read as a shikha, a religious marker, rule 3)
A thread at the collar, wrist or ankle; any steel bangle (it reads as a kara); a ring with a stone; a chain or pendant
Any cap, turban or head covering, including a wedding safa
A moustache, beard or stubble: his look is clean-shaven, and painted Indian men often carry a moustache in our library; untested whether klein adds one unasked, so the audit counts it
Spectacles of any kind, and a wristwatch (the watch is Mummy's alone; check it never jumps to his wrist when they share a panel)
Lightened skin, above all in the present-day and Rukavat soft styles and under Lugdi's and Jadugar's lamps; compare every panel with the master's skin swatch

Logos, letters or numbers anywhere: on the shirt, the folder, the page inside it, the phone screen, the ticket; no railway badge, name plate or uniform (badges carry letters); no ruled lines on the page
Fine pinstripes or a flat blue tint where the five broad stripes should be; check the stripes survive in every pick
Shine or reflections on the folder (it is matte), and a clear or see-through folder
Period drift from the look's era: wide 1970s collars, flared trousers, long sideburns, a safari suit, a 1980s moustache
A steep high or low camera in his panels (it flattens his height and hides the lean)
A kurta with a sleeveless stand-up collar jacket (Mama ji's cut), and a sleeveless V-neck sweater (Mausa ji's and Masterji's)
Mama ji's umbrella, Tinku's scorebook, Mami's clipboard or Mummy's key ring in his hands
The folder held flat against his chest (Mami's shape), a third hand, or the folder painted as part of his shirt; count his hands in every pick
A broad build, a belly, a rounded back (Masterji's curve) or forearms on his knees (Mausa ji's shape); folded hands, touching feet, or the head bobble as caricature
A hand reaching out of the panel towards the viewer, with or without his face in the frame (bible section 4: household hands never reach towards you; rule 7)
model_sheet: 0. FIRST, BEFORE ANY SINGLE SHEET (the comics review's order of work): the line-up of all ten as black shapes at phone width in the four height bands, and one strip per look with all ten as simple flat figures in that look's inks; then the trait-table dedupe; the owner approves the pictured line-up before any individual sheet. Papa's checks there: the tallest in the line-up, a head over Mummy, the lean visible, the two-eared head readable in black, his striped light top unlike any other top in Station and Cricket.

1. PREREQUISITES IN THE CODE (rules review, code-verified): cutscenes.py needs a per-panel seed bump and an eye-confirmed dot paint-out before any face-on panel (both exist only in portraits.py today); looks keyed by look, not by year; a refusal when a panel carries more than four reference pictures; Saal Bhar's own glossary section with the 'travel list' row; and a people-panel variant of the Lugdi and Cricket styles without 'dramatic angle'.

2. MASTER TURNAROUND, present day, full figure, standing, the folder in a hand at his side (painted into the master, so he and his prop take one reference slot): front; three-quarter; profile (the lean, the ears, the folder's length); back (the left parting, the grey sides, the stripes, the belt line, the folder's edge at his hip). Three seeds each (7100, 7203, 7319), picked by eye against the strip anchors only, then a forehead and skin close-up, a hand count, a stripe check and a stray-letter check. Whether klein can paint a multi-view sheet in one picture is untested; if not, one view per picture.

3. TWO-PERSON TEST before more panels are written: Papa with Mausi (chapter 1's pair) in the panel tier, recording the swap rate per anchor (ears, stripes, hoops, hair colour); the rules review's Nani with Mausa ji test runs alongside.

4. LINE-UP CHECKS FOR HIS PAIRS: beside Mummy (a head taller; line against square), Mausi (line against round; chapter 1), Mausa ji (line against block, seated; the ward chairs), Mami (lean against plumb, folder at the side against rectangle at the chest; chapter 5 and the album), Tinku (his dark brown skin beside hers).

5. POSES: walking a stride ahead, head turned up to a clock, the folder swinging; sitting angled to the door on the aisle end of a berth, the folder across his knees; ducking under an upper berth; laying the folder on a berth turned to the viewer and tapping it twice, face in frame (1.10); the guard's 'steady', palm down; lifting a hand to a passing van at night (the 2:10 halt); standing in a carriage doorway; the morning walk beside Captain sahab; asleep sitting back, the folder on his chest (tired).
6. EXPRESSIONS, head and shoulders, each with a small full-body thumbnail because faces drift: neutral, pleased, worried, cross, laughing, tired, moved, as written in posture.

7. OUTFIT VARIANTS in one standing pose: home (shirt untucked over drawstring trousers, rubber slippers); winter (the good charcoal jacket open over the striped shirt, grey wool scarf); wedding (the finer full-sleeved striped shirt, the good jacket open, polished shoes).

8. PROPS SHEET (its own reference pictures, painted before any panel; glossary rows first): the folder from straight above, three-quarter and edge-on; the page unfolded with its fold down the middle (1.11, 1.38); two folders side by side (the year's change); the plain black phone face up (dark blank screen) and face down; the steel cup of chai; the steel water bottle; the small folded blank ticket.

9. PER-LOOK REFERENCES, made from the picked master with the edit model (Flux2KleinEdit), never asking the painter to change style and keep a face in one step: LUGDI x4 (front, back, seated at a berth, laying the folder down; his chapter); RUKAVAT, STATION, CRICKET, JADUGAR x1 each (three-quarter, standing, for the silent presences); the present-day master doubles as the face chip. About eight references. A panel carries at most two people from references plus a place (klein takes four reference pictures).

10. FAR SPEC (for when he is small and no reference slot is free, painted from words): 'a tall thin figure leaning forward, a light shirt in broad dark stripes over dark trousers, a short pale-blue folder at his side'; checked only for the silhouette and the two value blocks.

11. FACE CHIP: a 512 x 512 head-and-shoulders portrait from the master, which needs a present-day template in portraits.py (WORLDS has none today); close-up check of forehead, skin, ears and age before it is used on any bubble or card note.

All painting through ~/.claude/heavy-queue/heavyq only, one heavy job on the Mac at a time, and only after this workflow and any browser checks have stopped (mac-memory-limit); the owner approves the pictured parts sheet before any panel is painted.
best_scenes: 9:30 PM, THE JUNCTION (1.08): the train comes in; his lips count the coaches in Tamil and he is already standing where S4 will stop, the folder at his side. 'Sixteen of us have twelve berths. 9:40, not 9:45.'

THE BERTH EXCHANGE (1.13, the players' judge asked for the household to talk to each other): Mausi, 'Lower berth for me, obviously.' Papa, 'Didi, lower berth 33 is already yours.' Then the ask for the other two.

THE DEAD PHONE (proposed 1.10, before D2): the man of time without the time. Mummy, silent, lifts her wrist and shows him her father's watch; he lays the folder on the lower berth, turned to you, taps it twice and takes his hand away, face in frame: 'My battery has died. Tonight, you are in charge.' The year turns here.

THE LONG HALT, 2:10 AM (1.25 and after D5; wordless): as the train starts again he stands in the carriage doorway and lifts a hand to the red lamp of a goods train's last van going the other way, then keeps looking down the dark line a beat longer than he needs. The colony-gate boy, on the page, without a word: the panel that keeps him from being the stock railway dad.
DAWN AT NANI'S GATE (1.39): his tea already poured on the step before he reaches it; Nani knew his arrival to the minute. The one time someone else keeps time for him.
THE WARD CHAIRS (ch2, silent): Papa and Mausa ji side by side through the night, two men who married in, not one word, face-on: a two-person panel the strip has no people in today.
SATURDAY 9:00 (ch3, silent, in the outcome painting): small but face-on across the platform, he looks up at the clock and lifts a hand as the shutter goes up, the guard's wave given to Mummy.
8:55 AT THE LANE GROUND (ch4, silent): first there with the water bottle; Captain sahab says nine; Tinku scores him, and he laughs, silently.
BEFORE THE GUEST TRAINS (ch5, silent): alone under the platform clock in the dark, face-on, no guests in the frame; then his own two-person beat, giving Tinku the ticket for the course's first day.
THE ALBUM (its own panel, never Nani's): 'Four trains this year. Nobody had to remind you once.', the nearest he comes to saying he is proud of you, still in numbers.
never_does: Says 'I missed you', 'I'm proud of you' or 'sorry' in words; he books, times or lays something down instead
Is late, runs for a train, says 'hurry', or books anything the night before
Raises his voice; when cross he goes quieter and counts down the minutes left, with the guard's 'steady' hand
Sends a voice note, a sticker, a forward he has not read, politics or false news

Splits the family at night or sends anyone alone through a train after lights out; so the draft's quiet-coach decision (1.20) goes against him, and the players' and chapter 1 checks' fix ('One spare pillow. Who gets it?', inside the lit bay) fits him
Doubts a report of harassment, of being followed or of a dowry demand, or calls one a misunderstanding (rule 22); he never comments on a card's hard fact at all
Sits on a card, or is the comic one while he asks (rule 37); his dry jokes are about himself or clocks, never at anyone's cost
Calls you beta or any gendered word, uses a Hindi form that marks your gender, or says whether you travel on his pass (rules 8 and 66)
Holds anything out towards you, even with his face in the frame (bible section 4)
Gives a rule for choosing in his ask, names a card person, or uses a card note's words in a bubble (rules 36 and 37)
Uses a temperament word about a person ('shy', 'moody'); his notes log what someone did, against the minute
Reads his list aloud in public, lets the page get wet, or holds the folder flat to his chest
Carries an umbrella, wears a watch or spectacles, grows a moustache, or wears a kurta with a sleeveless jacket
Times the dal: it is the one thing he does by taste
Talks money or haggles (prices are Mummy's; he times)
Is made a joke for his phone habits or his age (the 'couple who cannot work technology' cliché the realism notes warn against)

cast.name: Mama ji (मामा जी), 47
cast.role: Household member, round. Nani's youngest child and only son; Mummy's younger brother; Mami's husband; the bride's father. Chapter 5's asker: all eight wedding-week decisions, in the Jadugar look. Heard in the present-day opening (1.03, 1.04); painted, without a line, in the album. In chapter 2 he does not speak, because each household member speaks in one chapter until rulebook Q11 is answered (rule 10): Nani's phone rings at 2.24 ('Mama ji's call. Worried, as always.'), and if the owner allows it a wordless split panel paints him, so he is a person there and not only a ringing phone. First-use label: 'Mama ji, Mummy's brother' | 'मामा जी, मम्मी के भाई' (rule 65: 'Mama' can read as 'mother' in English). Never on a card (rule 10). Never the comic one (rule 37). Painter role word: 'the broad-chested man'. It names his build only, so it summons no place, trade, title or relation: 'the city uncle' would grow a skyline in Nani's lane (rules review), 'uncle' is a relation and may add a child (comics review), 'the round uncle' invites the pot-belly gag, and 'the bride's father' names a bride (ROLE already gives the old take's Rani 'the bride').
