cast.essence: The youngest, who left Nani's town for the city at twenty and has loved his family by phone ever since. He sells water pumps to builders, and his real stock is his phone book: every tent man, cook and bandmaster he has ever met, known by first name and by how their mothers are. Generous with money, with numbers and with feeling; sure that more is safer; worried about everyone but himself. In five words: the worrier who rings first. He is one of the two elders who say feelings out loud (Mausi says her hurt; he says his love: 'Amma, I missed you'), and he hugs everyone he can reach. His contradiction: he worries about everything, but plans nothing. He makes every number bigger and leaves the how to others, because doing the how would mean being there. The other half of it is his gift: nobody plans less, and nobody else can make the whole district turn up.
cast.backstory: Born in 1979 in Nani's town, the youngest of three. His sisters half raised him while Nani ran the grocery in her front room; Mausi still calls him 'Munna', and Nani and Mummy call him 'Chhote'. He was the one expected to take the grocery on. Instead, in the summer of 1999, the year Mummy opened her shop, he took the night train to the city for a sales interview, in a shirt Masterji stitched free 'for luck'. He reached the city in the first monsoon without an umbrella and was soaked through at the interview. He got the job anyway, still says it was the shirt, bought a big black umbrella that evening, and has carried one like it every day since, rain or not. This one is the third. Nani ran the grocery alone until 2016. He has never said he minds; he sends money to everyone instead. In 2000 he disputed a friend's bill line by line at a city hospital's billing counter; the young woman behind it made him read it line by line, and he came back the next day with the right change and a box of sweets (Mami's file). They married in 2001 at Nani's house, in Nani's lane, and Mami's family travelled a night by train to a town they had never seen to fill it. He has owed them a loud welcome ever since. Today he is area sales manager for a water-pump dealer, out at building sites by auto from nine till dark, phone at his ear. He lives with Mami, who manages a hospital billing desk, and their daughter, 24, in a two-bedroom flat high up in a city housing society whose lift breaks every monsoon. He rings Nani at eight every morning before his first site; she says 'बस, सब ठीक' and hangs up first (Nani's file). He sends Mummy stock leads, and money she never spends: it sits in its own account (Mummy's file). He books his train the night before and rings Papa to fix it; Papa fixes it, says nothing, and meets the train himself at 5 am (Papa's file). He forwards every weather warning for Nani's district. His daughter works in the city, chose her own match, and marries in December. She is never drawn, named or put on a card, and her wedding carries no talk of gifts to anyone, because the household is never the one doing the wrong (rule 27). Chapter 5's 'talk of a dowry' belongs only to the relatives' own past, on their cards. In June, after Nani's fall, he moved the wedding from a city hall to Nani's house, as his own had been, and lost the hall's advance. Mami mentions the advance; he never does.
cast.want_fear_contradiction: WANT THIS YEAR: his daughter married from Nani's house, with every one of them there and the lane too, more people than anyone expects. In his own words to Mami: 'This time Amma doesn't catch a train.' WANT FROM YOU: to hear 'Sorted, Mama ji' so he can stop worrying. You are his eyes in Nani's town, the one he rings instead of his sister. FEAR: that Nani grew old while he was on the phone in the city; that he is the son who was not there. In May he is not there. He is on a waitlisted ticket, booked the night before, when she slips on her back step, and he reaches her the day after she is home. CONTRADICTION ('X, but Y'): he worries about everything, but plans nothing. It shows the same way every time: a bigger number, then the job handed to someone else ('Ek kaam karo...'). Under it, the competence that keeps this from being 'the man who has to be managed' (India review): he cannot plan, but he can make anyone come. The cook and the tent come in December's busiest week because he rang them by name, and his bigger number is right once: the lane comes for Nani's cake and fills the ten extra chairs he had stacked by the gate. Mami is right about the plates; he is right about the people. Under that: the man who is never still stands still only twice in the year, with Nani's palm on his head at her gate and on the gate step at midnight beside Mausa ji. MEMORABLE TEST (method notes, section 4): you can draw him in five strokes (a round body, a raised right elbow, the hanging umbrella line, the hair wave, the moustache bar). His quoted line is '60? 70 kar do!' | 'Sixty? Make it seventy!'. His friction is with Mami (they bicker in public) and his tenderness is with Mami (they decide in private, and he is the only person allowed to write on her list). He changes across the year from phone to presence, and the silhouette shows it: the same raised right arm holds the phone at his ear in January and May and beckons people in at Nani's gate in December. At 5.27 he hangs the umbrella on Nani's gate. Players who would say 'I know this person': Shruti (27, grew up in Mysuru, lives in Bengaluru: her uncle who left for the metro, or herself in twenty years) and Ravi (26, runs his family's phone shop in Indore: the uncle in the city who rings the shop ten times a day, and who also knows every supplier by name). Round.
relationships: NANI (he says 'Amma' and आप; she calls him 'छोटे', Nani's file): her youngest, who left at twenty and rings at eight every morning to worry; she answers 'बस, सब ठीक' and hangs up first. Friction: after the fall he wants her moved into his flat high up in the city, and she will not go ('Your flat is yours. My bed is mine.', Nani's file); his lift breaks every monsoon, and she knows it. Tenderness: she keeps his school cricket bat behind her door. He is the one person who never talks over her: he lets her finish, then repeats her last two words back. With her, in every language mode, he slows to short whole sentences, the only person he slows down for (in Hindi mode he still says the numbers in English, 'अम्मा, सेवेंटी लोग'; English mode keeps the slowing, so the beat reaches every player). The greeting (India review: no greeting had replaced touching feet): at the blue gate in December he bends, and she lays her palm on his head without a word (she does not speak in chapter 5, rule 10). It is the first time all year he is still, and he says it out loud: 'Amma, I missed you. So much.'

MUMMY (he says 'Didi' and आप, softened with 'na'; she calls him 'Chhote' and तुम, and 'Chhote ji' with आप when she is angry, Mummy's file): the elder sister who half raised him while Nani ran the counter. Friction: he solves with money, she with time. He sends money she did not ask for, and she has never spent a rupee of it; it sits in its own account (Mummy's file, which proposes that in December it comes back as the two advance envelopes for the tent and the cook, his own money, and she says nothing). In July, when her shop floods, he sends two drainage pumps through Papa's parcel office; she keeps the pumps and puts his money in the same account. Tenderness: she is the first person he rings about anything ('Didi!!'), before Mami, before you.

PAPA (he says 'Jija ji' and आप; what Papa calls him is for the family's address table, since Papa's file sets none): brothers-in-law with opposite clocks. Papa books in January; Mama ji books the night before and rings Papa to fix it, and Papa always fixes it and says nothing (Papa's file). He calls Papa 'the family's railway' and means it as the highest praise. Papa meets his train himself at 5 am on every visit, and he hugs Papa on the platform, which Papa bears with his list held flat to his chest. Shared silence: in May, Papa could not confirm his waitlisted ticket, and that is why he reached Nani a day late; neither has ever mentioned it. Tenderness: at the wedding he puts Papa at the gate with the guests' train times, the one job he trusts to nobody else.

TINKU (he says 'Tinku' and तुम; she says 'Mama ji' and आप, Tinku's file): the uncle who brings gifts too expensive to use; one is still in its box. She scores his promises ('You said March, Mama ji. Nil for one.'). Friction: at every family function he introduces her as 'our youngest', the one thing that makes her lose her temper ('I'm not the youngest. I'm the scorer.', Tinku's file). Tenderness: when Captain sahab says the district should see her scorebook, he sends her the scorers' course form that same night. When the letter comes in December he makes her news bigger, as he makes everything bigger ('DISTRICT LEVEL!!!'), and from then on he introduces her by her job, as he introduces you: 'Meet the district scorer!' (proposed, outside any decision beat). It embarrasses her, and she keeps the message. In the wedding week, when his numbers keep growing, she quietly keeps the real count for him (Tinku's file).

MAUSI (he says 'Badi Didi' and आप, since plain 'Didi' is Mummy; she calls him 'Munna' and तुम in front of everyone, Mausi's file): the eldest, who half raised him too and still scolds him for leaving for the city at twenty. He paid for the benches in her tuition room with his first salary, and she tells every pupil so. Friction: she tells everyone what city life costs; he tells everyone how many people she feeds. Tenderness: she still packs him food for the train home, and he eats it before the train leaves the platform. They are the family's two elders who say feelings out loud, in different keys: she says her hurt, he says his love, in different words (his Hindi is not her proposed 'बहुत याद आई।'). In panels they are both round and both in the middle height band, so they are told apart by motion: she is wide and planted, he is always mid-stride with a raised elbow, and he is never painted still beside her.

MAUSA JI (he says 'Bade Jija ji' and आप; Mausa ji calls him 'Chhote' and तुम, the one nickname he uses, Mausa ji's file): taught him to ride a scooter at fifteen. Mama ji earns the most now, and Mausa ji still pays for the tea first; Mama ji lets him. It is the one number he never makes bigger. Friction: when Mama ji tries to pay him for the wedding's lighting work, Mausa ji walks off mid-sentence (Mausa ji's file). Tenderness: at midnight in the wedding week, the man who never stops talking sits beside Mausa ji on the gate step for two silent minutes, the only quiet of his week; and he hugs Mausa ji at every arrival, which Mausa ji answers with 'Hmm.'

MASTERJI (he says 'Masterji' and आप; Masterji calls him 'Mama ji', the lane's word, Masterji's file, and the address table settles whether तुम goes with it): stitched his 1999 interview shirt free 'for luck', and Mama ji still says it was the shirt; Masterji keeps the 1999 slip in his register. Friction: now Mama ji orders from the city by phone, sends photographs of cloth and wants it 'by Friday'; Masterji says city cloth photographs better than it wears. Tenderness: Masterji cuts the December wedding kurta himself, early, in Mama ji's own big check. They never meet in the strip, since Masterji is chapter 3's voice.

CAPTAIN SAHAB (he says 'Captain sahab' and आप; Captain sahab greets him 'Catch?' and says तुम, Captain sahab's file): years ago, in a family match on the lane, Mama ji dropped a catch off the last ball. He blames the sun, with a different reason every year. Friction: he has promised the lane cup a proper trophy every year since, and it has never come ('Catch, and the trophy. Both dropped.'). Tenderness: Captain sahab is the one person in his year who never asks him for anything, which he finds restful; every visit Captain sahab throws him the old ball without warning, and he drops it. Outside chapter 4, so the title's clash with a captain question there (rule 36) does not arise.

MAMI ('Boss' in front of the family, तुम both ways, as the realism notes ask of every married pair; her name stays off screen; she calls him no name, and 'your Mama ji' to the young ones, Mami's file): they met in 2000 over a disputed bill at her counter and married in 2001 at Nani's house. He promises, she plans; he says seventy, she counts sixty. They bicker in front of everyone and decide everything in private, and in private, only there, his numbers come down ('ok 65 / ok ok 60'). She is the calm one; he is the worrier. He is the only person allowed to write on her list, in his own hand, and she always ticks his item first (Mami's file). She is the only person he tells he is afraid ('I wasn't there, Boss. Again.', the night of the fall). The script is turned over without making him the one who is managed: each is right once. She is right about the plates (sixty at dinner, 5.27); he is right about the people (the cook and the tent, 5.13; the lane in his ten extra chairs at the cake). Their turns sit in different panels: his at 5.27, hers at the cake, where nobody comforts her (Mami's file), so he does not put an arm round her there. In panels his round mid-stride shape and her tall upright line are opposite top anchors, and she is half a head taller.

YOU (he says तुम, only in rule 66 shapes; you say 'Mama ji' and आप): he rings you, not his sister, when something has to be done in Nani's town. 'Sorted, Mama ji' is the sentence he most wants to hear. His worry lists name everyone (Amma, Didi, Jija ji, Tinku) and never ask how you are, because you are the one he is asking; Nani closes that in the album ('Aur tum.'). He hands you the week through Mami, whose hands reach towards you, because household hands never do (bible section 4). He introduces you to guests by your job, never a family word: 'In-charge se milo!' | 'इंचार्ज से मिलो!' | 'Meet the in-charge!' (outside any decision beat, with the guests off the panel, since they could be card people). You send one message back, in English, where he sends five (your file).

HIS DAUGHTER (off screen; 'beti' or 'she', never a name): 24, works in the city, chose her own match, with both families' blessing, in March. Never drawn, named, described or put on a card. He rings her twice a day. He cannot finish a sentence about her leaving home, so he talks about the guest list instead.

MAMI'S SIDE (chapter 5's circle, after the cast map's change): in 2001 they travelled a night by train to Nani's house for his wedding, so he welcomes them louder than his own, and that is half of 'make it seventy'. In the strip he never names, points at or describes anyone on a card (rule 36), and they are never painted near a circle: his 'Aaiye' at the gate is painted with him beckoning towards someone off the panel. His judging notes on them stay in his idiom, party manners, and land as often on men as on women (rule 22).

THE TENT MAN AND THE COOK (proposed minor people of his phone book, never on a card and never a joke; the India review asks for the wedding's cook and tent man as people): men he has known for years by first name, whose families he asks after before any business. The writers name them from rule 21's mix. On screen they are their work (the tent up and the cook's kettle steaming at 5.13), and, if the writers want them, one face-on panel each away from any circle.
cast.year_arc: JANUARY (present-day opening): face-on on the household screen (1.03), mid-stride with the phone at his right ear and the umbrella on his forearm. His message card (1.04) copies Nani's words back with his own marks: 'December!! / My daughter's wedding. / Everyone comes!!'. MAY, CHAPTER 1 (Lugdi, the night train): not on it. He booked a waitlisted ticket the night before and will come a night later. Unseen and unheard (rule 10). MAY, CHAPTER 2 (Rukavat, the ward): Nani slips on the evening the family arrives, and he is still in the city. At 8 am her phone rings on the locker: 'Mama ji's call. Worried, as always.' (2.24). Decision 7 is who explains her medicines to him. If the owner allows it, a wordless split panel paints him face-on on a high city balcony at dawn, phone to his ear, umbrella hooked on the rail, so he is there as a person (comics review). The ward half is written without his name, because looks() adds his whole look wherever his name appears. This is the chapter that turns his year: he was not there. He reaches her the day after she is home, asks her to move into his flat, and she refuses. JUNE (off screen): he moves the wedding from a city hall to Nani's house, as his own was in 2001, and loses the hall's advance: since she will not go to him, he comes to her. JULY, CHAPTER 3 (Station): off screen. Two drainage pumps reach Mummy's flooded shop through Papa's parcel office; she keeps the pumps and puts his money in its account. AUGUST, CHAPTER 4 (Cricket): off screen. He sends Tinku the scorers' course form the night Captain sahab praises her book. The draft's card at 4.28 is cut (rule 10). NOVEMBER (off screen): from the back of autos between sites he rings every tent man, cook and band he knows, by first name, asking after each family first, and books them for December's busiest week, when nobody else can. DECEMBER, CHAPTER 5 (Jadugar, his chapter): his phone goes into his pocket at Nani's gate and stays there all week, never painted and never in a bubble: he is here now. At the blue gate Nani lays her palm on his bowed head and he says it out loud ('Amma, I missed you. So much.'), the first still moment of his year. Then the chapter's one shout, '60 guests? 70 kar do!' (5.03), and Mami hands you her list. All week the raised right arm that held the phone all year beckons people in; he hugs everyone he can reach; the umbrella stays on his forearm in every panel, indoors and out. The worry walks at the tins (5.11) and the band's money (5.21) are one worried pose, the same in both halves of the twin (rule 37). Friday morning (5.13): the cook's kettle is steaming at dawn and the tent is up, because he rang. On the last night (5.27) he hangs the umbrella on Nani's gate and walks back to the canopy without it, the first time all year, and his tic turns round: in the on-time band, 'Sixty plates. For sure.' | 'साठ थालियाँ। पक्का।', the worrier no longer asking. At the cake (5.28) the lane comes and fills the ten extra chairs he had stacked by the gate since 5.01, his bigger number right once, in the background only, because 5.28 is Nani's. ALBUM (present day): if the album has a family picture, he is in it, small, face-on, hands free, and the umbrella is propped behind Nani's door beside his old school bat in the same picture, a detail and never a picture of its own. He has no album line (the album keeps two: Nani's count and your reply). In one line: from worrying at a distance with a phone at his ear to standing in her lane with the same arm raised, calling everyone in.

voice.register: Fast, warm and run-on: a man walking between two building sites with his right arm up, talking to someone far away. His shape is the job that grows and the worry that stacks. Inside one bubble he chains clauses with commas, and the 'ek kaam' he started with becomes three ('Ek kaam karo, gate pe raho, sabko andar lo.'); his questions are worry checks about named people, stacked, and he waits only for the answer to the last one, 'Pakka?'. A long thought runs on into a second or third bubble, picked up with 'aur' or, once a scene at most, 'aur haan'. Every bubble still ends cleanly, on a full stop, a question mark or a '!', so on a phone nothing looks cut off. That is what tells his long runs from the other three: Papa's are whole sentences in order with the times in them, Masterji's a verdict and a wander, Mausi's a tripled word and a question she answers herself; his is a list that keeps growing and a stack he waits on, and he never answers his own question. The common fillers (arre, achha, haan, chalo, dekho, bas, theek hai) come into his talk the way they come into anyone's; what marks him is the shape and where his words come from: people, health and city logistics. Feeling is said out loud, warmly, to one person at a time, with a hug: he is one of the two elders who say it in plain words (Mausi says hers to the whole room, loud; he says his to one face). Fear he says only to Mami. Humour is big and kind and aimed at himself (he plans nothing, he talks too much, he cannot say no to sweets), never at anyone's age, town, shop or work. He talks most to people far away, Mummy first ('Didi!'); in chapter 5, with the phone in his pocket, to everyone at the gate. With Nani alone he slows to short whole sentences, the only person he slows for, and lets her finish before he speaks. When cross he does not go quiet or slow (that is Mami's tell in his chapter): he still asks after the other man's family first, then the run-on stops dead and breaks into single words, one downward chop of his free hand on each ('Aaj. Abhi. Yahin.'). Never at family, a woman, a worker's dignity or anyone on a card. When anyone brings a report of harassment or a dowry demand he believes it at once and moves ('Main aa raha hoon. Abhi.'), with no 'Pakka?' and no question back (rule 22). His voice is never raised except the chapter's one shout at 5.03 (rule 35). Warm, and never the comic one while he is the asker (rule 37).
voice.mix: The most English elder. Hinglish: a whole English clause first, at speed, then a Hindi landing ('Don't worry, Bade Jija ji ko bulao.'). His English carries the jobs and the comfort (don't worry, no problem, sorted, last minute, booking, advance, I'll miss you), and his Hindi lands on family, food and health (Amma, Didi, ghar, sab, khaana, dawai, man, roz). Like most city people under fifty he also builds everyday verbs from an English word with kar or ho, and his are people and logistics verbs: 'miss kiya', 'call karo', 'book kar dijiye', 'check hua', 'dispatch kar dijiye'. Mummy's English verbs are the shop counter turned on home things ('MCB check karo', 'mains off karo'), so the two stay apart by what they turn into verbs, not by who may use the pattern. Mami, the other whole-clause switcher, runs the other way: a Hindi clause, then an English status. 'Ek kaam karo' to you, Tinku and Mami; 'Ek kaam kijiye' to vendors and elders. Everyday Urdu-rooted words are his too, as they are the whole town's: 'zaroor aaiye', 'fikr mat kijiye', 'kasoor', 'ain waqt'. Figures in Hinglish bubbles are digits ('60? 70 kar do!'), because romanised 'saath' is also 'with'. He cheers good news by making it bigger, not with 'Badhai ho' or 'Congratulations', which go to Mummy and Mami if the owner allows them, so he does not echo them in a shared panel. HINDI MODE: everyday spoken city Hindi in Devanagari that keeps the English loan words a Hindi-first reader already knows (नो प्रॉब्लम, सेट, एक्स्ट्रा, प्रमोशन, बीपी, टेंट, लिस्ट, वेटिंग, डिपार्टमेंट, क्रेडिट), so he still sorts in Hindi; where his Hinglish has a whole English phrase, Hindi mode uses the Hindi a Devanagari speaker would say ('बहुत गर्व है', 'सबकी याद आती है'), never English spelled out in Devanagari; 'चिंता मत करो', 'चिंता नहीं' or 'फ़िक्र मत कीजिए' for 'don't worry'; with Nani, whole Hindi sentences and आप. ENGLISH MODE: plain British English with his rhythm; 'oh, and' for 'aur haan'; 'Do one thing' at most once a chapter (his one Indian-English turn), otherwise 'One small job'; 'Oho!' stays; kin words stay as they are (Didi, Jija ji, Amma, Boss); never a spelled accent and never a word-for-word line ('everyone must come', not 'everyone comes').
tics: The job that grows: 'Ek kaam karo,' and the one job becomes two or three in the same comma chain ('Ek kaam karo, gate pe raho, sabko andar lo.'). The 'ek' is an idiom, not a count. 'Aur haan' (English mode 'oh, and') carries the run into one more bubble at most once a scene; every bubble ends on a full stop, '?' or '!', never on a trailing comma.

Stacks worry questions about named people and waits only for the last answer: 'Amma ka BP check hua? Dawai? Koi saath hai? Pakka?'. He never answers his own question (Mausi's shape) and never asks how you are (Nani's 'Aur tum.' closes that in the album). Each person in the stack gets a verb or a noun with them ('Amma ka BP check hua?', 'Amma andar hain?'), never a bare kin word. To you, Mummy is 'Tumhari Mummy' ('Tumhari Mummy kaisi hain?'), because 'Didi, kaisi hain?' said aloud, or with a comma, is him calling you Didi, and कैसी then gives you a gender.
Ends a worry stack, or a reassurance he is given, with 'Pakka?' ('Sure?'); at 5.27 it turns round into a statement. Never after a report of harassment or a dowry demand (rule 22).

People first, then business: every vendor gets 'Ghar mein sab theek?' and a question about their own people (a mother's knee, the children's exams) before 'Achha.' and the job. Names, not numbers, are his stock, and he keeps it even when cross ('Aa gaye, bhai? Ghar mein sab theek? Achha. Tent. Abhi.').

Makes everything bigger in words, never in figures: aur, sab, sabko, extra, poora, 'phir aur upar, phir sabse upar'. 'Full' ('full fit') in at most two lines a chapter; the rest of the time 'poora'. The plus-ten is a gesture, the flashed open hand, with no figure said; the only spoken figures in his year are 5.03 and 5.27.
Hands the how to someone else in the same breath: 'Bade Jija ji ko bulao.', 'Credit Jija ji ka.'. He plans nothing; he knows who can.

Credits people out loud by their job, to whoever is near: 'In-charge se miliye!', 'Ghar ke station master se miliye!' (Papa the parcel clerk, promoted in words), and from December 'District scorer se miliye!' (outside any decision beat, guests off the panel).
'Oho!' for good or bad news, by tone: rising with the arm up when a job lands, a falling 'Oho.' with a hand to his forehead at bad news. 'Aaiye' once at the gate, never three times.
Never talks over Nani: he lets her finish, then repeats her last two words back.
Hugs everyone he can reach while he says it out loud (a stage direction, never a word). Never you: household hands never reach towards you (rule 7).
catchphrases: 'Ek kaam karo, ...' | 'एक काम करो, ...' | 'Do one thing, ...' The one job that becomes three before the full stop. 'Ek kaam kijiye' to vendors and elders; in English mode 'Do one thing' once a chapter, otherwise 'One small job,'.
'Pakka?' | 'पक्का?' | 'Sure?' The end of every worry stack. Turned round once, at 5.27: 'Pakka.' | 'पक्का।' | 'For sure.' Never said after a report (rule 22).

'60? 70 kar do!' | 'साठ? सत्तर कर दो!' | 'Sixty? Make it seventy!' His quoted line and his only catchphrase with a number, said once, at 5.03, the chapter's one shout, with the open hand flashed. The owner is asked whether to keep both marked figures (matrix open point).
voice.exclamation: 'Oho!' | 'ओहो!' | 'Oho!' (the same in every mode). For good news and bad, and the tone tells which: a rising 'Oho!' with the arm up when a job lands, a falling 'Oho.' with a hand to his forehead at a delay or a worry. It is a sound with no word in it, so it has no religious sense, and no one else in the cast has it as their exclamation. Guard: never run on into a god-word, and never the city man's reflexes 'Thank God', 'Oh God', 'Oh my God', 'OMG', 'God bless', 'Shukar hai' or 'Bhagwan ka shukar' (rule 3). Each person keeps one exclamation of their own, so he does not use the others' ('Kamaal hai.' Papa, 'Arre waah.' Captain sahab, 'Haaye!' Mausi, 'Had hai!' Mummy, 'Baap re.' Nani, 'Hain?' Mausa ji, 'Uff.' Masterji, 'Gazab!' Tinku, 'Ish.' Mami, 'Badhiya.' you). A plain 'arre' in the middle of a line is free, as it is for anyone. Thanked, he opens on his own sound, 'Oho, no no!', not on Mummy's 'Arre, isme kya'.
voice.sorry_thanks_love: SORRY: in plain words, out loud, then the blame made bigger: 'Sorry, Didi, poora kasoor mera.' | 'सॉरी, दीदी, पूरा क़सूर मेरा।' | 'Sorry, Didi, it's all my fault.'. Said to whoever he let down, in front of everyone, and to the next person in the same breath ('Jija ji, aapse bhi sorry. Aapki neend kharab ki.'); to you the same, plainly ('Sorry, In-charge, phir last minute. Mera kasoor.'). Mausi's sorry is the tripled 'Sorry, sorry, sorry!' with food held out; his is one 'sorry' and the whole blame. THANKS: a plain 'Thank you' to anyone who helped, with a word for their people: 'Thank you, [Name] bhai! Maa ji ka khayal rakhiye.' | 'थैंक यू, [नाम] भाई! माँ जी का ख़याल रखिए।' | 'Thank you, [Name] bhai! Look after your mother.'. For family, the thank-you is the room hearing what they did: 'In-charge se miliye!' | 'इंचार्ज से मिलिए!' | 'Meet the one in charge!'; for Papa 'Ghar ke station master se miliye!' | 'घर के स्टेशन मास्टर से मिलिए!' | 'Meet our very own station master!'. Thanked himself, he brushes it off with his own exclamation and gives it away: 'Oho, no no! Credit Jija ji ka, Boss ka, sabka!' | 'ओहो, ना ना! क्रेडिट जीजा जी का, बॉस का, सबका!' | 'Oho, no no! Credit's Jija ji's, and Boss's, everyone's!' ('Arre, isme kya' is Mummy's brush-off, so he does not echo it). To Mami in private, a plain 'Thank you' after what she did, said back to her. LOVE: said in plain words, one to one, with a hug: 'Amma, aapko bahut miss kiya.' | 'अम्मा, आपके बिना एक दिन भी मन नहीं लगा।' | 'Amma, I missed you so much.'; at a parting 'Didi, I'll miss you.' | 'दीदी, आपके बिना मन नहीं लगेगा।' and the worry stack after it; to Mami in private, what she did said back to her ('Aaj poora ghar tumne sambhala. Maine dekha. Thank you.'). Mausi's love is 'Haaye! Bahut yaad aayi.' to the room; his is 'bahut miss kiya' to one face. 'Bahut' is the commonest word in the language and free to both; the phrase 'bahut yaad aayi' is hers, and his Hindi mode keeps 'एक दिन भी मन नहीं लगा', not her 'बहुत याद आई'. FEAR: only to Mami ('Main wahan nahi tha, Boss. Phir se.').

Single common words are not owned: arre, achha, haan, chalo, dekho, suno, bas, theek hai, sorry, thank you, tension, fikr, waqt and zaroor are free mid-line.

Other people's shapes: answering his own question or tripling a word (Mausi); the number before the noun (Papa, Tinku); items as 'thing, status' (Mami); closed verbless fragments outside his cross beat (Nani, Mausa ji); tea as his care (Nani's sorry, Masterji's love); a sugar joke about the tea itself (Nani and Papa have one).

Religious words and exclamations (rule 3): 'Thank God', 'Oh God', 'Oh my God', 'OMG', 'God bless', 'Hai Ram', 'Bhagwan', 'Shukar hai', 'Inshallah', 'Mashallah', 'Rab', 'Wahe Guru', 'Jesus'; in English mode also 'Gosh', 'Good Lord', 'Thank goodness', 'Thank heavens', 'Heavens'.
'Main hoon na' as a line of comfort: in his mouth it is heard as the film, so his comfort is 'Don't worry' and a job handed on.
Dowry or ritual words: 'dahej' | 'दहेज', 'lena-dena' | 'लेन-देन', 'kanyadaan', 'vidaai', 'phere', 'mandap', 'shagun', 'baraat'; nothing at all about gifts for the groom's side (rules 22 and 27).
His daughter's name or looks, or 'giving her away'.

Rule 66 checker flags on his lines to or around you, each for a native reader to clear: 'पक्का?' and 'अच्छा।' (words that never change); 'सब तुम्हारे भरोसे।' (भरोसे agrees with भरोसा); 'सबको जगह मिलनी चाहिए।' (agrees with जगह); 'तुम्हारी मम्मी कैसी हैं?' (तुम्हारी and कैसी agree with मम्मी); 'अम्मा अंदर हैं?'; 'पंप भेज रहा हूँ' (about himself); 'नौकरी लगी?' and 'अम्मा ने दवाई ली?' (they agree with नौकरी and दवाई); 'पूरा हफ़्ता इन्होंने चलाया।' (a ने past that agrees with हफ़्ता; but you are the doer, and rule 66 allows तुम-lines only as commands, 'who should' asks and lines where you are not the doer, so this line waits on the owner adding 'a past with ने, where the verb agrees with the thing' as a fourth shape, or on the native reader clearing it onto the build's cleared list; no wording change is needed if the owner agrees).
All of these go into the one family address table the India review asks for, signed off by the Hindi-first readers and the South Indian reader (rule 65).

habits: Device: a big plain black phone in a thick black rubber case with one corner cracked on a site, painted with the screen dark and no logo, every word live text laid on top (rule 30). In chapter 5 it stays in his trouser pocket: never painted, never typed on screen.

Script: English and Roman Hinglish, never Devanagari (Nani's voice-typed Devanagari is the contrast). In the game's Hindi mode his messages show in Devanagari and keep his bursts and marks; where his Hinglish types a whole English phrase ('so proud', 'miss you all'), Hindi mode shows the Hindi a Devanagari typist would use ('बहुत गर्व है', 'सबकी याद आती है'), and single loans he would say anyway stay (बीपी, टेंट, वेटिंग, प्लीज़).
Shape: the run-on typed as a burst. Four or five short messages, each one clause of it, 'aur haan' a message of its own at most once a burst, then 'calling' before you can reply.

The first message is the person's name, capitalised, with his doubled mark ('Didi!!', 'Jija ji!!', 'In-charge!!', '[Name] bhai!!'); everything after it is lowercase, kin names included ('amma', 'nani', 'chhote'), with no full stops. To Mami in private the name comes with no mark at all ('Boss').
Marks: '!!' is his; a worry question takes one '?', because '??' is Mausi's; never '!!!'.

Numbers: his bigness is typed in words (sab, everyone, extra), never as figures and never as the plus-ten. A digit appears only when a fact someone must act on cannot be said another way, and then he would rather ring.

Emoji: 🎉 for good news, ‼️ for worry, and 🤗 (a face with no person, gender or skin tone) for love typed in words ('miss you all 🤗'): he is the only one in the family who types love. Never a person emoji; no folded hands until the owner rules (realism notes).
Capitals once a year, for joy (Tinku's course letter), never in anger: all caps reads as shouting, the 'aggro uncle' trap (realism notes).

Voice notes from the back of an auto between sites, starting mid-word because he presses record late; shown as a voice-note strip with their words as live text, and they run on like his speech ('...aur haan, ek kaam aur,').

Forwards: only weather warnings for Nani's district, each with one line of his own ('amma ko andar rakhiye na!!'), the warning painted blank. Never politics, religion, gods, famous faces or false news (rule 3; caricature traps).

When: just before his eight o'clock call to Nani, at red lights, and late at night after Mami's list. He replies in seconds or not at all, because he rings instead, and never reads a long message to the end ('ok ok call me').

Short forms: 'pls', 'ok ok', 'msg'. English verbs with kar come into his typing as into his talk ('book kar dijiye pls'); 'ok ok call me' stays as it is, because the readers marked it true. No spelled accent and no typo played for laughs.
Thanks and sorry are typed plainly too ('thank you', 'sorry didi'), never as a code.
In private with Mami, and only there, his asks come down, in words: 'sabko?' becomes 'ok sab nahi' becomes 'tumhari list'.
The game has no group chat (owner, 23 Oct). On screen he is single messages on a painted blank phone or a message card under a panel, and a message on the player's own phone waits on rulebook Q9.

look.build: Middle height band. The comics review's four bands replace ten false-precise ranks: tall (Papa, Mami, Captain sahab), middle (Mausi, Mama ji, Tinku, Mummy), short (Mausa ji, Masterji), smallest (Nani). Exact gaps are set only for pairs who share panels: Mami is half a head taller than him (her file agrees). Broad-chested and solid, with a thick neck and heavy forearms from carrying sample pumps. His waist is a middle-aged solid one, never a pot-belly gag (realism notes: older men in Indian ads as 'the unfit uncle'). Base shape: round (round face, round shoulders, arms that open wide). Round is held by a woman and a man, Mausi and him; because they are siblings in one band and share December's panels, he is told apart by motion: always mid-stride with the right elbow raised, never painted still beside her. As a black shape at phone size: a round body, a raised right elbow at the head, and a long umbrella line hanging from the other arm, thicker where its folded cloth bunches.
look.face: A round face with full cheeks and a short, slightly heavy jaw. Three features, which are close-up details for the face chip and inserts: (1) a thick black moustache, neatly trimmed, its ends stopping at the corners of his mouth, over a clean-shaven chin. It is the only moustache without a beard in the speaking cast (Mausa ji's white moustache is joined to his beard): not curled, not pencil-thin. (2) The family's thick, straight, dark eyebrows, shared by Nani's line (Nani, Mausi, Mummy, Tinku). He lifts them high when he worries, painted without forehead creases. (3) Deep laugh lines fanning from the corners of his eyes, so his grin reaches his eyes before his mouth. Age shows in the laugh lines and a little weight under the jaw, so that the jet-black hair does not make him read 35 (painted ages read young). No forehead lines and no lines between the brows anywhere in his words: creases there can come back as painted stripes that read as a sect mark (rules review). At strip size only the moustache bar survives; the rest is the face chip's job.
look.skin: PROVISIONAL until one painted swatch strip settles the whole family (comics review: settle it on a strip, not in words). Proposed depth: medium brown with a warm undertone, darker on his forearms and the back of his neck from years on building sites. Painter words: the tested base first, 'South Asian features and warm brown skin', then the depth, 'of a medium-brown depth' (rules review: only the base phrase is tested against whitening). Why one step deeper than the cast map's 'warm light brown': soft looks pale light-brown skin first, and the city couple as the family's two lightest people reads as the colourism script (fair, city, money) in a game about fairness. But deepening him alone leaves Mami as the lightest adult, the same script (all three reviews). So the proposal for the strip is that neither city in-law is the lightest person in the family; if the strip keeps a light-medium tone, it belongs to someone in Nani's town. Mummy's, Mausi's, Masterji's and Mami's files still call him 'warm light brown'; they are updated from the strip, not from this file. Nobody's skin is ever 'golden' (Jadugar's gold can paint gold skin).
look.hair: Thick jet-black hair swept up and back in one solid wave at the front, standing a finger's width above his forehead, cut short at the sides and at the back of the neck. He dyes it; that is never said on screen. From behind: short, neat black back and sides. It is a strip anchor: a dark mass with a bump on top. The painter's sentence: 'thick jet-black hair swept up in a wave at the front and cut short at the sides'.
look.glasses_jewellery: None. No spectacles: Nani and Masterji hold them, and he never reads anything long; he rings instead. (The draft's reading glasses he will not buy, and the phone held at arm's length, are struck: six files gave that quirk.) No wristwatch: his phone is his clock, and the watch is Mummy's anchor. No ring (a stone ring reads as astrology). No chain (a gold chain on a man is the showy businessman stock figure). No bracelet, no thread on the wrist, no earring. Bare wrists and hands belong to his look: the only things on him are the umbrella on one forearm and, outside chapter 5, the phone in his hand.
outfits: EVERYDAY (the city, the opening, chapter 5 by day): a long-sleeved cotton shirt in a large cream and dark chocolate-brown check, each square about a hand wide, buttoned at the wrists, worn untucked; one empty chest pocket. Plain dark chocolate-brown cotton trousers. Dark brown leather lace-up shoes. The sleeves are buttoned, not rolled, because rolled sleeves on a moustached man in a checked shirt are the old take's Ramesh word for word. The painter's word for the pattern is 'large cream and dark-brown gingham, squares about a hand wide', since 'checked' and 'check' each have a second meaning (a tick mark, a bank cheque) under the glossary rule.
WINTER NIGHT (chapter 5 after dark): the same check shirt under a plain dark chocolate-brown zip jacket worn open so the check shows down the front.

HOME (Nani's house early in the morning): a plain cream half-sleeve cotton T-shirt with nothing printed on it, dark chocolate-brown track pants, plain grey rubber flip-flops; his shoes are left at the door.

WEDDING NIGHT (5.20 to 5.28): his signature at its signature scale in a finer cloth (comics review: comics keep the costume): a knee-length kurta in the same large cream and dark-brown check, hand-wide squares, in a cotton-silk with a soft sheen, cut by Masterji; dark chocolate-brown straight trousers; polished dark brown leather shoes. No jacket over it: the sleeveless jacket with a short upright collar is Papa's occasion cut, and a fine check reads flat at phone size. No head covering of any kind (never a wedding safa), no garland, no shawl, no thread on the wrist. No red on him, so nobody is mistaken for part of the unseen bride's party.
THE CITY IN THE MONSOON (only for the wordless chapter 2 balcony panel, if the owner allows it): the everyday check, with the umbrella hooked on the balcony rail.
look.colour_key: Signature: a large check of cream and dark chocolate-brown, a strong light-and-dark pattern over dark trousers, plus the black umbrella. Changed from the draft's tan and chocolate because a mid-tone check drifts (rules review, the drift sheet) and a light-and-dark check reads as a pattern at strip size. NOW: cream and dark-brown check, dark chocolate trousers, black umbrella. JADUGAR (chapter 5, his chapter; provisional until one Jadugar string is settled, since the chapter JSON says 'crimson, gold and black' and the code says vermilion, magenta, indigo night, emerald and old gold): the check in the poster's paper cream and its black-brown, which holds under either string. Old gold appears only as bulb light on the umbrella's steel tip, never in his cloth: old gold already sits on Nani's, Mummy's, Mausi's and Tinku's keys (comics review). Never crimson, vermilion or magenta on him (magenta is Mausi's; red is the bride's side and the chapter's curtain). LUGDI (only if Q11 opens): a marigold-cream and deep violet-brown check, indigo trousers. STATION (not used): cream squares crossed by broad blue-black bands, solid blue-black trousers, the umbrella and hair solid black. CRICKET (not used): a chalk-white and deep-brown check, never cherry red (Captain sahab's). RUKAVAT (only for the wordless balcony panel): a cream and teak check, deep teak trousers, never the signal orange (Mausa ji's orange). In every look the pattern and its light and dark values hold even when the colour goes. All of it is checked on the six look strips, with all ten people side by side as simple figures, before any master (comics review).
look.prop: THE BIG BLACK UMBRELLA. A long folded umbrella, its black cloth fat and bunched under its strap, so it reads as an umbrella and never as a stick, with a curved dark wooden handle, a short steel tip that always shows, and no markings; about as long as his leg. Its story: he reached the city in the 1999 monsoon without one, was soaked at his first interview, bought this kind that evening, and has carried one every day since, rain or not. This is the third, the same as the first. It is his worry as an object, the 'in case' he never puts down. How it is carried: always hanging by its handle from his forearm. Never held by the handle in his hand (that is a magician's cane, and Jadugar is a magic-show bill whose ROLE already has a magician; comics review), never leant on, never planted upright (that is Nani's cane). In chapter 5 it stays on his forearm in every panel, indoors and out, until 5.27, so each twin's two lead-ins match (rule 37) and its absence lands. Its arc: at 5.27 it hangs on Nani's gate by its handle and he walks back without it; in the album it is propped behind Nani's door beside his school cricket bat, a detail in the family picture. Its masters: he is painted with it on his forearm, so in a panel he and the umbrella take one reference slot (comics and rules reviews); a second, hands-free master serves 5.27 and the album. Sides: the left forearm is a preference to check, never what tells him apart, because layouts get mirrored (comics review). HIS SECOND OBJECT: the phone, a plain black slab in a thick black rubber case, screen dark, at his right ear with the elbow up, in January, in May and in his messages only. In chapter 5 it is in his pocket and the same raised right arm beckons people in, so the silhouette keeps its raised elbow while its meaning turns from calling at a distance to calling people in. GLOSSARY: only shared objects get rows, under keys nobody else uses (rules review): 'black umbrella' (his), and one merged 'mobile phone' row for the whole cast if the merged glossary keeps one. His clothes live only in his LOOKS entry (gingham, kurta, zip jacket, lace-up shoes, flip-flops), so they never collide with other people's rows ('chappals', 'kurta' and the upright-collar jacket are each defined in several files). WORDS KEPT OUT OF HIS PROMPTS, because old glossary rows fire on them in terms() (code-verified by the rules review): 'flat' (an apartment building), 'floor' (Dadi's Nashik bedroom), 'stands' or 'standing' (spectator stands), 'seat', 'cover', 'watch', 'bench', 'match', 'passes', 'wheel'; also 'canopy' for the umbrella's cloth (the lane's canopy is in the same prompts), 'wedding', 'city' (except the balcony panel, where the city is the place) and 'stage'. REFERENCE PICTURES: the umbrella alone in four states (closed and strapped with its cloth bunched; hanging from a forearm; hanging on a gate by its handle; propped behind a door), made with paint-ref and picked against its checklist: one umbrella, black, strapped and bunched, curved wooden handle, steel tip showing, leg length.
look.silhouette: STRIP ANCHORS (what a full-figure pick is checked against, comics review): (1) a broad round figure mid-stride; (2) the right elbow raised at the head, with the phone in January and May and beckoning in December; (3) a long black umbrella line hanging from the other forearm, thicker where its cloth bunches; (4) the jet-black hair wave as a bump on top and the black moustache bar; (5) the big light-and-dark check torso over dark legs. In five strokes: circle, raised elbow, hanging line, bump, bar. FAR SPEC (for when he is small and painted from words): a round figure with a dark top, a light checked torso, dark legs and a thin black line hanging from one arm. It reads as a black shape at phone size and in Station's two inks. It is the opposite of Mami's anchors (a tall upright line, a clipboard flat to her chest), the person he shares most panels with, and he is never painted still beside Mausi, who is also round and in his height band.
look.shoes: Everyday: dark brown leather lace-up shoes with thick rubber soles, dust on the toes from building sites. Indoors at Nani's: plain grey rubber flip-flops, the shoes left at the door (defined in his LOOKS entry only, so no 'chappals' row collides). Wedding: polished dark brown leather shoes. Never sports shoes (the painter puts logos on them). Never embroidered wedding slippers, which lean regional.

posture.stance: Weight forward on the balls of his feet, as if about to walk off. Chest out, shoulders a little rounded from years of leaning into phone calls. Right elbow up (the phone, or in December the beckon); the umbrella hanging from the other forearm; feet apart, toes out. He is never still except twice in the year: bowed under Nani's palm at her gate, and on the gate step at midnight beside Mausa ji.
posture.sitting: He barely sits. When he does, he sits on a plastic chair turned half round, one arm hooked over its back, his body turned towards the gate as if someone is about to arrive, one knee bouncing; the umbrella hangs from the forearm on the chair-back. (The draft's 'front edge, never leaning back' is struck: eight files gave it.) Never with the umbrella planted upright between his knees: that is Nani's cane at her side, and the two must not echo.
posture.walk: Fast, short, heavy steps, talking as he walks and walking as he talks. He turns in a tight circle when he worries, and walks out of a panel and back in. In a lane he walks down the middle of it, beckoning to both sides.
gestures: The plus-ten: his free hand flashes open twice, five fingers and five, as he raises a number. Nani counts heads with one finger; he adds them ten at a time.
The beckon (December): right hand up by his head, fingers curling in towards himself twice, calling people in. Never palm up and pushed outward, which in Jadugar is a magician presenting.

The hug: both arms round whoever arrives, Papa (who bears it with his list held to his chest), Mausa ji (who says 'Hmm'), Tinku (who ducks out); painted people only, never towards the viewer, because the player is never painted and household hands never reach towards you.
He wipes his forehead with the back of his wrist, the umbrella swinging on that arm.
Relief: head tipped back, eyes shut, cheeks blown out in one long breath.
Cross: one downward chop of the free hand on each single word, walking straight at the problem.
expressions: NEUTRAL: mid-stride, brows level, mouth moving, eyes already on the next thing.
PLEASED: arms thrown wide, the umbrella swinging, a grin under the moustache that crinkles his eyes shut.
WORRIED: brows lifted high, walking a tight circle, his free hand rubbing the back of his neck. This is the one pose for both halves of twin C (5.11 and 5.21).

CROSS: he stops circling and walks straight at the problem, chin forward, the free hand chopping once on each single word; never a raised voice, never at family, a woman or anyone on a card. Mami goes still and slow when cross, so in their shared chapter the two tells never match.
LAUGHING: head back, a big laugh from the chest, a slap on the nearest shoulder or his own knee.
TIRED: on Nani's gate step at night, elbows on his knees, hands hanging between them, the umbrella still on one forearm, head bowed.

MOVED: he says it out loud and does not hide his wet eyes ('Amma, I missed you. So much.'), then a hug. Under Nani's palm he is still, bowed. (The draft's silent turn to the wall is struck: the comics review gives him the overt register, so the rest of the cast's silent love reads as character and not as the house style.)

across_looks: WHAT MUST SURVIVE IN EVERY LOOK, as strip anchors, strongest first: (1) the round mid-stride silhouette with the raised right elbow and the hanging umbrella line; (2) hair as a shape, the jet-black wave up at the front with short sides; (3) the black moustache bar; (4) the large light-and-dark check over dark trousers; (5) the umbrella, painted from its own reference, bunched cloth and steel tip; (6) height: half a head under Mami whenever they share a panel; (7) colour: cream and dark brown, or the look's nearest light and dark inks. CLOSE-UP DETAILS, for the face chip and inserts only and never used to pass or fail a full figure: the laugh lines, the eyebrows, the phone's cracked corner, the umbrella's handle and strap, the shoes.

NOW (master sheet, face chip, household screen 1.03, album): as written. STYLE['now'] bakes in cool rainy-evening blues; his sheet needs plain daylight, and portraits.py has no present-day template yet.

The magic-bill look turns a moustached man into the poster's magician, so: 'present-day clothes' is named every time; the moustache stays trimmed; the umbrella always hangs from his forearm with its bunched cloth and steel tip, never in his hand (a cane) and never thin like a wand; no stage, curtain or spotlight is ever centred behind him (at 5.14 and 5.21, which sit by the stage, the stage goes to the far side of the frame, side-on, and he faces across it, not out of it); the beckon never becomes a presenting palm. The look's chromolithograph glow can pale or gild skin, so the skin words go in every prompt.

LUGDI, STATION, CRICKET: not used while rule 10 stands. The colour key gives each, so a model sheet exists if Q11 opens. Pulp styles push moustaches towards a villain's: keep his trimmed.

ORDER OF WORK (comics review): the line-up of all ten as black shapes at phone width in four height bands, and the six look strips with all ten side by side, come before his master; collisions are settled on the strips, not in this file.

SET THE FACE ONCE: one master in the present-day style, then one reference per look made from it with the edit model, so the painter is never asked to change style and keep a face in the same step (method notes).

[STORY_NO]'. Test both tiers on the 5.03 pair (him and Mami) first and record the swap rate (comics review). Never 'wedding' in a chapter 5 prompt: it invites ritual imagery (rules review; rule 3). painter_avoid: These are the audit checklist, never words in the prompt (naming a thing draws it).

A forehead dot, a vertical mark, ash stripes or a paste line on the forehead. FLUX painted a dot on men too (jadugar-salim). Check every panel's forehead, hairline and neck close up and paint confirmed marks out.
Lightened or pale skin, or a European face, in any look, most of all in Now and Rukavat. Compare every pick against the family swatch strip and his master.
Any head covering: turban, wedding safa, cap, skullcap, a magician's turban or top hat.
A garland, wrist thread, ring, chain, bracelet, earring, wristwatch or spectacles.
A beard, stubble, or a curled, handlebar or pencil moustache.
Logos or letters on the phone, shirt pocket, shoes or umbrella; a lit phone screen; lettering anywhere (rule 30). Any phone on him in chapter 5.
A pot belly, sweat patches, a drunken or dancing wedding-uncle pose.

A cape, sequins, a bow tie, white gloves, a wand; the umbrella held by its handle in his hand, leant on, opened, painted as a walking stick or a magician's cane, or with its cloth thin and tight like a stick; two umbrellas.
A stage, curtain or spotlight centred behind him; a presenting palm (up and pushed outward).
Three hands, or the phone and the umbrella in one hand. Count hands in every pick.

Attribute swaps with Mami (her indigo print or clipboard on him, his check on her), with Mausa ji (white hair or a beard on him) and with Mausi (her copper puff or big flowers on him, his check on her).
Reading as 35: if the jet-black hair makes him young, add age to the face words, never grey to the hair.

A likeness of the old take's Ramesh. His words were close (LOOKS: 'a 48-year-old Indian man with a greying moustache and a checked shirt'; the portrait: 'a thick black moustache, a checked shirt with the sleeves rolled'). Keep design-system/assets/pulp-ramesh.webp and every old Ramesh picture out of his reference folder, and compare every pick against it so an accidental likeness is caught (rules review).
A skyline or tower blocks in Nani's lane (what 'the city uncle' would have summoned).
Any figure who could be a card person beside him in a panel next to a circle: the guests he welcomes stay off the panel (rules review).

Not yet tested: whether klein can paint several views in one picture; if not, paint each view separately from the same words and pick to match.

5.03, the gate: the chapter's one shout, '60 guests? 70 kar do!', while Mami beside him, face-on, holds her list out to you. The quickest read of both of them.

2.24, the ward at 8 am (chapter 2, wordless for him): Nani's phone rings on the locker, 'Mama ji's call. Worried, as always.' If allowed, the split panel paints him on a high city balcony at dawn, phone to his ear, umbrella on the rail: the son who was not there, seen as a person.
The worry walks at the tins (5.11) and the band's money (5.21): one worried pose, a tight circle, the same in both halves of the twin.

5.27, the gate at night: he hangs the umbrella on the gate and walks back to the canopy without it. 'Sixty plates. For sure.': the first time all year he stops asking.

The album: him small and face-on in the family picture, hands free, the umbrella behind Nani's door beside his old school bat.
The opening (1.03, 1.04): mid-stride on the phone on the household screen, and his message card copying Nani's 'Everyone comes' with his double marks.
December, as messages: Tinku's course letter, 'DISTRICT LEVEL!!!', and her 'its a course mama ji'.
never_does: Never sits on a card or is one of the equal two (rule 10). Never names, points at or describes anyone on a decision's cards in a bubble before or during that decision (rule 36).
Never the comic one in his own chapter (rule 37): his habits are shown warm, never as a gag. No pratfall, no dance, no drunken wedding uncle, no pot-belly joke.
Never asks for, accepts, excuses or doubts a dowry demand, and never doubts a report of harassment (rule 22). His daughter's wedding carries no talk of gifts to anyone (rule 27).
Never says no to a guest or shrinks a list in public; never leaves anyone off.
Never shows off money: no gold, no cash in his hand, no talk of his car or his flat.
Never looks down on Nani's town, Mummy's shop or Papa's punctuality, and never makes age a joke.
Never loses his temper at family, at a woman, at anyone on a card, or at a worker's dignity; never raises his voice except the one shout at 5.03.
Never talks over Nani.
Never hides that he is moved, and never says he is fine when he is afraid (he tells Mami).

Never gives you a gender (no beta, bhanja, bhanji, bachcha, bhai, champ; no 'tum aa gaye?' or 'thak gaye?', rule 66). Never touches you or hands you anything (rules 7 and 8; household hands never reach towards you).
Never asks how you are: that belongs to Nani's 'Aur tum.' in the album.
Never names, shows or describes his daughter.
Never wears a head covering, garland, thread, ring, chain or anything religious, marital or branded (rule 3).
Never on the phone in chapter 5, painted or in a bubble.
Never types in Devanagari or sends a long typed message; never forwards politics, religion, gods or false news; never sends a person emoji.
Never holds the umbrella by its handle in his hand, and never parts from it before 5.27 (on the balcony it hangs on the rail at his elbow).
