voice_changes: COMMON FILLERS FREED (cast-wide 1): the never list no longer takes common words from him or gives them away. Arre, achha, haan, chalo, dekho, suno, bas, theek hai, sorry, thank you, tension, fikr, waqt and zaroor are free in the middle of a line; only set phrases stay with their owners ('Arre waah.', 'Kamaal hai.', 'Suno, suno, suno!', a one-word 'Theek.', 'Bas.' as a closer, and the rest listed). 'Achha' and 'Pakka' are no longer his alone; what stays his is the place they sit: 'Achha.' as the hinge from people to the job, 'Pakka?' at the end of a worry stack.

THE SHAPE, NOT A TAG (real India 1): 'aur haan' now comes at most once a scene and every bubble ends on a full stop, '?' or '!', so nothing looks cut off on a phone. In the test set 'aur haan' is in 1 line of 12 (it was 8) and no bubble ends on a comma. His long run now shows inside one bubble as the job that grows ('Ek kaam karo, gate pe raho, sabko andar lo.') and the worry stack that waits on 'Pakka?', which still reads apart from Papa's ordered sentences, Masterji's wander and Mausi's triple.

ENGLISH VERB WITH KAR OR HO ALLOWED (cast-wide 2): 'miss kiya', 'call karo', 'book kar dijiye', 'check hua', 'dispatch kar dijiye'. He is told apart from Mummy by what he turns into a verb (people and logistics) against hers (home things in counter English). 'ok ok call me' is kept as it was, because the readers marked it true.

SORRY AND THANKS IN PLAIN WORDS (cast-wide 3): sorry is a plain 'Sorry, Didi, poora kasoor mera.' and, to you, 'Sorry, In-charge, phir last minute. Mera kasoor.'; thanks is a plain 'Thank you, [Name] bhai! Maa ji ka khayal rakhiye.', a 'Thank you' to Mami in private, and when he is thanked his own brush-off, 'Oho, no no!', before the credit is given away (it was 'Arre, isme kya!', Mummy's brush-off in the same moment). Credit by job stays for family, as his way of letting the room hear it, not as a trade code.

CONGRATULATIONS (cast-wide 4): 'Badhaai ho' is off his never list (rule 3 does not bar everyday phrases); it and 'Congratulations' are left for Mummy and Mami if the owner allows them, and he cheers by making the news bigger ('Ab promotion, phir aur upar, phir sabse upar!').

RULE 22 GUARD ADDED (Hindi and rules note 2, cast-wide 5): never 'Pakka?', 'Sach mein?' or any question back after a report of harassment or a dowry demand, and no proof words near a report beat. A believe-first sample is added: 'Didi, main aa raha hoon. Abhi.' / 'Aap unke saath rahiye.' The register says it too.

LOVE LINE (real India 2): 'Amma, I missed you. Roz.' became 'Amma, aapko bahut miss kiya.' | 'अम्मा, आपके बिना एक दिन भी मन नहीं लगा।' | 'Amma, I missed you so much.', as a city son says it. 'Roz' was bending the line only because 'bahut' had been given to Mausi; 'bahut' is the commonest word in the language and is his again, while Mausi keeps her phrase 'bahut yaad aayi' (the matrix strike of his 'Bahut' is undone for this line). Typed love in Hinglish became 'chhote roz miss karta hai'.
RUMOUR LINE (real India 3): moment 8 is now 'Oho. Band? Mithai wale bhai theek toh hain? Pakka?', a reaction first and the shopkeeper himself, not a jump to his mother.

'FULL' CUT DOWN (real India 5): 'full' is in one test line ('Full fit!') and at most two lines a chapter; the sorry is 'poora kasoor', the tea is no longer 'full meethi', the gate order no longer says 'full'.

LONE KIN WORD TO YOU FIXED (Hindi and rules note 1): moment 10's bare 'Didi?' became 'Tumhari Mummy kaisi hain?' | 'तुम्हारी मम्मी कैसी हैं?' | 'How's your Mummy?' (9 counted words). 'Didi kaisi hain?' was tried first, but said aloud, or with a comma, it is him calling you Didi, and the feminine कैसी gives you a gender. The tics, never list and address table now bar a kin word alone, or 'Didi' before a verb that agrees with a person, in a bubble to you; 'Didi ki dukaan' in moment 9 is a possessive and stays (later mended to 'Mummy ki dukaan': to the child of the house an uncle says 'Mummy', as moment 10 does).

HINDI MODE TYPING (Hindi and rules note 3): 'सो प्राउड 🤗' became 'बहुत गर्व है 🤗' and 'मिस यू ऑल 🤗' became 'सबकी याद आती है 🤗'; Hinglish keeps 'so proud' and 'miss you all'. The mix now says Hindi mode never spells a whole English phrase in Devanagari.
टिकट ONE GENDER (Hindi and rules note 4): the Papa tease is now 'अगले साल का टिकट भी बुक कर लिया? / मेरा भी कर दीजिए।', masculine like Papa's file, so it cannot read as a slip.

ENGLISH MODE DE-TRANSLATED (cast-wide 10, real India 4): 'everyone comes!!' became 'everyone must come!!' (Hinglish 'sabko aana hai!!'); 'Meet the family's railway!' became 'Meet our very own station master!' (Hindi 'घर के स्टेशन मास्टर', which also settles the open question on the gender of रेलवे, and promotes the parcel clerk in words, his habit of making things bigger); 'Meet the in-charge!' became 'Meet the one in charge!'; the chairs joke reads 'Short of chairs? People stand, dinner's over sooner.'; 'All on you.' became 'It's all in your hands.'.

HINDI MODE FOR LOW-ENGLISH READERS (cast-wide 11): he keeps the loans most readers know (नो प्रॉब्लम, सेट, एक्स्ट्रा, प्रमोशन, बीपी, टेंट, वेटिंग) but Hindi mode says 'भेज दीजिए' for 'dispatch'. 'Credit' stays क्रेडिट in Hindi mode, a loan the Hindi reader knows, because 'सारा काम' made the Hindi drift from the Hinglish.

SHARED BITS SPLIT (cast-wide 6): moment 11's 'Paani hi tha', one of four 'only water' lines, became 'Lagi toh nahi?', his worry going to the child; moment 4 no longer jokes about the sugar in the tea (Nani and Papa share that joke) but at himself ('Boss ko mat bataiye').
URDU-ROOTED WORDS SHARED (cast-wide 8): he now says 'zaroor aaiye', 'fikr mat kijiye', 'kasoor' and 'ain waqt' as everyday town words; a new inviting sample carries the first two.
VERBS BACK IN (cast-wide 9): his comfort and worry lines keep 'hai' and 'hoon' ('Amma andar hain?', 'Pump bhej raha hoon', 'Sabko jagah milni chahiye').

RULE 66 FLAG (cast-wide 0): the never list now bars any participle before रहो, रहना or रहिए ('खाते रहो' as well as 'खड़े रहो', 'बैठे रहो') and a 'we' that takes you in with a gendered verb; the credit line about you is a ने past ('इन्होंने चलाया').
WARMTH ADDED: a plain thank-you to Mami after what she held together, a word for the cook's mother after the thank-you, the invitation that asks for everyone, and a sorry to Papa for his lost sleep.

KEPT AS THE READERS MARKED IT TRUE: 'Pakka?'; 'Oho!'; 'Boss' for his wife; 'Ghar mein sab theek? Maa ji ka ghutna?' to every vendor; 'Aa gaye, bhai? Ghar mein sab theek? Achha. Tent. Abhi.' word for word; the chairs joke, now with the verb it was missing ('Kursiyaan kam padin toh log khade-khade khaayenge. Jaldi niptega!'); 'Didi!!', 'ok ok call me' and 'DISTRICT LEVEL!! 🎉🎉'. Also kept: his essence, want, fear and contradiction (worries about everything, plans nothing; makes anyone come); 'Ek kaam karo'; the stacked worry questions he never answers himself; people before business; the cross tell; slowing only for Nani; fear said only to Mami; the two marked figures; the address table.

CHAIRS JOKE MENDED (Hindi and rules): 'log khade-khade, khaana jaldi niptega' had no verb after 'khade-khade' and read as broken Hindi, not as his run-on. It is now 'Kursiyaan kam padin toh log khade-khade khaayenge. Jaldi niptega!' | 'कुर्सियाँ कम पड़ीं तो लोग खड़े-खड़े खाएँगे। जल्दी निपटेगा!' (9 words); the future agrees with लोग, not with you.

THANKED, HIS OWN SOUND (Hindi and rules): moment 7 opened on 'Arre, isme kya!', Mummy's brush-off in the same moment, and its Hindi said 'सारा काम' where the Hinglish said 'Credit'. It is now 'Oho, no no! Credit Jija ji ka, Boss ka, sabka!' | 'ओहो, ना ना! क्रेडिट जीजा जी का, बॉस का, सबका!' | 'Oho, no no! Credit's Jija ji's, and Boss's, everyone's!' (8 words).

'JUST CHECKING IN' OUT (real India): it is American office English. The worry call to Mummy now opens 'Haan, Didi! Bas aise hi phone kiya, kuch khaas nahi.', as the Hindi mode already had it; English mode 'Didi! Just thought I'd ring, nothing special.'

RULE 66, THE ने PAST (cast-wide): 'Poora week inhone chalaya' | 'पूरा हफ़्ता इन्होंने चलाया' marks no gender, since the verb agrees with हफ़्ता, but you are the doer, and rule 66 names only three shapes. No wording change; it waits on the owner (see OPEN).

OPEN, for the owner and readers: may rule 66 add a fourth shape, 'a past with ने, where the verb agrees with the thing' (here 'Poora week inhone chalaya'; the same shape sits in Tinku's, Mausi's, Papa's and Mummy's files), or should the native reader clear each such line onto the build's cleared list? Keep both marked figures (5.03 and 5.27)? May 'Badhai ho!' and 'Congratulations.' go to Mummy and Mami? A Hindi-first reader checks 'घर के स्टेशन मास्टर', 'फ़ुल फ़िट', 'नो प्रॉब्लम', 'एकदम मिठाई', 'वेटिंग भी चलेगा' and 'Kursiyaan kam padin'; 🤗 is proposed as his and no other file claims it; every joke still waits on rulebook Q5.

cast.name: Tinku (टिंकू), 21
cast.role: Your younger sister. On first sight she is labelled 'Tinku, your sister' | 'टिंकू, आपकी बहन'. This replaces the draft's 'Tinku, the youngest', which is not a relation (chapter 1 check, rule 65), and it still gives you no gender. She is in the household. She asks all of chapter 4, the lane cup, in the Cricket look, and she is one of its two judging voices, with Captain sahab (rule 22). She is one of the three women askers (rule 37). A round character. She is never on a card, never the comic one, and never doubts a report. Painter's role word: 'the ponytailed young woman'. It names her strongest anchor and no trade, place, title or relation. 'The young scorer' would pull cricket kit or a scoreboard into the flood and the drain (rules review), and 'the young woman' alone is already Tara's in ROLE in cutscenes.py.
cast.essence: The family's scorer. She is a final-year commerce student who works Mummy's Saturday counter and has kept the lane cup's book since she was twelve. She keeps a tally of everything: runs, promises, Papa's corrections, who said what and when. Ask her about herself and she answers with somebody else's score. She is the third woman of Nani's line to sit at a table keeping count (Nani at her grocery counter, Mummy at the shop, Tinku at the scorer's table), and the only one keeping it for a game rather than a till. The picture a reader keeps: a wiry young woman on a plastic chair with her knees drawn up and a wide book across them. Quoted line: 'Third time. Three-nil.' | 'तीसरी बार। तीन-ज़ीरो।' | 'Teesri baar. 3-0.' Players who would say 'I know this person': Meena, for the quiet skill with numbers, and Ravi, the younger one at the counter of a family business.
cast.backstory: Tinku was born in 2005 in the junction town, a month early and small, six years after Mummy opened the shop. Nani held her and said she was as light as a tinka, a straw, and that a straw bends and does not break. The family turned tinka into Tinku. It is Nani's pet name, about smallness, so it carries no 'tomboy' story (Hindi-first readers still check how it reads to players; owner question 1). The name has stuck to her the way 'the youngest' has, and she minds both. At eight she sat on the shop counter counting fuses into tens. Every summer until the grocery shut in 2016, Nani taught her to keep accounts in the grocery's old cloth-bound ledger, and Tinku still crosses her sevens the way Nani does. When she was twelve, the lane cup's old scorer could no longer see the far end of the lane. Captain sahab handed the book to the girl who had been keeping her own tally on the wall in chalk. She has scored every cup since, and this August is her tenth. She buys a new scorebook every season. The nine old ones stand in a row on the shelf above her bed, and the back page of every one is blank: the page a scorer keeps for her own notes. She is in the final year of a BCom at the town college. Every Saturday she works the shop counter for a day's pay. Her first three months of that pay bought a cheap plain pair of black headphones from a mobile shop on the station road, so she can follow the commentary on her phone while she scores (the radio is Nani's). In March she found the form for the district cricket association's scorers' course. She printed it, folded it into the back of the scorebook, and has not filled it in. Its last date is 20 August. Everyone calls her Tinku. Her given name is used only at college and is never shown, because the household marks no community (rule 21).
cast.want_fear_contradiction: WANT, THIS YEAR: to count as more than 'the youngest', with a place on the district association's scorers' course (owner question 2). WANT FROM YOU: to be treated as an equal. On cup day she hands you the decisions ('Today, your call') to see what you do with them, and she is scoring you while she asks. FEAR: being 'the youngest' for ever, left in the junction town keeping everyone else's numbers while everyone calls you. Under that: that she is only useful for counting other people's things. CONTRADICTION: she keeps exact score of everyone else's game, but never writes down her own. It shows the same way every time. Asked about herself (her marks, her plans, the form), she answers with somebody else's score ('My marks? Papa's corrected four times today.'), and the back page of her scorebook stays blank. This contradiction is hers alone in the cast; the player's file keeps only 'everyone calls you, nobody asks' (comics review). THE COST, ON SCREEN (India review: every capable woman pays one real price): her silence nearly loses her the course. The form has sat in the back of the book since March, and its last date is 20 August. She sends it only on cup night, after Captain sahab says the district should see her book (chapter 4, proposed). Her year turns there, and it pays off in December, when the letter comes and she writes on the back page for the first time (chapter 5).
relationships: NANI: Nani taught her accounts on the grocery's old ledger, every summer from eight to eleven, and gave her her name. Tinku keeps Nani's carrom scores and medicine times (8, 2, 8) inside the scorebook's front cover. She is the only grandchild who drops every English word for Nani: plain polite Hindi, आप, every word in full. Nani is the only person she switches her phone to the Hindi keyboard for. Nani calls her 'scorer' | 'स्कोरर', the one English word Nani took up for her, and never 'the youngest'. Friction: Nani cheats at carrom, and Tinku writes it down. Tenderness: after the fall, Tinku knows every dose without looking, and when Nani comes home from the ward Tinku is at the door: 'Eighty, not out, Nani.' (proposed; see year_arc). Nani greets her with a hand on her shoulder, never on her head (rules review: an elder's hand on a head reads as a blessing).

MUMMY: Tinku works her Saturday counter and keeps the stock tally on her phone. Mummy is hardest on her because Tinku is most like her: both answer every question with a number, Mummy with a time or a price, Tinku with a score. Friction: both want to hold the count. In the July flood they argue over whose tally of wet stock is right, and both are. Tenderness: Mummy pays her a full day's rate every Saturday, the same as any hand, and Tinku knows that is Mummy's way of saying she is good at it. Tinku grew past her at fifteen, by a clear half head, and Mummy pretends not to notice (Mummy's file). She says आप to Mummy, exactly as to Papa.

PAPA: she is the only one who can make him laugh, by scoring his corrections ('Papa, that's the fourth not-9:45 today.'). He taught her to read a timetable at seven, and she taught him to read a scorebook at fifty. She reads his messages with full stops correctly and explains them to the family: 'He's not cross. That's just his full stop.' Friction: he wants her to sit the railway's recruitment exam for a safe job, and she has not told him about the course (the same exam as Papa's file; the draft's bank exams did not match). Tenderness: on the night train he counts the family, she counts them again behind him, and they nod to each other. In December he books her train to the course without being asked (Papa's file, proposal). She says आप and 'Papa'.

MAMA JI: the uncle whose gifts are too expensive to use; one is still in its box. She scores his promises: 'You said March, Mama ji. Nil for one.' Friction: he calls her 'the youngest' at every family function, and it is the one thing that makes her lose her temper (she reads him his whole record, fast). Tenderness: in December, when his numbers keep growing, she quietly keeps the real count for him, and it matches Mami's. She says आप and 'Mama ji'.

MAUSI: Tinku did her Class 3 sums in Mausi's tuition class in her front room. Mausi still checks her sums, tells everyone her marks ('Sau mein sau, hai na?' is Mausi's tease, so Tinku no longer uses it) and asks about her plans three questions at a time. Tinku answers with a score. Friction: Mausi talks over her. Tenderness: Mausi remembers that at nine Tinku wanted to be a cricket commentator, and she is the only one who still brings it up. आप, 'Mausi'.

MAUSA JI: they watch matches side by side without talking. She scores, and he says 'Hmm' at every wicket. He is the only adult who never calls her 'the youngest', and the only person she lets turn the pages of her scorebook. आप, 'Mausa ji'.

MASTERJI: he stitched her first school uniform, and he still says she is too thin for any pattern. She brings him his eleven o'clock tea on Saturdays, and he checks the time by it. Friction: he says she slouches over that book. Tenderness: in the flood week she counts his wet bolts of cloth too, without being asked. आप, 'Masterji'.

CAPTAIN SAHAB: he taught her to keep the lane cup's book at twelve, and in August he says the district should see it. She teases him about his one state trial ('Your one trial again, Captain sahab?'; no year on screen, rule 2), always with आप. She is the successor he has not named. Friction: she once scored a no-ball against his own lane in front of everyone, and he has never said she was right. Tenderness: he gives her his chair in the shade. Their voices never cross: he makes the calls (the toss, 'Straight bat', the umpire's verdicts) and she keeps the score; the toss line is only ever his (comics review). In a panel the painter tells them apart by shape: her seated angles, ponytail and wide book against his tall, standing, side-on figure, hat and ball, both against one mid-grey plastered wall.

MAMI: Mami thinks Tinku should do a proper accounts course, and says so at every function. Tinku keeps a tally of how often: 'That's four, Mami.' Friction: Mami asks her to take the headphones off for the wedding week, and she does not. Tenderness: the two list-keepers end the wedding checking each other's counts, and Mami's sixty matches Tinku's sixty. आप, 'Mami'.

YOU: her older sibling, and her rival for being the one everyone calls. She keeps one tally nobody knows about: how many times the family called you this year. She uses no address word for you, or 'oye' (you answer 'oye, scorer', in the You file). Never bhai, bro, didi or bhaiya (rule 8), and no longer 'suno', which is Mausi's and Mummy's (comics review). She says तुम to you, as many brothers and sisters close in age do. One Delhi speaker in the realism notes used आप for her elder brother (source [5]), so Hindi-first readers settle it (rules review). In Hindi her तुम lines to you are only commands, 'who should' questions and lines where you are not the doer (rule 66). Never तू, which can carry contempt (realism notes 1.1, sources [3] and [5]). You say तुम to her. Friction: Mama ji calls you, not her. Tenderness: in August she hands you the calls, and in December you are the first person she tells about the letter, before Mummy. You are the only one who names her habit out loud ('Scorer, write your own score too.', in the You file).

THE LANE SIDE (chapter 4's circle): she knows all ten from ten years of scoring. In her own bubbles she never names, points at or describes anyone on a decision's cards before or during that decision (rule 36). Her judging notes stay in game words, fall as often on men as on women (the chapter 4 check counted 2 and 2), and never touch the job being asked. None of them is painted near her in a decision's lead-in (rules 32 and 36).
HER COLLEGE FRIENDS: never drawn and never named. They are the ones who get her stickers and voice notes.
cast.year_arc: OPENING (January, present day): face-on on the household screen with the label 'Tinku, your sister'. In the kitchen beside Papa she holds her shut scorebook and says 'August 15. Lane cup. I'm scoring.' | '15 अगस्त। गली का कप। स्कोर मेरा।' (draft 1.04). CHAPTER 1 (May, Lugdi, the night train, coach S4): on the platform she counts heads behind Papa. In the coach she lies on her stomach on an upper berth, ponytail hanging over the edge, headphones round her neck. A proposed exchange, so that the household talks to each other (the players' judge asked for this): Papa gives the count, fourteen people and ten berths (bible section 8; the draft's sixteen and twelve are gone), and Tinku answers without a number: 'Counted twice, Papa.' | 'दो बार गिने, पापा।' | 'Do baar gine, Papa.' [WAITS rulebook Q11: while it is open she may speak only in chapter 4; until then she is painted and silent here]. CHAPTER 2 (May, Rukavat, the ward night): she is at Nani's house with the cousins and the little ones. At 8 am comes one message card in Devanagari with Nani's medicine times, the only Hindi-keyboard message in the take [WAITS Q11]. When Nani comes home she is at the door, small but face-on: 'Eighty, not out, Nani.' | 'अस्सी, नॉट आउट, नानी।' | '80, not out, Nani.' Here 'not out' means Nani came through the fall. The line moved from the album, which now keeps only Nani's count and your reply (comics review) [proposal; WAITS Q11 and rulebook Q5 on jokes, though the line is written warm]. CHAPTER 3 (July, Station, the flood): at the Saturday counter beside Mummy, sleeves pushed up, jeans rolled to mid-calf, keeping the wet-stock tally. The two who are most alike argue over whose count is right, and both are. When the shutter goes up: 'Shutter up at nine. Not out, Mummy.' [WAITS Q11; otherwise painted and silent]. CHAPTER 4 (15 August, Cricket, the lane cup): her chapter; she asks all eight decisions. A proposed wordless panel before 4.02 shows her own past (comics review: one wordless panel each for the five at risk of reading as stock): the shelf above her bed with nine worn scorebooks in a row and a gap for the tenth, no people. She wakes you ('Up! Cup day.', 4.02), hands you the decisions ('Two targets. Today, your call.', 4.04) and scores your calls while she asks. She is painted face-on or three-quarter in her chapter, seated knees-up with the book, not from behind as draft 4.04, 4.06, 4.15 and 4.26 have her (the players' judge: every asker seen from behind; owner answer 6). Fixes adopted from the continuity read: 4.05 becomes 'Ten to pick from.' | 'चुनने को दस।', decision 2 becomes 'Three fielders, one a keeper.', and the captain stage is dropped from decisions 1 and 5. That stage clashes with Captain sahab's title (rule 36), and the making judge says it cannot be built. The turn: at 4.26, at dusk, the scorebook lies open on her knees for the first time, turned to the blank back page. Proposed for Captain sahab, off the panel at 4.27, in his own chapter: 'That book. Show the district.' | 'वो किताब। ज़िले को दिखाओ।' That night she sends the form, five days before its last date [proposal]. CHAPTER 5 (December, Jadugar, the wedding week): a plain envelope, painted blank, arrives at Nani's house. The letter's words are live text, 'Scorers' course: selected. March.', with no name on it. She tells you first, under the tent lights. Then she writes on the back page for the first time, with the pages turned away (rule 30) [WAITS Q11 for any line]. She wears the headphones all week, though Mami asked her not to. ALBUM (5.29): she is not in it; the album is Nani's. HOW SHE CHANGES: she goes from keeping everyone's score and hiding her own to writing her own line; from 'the youngest' to 'the scorer' and 'your sister'; and, with you, from rival to equal. LINES: in chapter 4, about 10 bubbles plus her question balloons on the plain decisions (hard decisions use the plain box, rule 37); in the opening, 1; in every other chapter 0 to 2, all waiting on Q11. OWNER QUESTIONS: (1) Does the name Tinku lean male for Hindi-belt players? If readers say yes, keep it with Nani's reason above, or choose a pet name they hear for girls as often as for boys. (2) Her want is the district scorers' course. Does it suit her, or should her want stay inside the family? (A fallback: taking over the shop's books from Mummy.) (3) Should her silent and spoken appearances outside chapter 4 go ahead (rulebook Q11)? (4) 'Eighty, not out, Nani.' at Nani's homecoming (rulebook Q5). (5) Tinku says आप to both Mummy and Papa, so the household keeps respect equal, and तुम to you. Is that right for this family? (6) Hindi-first readers should confirm तीन-ज़ीरो over the cast map's formal तीन-शून्य. (7) Over-ear headphones or a neckband earphone (India review; see revision notes).

voice.register: Quick, warm and teasing: the fastest young voice in the house, and the one that sounds most like a 21-year-old at a small-town college. She talks in short, quick lines, mostly three to eight words, with the verb kept in more often than not, and many of them are questions. Her own shapes: (1) the tally tease, someone's habit counted to their face and softened with 'haan?' ('Papa aaj 4 baar tok chuke. Record.', 'Achha Mami, aaj ye 4 baar, haan?'); (2) the quick English question when something happens again ('Seriously? Phir se?'), which is also how her cross run starts; (3) the dodge: asked about herself, she answers with somebody else's count; (4) now and then, once a chapter at most, a live commentary aside from the commentator she wanted to be at nine ('Aur ye gaya!'). Feelings come in plain words, often English ones, and the joke comes after, never instead ('Sorry, meri galti. 14 nahin, 15.', 'Thank you.', 'Jaldi aana, yaar. Main din ginungi.'). Cricket is how she sees the lane cup and how she talks with Captain sahab, who gave her the book; with everyone else it shows only in her counting. In chapter 4 her questions are the decisions themselves, asked plainly with no tag (rule 37), crisp and warm, never the comic one. To Nani she slows into whole, careful, polite Hindi sentences with -इए, no English and no tag. Moved, she goes very short and plain ('March. Jawaab: haan.'). Cross, she gets faster but not louder (Mausi is the one who gets louder): flat and exact, she reads out the record in two or three chained bubbles, then the book snaps shut and the ear cups go on. She talks most to you, as an equal and a rival; then to Nani, in polite Hindi.
voice.mix: Young small-town Hinglish, the way a final-year commerce student talks at home: a Hindi frame with short English clauses dropped in ('Seriously?', 'Wait, wait', 'not now', 'No way') and the everyday English verb with kar or ho ('call kiya', 'miss karungi', 'try karo', 'relax kijiye'). Her counting words are a scorer's (baar, ginti, score, total, record); the cricket words (run, over, wicket, keeper, innings) come out on cup day and with Captain sahab, never as a code for a feeling. Commerce words stay out of her speech (stock, bill, balance, hisaab, profit), so the shop family's talk does not tip into the trader idiom; 'tally' and 'total' stay because a scorer uses them. No trending slang ('literally', 'vibe', 'bestie'): her quickness is in the teasing and the counting (realism notes, section 7). The common fillers are hers as much as anyone's (arre, achha, chalo, bas, theek hai, haan), and so is everyday Hindustani (fikr, zaroor, waqt). With Nani: plain polite Hindi, आप, every word in full, no English except Nani's own nouns (doctor, BP) and the one '80, not out, Nani.' at the homecoming. With Mummy, Papa and the other elders: the same Hinglish with आप and ji, her English kept to a word or two ('Seriously, Mama ji?', 'Papa, please, not now.'); her teasing rides on counts, so it never needs a familiar 'you' to an elder. With you: तुम and 'yaar', in commands, 'who should' questions and lines where you are not the doer (rule 66). Hindi mode: natural Hindi that a reader with little English follows easily. Her English clauses turn into Hindi ('Seriously?' is 'सच में?', 'Wait, wait' is 'रुकिए, रुकिए', 'Relax' is 'आराम से'); only the loans every Hindi reader knows stay (सॉरी, थैंक यू, स्कोर, रिकॉर्ड, पार्टी, स्पीकर, and रन, विकेट on cup day), and she says तीन-ज़ीरो, not the formal तीन-शून्य (Hindi-first readers confirm). Hinglish mode: every number is a figure ('3 baar', '4 chammach'), so a number is never misread as a word. English mode: plain young Indian English, numbers as words, 'haan?' and 'yaar' kept, and 'zero' rather than the British 'nil'.
tics: The tally tease: counts someone's habit out loud, to their face, then 'haan?': 'Achha Mami, aaj ye 4 baar, haan?' | 'अच्छा मामी, आज ये चार बार, हाँ?' | 'Okay, Mami, that's four times today, haan?' Only counts, scores and totals, never an ordinal, a clock time or a price.
Ends a tease with 'haan?' | 'हाँ?', in every mode. Not on a moved line, not to Nani, and not on a chapter 4 question.
The quick English question when something happens again: 'Seriously? Phir se?' | 'सच में? फिर से?' | 'Seriously? Again?' It is how her cross run starts.
The dodge, her contradiction: asked about herself (her marks, her plans, the form), she answers with somebody else's count, a different person each time: 'Main? Papa aaj 4 baar tok chuke. Record.'
Says 'Kitaab mein.' when anyone makes a promise: it is written down now. Never after a report of harassment or a dowry demand (rule 22).
Hands a choice over with 'Faisla tumhara.' It is a test, not a shrug: she scores what you do with it.

The commentary aside, at most once a chapter: calls a small household moment live, in the present tense, like a commentator: 'Aur ye gaya!' | 'और ये गया!' | 'And there it goes!'; 'Aur Mama ji gate par! Kya entry!'
Says the feeling first, in plain words, then the joke or the fact: 'Sorry, meri galti.' before the corrected count; 'Thank you.' before the thing she is thanking you for.
When cross: faster and flatter, never louder; the record in two or three chained bubbles, then the book shut and the ear cups on.
catchphrases: 'Kitaab mein.' | 'किताब में।' | 'In the book.' (when anyone promises something; verbless, so it marks no gender)
'Seriously? Phir se?' | 'सच में? फिर से?' | 'Seriously? Again?' (new, from the readers' note; the start of her cross run, most often at Mama ji)
'Faisla tumhara.' | 'फ़ैसला तुम्हारा।' | 'Your call.' (you are not the doer; the rule 66 checker flags तुम्हारा at a sentence end and a native reader clears it, since it agrees with फ़ैसला)
voice.exclamation: 'Gazab!' | 'ग़ज़ब!' | 'Brilliant!' Kept: the readers marked it as ringing true, and it sounds like UP, which suits a junction town. Nobody else in the cast takes it as their exclamation. Bright for a good surprise (a cousin's job, a phone call, the last ball); flat and ironic for a bad one (the lights going out: 'Gazab! Batti gul, khel band.'). Typed, it stretches: 'gazabbb'. Religious meaning: none in everyday Hindi, where it means 'amazing' or 'unbelievable'. Guard: never in 'ग़ज़ब ख़ुदा का' or 'ख़ुदा का ग़ज़ब' ('God's wrath'), and never followed by any name. The English 'Brilliant!' avoids every mild word that hides a holy name (Gosh, Blimey, Crikey, Goodness). A Hindi-first and an Urdu-speaking reader confirm; fallback 'Zabardast!' | 'ज़बरदस्त!' | 'Terrific!'.

Fifteen, not fourteen.' To an elder, the same words with the name ('Sorry, Papa. Meri galti.'). To Nani, in Hindi only: 'Nani, galti ho gayi. Abhi theek karti hoon.' | 'नानी, ग़लती हो गई। अभी ठीक करती हूँ।' | 'My mistake, Nani. I'll put it right now.' One sorry and no food in her hand, so it never sounds like Mausi's 'Sorry, sorry, sorry!' with a plate held out. To Captain sahab, the same plain words turned round: 'Galti meri, Captain sahab.' | 'ग़लती मेरी, कप्तान साहब।' | 'My fault, Captain sahab.' THANKS: a plain 'Thank you', then the thing she is thanking for: to you, 'Thank you. Kal raat ki dawai tumne sambhali.' | 'थैंक यू। कल रात की दवाई तुमने सँभाली।' | 'Thanks. You handled last night's medicines.' (the ने past agrees with दवाई, so it gives you no gender; you are its doer, so it waits on the owner's rule 66 ruling, as her address note on you says). To an elder, 'Thank you, Mausa ji.' with the name. To Nani, in Hindi: 'Nani, aapne bacha liya.' | 'नानी, आपने बचा लिया।' | 'Nani, you saved me.' WHEN SHE IS THANKED: she brushes it off and puts the credit in someone else's column, which is her contradiction again: 'Arre Masterji, kuch nahin. Bas gin liya.' | 'अरे मास्टरजी, कुछ नहीं। बस गिन लिया।' | 'Oh, it's nothing, Masterji. I only counted.' When Captain sahab thanks her for the book, the credit in his column and the blame in hers: 'Sab aapka sikhaya hai, Captain sahab.' / 'Galtiyaan bas meri.' | 'सब आपका सिखाया है, कप्तान साहब।' / 'ग़लतियाँ बस मेरी।' | 'You taught me all of it, Captain sahab.' / 'Only the mistakes are mine.' (not 'Kis baat ka?' or the book, which are his own words in the same moment). LOVE: plain and short, never in a cricket code. To you at a parting: 'Jaldi aana, yaar. Main din ginungi.' | 'जल्दी आना, यार। मैं दिन गिनूँगी।' | 'Come back soon, yaar. I'll be counting the days.' (a real idiom in both languages, her counting turned tender). After a hard week: 'Baitho, yaar. Tumne bahut kiya.' The one love line in cricket is the birthday saying everyone in India knows, once a year, when Nani comes home: '80, not out, Nani.' | 'अस्सी, नॉट आउट, नानी।' | 'Eighty, not out, Nani.'

Mummy: 'Mummy' | 'मम्मी', आप, the same as to Papa, so respect is equal between the parents (realism notes 1.1, source [6]). When Mummy is cross she calls her 'Tinku ji', with आप, and Tinku knows at once that she is in trouble.
Papa: 'Papa' | 'पापा', आप.
Mama ji: 'Mama ji' | 'मामा जी', आप. Mami: 'Mami' | 'मामी', आप.
Mausi: 'Mausi' | 'मौसी', आप. Mausa ji: 'Mausa ji' | 'मौसा जी', आप.
Masterji: 'Masterji' | 'मास्टरजी', आप. Captain sahab: 'Captain sahab' | 'कप्तान साहब', आप.

You (the player): mostly no address word. When she wants one, 'yaar' | 'यार', the everyday word that young women and men all over north India use to a sibling or a friend, which marks no gender (the owner and the readers clear it under rules 8 and 66). 'oye' | 'ओए' only now and then, mostly typed, never to an elder. तुम, because 'elder' in her file means a generation up (Hindi-first readers settle it). Her Hindi to you is commands (उठो, चुनो, बैठो, आना), 'who should' questions (कौन देखे?) and lines where you are not the doer (फ़ैसला तुम्हारा). Two lines wait on the owner: 'तुमने बहुत किया।' and 'दवाई तुमने सँभाली।', pasts with ने where you are the doer and the verb agrees with the thing done, so they mark no gender, but rule 66 names only three shapes; the owner either adds this as a fourth shape or the native reader puts each line on the build's cleared list (no wording change if the owner agrees). Never बेटा, भैया or दीदी. You call her 'Tinku', and 'scorer' at most once a chapter.
People on the cards: first names only, and only in rule 38's fixed line after a pick, never before or during a decision.
While rulebook Q7 is open, nobody calls Tinku 'beta' either, so you are not the only one without a pet name.

habits: Her phone: a plain phone in a plain dark case, one corner of the screen protector cracked. It is painted with a blank screen and every message is live text (rule 30). No brand, app name, app look or 'forwarded' label (rule 3).
Two thumbs, fast. A one-word holding reply within seconds ('k', 'ok'), and the real reply comes later.

Roman Hinglish, all in lowercase, with no full stops: a new line for each thought, one question mark at most and never two. Never all capitals, which people her age read as shouting (realism notes 2.1).
More English than her speech: whole short English phrases sit here that she would say only in part aloud ('called u again', 'form sent', 'miss u').
Her numbers, typed: always digits, and only counts, scores and totals, in shorthand (3-0, 14/14, 1 mein 0, 2x). No clock times, durations or prices, in typing as in speech.

Stretched letters for warmth and for her exclamation: 'yesss', 'nooo', 'thank youuu', 'gazabbb'. Short forms: k, ok, idk, u, ur, pls, lol, no. for 'number'. To elders she types 'aap' and 'aapne', never 'u'.
Plain sorry and thanks type the way she says them: 'sorry yaar', 'thank youuu', then the reason on the next line.

Emoji: few, and only faces and objects: 🙂 😐 😂 😅 🏏. No thumbs-up: to people her age it reads as cold. No person emoji, since one carries a gender and a skin tone. Stickers go only to her college friends, and only drawn objects (a cup of tea, a duck for out-for-nil), never a famous face (rule 3).
To Nani she switches to the Hindi keyboard: Devanagari, whole words, the full stop (।), no emoji and no English. Then she calls anyway. Nani is the only person she does this for.
To Papa she copies his layout of one fact a line, but keeps her lowercase and drops his full stops, as a tease. She is the one who tells the family that his full stops do not mean he is cross.
Voice notes: never to elders (realism notes 2.3), only to friends. She plays Mausi's long voice notes at double speed.
When: late at night and between lectures. Never at the table while Nani is speaking; she is not a phone addict (the cast map's caricature guard).
She never forwards anything. She sends a photo of a total instead (painted blank, with the figures as live text). Almost no typos, and her numbers are always right.
The family group can be mentioned but never shown (owner, 23 Oct; rule 47). If the story needs her post, it becomes a single message card.

look.build: Height band: middle (comics review: four bands, not ten ranks). Exact gaps only for the people she shares panels with: a clear half head taller than Mummy (she grew past her at fifteen, Mummy's file; 'a little' would not paint) and half a head shorter than Papa. Slight and wiry, with long arms and sharp elbows and knees, so she reads as all angles. Her base shape is the triangle, which she shares with Nani and Captain sahab. She and Nani are never painted at the same size in one panel. She is an adult of 21, with an adult face and a woman's proportions, and must never be painted as a schoolgirl (rule 12).
look.face: CLOSE-UP DETAILS ONLY (for inserts and the face chip; at strip size they vanish, comics review): a narrow oval face with a pointed chin and high cheekbones; a small gap between her two front teeth that shows when she grins, which is hers alone in the cast (Mausi's file must drop its matching gap, comics review); a small pale nick through the outer end of her left eyebrow, from a tennis ball at fourteen, which is secondary because the painter may drop it; quick dark-brown eyes, usually narrowed a little, as if checking a total. Her eyebrows are thick, straight and dark, the mark of Nani's line (Nani, Mausi, Mummy, Mama ji, Tinku). They tie her to the family and are nobody's personal feature. A clear forehead with a few loose short strands of hair at the temples, and nothing between the brows. No make-up.
look.skin: Dark brown, like Papa's: the darkest skin of the women in the household. Painter words every time: the tested phrase first, 'South Asian features and warm brown skin', then the depth words 'dark brown in tone' (rules review: only the first phrase was tested against whitening, flux-portrait-biases). She is never lighter in any look. Check hardest in STYLE['now'] and Rukavat's 'sunday' style, the soft styles that whiten skin, and under Lugdi's and Jadugar's lamp light. Compare every pick with her master's skin swatch, not with words.
look.hair: Thick, straight black hair pulled up into a high ponytail at the crown, tied with a plain black elastic and hanging loose to between her shoulder blades. It swings when she moves. The shape is a bump at the crown and a swinging tail, and it is her anchor from behind and in silhouette: hair shape held in every look on the team's drift sheet (method notes). It is the same high ponytail every day of the year: messier at home and on the train, neater with one plain black clip at the wedding. Painter sentence: 'thick straight black hair pulled up into a high ponytail tied at the crown, loose and swinging'. For writers: never a plait (Nani's anchor), a bun (Mummy's), short hair, or hair worn down.
look.glasses_jewellery: No spectacles; the cast's spectacles belong to Nani and Masterji. One tiny plain silver stud in each earlobe (a close-up detail), and nothing else: no chain, ring, nose stud, bangle or watch (she reads the time off her phone). Nothing on her wrists, because a black elastic or thread on a wrist can read as a protective thread, and a plain steel band as a kara (realism notes 5.1, source [22]). WORN, NOT HELD: a cheap plain pair of matte black over-ear headphones, unmarked and with no lights, resting round her neck with the ear cups on her collarbones. She bought them with her first three months of Saturday pay, for the commentary she follows on her phone while she scores; the radio is Nani's (India review). They count as worn, so they never also appear in a hand, and they go on her head only when she is cross. Kept over a neckband earphone for the reason in the revision notes; owner question 7.
outfits: EVERYDAY (her signature, in most panels): a dark petrol-blue crew-neck cotton T-shirt with solid black raglan sleeves to just above the elbow (the black runs in a diagonal seam from the underarm to the collar), with no print and no letters; pale faded blue straight jeans rolled once at the ankle; plain white canvas lace-up shoes; the headphones round her neck.
SATURDAY SHOP COUNTER (chapter 3): the same, with the sleeves pushed up. In the flood her jeans are rolled to mid-calf and her shoes are swapped for dark blue rubber slippers.

HOME AND THE NIGHT TRAIN (the opening's kitchen, chapter 1's berth): the same petrol-blue raglan T-shirt, older and softer, over plain grey cotton track pants with no stripes; dark blue rubber slippers; socks on the berth.

WINTER (January and December mornings): a plain black zip-up hoodie worn open over the T-shirt, hood down, no print, no drawstrings. The open black front keeps her dark top edge over the petrol-blue body.

WEDDING WEEK (chapter 5): her signature colour and pattern at its usual scale, in a finer cloth (comics review: the costume stays). A straight dark petrol-blue cotton-silk kurta to the knee with black three-quarter sleeves and a narrow black edge at the hem, over black churidar. A plain black cotton dupatta laid over both shoulders and pinned at each shoulder so it falls straight down her back, never over her head and never across her chest, because the one diagonal across the chest in the cast is Mummy's (comics review). Plain black sandals with no heel; one plain black clip at the base of the ponytail; the tiny silver studs; the headphones still round her neck, though Mami asked her not to. No bangles, no mehendi. Not red, so nobody mistakes her for the bride, who is never shown. This replaces the kurti over jeans: at a small-town home wedding Nani and Mummy would send her back to change, and it reads as the rebel-girl cliché (India review).
look.colour_key: Her colours: a dark petrol-blue body (a dark greyish blue with only a hint of green, bluer and darker than the draft's teal), solid black sleeves, black headphones, pale faded blue jeans, white shoes, and the scorebook's dark brown binding with a cream page edge. Her value stack is what carries her, and it holds even in two inks (comics review): a dark top edge (black sleeves and headphones), a mid-dark body, light legs, white feet, and the black ponytail above. The body colour is the weakest anchor, because mid tones drift (rules review), so her checklist leads with the ponytail, the black sleeves and the white shoes. PROVISIONAL: the chapter look lines and the code STYLE disagree (rules review: Cricket 'slate-green and chalk-white' against 'deep outfield greens, chalk white and cherry red'; Jadugar 'flat crimson, gold and black' against vermilion, magenta, indigo night, emerald and old gold). This key is checked again on each look's strip once one string per look is settled. Look by look, against the code STYLE as it stands: NOW (clean ink, soft flat fills): true petrol blue, black, pale blue, white. LUGDI (violet and indigo shadow, vermilion and marigold lamplight): the body sinks towards indigo, so the lamp catches the cream page edge, the white shoes and the outline of the ponytail; keep the body cooler than the lamps. STATION (enamel blue and black on cream): the body a mid halftone of enamel blue, the sleeves and ponytail solid black, the jeans a light halftone, the shoes the cream of the paper, the book a dark block with a cream edge. JADUGAR (vermilion, magenta, indigo night, emerald, old gold): petrol blue sits between Mami's indigo and Nani's emerald, so light her with the lamps and check her on the Jadugar strip beside both before any master (comics review). CRICKET: petrol blue is bluer than outfield green or slate green but close to slate in value, so she is never painted against grass. Her shared panels with Captain sahab use one mid-grey plastered wall, against which her white shoes, black sleeves and his white hat all read (comics review); a whitewashed wall would swallow his hat. Captain sahab is the only cherry red. RUKAVAT (teak, faded teal, cream, one signal orange): her body fades towards the palette's teal, and the black sleeves stay the darkest thing in the panel. Never the signal orange, which in chapter 2 belongs to Mausa ji's orange. The draft's ochre book is gone: ochre sat too close to the yellow the game uses to mean 'chosen' (rule 38).
look.prop: THE SCOREBOOK: a wide oblong cloth-bound book, about twice as wide as it is tall, that opens sideways like a ledger, with a plain dark brown cloth binding worn pale at the corners and a cream page edge. The wide shape is the anchor, not the colour (comics review). A short plain unpainted wooden pencil is tucked into the spine. She buys a new one every season and has done since she was twelve; this is the tenth, and the nine old ones stand above her bed. Inside: pale, blank pages with no ruling, because ruled lines invite painted digits (rules review) and every figure is live text (rule 30). Nani's medicine times and Papa's 'not 9:45s' are kept inside the front cover (story only, never painted). The back page, a scorer's own page, stays blank until December. HANDS: shut and clamped under her arm, or across her knees when she sits. The pencil is in her other hand, or between her teeth, and then in no hand. Left and right are a preference to check, never what tells her apart (comics review). GLOSSARY ROWS, keyed only as written (rules review): 'scorebook': 'The scorebook is a wide oblong cloth-bound book about twice as wide as it is tall, with a plain dark brown cloth binding worn pale at the corners and a cream page edge; it opens sideways like a ledger, and its pages are pale and blank.' 'scorer's pencil' (not 'pencil', which would fire on the calendar's pencil rings): 'The scorer's pencil is a short plain unpainted wooden pencil.' Both rows avoid the old trigger words 'cover', 'flat', 'seat' and 'box', and the probe run on them found no old row firing. Her master is painted holding the book, so she and her prop take one reference slot (comics review). Its thick wide block keeps it apart from Papa's floppy clear sleeve and Mami's rigid clipboard. SECONDARY: her phone (plain, in a plain dark case, screen blank).
look.silhouette: Seated, which is her default and her front image (comics review: from the neck up she is the stock game young person; what is hers alone is the scorer's pose): a slight figure on a plastic chair with her knees drawn up and her feet on the front edge of the chair, a wide oblong book across her knees, a high ponytail sticking up and back from the crown, and the bumps of the ear cups at her neck. A stack of angles. Standing: slim and upright, weight on one hip, the wide book clamped under her arm as a horizontal block, and the ponytail. The black-shape test at phone size: the knees-up seated block with a wide book on top, and the bump of the high ponytail, are two things nobody else has. FAR (small in a crowd, painted from words with no reference; comics review): a slight figure with a high black ponytail, a dark top edge over a mid-dark body, pale legs and white shoes, seated knees-up if sitting. Beside Captain sahab, the other face in her chapter, her seated angles and ponytail stand against his tall, standing, side-on figure and his hat brim, so the painter cannot swap them.
look.shoes: Plain white canvas lace-up shoes with thin white rubber soles, scuffed grey at the toes, with no stripes, no logo and no coloured heel tab. At home, on the train and in the flood: dark blue rubber slippers with plain straps. At the wedding: plain black sandals with no heel. On the train berth her shoes are off and her socks on.

posture.stance: Weight on her right hip, the book clamped under her arm, head tilted a little as if checking a total. She rises onto her toes when a ball is in the air. She is never quite still: the ponytail is always moving.
posture.sitting: Her default, and her front image: knees drawn up on a plastic chair, feet on its front edge, the scorebook across her knees, leaning forward over it. Cross-legged on a durrie at lunch. On her stomach on an upper train berth, ponytail hanging over the edge. At home, sitting low on a durrie beside Nani's armchair with her back against its side (written so because 'floor' would pull in the old take's Nashik bedroom, rules review). She never takes Nani's chair.
posture.walk: Quick short steps, ponytail swinging. She often walks backwards for a few steps while she finishes a sentence to someone behind her. The book is under one arm, so her free hand can hold up a score.
gestures: Spins the pencil once round her thumb before she says a score. It replaces the draft's double tap, which Papa and Mausa ji also had (comics review). A close-up gesture.
Holds up fingers to show a score, three for 'third time', with the other hand closed. Nani counts heads with one pointing finger; Tinku shows totals with an open hand.
Slides one ear cup up off her ear when she is really listening, and back down when she is done with the conversation.
Holds the pencil between her teeth while she thinks, and then it is in no hand.
Lifts the pencil once when the umpire signals, as a scorer does to acknowledge it (team knowledge, not from an opened source).
expressions: Neutral: chin down over the book, ponytail still, the pencil turning in her fingers, eyes narrowed a little.
Pleased: a quick grin that shows the gap in her teeth; up off the chair onto her toes, a fist round the pencil.
Worried: the shut book pressed to her chest with both arms, shoulders up, the pencil between her teeth.

Cross: fast, not quiet (comics review: most of the house goes quiet when cross). She reads out the whole record in one breath, snaps the book shut one-handed and pulls both ear cups up over her ears, the only time the headphones go on her head.
Laughing: head back, ponytail swinging behind the chair, one hand over the gap in her teeth, knees pulled up.
Tired: slumped sideways on the plastic chair, the book open face down on her knees, headphones round her neck with nothing playing.
Moved: looks down at the book and runs her thumb along its edge, and does not look up. The one time she cannot keep score.

across_looks: 1. The high ponytail at the crown: the strongest anchor. Hair shape held in every look on the team's drift sheet (method notes).
2. The seated scorer's pose, knees drawn up with a wide book across them: her front image, and her default in chapter 4 (comics review).
3. The dark top edge: solid black raglan sleeves and black headphones over a mid-dark petrol-blue body, even where colour is gone (Station).
4. Light legs and white shoes under the dark top.
5. The wide oblong dark brown scorebook with its cream page edge, whenever the scene has it, painted into her master so it travels in her reference.
6. Skin: 'South Asian features and warm brown skin, dark brown in tone' in every prompt.
7. A slight, wiry, angular build.
8. A clear forehead, a clean hair parting and bare wrists.

STRIP ANCHORS (checked on every full-figure pick, where a standing figure is roughly 200 screen pixels tall, comics review): items 1 to 5. CLOSE-UP DETAILS (checked only on inserts and the face chip): the family eyebrows, the tooth gap, the eyebrow nick, the silver studs, the pencil spin.
ALLOWED TO DRIFT: the exact face. The reference picture carries the face, which is the least stable anchor (method notes).
LOOK STRINGS FIRST: one string per look must be settled (the chapter look lines against the code STYLE, rules review) before her colour key or any reference is trusted.

HOW EACH LOOK IS MADE: each look's reference is made from the present-day master with the edit model (Flux2KleinEdit), never painted fresh. Order: Cricket first (her chapter), then present day (the opening), then Station, Lugdi, Rukavat and Jadugar as rulebook Q11 allows.

CRICKET: story panels use STORY_STYLE['cricket'], the gouache sports annual. Faces hold better there than in the halftone 'photograph' portrait template, which washes faces out (inventory painter notes).
PRESENT DAY: STYLE['now'] bakes in 'cool rainy-evening blues', but her January kitchen needs a present-day entry with no fixed weather (inventory painter notes; checked in cutscenes.py).
cast.painter_prompt: LOOKS ENTRY (body and clothes only, word for word every time; the code puts the role word 'the ponytailed young woman' in front of it; stance, hands and props go in the scene words, rules review): a slight, wiry 21-year-old Indian woman with South Asian features and warm brown skin, dark brown in tone, a narrow oval face with a pointed chin, high cheekbones and thick straight dark eyebrows, a clear forehead with a few loose strands of hair at the temples, long arms and sharp elbows and knees, thick straight black hair pulled up into a high ponytail tied at the crown, loose and swinging, one tiny plain silver stud in each earlobe, plain matte black over-ear headphones resting round her neck with the ear cups on her collarbones, a plain dark petrol-blue crew-neck cotton T-shirt with solid black raglan sleeves to just above the elbow and no print, pale faded blue straight jeans rolled once at the ankle, and plain white canvas lace-up shoes with thin white rubber soles. MASTER SCENE (her front image, in the present-day style): She sits on a white plastic chair against a plain mid-grey plastered wall, her knees drawn up and her feet on the front edge of the chair. A scorebook lies shut across her knees under her left hand, and a scorer's pencil is in her right hand. She looks straight out at the viewer with a small grin that shows a gap between her front teeth. Her head is about a third of the way down the picture, with plain wall above it. Then the look's STYLE string word for word, then STORY_NO. PANEL TAG (30 words, for panels where her reference picture is supplied, comics review): wiry 21-year-old Indian woman, South Asian features and warm brown skin, dark brown, high black ponytail, black headphones round her neck, petrol-blue T-shirt with black sleeves, pale jeans, white shoes. The glossary probe (glossary_probe.py's method) finds no old row firing and no undefined need-list word in any of the three.
painter_avoid: A forehead dot or bindi. FLUX.2 klein paints one on nearly every Indian woman whatever the prompt says. Check every face close up (forehead, hair parting, neck). The dot paint-out (DOTS) and the per-face seed bump (SEED_BUMP) exist only in portraits.py; cutscenes.py has three fixed seeds and no dot clean-up (rules review, confirmed in the code). Before any face-on panel of her, the panel painter needs a per-panel seed bump and an eye-confirmed paint-out, and a person reads every forehead, since Station's halftone dots defeat an automatic finder.
Sindoor or any colour in the hair parting, or any marriage marker (mangalsutra, toe rings, glass bangles, chooda). She is unmarried, and the household shows no marker at all (rule 3).

Any religious or caste mark or object: tilak, a thread on the wrist or ankle, a plain steel band that reads as a kara, a pendant, rudraksha or tulsi beads, a head covering, a dupatta over the head (rule 3; realism notes section 5). At the wedding the dupatta is pinned at both shoulders and falls down her back.
A neckband earphone or any thin black band round her neck, which can be painted as a black-bead chain.

Lightened skin. Write 'South Asian features and warm brown skin, dark brown in tone' every time. The worst risks are STYLE['now'] and Rukavat's 'sunday' style, which lacks the skin words; check under the lamp light of Lugdi and Jadugar too.

Logos, letters or numbers anywhere: on the T-shirt (raglan T-shirts get painted as sports jerseys with numbers), on the headphones, on the shoes (stripes, ticks), on the scorebook's binding and pages (blank, no ruling), on the phone (a plain dark case, never clear). No red-and-black striped pencil, which looks like a brand.
A T-shirt that comes out green, teal or emerald, or anything else the word 'petrol' might summon: it is a dark greyish blue.
A cricket jersey, cap, whites or pads. She is the scorer, not a player, and the old take's Rani is the cricketer in whites.
A school-age look. Painted ages drift young, so no school uniform, no pinafore, no two plaits; check that she reads as 21.
A plait or a bun (Nani's and Mummy's anchors), short hair (Tara in the old take), or hair worn down.
A third hand. The headphones are worn; the book has one hand or her knees; the pencil is in one hand or her teeth. Count hands in every pick (the three-hands lesson).
Headphones on her head (except in the 'cross' expression), or headphones in a hand.
A nose stud, big earrings, more than one stud per ear, make-up, nail colour, mehendi.
Grass behind her in Cricket, and a whitewashed wall behind her when Captain sahab shares the panel: use one mid-grey plastered wall.

Swapping features with Captain sahab when they share a panel (painters mix up attributes between two people; method notes 5.2). Check that the hat, red polo and ball stay on him, and the ponytail, headphones and book stay on her.
Lane players, or anyone who could be a card person, in the background of her decision lead-ins (rules 32 and 36).
A hand or object reaching out of the frame towards the viewer, which would read as yours (rule 7). Papers meant for you lie face up, facing the viewer.
An elder's hand on her head, which reads as a blessing (rule 3). Nani's greeting is a hand on her shoulder; in the homecoming panel Nani's hands stay on her cane.

Names in a prompt. Her own name gets painted as lettering; any person's name, possessives included, makes looks() add that person's whole look (rules review). So 'Nani's chair' is written 'an empty cane armchair', and people-free panels carry no names.

The old glossary's trigger words in her scene words: 'seat', 'cover', 'flat', 'floor', 'stands', 'watch', 'match', 'bench', 'box', 'card', 'ground', 'run', 'bat' (each appends an old-take row or is on the need list; rules review probe). Write 'front edge of the chair', 'binding', 'oblong', 'durrie', 'sandals with no heel'.
'Border' anywhere in her clothes, which fights STORY_NO's 'no border'. Her kurta hem has a black 'edge'.

FRONT IMAGE AND MASTER: the seated scorer in the present-day style, knees drawn up on a white plastic chair against a plain mid-grey plastered wall, the scorebook shut across her knees, the pencil in her other hand, face-on (the master scene in painter_prompt). EXPRESSIONS, head and shoulders, each written as what her body does: neutral, pleased, worried, cross (headphones on her head), laughing, tired, moved.

PROPS, each its own people-free reference: the scorebook shut (binding, spine with the pencil, cream page edge); the scorebook open (pale blank pages, nothing written), including the blank back page; the headphones; the pencil; the phone in a plain dark case with a blank screen.

Nothing written anywhere.'

never_does: Sits on a card or is one of the equal two (rule 10).
Plays the comic one in her own chapter (rule 37). Her teasing is warm, aimed at family habits, never at a card person or a group of people.
