cast.name: Mausi (मौसी), about 55, chapter 1 voice
cast.role: Chapter 1's voice (May, the night train to Nani's, painted in the Lugdi look). Mummy's elder sister and Nani's eldest child. She speaks the chapter's one shout (rule 35) and gives half its judging notes, six in draft 1, each with her face chip; Papa, the asker, gives the rest, so chapter 1's remarks come from a woman and a man (rule 22). She is never the asker (rule 37), never on a card (rule 10), and never names a card person in a bubble (rule 36). Two things set her voice apart from the rest of the cast: in chapter 1 she is the voice with no numbers (Papa owns the figures, so the speaking pair never sound alike), and in a family that shows love only by deeds she is the one who says what she feels out loud. First-time label: 'Mausi, Mummy's elder sister' | 'मौसी, मम्मी की बड़ी बहन' | Hinglish 'Mausi, Mummy ki badi behen' (rule 65); plain 'Mausi' after that, with a tag on every bubble (rule 34). Painter's role word: 'the copper-haired woman', taken from her look. Never her name (names get painted as lettering), and never 'the aunt', because a relation word can paint a second person, the same reason Mausa ji's file gave up 'the aunt's husband' and Mummy's gave up 'the mother'. Flat by design, as a chapter voice: one want, one fear, one contradiction that shows the same way every time, and one turn in December. Marks carried from the chapter 1 check: [BREAKS rule 9: a family voice who is not on the household screen] [WAITS rulebook Q11: if the household may speak in every chapter, the chapter voices go]. Rule 33's 'seen only from behind in a world' no longer binds her face: the owner's 26 Oct answer 6 says characters are drawn from their own model sheets, and the bible already says 'The chapter voice is painted face-on' (bible.md line 78), though rule 33's text still needs rewriting.
cast.essence: Nani's eldest, who has taught the junction town's smallest children in her front room for thirty years and talks to every room as if it were Class 3: the loudest, fastest person in the family, a basket bag on her arm, who never lets you finish a sentence and remembers every word of it a year later. The type in five words: the loud aunt who feeds. What makes her not the type: talking over you is how she listens, her memory is exact, and she is the only one in a family of quiet deeds who says what she feels out loud, her hurt included ('Amma calls your Mummy first!'), so loudly and so often that nobody takes it in.
cast.backstory: Born 1971, the eldest of Nani's three (Mummy 1974, Mama ji 1979). While Nani ran the grocery from her front room, Mausi did the younger two's homework at the back of the shop: she taught Mummy to read the clock and Mama ji his tables, and has not stopped teaching since. She wanted to be a schoolteacher; she married at 21 instead (1992) and moved to the junction town, where Mausa ji was posted as a lineman with the electricity board. In 1996 she started a tuition class for Classes 1 to 5 in her front room: a blackboard painted on the wall, a mat on the floor, two long benches Mama ji paid for with his first city salary, and a ceiling fan that Mausa ji swaps for a bigger one every summer (his file). That year she bought her basket bag at the junction's Saturday market to carry her pupils' exercise books home to mark, and she still carries a stack of them everywhere. She says she has taught a thousand children; Tinku has counted 612. You and Tinku both did your sums on her mat, so half the town calls her 'Madam ji' and the rest 'Mausi'. In 1995 she noticed the young railway parcel clerk lodging in her lane, the only bachelor who paid the milkman on the first of the month, and carried his proposal to Nani for her younger sister; Mummy and Papa married in 1997, and she mentions it at every wedding. Her two grown children (about 32 and 29) live elsewhere and come to family events by road. Her right knee aches from years on the floor mat with her youngest pupils (the realism notes record squatting and floor sitting as possible knee risks for older women); she now teaches from a chair and accepts the lower berth she pretends not to need. She is a little short-sighted and has never needed reading glasses: she reads with the page close to her face, and nags Mausa ji about the reading glasses he will not wear (his file). She wakes at four, as Nani does, which is why Nani rings her, not Mummy, on nights she cannot sleep; Mausi has never thought that counts for anything. The morning Nani's 'Everyone comes' arrived in January, she cut limes and set a jar of lime pickle in the sun on her roof, made to Nani's own recipe without asking Nani for it, for the first time in her life; it has been maturing up there ever since, and in May it rides to Nani's in her basket bag.
cast.want_fear_contradiction: WANTS THIS YEAR: to be first through Nani's door for the eightieth with her basket bag, the January jar of lime pickle inside, and be the first one Nani thanks. The fall that evening (1.40) cancels the party and the jar goes onto Nani's kitchen shelf unopened, so her want waits until December. WANTS FROM YOU: your news first-hand. She lives in the same town and still hears it second-hand on her daily call with Mummy; on the night train she asks for it straight ('Now tell me. Straight to me.') and then talks over the answer. FEARS: that she, the eldest, is the daughter Nani puts up with while Mummy is the one Nani relies on; and that she talks so much that nobody hears her. Unlike everyone else in the family she says the first fear out loud, more than once ('Amma calls your Mummy first!'), and that is exactly why nobody hears it: it sounds like the rest of her noise. CONTRADICTION ('X, but Y'): she never lets you finish a sentence, but remembers every word of it a year later. It shows the same way every time: her bubble starts over the end of yours (your line trails off, 'Mausi, wo…'), and later she quotes your exact words back ('Last year you said…'). ITS COST: whatever you were about to say on the carriage step never gets said, and she never learns what it was. HABIT OF SPEECH: says her first word three times. LINE PEOPLE QUOTE BACK: 'Suno, suno, suno!' | 'सुनो, सुनो, सुनो!' | 'Listen, listen, listen!' (the tripled 'suno' is hers alone in the cast; she calls Mausa ji 'Aji', not 'suno ji'). I KNOW THIS PERSON (a prediction for real readers to confirm): Sunita, the small-town tailor of 41, whose lane will have a woman who runs tuition from her front room and feeds whoever sits down, and whose family she would not want mocked; so Mausi is never the butt of the joke. FLAT OR ROUND: flat by design, with one contradiction and one turn: in December, when Nani thanks her first in front of the whole kitchen, the woman who says everything out loud says nothing at all, because for once she has been heard.
relationships: Nani ('Amma'): her mother. Mausi says 'Amma' and आप; Nani calls her 'Badi' (the eldest) and says तुम. When they meet, Mausi bends and Nani lays her palm on her head (a greeting families of many communities use, kept between painted people). Friction: Nani relies on Mummy for decisions and on Mausi for dinner, and Mausi minds, out loud; she brings food to be thanked and is thanked last. Tenderness: they both wake at four, and Nani rings Mausi, nobody else, when she cannot sleep. The player sees it on the ward night (a proposed line for Nani's writer: 'Ring my eldest. She'll be awake too.' | 'बड़ी को फ़ोन लगाओ। वो भी जगी होगी।'); Mausi never learns that the player saw it. December pays it off: Nani tastes the May pickle and thanks her first, in her own idiom (proposed for Nani's writer: 'Badi ne banaya.' | 'बड़ी ने बनाया।' | 'My eldest made this.').

Mummy ('Chhoti'): her younger sister by three years. Mausi says 'Chhoti' (little one) and तुम; Mummy says 'Didi' and आप, as Mummy's own file has it (the India review found the two files disagreed). In English mode Mausi says 'your Mummy' when she speaks of her to you. Friction: rivalry dressed as concern ('Chhoti, you work too hard', which means 'Amma calls you first', and once a chapter she says the second half out loud). Tenderness: a daily phone call both look forward to, and Mausi chose Mummy's husband for her.

Papa (no address word): her younger sister's husband, a year older than her, whose proposal she carried. She says आप and uses no address word to his face; to you she calls him 'tumhare Papa'. 'Tinku ke Papa' is dropped: naming a man by his child is how a wife names her own husband, and families name a man by the eldest child, not Tinku (the India review and Mummy's file). He calls her 'Didi' and says आप (his file), because the relation outranks the year. Friction: she overrules his berth chart every trip and boards at the last possible minute, 9:40 for a 9:40 train. Tenderness: he books her a lower berth for her knee in January, before she asks, and never says so; on this train she finds out. The numbers stay in his lines, never in hers.

Mama ji ('Munna'): the youngest, whom she half raised. She still calls him 'Munna' (his childhood pet name, used in many communities; readers confirm) in front of everyone and says तुम; he calls her 'Badi Didi'. Friction: she scolds him for leaving for the city at twenty. Tenderness: he paid for the benches in her tuition room with his first salary, and she tells every pupil so.

Tinku ('hamari topper'): her niece, who did her sums on Mausi's mat. Mausi calls her 'Tinku' or 'hamari topper' (our topper), says तुम, and tells everyone she came top again, which Tinku hates; Tinku says 'Mausi' and आप. Friction: Mausi still checks her sums. Tenderness: Tinku keeps the true count of Mausi's pupils (612), the kind of tally that is Tinku's, never Mausi's, and Mausi pretends not to know.

Mausa ji ('Aji'): her husband since 1992, about 58. They say तुम to each other, both ways (the even-respect rule the realism notes set for couples in this family). She calls him 'Aji' | 'अजी', never his name, and never 'suno ji', because the tripled 'suno' is her catchphrase (comics review); he uses no address word for her, and to you calls her 'tumhari Mausi' (his file). Friction: she tells everyone his blood pressure, sends him pill reminders and nags him about his reading glasses. Tenderness: she talks and finishes his sentences and he lets her; on night trains they hold hands when they think the carriage is asleep; every summer he wires a bigger fan into her tuition room.

Mami ('Bhabhi'): her younger brother's wife. Mausi says 'Bhabhi' and तुम; Mami says 'Badi Didi' and आप, as Mami's own file has it (Mummy is Mami's plain 'Didi'). Friction: Mausi thinks city people waste money; Mami thinks Mausi feeds people too much. Tenderness: in the wedding week Mausi's basket bag feeds Mami's list and the two run Nani's house together, allies, never women set against women.

Masterji: her tailor for decades. He calls her 'Behenji' (readers confirm); she says 'Masterji' and आप. Friction: she complains about every fitting. Tenderness: she comes back every time, and in the flood week she brings his lunch to the counter with Mummy's.

Captain sahab: a lane elder of the junction town. He calls her 'Madam ji', as her old pupils do, and she is secretly delighted; she says 'Captain sahab' and आप. Friction: she once sent him a two-minute voice note about when to send the lane side's lunch; he replied '9 am'. Backstory only: she is not in chapter 4.

You: her younger sister's elder child, and her old pupil. She says तुम to you, with no address word, or 'suno'; you say 'Mausi' and आप, with -इए. Friction: she hears your news only through Chhoti, so she asks for it straight and then talks over your answer, and never hears the end of what you meant to say. Tenderness: she says she missed you, out loud, the moment she sees you ('Haaye! Bahut yaad aayi.'), remembers what you said a year ago word for word, and keeps the place beside her for you. She never touches you, because you are never painted (rule 7), and holds things out towards you only with her face in the frame.

The chapter 1 cousins (the circle, on the cards): Nani's sisters' and brother's grandchildren, aged 27 to 37, whom she has fed at every family function since they were small. Her judging notes are what she saw at the table and on trips, in a report-card voice ('Never sits still for long.'). She never names or points at one in a bubble (rule 36), never offers them food in a painting (the bay is the card people, so it stays out of frame, rule 32), and her notes fall on women and men equally (three and three in draft 1).

Her own two children (about 32 and 29): off screen. They come by road, so they are not in the train's headcount and never on a card (her note would then be a mother's verdict on her own child, a different kind of note). If the owner wants a speaking person in their thirties, her elder child is the natural one (cast map).
cast.year_arc: JANUARY (the opening, present day): not on the household screen and not heard. The morning Nani's 'Everyone comes' arrives she sets a jar of lime pickle in the sun, to Nani's recipe; it is never shown until it rides in her basket bag in May. MAY, CHAPTER 1 (Lugdi, the night train): her chapter. She boards at 9:40 for the 9:40 train with the basket bag and the chapter's one shout, a shout with no numbers in it; tells you out loud that she missed you; finds the lower berth Papa booked for her in January and goes silent for once; marks a stack of her pupils' exercise books on her berth by the night lamp as the bay settles (a teacher in one wordless picture); sits up on the carriage step at the long halt (she and Nani both wake at four), says her hurt out loud ('Amma calls your Mummy first!'), asks for your news straight, talks over it, and quotes back what you said last year. At dawn her basket bag is already on the front step (1.37), because she was first through the gate: the one time an object stands in for her. That evening Nani slips on the wet back step (1.40). The party is off, the pickle jar goes onto Nani's kitchen shelf unopened, and her want waits. MAY, CHAPTER 2 (Rukavat, the ward night, Mausa ji's chapter): all night she is at Nani's house feeding the full house, which also answers the review's 'where is the family'. At four Nani, sleepless, has her rung (the proposed line in relationships): the player learns that Mausi's fear is false; Mausi does not. At first light she is at the ward door, small, face-on and silent, the basket bag on her arm, Mausa ji beside the door seen from behind [WAITS rulebook Q11: she does not speak, so rule 10's one speaking chapter holds]. JULY, CHAPTER 3 (Station, the flood): one small silent panel at Mummy's counter, holding a foil parcel of lunch out to Mummy with Masterji's beside it; no hired hands in the frame, since they may be card people (rule 32) [WAITS rulebook Q11]. 15 AUGUST, CHAPTER 4 (Cricket, the lane cup): not seen. The lane cup is Captain sahab's and Tinku's, and her basket bag has had its one object beat. DECEMBER, CHAPTER 5 (Jadugar, the wedding at Nani's house): she runs Nani's kitchen while Mami runs the list. Her payoff has its own panel before the cake (chapter 5's writer numbers it, about 5.25 or 5.26) [WAITS rulebook Q11]: the May jar comes down off Nani's shelf for the feast, Nani tastes it and thanks her first in front of the whole kitchen ('Badi ne banaya.', Nani's writer owns the line), and Mausi gives her one silent panel of the year, palm pressed to her chest. She has no part in the cake at 5.28 and no line in the album: the candle box is Nani's alone, and the album keeps its two lines (Nani's count and your reply), as the comics review asked. WHAT CHANGES: in January she is the loud one who hears everything second-hand and says, too loudly to be heard, that she is only tolerated. By December she has been thanked first, for the one thing she made without asking, and for once she has nothing to say.

voice.register: Hindi-first; the loudest and fastest voice in the cast, warm and bossy like a front-room tuition teacher with her Class 3. She talks in bursts: two to four bubbles of short closed sentences, most ending on ! or ?, the first bubble starting over the end of yours. Her shape: she says a word twice to push the room along ('Chalo, chalo!', 'Na, na!'), asks a question and answers it herself before anyone can, and tags a statement 'hai na?' and moves on before anyone replies. A triple is kept for a peak, at most once a scene, and 'Suno, suno, suno!' is the one the family quotes back. Her long run is a string of short loud sentences, never a comma chain (Mama ji's run-on) and never a list (Mummy's jobs, Mami's statuses). The common fillers come and go in her lines as in anyone's (arre, achha, haan, chalo, dekho, suno, bas, theek hai); what marks her is the shape and the classroom and kitchen her words come from, never a word she owns. Pace quick and rising. When cross she gets louder and faster, the only one in the family who does; when moved she goes silent, the only time she does. No numbers at all, not even ordinals. One shout bubble a chapter at most (rule 35, which is 1.09), and never a whisper, because she cannot whisper. Each bubble is at most 10 words (rule 62), so a longer thought becomes more bubbles. She is never the asker (rule 37) and never reacts to who was picked (rule 39).
voice.mix: A Hindi frame with single English words in it, the older speakers' pattern in the realism notes (1.1). Her English carries feeling and school, not trade: sorry, tension, first class, topper, homework, copy (exercise book), class, teacher, fail, late mark; in chapter 1 also the travel nouns berth and chart. The everyday English verb with kar or ho comes to her as it does to any schoolteacher, with school verbs: 'top kiya', 'check karo', 'fail ho gayi', 'pass ho gaya' (of you only as a command, since a past said of you would mark a gender). Mummy is told apart by what she turns into counter English, not by owning the pattern. She never switches a whole clause into English (Mama ji's and Mami's way). Her Hindi is everyday small-town Hindustani with a teacher's words in it (inaam, bujho, copiyan, 'kaan pakdo', 'khaali pet'), and the town's ordinary words fikr, waqt and zaroor come to her plainly too; never spelled to sound funny. The tag 'hai na?' is a habit of hers, not a word she owns; in English mode it becomes the Indian English 'right?'. In Hinglish mode she reads as Roman Hindi with those English words (how a Hinglish bubble looks waits on rulebook Q6). A Hindi-first reader reads every line aloud (rule 65).
tics: Says a word twice to hurry, refuse or soothe, the way real Hindi does: 'Chalo, chalo!', 'Na, na!', 'Aao, aao.', 'Sorry, sorry!', or a name twice ('Munna, Munna!', 'Bhabhi, Bhabhi!'); to elders 'Chaliye, chaliye!'. The triple is saved for a peak, at most once a scene: 'Suno, suno, suno!' to call the room (the one the family quotes back), or 'Na, na, na!' at news she will not have. 'Haay' is never doubled or tripled, because हाय-हाय is a lament and a protest chant.

Asks a question and answers it herself, like the riddle-setter she is every morning, blurting the answer before anyone can guess: 'Kiski? Hamari!', 'Main padosan hoon? Nahin!', 'Andhera? Koi baat nahin!', 'Chai ya halwa? Halwa!'. The one question in the year she cannot answer herself is 'Kisne karwaayi?' at the lower berth, and then she goes silent.
Ends a statement with 'hai na?' and is gone before anyone answers; in English mode, 'right?'. Not on every line: a few a scene at most.
Quotes people back word for word: 'Pichhle saal tumne kaha tha…'. Her memory is exact; she never misquotes.
Says what she feels, out loud, to the whole room: love ('Bahut yaad aayi'), hurt ('Amma pehle Chhoti ko bulaati hain!'), sorry. Silent only when moved, palm to her chest.

Runs the room like her class: marks the late ('Late mark!'), sets the classroom's punishment in fun ('Kaan pakdo!', to Munna or Tinku), grades a favour ('Ekdum first class!', at most once a chapter), now and then fails herself when she is wrong ('Aaj teacher fail!'), and measures a loss by her pupils ('meri class ka inaam'). Her teaching is in her mouth, not only in one wordless picture, so she is more than the loud aunt who feeds. But the classroom is one of her two sources, never her stamp: about one line in four reaches for it at most, and the kitchen and her exact memory of what people said carry the rest (the flood is 'Achaar ke martbaan upar!', not her pupils' exercise books; being wrong is 'Galat kaun nikla? Main!').
Worries in quick questions about the body and the belly, and answers for you if you are slow: 'Kuch khaya bhi? Nahin?', 'Chot toh nahin lagi?'.

Food as punctuation: 'Pehle khao' (the only 'Pehle' that is hers; 'Pehle ___' as a courtesy is yours), 'Khaali pet baat nahin!', 'Muh meetha karo!', and something held out as she says it, her face in the frame. 'Haay' never comes just before she holds out food.
Report-card verdicts on habits, never on character, in all her judging notes ('Never sits still for long.').
'Hamara, hamari' (ours) for anyone she is proud of ('hamari topper'), but never of you, since it would mark your gender.
She always has an answer and almost never says 'pata nahin', which is why 'Kisne karwaayi?' silences her.
When cross: louder and faster, hand on hip, the basket bag set down hard, and her own catchphrase fails ('Koi sunta bhi hai? Nahin!').
catchphrases: 'Suno, suno, suno!' | 'सुनो, सुनो, सुनो!' | 'Listen, listen, listen!' (her opener and the line people quote back; her one regular triple. Anyone may say 'suno' or 'chalo'; the tripled call to the room is hers)
'Maine kaha tha na?' | 'मैंने कहा था न?' | 'Didn't I tell you?' (whenever something she predicted comes true, good news above all)

'Pichhle saal tumne kaha tha…' | 'पिछले साल तुमने कहा था…' | 'Last year you said…' (the quote-back; it marks no gender, because with तुमने the verb agrees with what was said; you are the doer, though, so it waits on the owner's rule 66 question in address 0). None of the three has a number in it.
voice.exclamation: 'Haay!' | 'हाय!' | English mode 'Haay!' too, the way Mami keeps 'Ish'. Spelled short, the way the cry sounds in a Hindi-belt town, not the film spelling 'Haaye' that makes her the screen's Punjabi aunty. For sympathy, surprise and delight, and just before she says a feeling ('Haay! Bahut yaad aayi.'). At most once a scene, and never just before she holds out food. Nobody else in the cast uses it. It has no religious meaning on its own; the guard is that it is never followed by a name of any kind or by 'Maa': no 'Hai Ram', 'Haay Ram', 'Haay Rabba', 'Haay Allah', 'Haay Maa', 'Ui Maa'. Never doubled or tripled (हाय-हाय is a lament and a protest chant). Keeping it in English mode also ends the old mix-up of her 'Oh!' with Mama ji's 'Oho!'.
voice.sorry_thanks_love: SORRY: plain and doubled, food held out as she says it, her face in the frame: 'Sorry, sorry! Pehle khao.' | 'सॉरी, सॉरी! पहले खाओ।' | 'Sorry, sorry! Eat first.' To an elder: 'Sorry, sorry! Pehle khaiye.' Tinku and you now say a plain 'sorry' too; hers is told apart by the double and the food, not by owning the word. Wrong in front of everyone, she says so first and loudest, her own question answered at once: 'Galat kaun nikla? Main! Sorry, sorry! Pehle khao!'; now and then she fails herself as a teacher instead ('Aaj teacher fail, hai na?'). THANKS, GIVEN: plain words, out loud, to the whole room: 'Bahut achha laga!' | 'बहुत अच्छा लगा!' | 'So nice of you!' ('Bahut achha kiya.' is Mummy's thanks, so the sisters' words differ, and with लगा you are not the doer); and her teacher's grade 'Ekdum first class!' | 'एकदम फ़र्स्ट क्लास!' | 'First class!' at most once a chapter, so the grade stays a treat and never turns into a code. 'Thank you' is not her habit at home, as it is not for most of her generation; she says it to a stranger like anyone. WHEN SHE IS THANKED: she wants it heard: 'Achha? Zor se kaho! Amma bhi sunein!' | 'अच्छा? ज़ोर से कहो! अम्मा भी सुनें!' | 'Really? Say it louder! Let Amma hear too!' Only Amma's thanks, in December, makes her silent. LOVE: said out loud, to the whole room: 'Haay! Bahut yaad aayi.' | 'हाय! बहुत याद आई।' | 'Haay! I missed you so much.' At a parting, the same key: 'Abhi se yaad aa rahi hai!' | 'अभी से याद आ रही है!' | 'Missing you already!' Mama ji's love is warm and one to one, with a hug; hers is loud and to the room, with food.

chalo, chalo / chaliye, chaliye | चलो, चलो / चलिए, चलिए | come on, come on (चलिए to elders)

na, na / na, na, na | ना, ना / ना, ना, ना | no, no / no, no, no (the triple only at a peak)

maine kaha tha na? | मैंने कहा था न? | didn't I tell you?

sorry, sorry | सॉरी, सॉरी | sorry, sorry
bahut achha laga | बहुत अच्छा लगा | so nice of you (her everyday thanks; 'bahut achha kiya' is Mummy's)

arre, achha, haan, dekho, bas, theek hai | अरे, अच्छा, हाँ, देखो, बस, ठीक है | everyone's fillers, in the middle of her lines like anyone's ('arre' only as a filler: as an exclamation on its own it is Captain sahab's, matrix 2.15, and hers is 'Haay')
berth, chart | बर्थ, चार्ट | chapter 1's travel nouns, the same in every mode
never: Any doubt of a report of being followed or harassed, or of a dowry demand: no 'sach mein?', 'pakka?', 'galatfehmi', 'misunderstanding', 'imagined', 'chhodo', 'jaane do', 'hota rehta hai' about it. She is the first to believe, and the hard topic never reaches a bubble or a story panel anyway (rule 26); she has no line in the lead-in or settle of a hard decision. Her 'Na, na!' and 'Ye nahin chalega!' are for harmless news only.

Any religious word or exclamation (rule 3): no Hai Ram, Haay Ram, Haay Rabba, Bhagwan, Allah, Rab, Wahe Guru, Ishwar, Jesus, tauba, 'shukr hai', 'Ui Maa', 'Mata ji' as a goddess; in English mode no Gosh, Golly, Goodness, Oh my, Heavens, Lord, Thank God. No caste word, no brand.
Any number in speech: no figures, no counts, no years (rule 2), no ordinals ('teesri class' is struck), no 'ek-ek', 'teen baar' or 'sau mein sau'. 'First class' stays as an idiom of praise.

Any word that gives you a gender: beta, bachcha, bhaiya, didi, raja, rani; 'hamara/hamari' of you; any verb or adjective that agrees with you: kitne/kitni bade/badi ho gaye, aa gaye/aa gayi, thak gaye/gayi, -oge/-ogi, khaate/khaati raho (rules 8 and 66). 'How grown up you've got' becomes 'Chehre pe thakaan.'

Other people's set phrases, so the blind sort can tell her apart. These are phrases, not fillers: arre, achha, haan, chalo, dekho, suno, bas and theek hai are everyone's. Kept out (an exclamation here is barred only as her habitual cry; the word itself stays free): 'Arre waah' and 'Arre!' as an exclamation on its own (Captain sahab's, matrix 2.15; hers is 'Haay!'), 'Ek-ek karke' and 'Pehle ___' as a courtesy (yours; she keeps only 'Pehle khao'), 'Lo. Aadha.' and a one-word 'Theek.' bubble (Mausa ji's), 'aur haan' as a joiner, 'Oho!', 'full' and a one-word 'Roz.' (Mama ji's), 'Kamaal' and 'Reached?' (Papa's), 'Had hai!', 'Ye mere hisaab mein' and 'Iska bill nahin' (Mummy's), 'Gazab!' and the 'haan?' tag (Tinku's), 'Not out', 'Next ball', 'Well played' (Captain sahab's), 'Baap re', a closing 'Bas.', 'Chai piyo', 'Main yahin hoon', 'Khush raho' (Nani's), 'Uff' and 'Jeete raho' (Masterji's), 'Hain?', 'Mazboot', 'Galti hui', 'Ho jayega' (Mausa ji's), 'Ish', 'Tick', 'Correct?', 'pending', 'Congratulations' (Mami's), 'Badhiya' as a one-word verdict and 'Shukriya' (yours), 'Badhai ho' (Mummy's, if the owner allows it), and 'Mubarak ho' (unused for now: it and 'Badhai ho' are both everyday congratulations and take one ruling, and an Urdu-speaking reader checks that both sides are treated alike, India verdict 3).
A whole English clause (Mama ji's and Mami's way): her English stays single words, and school verbs with kar or ho.
A comma chain or a list: her long run is short closed sentences, never Mama ji's run-on or Mummy's and Mami's lists.

Character words or verdicts on anyone: aalsi, kaamchor, raub, besharam, badchalan, chalu; nothing on anyone's morals, marriage or dress; no sentence about ladkiyan, ladke, aurtein or mard in general (rule 22). Her talk is energy and care, never gossip about people.

habits: Device: a big-screen Android phone in a plain flip case with no markings (rule 3). She reads it held a hand's width from her nose, since she is short-sighted and wears no glasses; that distance is her phone trait (six files share 'font at its largest', so it is not). Painted blank; every word on it is live text (rule 30).

Mostly voice notes, long ones, the phone held flat under her chin like a plate and spoken at full volume so the whole room hears. They open 'Haan suno....' and close '....chalo, khana kha lena 😊'. On screen a voice note is a live-text card: a play mark, a long bar and her first words, with no length figure, so no number reaches her lines.
When she types: Roman Hinglish, all lowercase except 'OK', spelled the way she says it ('haay', not 'haaye') and always in full, never short forms like 'h' or 'k' (Masterji's and Tinku's).

Punctuation: four dots '....' between every phrase instead of full stops or commas; double question marks '??', which are hers (Mama ji keeps '!!'). One long message, never a burst of short ones (Mama ji's), never one item a line (Papa's), never a list (Mami's); the one exception waits on the owner, if message cards are held to the 10-word cap (habit 9). She types her doubles too, with no commas ('jaldi jaldi', 'abhi abhi'), the one triple the family quotes ('suno suno suno'), and her self-answered question ('kaun jeeta?? hamari topper').
No figures, even typed: no times, no counts, no prices. Her daily send is a riddle, not a sum.

Emoji: 😊 at the end of nearly everything, even bad news (the family knows to read past it); 😋 for food. Never 👍 (Mummy's), never a person emoji (it carries a gender and a skin tone), and 🙏 not at all until the owner decides (realism 2.2).

Her one daily send is her own: 'aaj ki paheli' (today's riddle), a traditional children's riddle in words to the family group early each morning, whose answers she marks by voice note at night. Never a good-morning flower (Papa's), never gods, politics, a famous face, false news or a home remedy (rule 3; realism 2.2).
Timing: replies within seconds all day, answers a one-word message with a long voice note, and is sending from four in the morning. No reply means she is cooking.
Typos: autocorrect turns her Hinglish into English words and she sends it anyway; it is never shown as a joke on her.

The family group is mentioned, never shown (owner, 23 Oct). A message reaches the player as one message card. No mole or mark anywhere on the face, since a mark near the brow reads as a bindi, and no lines between the eyebrows, which can come back as a painted tilak (rules review). Her forehead is smooth and bare; her age shows in the eyes, the cheeks and the chin.
look.skin: Always written with the tested words 'South Asian features and warm brown skin', then her depth after them: 'a medium-deep brown' (flux-portrait-biases: those exact words fixed whitening; the rules review found the cast's other variants untested). Darker than Mummy and Mama ji (both warm medium brown in their files now), lighter than Nani and Papa. Her copper hair is an extra whitening risk, because red-brown hair pulls the painter towards a pale face, so the skin words go straight after the hair words, and every pick is checked close up against her master swatch, not against the lamp light: Lugdi's marigold and Jadugar's tent lamps recolour skin too.
look.hair: Hair dyed the even dark copper-brown of home hair dye, a little grey at the temples. It is brushed up and back off her forehead into a full soft puff with no centre parting, and the rest is twisted up at the back of her head and held in a big plain dark brown plastic claw clip, the loose ends fanning out above the clip. From the front her head reads as one full round of hair a little wider than her face; from behind, a copper twist and the clip high on the back of her head, well clear of Mummy's big low bun at the nape. The painter's words: 'dark copper-brown dyed hair brushed up off the forehead into a full soft puff, no centre parting, the rest twisted up at the back of her head in a big plain dark brown plastic claw clip'. Never 'henna' in a prompt (the painter may add mehendi to her hands), and never 'red' or 'vermilion' anywhere near her hair: red at a parting or hairline reads as sindoor. Changed from the open waves of the draft: open hair with big hoops reads as the city kitty-party aunty (India review), while a claw clip is worn by women of every age, region and community and keeps the round outline. The dye colour waits on an Indian reader (cast map).
look.glasses_jewellery: No spectacles, ever: she is a little short-sighted and reads with the page close to her face, so she has never needed reading glasses (refusing reading glasses and reading at arm's length was in six files; this is hers alone, and spectacles stay with Nani and Masterji). Her only jewellery: two medium plain gold hoop earrings, each about as wide as two fingers side by side, made of thick round gold wire as thick as a matchstick, so they read as two bright rings beside her jaw in any picture from the waist up (the comics review: thin hoops are a hairline at phone size; the India review: medium, not big). In a full-figure picture they are a close-up detail, not a strip anchor. Nothing else: a bare neck (no chain, so nothing can be painted as a mangalsutra), bare wrists (no bangle, since most bangles carry marital meaning and a steel one reads as a kara; no wristwatch, which is Mummy's), a bare nose, bare toes. The India review warns that a bare married woman of 55 can read as widowed to older Hindi-belt eyes; her hoops and claw clip are her strong non-marital objects, and plain thin gold bangles wait on the owner (owner questions).
outfits: SIGNATURE, every day and for travel (chapter 1, May): a cream sari of light printed synthetic, printed all over with big magenta flowers and dark green leaves, with a solid magenta edge two fingers wide; the everyday Nivi drape, pleated at the waist, its loose end over her left shoulder and hanging down her back to the knees, her head always uncovered; a plain magenta half-sleeve sari blouse. The loose end carries the same print, so no contrasting band crosses her chest (the diagonal belongs to Mummy's dupatta). When she gets to work she pulls the loose end round and tucks it into her waist at the front. Value: a light base, big dark flowers, a dark edge, which survives Station's two inks. Write 'edge', never 'border', which fights STORY_NO's 'no border, no frame'.
HOME and her tuition room: the same flower print on an older, softer, faded cotton sari, its loose end tucked into her waist all day; barefoot indoors.

COLD MONTHS ONLY (January and December): a plain cream hand-knitted cardigan worn open over the sari, sleeves pushed to the elbows. Never in May, July or August (the India review's hot-season note). Defined in her own look only; Mummy's cardigan is maroon wool, so the word gets no shared glossary row.

OCCASION, the wedding week (December): the signature at the signature scale in a finer cloth (the comics review: comics keep the costume): a cream silk-look sari with the same big magenta flowers and dark green leaves, a solid magenta edge with a thin line of gold along it, the same drape, head uncovered, the same hoops, the cream cardigan off stage. The light base keeps her apart from Jadugar's stage magenta and from anything bridal: a solid magenta or red silk sari with a broad gold edge reads as the bride (rules review). Never white or all-white, which with a bare forehead reads as a widow.

NEVER: a salwar suit (the draft's 1.09 'plain cotton salwar suit' is replaced, so her silhouette is the sari's flare and her colour is never Mummy's maroon suit); never letters, logos or pictures on any cloth.
look.colour_key: Her key is magenta flowers on cream, gold at the ears, and a magenta-and-white zigzag on her arm. The signature sari keeps its value and its pattern in every look and takes the look's nearest ink. NOW: cream base, magenta flowers and edge, dark green leaves, dark copper-brown hair, gold hoops. LUGDI (chapter 1; cutscenes.py STYLE: deep night violet and indigo shadows, hot vermilion and marigold lamp light): the cream catches the marigold lamp, the flowers and edge go hot magenta, the folds sink to violet, the hair is dark copper-brown catching marigold light (never vermilion: that is sindoor's colour, and this look already pours vermilion light; rules review), the hoops marigold. Her light shape is the cream base of the sari; she does not claim the brightest shape in the carriage, which Papa's and Mummy's files both claim, and that is settled on the Lugdi look strip. STATION (enamel blue and black on cream), if she is seen at Mummy's counter: her base is the cream paper; flowers, edge and blouse solid enamel blue; hair a dark halftone mass of the same shape; hoops two dark rings; the basket bag a dark-and-light zigzag. RUKAVAT (teak, faded teal, cream, one signal orange), if she is seen at the ward door: cream base, faded rose flowers, never the signal orange (that is Mausa ji's orange in chapter 2), and the skin words added, since the Rukavat panel style lacks them. CRICKET: not seen. JADUGAR (code: vermilion and magenta against a deep indigo night, emerald and old gold): the cream silk-look sari lit warm by the lamps so it never sinks into the indigo, the magenta flowers on it, the edge magenta with its thin gold line, hoops old gold; never solid magenta, which is the stage's colour. If chapter 5's look line ('flat crimson, gold and black') wins instead, the flowers print crimson on a light base, which still reads as a guest, never the bride. Still needed before any colour key is trusted: one agreed style string per look; chapter-1.json's Lugdi line ('flat red, mustard and night blue, coarse halftone') does not match cutscenes.py's STYLE['lugdi'].
look.prop: THE BASKET BAG: a bucket-shaped Indian shopping basket woven from thin plastic strips in a magenta and white zigzag, with two loop handles (one mended with a twist of white plastic tape), its top hidden under a folded plain cream cotton cloth that bulges over what is inside. She bought it at the junction's Saturday market in 1996, the year she started her class, to carry her pupils' exercise books home to mark; now it carries food as well, and she is never without it. HAND: hooked in the crook of one elbow, usually the right, that hand resting on the cloth as if guarding it; the other hand free to wave. Which side is a preference to check, never what tells her from anyone else (the comics review: the painter does not keep sides, and layouts get mirrored). CHAPTER 1 CONTENTS (painted, never named in a bubble before a decision): a squat clear glass jar of dark red-brown lime pickle with a plain white screw lid and no label, kept shut; thin parcels of food wrapped in plain silver foil; the steel thermos flask of tea (the glossary's 'flask'); and a stack of her pupils' exercise books in plain brown paper jackets, painted blank. It replaces the draft's steel tiffin carrier, which sat close to a cousin's 'Brought the steel tiffins' note, and it carries no birthday candles: those belong to Nani's file alone. Its one beat standing in for her is the dawn outcome at 1.37; everywhere else she is painted with it. The master is painted with the bag on her arm, so person and prop take one reference slot, and it also gets its own reference picture and its own glossary row.
look.silhouette: The widest figure in the cast: a full round head of hair (the puff in front, the clipped twist behind) on a broad, rounded body, the sari's loose end flaring off her shoulder, a bulging basket bag like a second, smaller round on one forearm, and the other arm up mid-gesture. In black at phone size: a round head, a wide body, a lump on one side, a raised arm on the other. Beside Papa (tall band, a thin vertical line with combed-down hair), with whom she shares chapter 1, the two read as opposites at any size. FAR SPEC, for when she is small in a panel and painted from words alone (the comics review): a round copper-brown head, a wide light sari shape with a dark edge, the basket bag; nothing else.
look.shoes: Dark brown slip-on chappals with one wide padded strap across the toes, soft and worn at the heel; barefoot indoors at home. Defined in her own look only, never as a shared glossary row (Nani's chappals are different). Feet show only in full-figure pictures, which are checked for toe rings.

posture.stance: Feet planted wide, weight on her left leg to spare the right knee, chest forward, chin up, the whole body leaning a little towards whoever she is talking to (towards the viewer when she talks to you); the basket bag hooked in one elbow, that hand resting on its cloth; the other hand up at shoulder height, stirring the air. Stance goes in the scene words of each panel, never in her fixed look (rules review).
posture.sitting: She drops down all at once with a thump (sound word 'dhamm' | 'धम्म') and sits deep and wide, right back against the berth wall, never perched on the front edge (eight files had the front edge; this is hers): right leg stretched straight out along the berth for the knee, left foot planted, the basket bag beside her, one arm along the berth back, taking up space. She pats the place beside her with her palm, the invitation she promised you a year ago. She gets up by rocking forward twice and pushing off with one hand, not as Nani does, in stages with a hand on her knee.
posture.walk: Quick short steps, hips rolling, the basket bag swinging on her forearm, talking over her shoulder as she goes; first through every door and first up every step, a hand on the rail, left leg leading. She never walks in silence.
gestures: THE STIR: one hand turns small circles in the air while she talks, faster as she gets louder, the palm open and the fingers spread when she wins an argument. Her one constant.
THE TUCK: when she is about to take charge she pulls the loose end of her sari round and tucks it into her waist at the front with both hands. It means 'Now listen'.

THE OFFERING ARM: a foil parcel held out at full stretch towards the viewer (always with her face in the frame, so the hand is plainly hers, rule 7), to Papa or to Mausa ji; never towards the bay, which is the card people and stays out of the frame (rule 32).

THE CLOSE READ: anything written (her phone, an exercise book) held a hand's width from her nose, eyes narrowed, no glasses; papers and screens painted blank. It replaces the arm's-length read, which six files shared.
THE STILL HAND: her palm pressed to her chest when she is moved, the only time her hands stop.

She touches the sleeve of whoever she is talking to (Papa's, Mausa ji's), never yours. She never greets with folded hands, which read as prayer (realism 6, rule 3): her greeting is both arms opened wide; with Nani, she bends and Nani lays a palm on her head.
expressions: NEUTRAL: mouth a little open as if about to speak, eyebrows up, body turned to the nearest person, one hand ready.
PLEASED: both arms flung wide, chin up, a wide open grin, the basket bag swinging.
WORRIED: mouth shut tight (the only time it is, apart from when she is moved), a hand pressed on the basket cloth, eyes going from face to face.
CROSS: louder, not quieter, the only one in the family whose anger is loud: a hand on her hip, the basket bag set down hard, chin out, forefinger wagging as at Class 3, mouth wide.
LAUGHING: head thrown back, eyes shut, a hand slapping her own knee, shoulders shaking.
TEASING: one eyebrow up, chin down, a sideways look, the stirring hand slowing.
TIRED: sunk deep into the berth, a hand rubbing her right knee, hair flattened on one side, eyes half shut, mouth still going.
MOVED: silent, palm pressed to her chest, lips pressed together, eyes wet, her hands still for once. Her one bubble-less panel a chapter.

across_looks: STRIP ANCHORS (check every full-figure pick against these only; the comics review split anchors by what survives at about 200 screen pixels a figure): (1) the round silhouette: a full round of hair on a broad body, the sari flaring off the shoulder; (2) the value: a light sari with big dark flowers and a dark edge, head uncovered; (3) the basket bag, a hand-sized round with a zigzag, on one forearm; (4) one arm up mid-gesture.

CLOSE-UP DETAILS (inserts and the face chip only): the two thick gold hoops; the open mouth; the claw clip; the family eyebrows; laugh lines and soft double chin; bare forehead, neck, wrists and nose; no spectacles; skin against her master swatch; her age, about 55.

MAY CHANGE look to look: the exact inks, the light, and the fine shape of the face, which only her reference picture carries (the method notes: hair, spectacles and pattern held across our five worlds; face shape, age and skin drifted).

LUGDI (chapter 1, her own chapter, face-on): hot magenta flowers on a marigold-lit cream, violet folds, dark copper-brown hair catching marigold light, marigold hoops. Hard lamp light from one side; keep her face lit, not lost in the shadow drama. Check the hairline close up in every pick for red.
RUKAVAT (chapter 2, small and silent at the ward door at dawn, if rulebook Q11 allows): faded rose on cream, never the signal orange; add the tested skin words.
STATION (chapter 3, small and silent at Mummy's counter, if Q11 allows): two inks, so shape and value carry her; the zigzag and the flower print must read at phone size.
CRICKET (chapter 4): not seen.

JADUGAR (chapter 5, Nani's kitchen, if Q11 allows): the cream silk-look flowered sari, lamp-lit against the indigo night; in this look 'basket' alone paints the rope-trick wicker basket and 'hoops' alone may paint magic rings, so always 'basket bag' and 'hoop earrings'.

NOW (her face chip on every note and bubble): the fixed look, word for word; the chip and the Lugdi panels must share the puff, the hoops and the print, because players meet her chip on the cards before and after they see her painted.

REFERENCES: one present-day master with the basket bag on her arm (person and prop in one slot), then one Lugdi reference (essential) and one present-day face chip; Rukavat, Station and Jadugar references only if Q11 lets her appear. Paint by scene with cutscenes.py paint-refs: at most two people from references in a panel (FLUX.2 klein takes four reference pictures), anyone else small, side-on or from behind, and never a card person. With Papa the contrast is built in (a tall striped line beside a wide flowered round); check both after every pick for swapped attributes.
cast.painter_prompt: TWO TIERS (the comics and rules reviews: long fixed looks make the painter swap traits between two people). The long text paints the master only; panels painted from her reference picture use the short tag. MASTER (present day; STYLE['now'] without its fixed rainy-evening light, since portraits.py has no present-day template): A character turnaround of one woman, the copper-haired woman, shown in five views side by side at the same size on a plain warm off-white background, evenly lit: from the front, three-quarter from her left, in profile facing left, three-quarter from behind, and from behind. She is a broad, soft, round-faced Indian woman of about 55, taller than average, wide in the shoulders and hips, with South Asian features and warm brown skin, a medium-deep brown, thick straight dark eyebrows, high round cheeks, laugh lines at the eyes, a soft double chin, a smooth clear forehead, and a wide mouth a little open as if mid-word. Her dark copper-brown dyed hair is brushed up off her forehead into a full soft puff with no centre parting, and the rest is twisted up at the back of her head in a big plain dark brown plastic claw clip, its ends fanning out above it, a little grey at the temples, fully uncovered. She wears two medium plain gold hoop earrings of thick round wire. She wears a cream sari printed all over with big magenta flowers and dark green leaves, with a solid magenta edge, wrapped in the everyday style, pleated at the waist, its loose end over her left shoulder and hanging down her back to her knees, a plain magenta half-sleeve sari blouse, and dark brown slip-on chappals. Her forearms, wrists and neck are bare. The basket bag hangs on her right forearm, her right hand resting on its folded cloth; her left hand hangs relaxed. Clean confident ink outlines, soft even colour fills, gentle paper grain, calm even daylight. (Then a reference ending of its own, without STORY_NO's 'One illustration panel, full-bleed', which fights five views: ' No text, no letters, no numbers, no words, no logos, no religious symbols, no writing anywhere.' The basket bag from its reference picture.) PANEL TAG (29 words, after her role word in any panel painted with her reference picture): 'broad round-faced Indian woman of about 55, South Asian features and warm brown skin, copper-brown hair in a round puff, gold hoop earrings, cream sari with big magenta flowers'. PANEL 1.09 (Lugdi), scene words with the tag: Night at a junction platform. The copper-haired woman (the tag) climbs up into the open doorway of an Indian sleeper carriage, its side painted one plain colour, face-on in the left third of the picture, her head a third of the way down, one hand gripping the upright steel grab rail beside the door, one foot on the top step, the basket bag hooked over her other forearm, her mouth wide open mid-shout, her eyebrows raised. Behind her one platform lamp. The plain carriage wall is empty in the upper right. Nobody else in the picture. (Then STYLE['lugdi'] and STORY_NO; her Lugdi reference and the basket bag's with paint-refs.) FIRST TEST before any more panels: one two-person picture, her with Papa at the berth beat, both from references with their tags; record, for each strip anchor, the share of picks that keep it, and how often the two swap traits.
painter_avoid: A forehead dot or any mark between or above the eyebrows: FLUX.2 klein paints one on nearly every Indian woman whatever the prompt says. Check every face close up by eye, and repaint with a new seed. The panel painter has neither tool today: DOTS and SEED_BUMP exist only in portraits.py, and cutscenes.py has three fixed seeds (rules review), so a per-panel seed bump and an eye-confirmed paint-out are added to cutscenes.py before any face-on panel of her; a person reads every forehead, since Station's halftone dots defeat an automatic finder. Never name the mark in a prompt.

Red in or along a hair parting, or a red streak at the hairline: with her copper-brown hair this is the likeliest sindoor misread, worst in Lugdi's vermilion lamp light. The look says 'no centre parting', no prompt puts 'red' or 'vermilion' near her hair, and every hairline is checked close up.
Lines between or above the eyebrows (they can come back as a painted tilak, rules review).
Anything at the neck (a chain, pendant or black beads read as a mangalsutra); check the neck.
Bangles of any kind on either wrist (glass, gold or steel; steel reads as a kara), a watch, or threads on the wrist or ankle; check the wrists.
Toe rings, a nose ring or a nose stud.
Mehendi patterns on hands or feet; never write 'henna' in a prompt.
The sari's loose end, or any cloth, over her head.

A white or near-white sari (with a bare forehead it reads as a widow); a solid red or solid magenta silk sari with a broad gold edge (reads as the bride, and solid magenta sinks into Jadugar's stage).
A tilak, ash, beads, a religious pendant or any religious symbol; folded hands (read as prayer).

Lightened skin or a European face, likeliest in Rukavat's soft gouache and wherever the copper hair pulls the painter: the tested skin words go in every prompt; compare with her master swatch; reject and repaint with a new seed.
Spectacles of any kind (they belong to Nani and Masterji); a gap in her teeth (Tinku's).

Letters, numbers or logos anywhere: on the basket bag, its cloth, the flask, the pickle jar (painters put printed labels on jars), the exercise books and their jackets (red ticks painted as plain strokes, never letters or marks out of ten), the phone, the sari edge, the carriage (rule 30). Each goes on the close-up stray-letter check.
The draft's steel tiffin carrier, salwar suit, open waves and thin hoops (replaced by the basket bag, the sari, the claw clip and thick medium hoops).
A third hand, or a hand nobody owns: count hands in every pick; a hand reaching out of the frame towards the viewer without her face in the frame reads as the player's (rule 7).
Figures of the bay or any cousin behind or beside her: they are the card people (rule 32).
The wrong basket or hoops: bare 'basket' paints Jadugar's rope-trick wicker basket, bare 'hoops' may paint magic rings; always 'basket bag' and 'hoop earrings'.
Painted too young, or as a comic figure: no gossip pose, no hand over the mouth, no pot-belly gag, no caricature aunty face.
Her name in a prompt (it gets painted as lettering), or a relation word such as 'the aunt' (it can paint a second person): the role word 'the copper-haired woman' only.

Words that fire the old take's glossary rows or sit on its need list (rules review, checked with its probe on this prompt): 'flat' (an apartment), 'cover' (a pulp novel), 'seat' (a lorry cab), 'floor' (Dadi's bedroom), 'stands' (cricket benches), 'watch', 'bench', 'match', 'coach' (write 'sleeper carriage'), 'border' (write 'edge'), 'ground' and 'sheet' (write 'background' and 'turnaround').
Looking like Mummy, her sister, who shares the brows: keep the round copper puff and high clip against Mummy's low bun, and magenta flowers on cream against Mummy's maroon.
model_sheet: ORDER OF WORK (the comics review: most failures are between people, so the cast comes before the person): (1) the cast line-up, all ten as black shapes at phone width in the four height bands, her in the middle band, approved by the owner as a picture; (2) the six look strips, all ten as simple figures in each look's inks, where her collisions are settled (Jadugar's stage magenta, old gold, Lugdi's brightest shape); (3) the trait table, one owner a trait, with her duplicates already struck in this file; (4) only then her master.

MASTER TURNAROUND (present day): front, three-quarter left, profile left, three-quarter back, back; full figure, the basket bag on her right forearm, on a plain background. Three seeds (7100, 7203, 7319), picked by eye against the audit checklist below. Not yet tested: whether klein paints five views in one picture; the fallback is five single-view paintings from the same words.
HEIGHT CHECK (inside the line-up): her shape beside Papa (tall band) and Mausa ji (short band), the two she shares panels with; beside Mummy (same band) the test is shape, not height.

POSES: standing with the basket bag on one forearm, the other hand stirring; climbing a carriage step (a hand on the grab rail, mouth open: the 1.09 pose); dropping down onto a berth and sitting deep, right leg out; patting the place beside her; the tuck (both hands at the waist); the offering arm (a foil parcel at full stretch towards the viewer, face in frame); the close read (blank paper a hand's width from her nose); marking a stack of blank exercise books on her berth under a night lamp, red ticks as plain strokes; the greeting (both arms wide); bending for Nani's palm on her head.
EXPRESSIONS as whole-body poses: neutral, pleased, worried, cross, laughing, teasing, tired, moved (as in posture).

FACE CHIP: head and shoulders, front and three-quarter, 512 by 512, present day, for every bubble and note she carries; checked close up for the forehead, the brows, the hairline, the ears (hoops only), the neck.

PROPS, each painted alone: the basket bag (front, three-quarter, and from above with the cloth folded back on the pickle jar, foil parcels, steel flask and the stack of exercise books); the pickle jar (shut, no label); the exercise books (plain brown paper jackets, blank pages, red ticks as plain strokes); the claw clip; the hoop earrings; the chappals.

OUTFIT VARIANTS: the signature travel sari; the faded home sari with its loose end tucked; the cream cardigan over the sari (January and December only); the cream silk-look flowered wedding sari with the magenta and gold edge.

FAR SPEC sheet: her as a small figure from words alone, round copper-brown head, wide light sari shape with a dark edge, the basket bag, to check that she still reads when she is not from a reference.

PER-LOOK REFERENCES from the picked master with the edit model (cutscenes.py paint-ref and pick-ref, Flux2KleinEdit), so the painter is never asked to change style and keep a face in one step: Lugdi first; the present-day face chip; Rukavat, Station and Jadugar only if rulebook Q11 lets her appear; the basket bag in Lugdi and in each look she appears in.

PIPELINE BEFORE HER FIRST PANEL (rules review): cutscenes.py keys ERA, LOOKS and ROLE by year and reads first-take-script.md, while Saal Bhar is a present-day story in five looks; REFS holds objects only and paint_refs() never checks klein's limit. So: looks keyed by look, panels read from the chapter JSONs, a person route in REFS, a refusal of any panel with more than four references, explicit lists of who is in each panel (looks() adds a fixed look whenever a name appears, possessives included), and the seed bump and dot paint-out. FILES (proposed): art/refs/copper-haired-woman-master.png, -lugdi.png, -chip.png, art/refs/basket-bag.png and basket-bag-<look>.png, with the seeds tried and the seed picked beside each. Every run goes through ~/.claude/heavy-queue/heavyq, one heavy job on the Mac at a time, only after this workflow and any browser checks have stopped (mac-memory-limit), and the owner approves the pictured sheet before any panel.

AUDIT CHECKLIST for every panel she is in, with a pass rate kept per look. Strip anchors first: (1) round silhouette, a full round of hair on a broad body; (2) a light sari with big dark flowers and a dark edge, head uncovered; (3) the basket bag, zigzag, no lettering; (4) copper-brown hair, no parting, hairline clean. Then close-up: (5) two thick gold hoops; (6) two hands, one free; (7) forehead, brows, neck, wrists, nose and toes bare; (8) skin against her swatch; (9) no spectacles, no tooth gap; (10) no letters or numbers, the jar and the books included; (11) looks about 55; (12) nothing swapped with the other person in the panel; (13) no card person in the frame. Which arm holds the bag is noted, never failed.

GLOSSARY ROWS to add before any panel, only for shared objects and only under keys nobody else uses (rules review: worn things collided between files, so her sari, blouse, hoops, claw clip, hair, chappals and cardigan live in her LOOKS entry alone): 'basket bag' (the prop line above); 'foil parcel' (a thin parcel of food wrapped in plain silver foil); 'pickle jar' (a squat clear glass jar of dark red-brown lime pickle with a plain white screw lid and no label); 'exercise books' (a stack of thin school exercise books in plain brown paper jackets, nothing written on them); 'grab rail' (the upright steel handrail beside a railway carriage's open door); 'sleeper carriage' (one shared definition with Papa's file). Reuse the existing 'flask' row. Re-run the glossary probe on every panel's final words.
best_scenes: 1.09, 9:40 pm, boarding (Lugdi): face-on in the sleeper carriage doorway, left third, the basket bag on her arm, the platform lamp behind her, nobody else in frame, the chapter's one shout: 'So few berths? For so many of us?' (no figures: Papa's 1.08 already says them).

A new beat straight after 1.09, before the circle page (not a lead-in, so rule 37's matched lead-ins for twin A at 1.13 and 1.25 stay as written): face-on towards the viewer, arms wide, the bay out of frame: 'Oh! I missed you so much.' Then she drops down onto the lower berth made up for her and sits deep, right leg out: 'A lower berth? For me? Who arranged this?' Papa, from behind: 'In January.' Her palm goes to her chest and she says nothing. It answers the review's 'the household never talk to each other in the train scenes'.

A new wordless beat after D1 settles (after 1.15), about 9:58 pm, lights dimming: she sits deep on her lower berth under the night lamp, marking a stack of blank exercise books, each held close to her face, red ticks as plain strokes, the basket bag open beside her; only the sound word 'shhh' from off panel. A teacher in one picture with no note word (comics review). Then, if rulebook Q5 allows, her joke on herself: 'Yes, I'm loud. That's how Class 3 hears.' Kept well clear of the hard decision at 11 pm (rule 25). Optional if Mausa ji may be seen in chapter 1 [WAITS rulebook Q11]: after D4 settles, night-lamp blue, her hand in his on the berth edge, him from behind.

Three new beats after D5 settles and before D6's lead-in, 2:20 am, the carriage step at the long halt, the steel flask beside her: (a) 'Can't sleep. Just like Amma.' and, laughing and meaning it, 'Amma calls your Mummy first!'; (b) the cut-off (You: 'Mausi, wo…' Mausi: 'Listen, listen, listen! Now tell me. Straight to me.'); (c) the quote-back, 'Last year you said: "Next time, right beside you."', she pats the step, and your 'Okay, Mausi.' At most 20 counted words a beat (rule 62); every word passes the note-word check against D6 to D8 (no phone, साथ, सबके, पास, बोल, platform or शहर).

1.37, the outcome painting at dawn (people-free, as written, and described without names so no fixed look is pulled in): 'a magenta-and-white basket bag on the front step of a house with a blue wooden gate, beside a tray of chai'. Her one object stand-in of the year: she was first through the gate. Then 1.40, the wet back step, and the party is off.
Chapter 2, first light at the ward door [WAITS rulebook Q11]: small, face-on, silent, the basket bag on her arm, Mausa ji beside the door from behind; two people, after Nani has had her rung at four.

Chapter 3, the flood week lunch [WAITS rulebook Q11]: small, face-on, silent, at Mummy's counter, a foil parcel held out to Mummy, a second one on the counter for Masterji; no hired hands in the frame (rule 32).

December, Nani's kitchen, before the cake (chapter 5's writer numbers it, about 5.25 or 5.26) [WAITS rulebook Q11]: the May jar comes down off the shelf, Nani tastes it and thanks her first in front of the kitchen ('My eldest made this.', Nani's writer owns the line); Mausi's one silent panel of the year, palm pressed to her chest. Two people, Nani and Mausi, one payoff in the panel. She is not at the cake (5.28) and not in the album.
never_does: Never doubts, questions or plays down a report of being followed or harassed, or a dowry demand, and never calls one a misunderstanding; she is the first to believe. Because the hard topic never reaches a bubble or a story panel (rule 26), this shows in what she never says and in her notes never touching it (her draft note on Kiran, the card with the report, is about cooking, never the report).
Never sits on a card, never names, points at or describes a card person in a bubble, and never uses a card note's words in a bubble before or during that decision (rules 10 and 36).
Never asks the decision's question (Papa asks in chapter 1, rule 37), and never reacts to who was picked (rule 39).

Never judges character: her notes are habits seen at the table or on a trip, in a report-card voice, never 'lazy', 'bossy', 'characterless' or a word on anyone's morals, marriage or dress; never anything about women or men in general (rule 22); her notes land on women and men equally.

Never interrogates you like the stock aunty: never asks about marriage, a match, your salary, your weight, your looks or anyone's skin colour. She asks whether you have eaten and slept, and for your news, and leaves your life to you.
Never sets women against women: her rivalry with Mummy is concern and a daily call, and Mami is her ally.
Never gives you a gender: no beta, bhaiya or didi, no verb that agrees with you (rules 8 and 66).
Never touches you, never holds anything out towards you unless her face is in the frame (rule 7), and never feeds the bay in a painting (rule 32).
Never whispers, never shouts twice in a chapter (rule 35), and never goes a whole panel silent except when she is moved.
Never hides what she feels: she is the one elder who says it in words, sorry and thank you included, though she still hands over food as she says them.

Never puts a number, a score or a year in her lines (Papa owns the figures in chapter 1; rule 2), and never borrows another person's signature line ('Reached?', 'Bas', 'Main yahin hoon', 'Ho jayega', 'pakka').
Never wears spectacles; never covers her head; never wears white, bangles, a chain or a watch.
Never says she does not know.
Never repeats what she was told in confidence: she remembers everything and passes on only what she was asked to.
Never forwards gods, politics, false news, a famous face or a home remedy; her one daily send is her own children's riddle.
Never the butt of the joke: the strip laughs with her, never at her loudness, her body or her age.

Never speaks outside chapter 1 while rulebook Q11 is open; her small silent appearances in chapters 2, 3 and 5 are marked [WAITS rulebook Q11], and her basket bag stands in for her only once, at 1.37.
