test_lines.hinglish: Haay! Achhi khabar? Kiski? Hamari! Amma ko abhi batao!
test_lines.hi: हाय! अच्छी ख़बर? किसकी? हमारी! अम्मा को अभी बताओ!

voice_changes: Triples cut back to doubles by default ('Chalo, chalo!', 'Na, na!', 'Aao, aao.', 'Sorry, sorry!', 'Munna, Munna!'), the way real Hindi repeats a word; a triple is kept for a peak, at most once a scene, and 'Suno, suno, suno!' stays the one the family quotes back. The test set now opens with a triple twice in twelve (moments 3 and 8, and 8 is a line the readers marked true) instead of eight times. Why: the real-India note, too many triples.

'Haaye' is now spelled 'Haay' in Roman letters (हाय is unchanged) and kept in English mode too, replacing 'Oh!'. It comes at most once a scene and never just before she holds out food, so the worry line and the good-news line lose it. Why: 'Haaye' is the film spelling of the Punjabi aunty, the very type the comics review named; keeping 'Haay' in English also ends the blur with Mama ji's 'Oho!'.

'Aji' now goes with आप: 'Aji, goli khaayi? Nahin? Haay! Abhi khaiye!', the typed 'abhi khaiye', and moment 4 with no तुम command ('Mujhe phiki chahiye.'). Why: a wife who calls her husband 'Aji' says आप to him. Mausa ji's file still has तुम both ways, which the note wants matched, so the family address table settles it.
The order to Papa and Mausa ji is now 'Chaliye, chaliye! Bade wale upar! Jaldi kijiye!'. Why: the Hindi note, चलो to a jija reads as a step down.

English tags are now 'right?' across her English lines ('Amma calls your Mummy first! Right?'), and 'Didn't I say so?' is now 'Didn't I tell you?', 'Absolutely first class' is now 'First class!', 'No tension!' is now 'Don't take tension!', and 'copybooks' is now 'notebooks'. Why: Indian English says 'right?' or 'na?', and the English-mode readers heard the rest as translated.

Common fillers are no longer banned for her: she says 'Achha?' (moment 7), 'arre' may come mid-line as anyone's filler (as an exclamation it stays Captain sahab's, matrix 2.15), and the never list now keeps out only other people's set phrases. The bans on arre, dekho, achha, bas, theek, chalo/suno as anyone else's, 'please', 'pata nahin', 'mausam' and 'barsaat' are gone ('pakka?' stays out only as doubt after a report). Why: cast-wide note 1. Fillers belong to everyone, and she is told apart by shape and word sources.

The English verb with kar or ho is now hers when it suits a schoolteacher: 'Phir se top kiya, hai na?', and 'check karo', 'fail ho gayi' in her uses. She still never switches a whole clause. Why: cast-wide note 2. It is the most common Hinglish pattern, and Mummy is marked by her counter English, not by owning the pattern.

Sorry and thanks are plain words. Sorry is 'Sorry, sorry! Pehle khao.', and since Tinku and you now say a plain 'sorry' too, hers is told apart by the double and the food. Thanks is now the everyday 'Bahut achha kiya!' (since mended to 'Bahut achha laga!', so that 'Bahut achha kiya' is Mummy's alone), with the teacher's grade 'Ekdum first class!' at most once a chapter. Why: cast-wide note 3, no thanks or sorry in a code more than once a chapter.

The town's words reach her plainly: 'fikr mat karo' to Chhoti, 'goli ka waqt' to Aji, and 'Jaldi aana. Zaroor!' in a new parting sample. Why: cast-wide note 8, so fikr, waqt and zaroor are not one tailor's badge.

Moment 2 drops the cold food ('Khana thanda!') for 'Ab aaye ho? Late mark! Kaan pakdo!', the classroom's own punishment said in fun. Moment 11 now worries ('Koi baat nahin! Chot toh nahin lagi?') instead of a second class joke. Why: cast-wide note 6, where five people reached for cold food in moment 2; the change also keeps her school words from becoming a gimmick.

The first time she names Mummy to you in a chapter, she says 'tumhari Mummy' and then 'Chhoti' ('Tumhari khabar, tumhari Mummy se? Kyon?'; the typed 'tumhari mummy se nahi'). Why: Nani's note, 'Chhoti' alone is opaque to the player-reader.

Lines get more of their verbs ('Abhi se yaad aa rahi hai!', 'Bachche aaj bhi tumhari benchon par baithte hain!'), and the shout ends 'Ye nahin chalega!' instead of 'Kabhi nahin!'. Why: cast-wide note 9 on verbless telegrams, and 'Kabhi nahin!' did not answer her own question the way a Hindi-belt aunt would.

Moment 3 keeps her own congratulation ('Naukri lag gayi! Maine kaha tha na?', now 'lag gayi' as it is said); 'Badhai ho' is left for Mummy if the owner allows it, and 'Mubarak ho' unused. Why: cast-wide note 4.

Kept word for word, as the readers marked true: 'Bahut yaad aayi'; 'Rishta main laayi thi. Berth bhi main laaun?'; 'Kaisi hoon? Batati hoon! Ghutna dukhta hai, dil nahin!'; 'Chehre pe thakaan! Kuch khaya bhi?'; 'Na, na, na! Band? Toh meri class ka inaam?'; 'Late mark!'; 'Ekdum first class!'; the riddle 'ek thaal moti se bhara'; the '....' typing with 😊; 'khana khaya?? kya kya khaya??'. Also kept: her essence, want, fear, contradiction, year arc, the shout's place, the lower-berth silence, the December silence, every never-rule on harassment and dowry reports, and the note-word limits.

Open points for readers and the owner: whether Mausa ji says आप back to her (his file says तुम); whether 'Meri class aise hi sunti hai' and 'Kaan pakdo!' to a grown brother sound right to a Hindi-first reader; whether 'Badhai ho' is allowed (owner); rule 66's fourth shape and rule 62 for message cards (owner, the entries below); whether 'Aji' sounds like the film wife (readers, the entry below).

Moment 9 is now 'Gali mein nadi? Haay! Achaar ke martbaan upar! Chalo, chalo!' | 'गली में नदी? हाय! अचार के मर्तबान ऊपर! चलो, चलो!' | 'Lane's a river? Haay! Pickles up! Come on, come on!'. Why: the Hindi note, where 'Arre' worked as an exclamation, which matrix 2.15 gives to Captain sahab, so her own 'Haay' takes its place; and the real-India note, where the classroom had become her stamp, so the flood reaches for the courtyard's pickle jars instead of her pupils' exercise books.

Moment 5 is now 'Galat kaun nikla? Main! Sorry, sorry! Pehle khao!' | 'ग़लत कौन निकला? मैं! सॉरी, सॉरी! पहले खाओ!' | 'Who got it wrong? Me! Sorry, sorry! Eat first!'. Why: the same real-India note; it was the third school line of four in the test set. Now two of twelve reach for school ('Late mark! Kaan pakdo!' and 'meri class ka inaam', both marked true and kept), and the rest come from the kitchen, her questions answered at once and her exact memory. 'Aaj teacher fail' stays a now-and-then habit (tic 5, sorry), and tic 5 now says the classroom is one of her two sources, never her stamp.

Rule 66: address 0 now sets out the owner's question on pasts with ने where you are the doer ('Pichhle saal tumne kaha tha', 'Kuch khaya bhi?', 'khana khaya??', 'Parathe rakhe, hai na?', and, until her thanks became 'Bahut achha laga!', 'Bahut achha kiya!' said to you): add it to rule 66 as a fourth shape, or have the native reader clear each line onto the build's cleared list. The lines' notes point there, and the cleared list now holds only lines where you are not the doer. No wording changed. Why: the Hindi note, rule 66 names only three shapes for तुम and the file had cleared these as 'a ने past', which the rule does not name.

Rule 62 and typed messages: typing habit 9 now asks the owner whether a message card is held to the 10-word cap, and samples 0, 3, 5 and 7 carry their split at her '....' into cards of 10 words or fewer, ready if the cap applies. No message changed. Why: the Hindi note, four of her messages run to between 13 and 20 words.

Masterji's word for her stays 'Behenji' (आप), and address 10 now says why and that Masterji's file, which has 'Mausi ji', is to be matched to it. Why: the two address tables disagreed, and 'Behenji' is what a neighbour of about sixty says to a schoolteacher of about fifty-five.

'Aji' now carries a readers' question (address 6, uses 28): if the Hindi-first readers hear the 1970s film wife in it, her lines to Mausa ji take 'Suniye' or no address word, still with आप. Why: the real-India note.

cast.name: Mausa ji (मौसा जी), about 58, chapter 2's voice
cast.role: Chapter 2's voice ('One night in the ward', the Rukavat look over a present-day district hospital). He is the second judging voice beside Nani, who asks all eight decisions; his four work verdicts sit on twin D's cards (2.16 and 2.28), so a woman and a man judge in that chapter (rule 22). Mummy's elder sister's husband: your mother's side, and married in, like Papa and Mami. While rulebook Q11 is open he speaks in chapter 2 only; he never asks a decision and never sits on a card; in every other chapter he is a silent, painted presence, small but face-on, never an object standing in for him. Label on first use: 'Mausa ji, Mausi's husband' | 'मौसा जी, मौसी के पति' (the cast map's label; chapter 2's JSON still tags 2.03 and 2.17 with the old 'Mummy's sister's husband', which the chapter writer updates), then 'Mausa ji' | 'मौसा जी' with his face chip on every bubble. Painter's role word: 'the bearded man', taken from his look as every role word now should be, with no colour word in it (rules review) and no relation word, since 'aunt' or 'uncle' can paint a second person. Flat by design (one chapter, read at a glance), with one contradiction held the same way every time and one change across the year that is painted at both ends. OPEN FOR THE OWNER AND READERS: (1) rulebook Q5, whether he may make his one dry joke; (2) rulebook Q11, which would remove the chapter voices; (3) the address words 'Amma ji' (his word for Nani), 'Chhote' (his for Mama ji), 'Bade Jija ji' (Mama ji's for him), 'Bhai sahab' (Papa's) and 'Jija ji' (Mummy's and Mami's), to be settled in the cast map's one address table that every file reads (India review); (4) whether 'Mausa ji' leans towards one community, since many Urdu-speaking families say 'Khalu', for a Hindi-first and an Urdu-speaking reader; (5) the silent cameos proposed in chapters 1, 3, 4 and 5; (6) the back-step bulb: the default is now that Nani's fall has no cause on screen or in writing, and the new lit bulb at her homecoming reads as care, not guilt; the owner may still ask for the old thread, but never in an outcome beat (rule 46); (7) whether Mausi's two grown children travel in chapter 1, and if so that they stay off the cards Mausi judges; (8) the sweet lime (mosambi) in place of the orange, and whether a strong thumb can peel one by hand (readers); (9) the plain dark olive shoulder cloth: readers confirm that a plain one-colour cotton cloth over a man's shoulders leans to no region or community; (10) his retirement: voluntary at 58, two years early; readers confirm the board's age.
cast.essence: A retired lineman, 34 years on the electricity board's poles and night shutdowns, with big scarred hands, who says two blunt words and does twenty kind things. He keeps the steel chairs outside the ward door all night so you can sleep, peels a sweet lime with his bare thumb and sets half of it down beside you, stands up when the doctor goes by, and leaves the room if anyone thanks him. The type in five words: the quiet uncle who fixes. What makes him not the type, the same way every time: blunt in words, but soft in deeds; and two things only a lineman carries, the night-gang habit of handing out halves of whatever fruit there is, and a scar from the day a dead line came back on under his hand, which is why nobody near him touches a switch until he nods. The line people quote back: 'Hmm. Ho jayega.' | 'हम्म। हो जाएगा।' | 'Hmm. It'll get done.' Who would say 'I know this person': Farida, the staff nurse, who has seen him outside her ward on a hundred nights (cast map); and Mr Natarajan, 61 and retired, who knows what the first year with no duty to go to feels like.
cast.backstory: Born in 1968 in a small town (never named, rule 3), the eldest of four. After Class 12 he took the state electricity board's lineman training; the job letter came in January 1992 and he married Mausi that November (married 34 years, cast map). For twenty years he climbed poles; for fourteen more he ran a line gang out of the sub-station near the railway junction, the man the night calls went to. On night shutdowns the gang shared whatever fruit someone had brought, and whoever peeled it handed out the halves; he still cannot eat a whole one, and he is the only one in the family who can take the thick peel off a sweet lime with his thumb. In 1998 a line he had shut down was switched back on while his hand was on it: a pale, shiny burn scar the size of a coin sits on the back of his right hand, and since that day nobody touches a wire near him with the switch on. He retired last December at 58 on the board's voluntary scheme, two years early, because his knees would no longer take the poles (team judgement: we assume a retirement age of 60 for his board and have opened no source; readers confirm). This is his first year with no duty roster, and he still wakes at five. He and Mausi live in a two-room house near the junction, fifteen minutes from Mummy's shop; the front room is Mausi's tuition class, whose fans he rewires every summer. Since he retired Mausi has hidden the stepladder, because of the knees; he borrows the neighbour's. Their two grown children (about 32 and 29) work in other cities, ring on Sundays and want their parents to move nearer them; he answers 'Hmm', which means no. What fills his day now: neighbours who call 'ek minute' for a switch, a fan or a meter; the customers with wiring trouble whom Mummy sends him, so he is never idle; twenty minutes asleep sitting up after lunch; cricket with the sound off. He takes a blood-pressure tablet, which Mausi tells everyone about. For thirty years he has fixed Nani's house wiring without being asked and held her spare house key (Nani's file), and every winter he fits a new rubber foot on her cane. Her lane knows him as the son-in-law who fixes things; a few still call him 'Lineman sahab'. In May, the evening of Nani's fall, he carried her to the auto at seven. The fall has no cause on screen or in writing (the default; see role, question 6). What it did to him: it frightened him that eighty is not a number that waits, and he has not said 'kal' (tomorrow) about a job since. Before she came home he had lit her back step and laid a rubber mat on it, and nobody has mentioned it. CHANGES FROM THE DRAFT AND THE CAST MAP, WITH REASONS (the review responses are under revision_notes): (1) the bible's 'slow, kind, few words' becomes 'blunt in words, kind in deeds', so his four harsh chapter 2 remarks fit (continuity read). (2) No spectacles at all, which leaves spectacles to Nani and Masterji. (3) 2.17 'I'm fine on this bench.' becomes 'The bench is fine.' | 'बेंच ठीक है।', to keep his never-'I' habit. (4) His card notes keep to work verdicts (see voice). (5) The orange becomes a sweet lime, and he sets the half down rather than holding it out. (6) The painter's role word is 'the bearded man'. (7) The olive shawl becomes a thin olive cotton shoulder cloth from February to November and an olive wool shawl in December, worn the same way all year, round the neck and over both shoulders.
cast.want_fear_contradiction: WANTS THIS YEAR: a quiet first year of retirement, useful and unthanked; under it, to still be the man people ring when the lights go, now that the board does not. WANTS FROM YOU: that you sleep while he sits up, and that you never thank him (if you do, he stands and leaves). By December the want turns: he sets a stack of chairs down for you and steps back, the first load he leaves you to share. FEARS: that his tongue undoes what his hands do, so he keeps it to two words; that retirement makes him a man who sits; and, after May, that Amma ji's time is shorter than any 'kal'. CONTRADICTION, shown the same way every time: blunt in words, but soft in deeds. He calls a man lazy, then peels a sweet lime and leaves you half. Every bubble of his is followed, in the same panel or the next, by something his hands do. He is never the silent patriarch: his few words always lead to an act, and he never has the last say on a family decision.
relationships: NANI ('Amma ji' | 'अम्मा जी', आप; she says आप to him, as to everyone who married into her family, Nani's file): for thirty years he has fixed her wiring unasked and held her spare house key, and every winter he fits a new rubber foot on her cane. When he arrives she lays her hand on his shoulder and he bows his head a little: the cast's greeting for an elder, in place of touching her feet (India review). Friction: she still orders him about as if he were 24 ('Ladder. Now.') and will not let him spend a rupee in her house; he says 'Hmm' and climbs, knees or no knees. Tenderness: she never thanks him, because she knows he could not bear it; she thanks him the only way he accepts, with the next job. On the ward night she sends him to sleep at 2 am; he does not go, and she does not ask again (Nani's file). Before she comes home he has lit her back step.

MAUSI (his wife; married 34 years; no address word from him, तुम both ways, equal): she talks, he says 'Hmm'; she finishes his sentences and he lets her; she is half a head taller, which he finds funny and never says. Friction: she tells everyone his blood pressure, and since he retired she has hidden the stepladder because of his knees; he borrows the neighbour's, and she knows. Tenderness: on night trains they hold hands when they think the coach is asleep (cast map); every summer he wires a bigger fan into her tuition room. She is the only one who can make him laugh aloud, with a story he has heard fifty times.

MUMMY ('Jija ji' and आप from her; no address word and तुम from him, as to his wife's younger sister): in 1999 he gave her her first wholesaler's name, and his is the only wiring advice she takes without arguing; the morning after the July flood her shutter does not go up until he has knelt at the switchboard and nodded, and she does not touch the switch before (Mummy's file; a silent beat while Q11 holds). Friction: she prices everything and he gives his work away for nothing, which she calls bad business to his face. Tenderness: she keeps fuses aside for him at cost and never lets him pay (Mummy's file), and sends him every customer with a wiring problem, so in retirement he is never idle.

PAPA ('Bhai sahab' and आप from Papa; no address word and आप from him; two years apart, equal): the two who married in sit side by side at every function, contentedly silent; Papa talks trains, he says 'Hmm' (cast map). Friction: his 'Ho jayega' with no time in it drives Papa quietly mad ('When?', Papa's file); after May the answer is 'Abhi.' Tenderness: on the ward night Papa takes the next steel chair so he is not alone, and neither speaks (Papa's file). Each is the other's way out of a crowded room ('Bhai sahab, chai?').

MAMA JI ('Chhote' | 'छोटे' and तुम from him, the one nickname he uses, since the scooter lessons; 'Bade Jija ji' and आप from Mama ji, Mama ji's file): he taught Mama ji to ride a scooter at fifteen, in 1994; Mama ji earns the most now and he still pays for the tea first (cast map). Friction: Mama ji solves with money, and when Mama ji tries to pay him for the wedding's lighting work he walks off mid-sentence. Tenderness: at midnight in the wedding week Mama ji sits beside him on the gate step for two silent minutes, the only quiet of Mama ji's week (Mama ji's file).

TINKU ('Tinku', the only first name he says, with तुम; she says 'Mausa ji' and आप): they watch matches side by side without talking, the television on mute and her radio commentary in her headphones; he says 'Hmm' at every wicket and is the only adult who never calls her 'the youngest' (cast map), and the only one she lets turn the pages of her scorebook (Tinku's file). Friction: she scores him ('Eleven Hmms, two words.') and he pretends not to hear. Tenderness: in December, when her scorers' course letter comes, his is the first reply in the family group, one word, his highest: 'Mazboot.'

MAMI ('Jija ji' and आप from her; no address word and आप from him): first to arrive and last to leave at her daughter's wedding, carrying chairs; she puts him on no list because he does everything that is not on it (cast map). Friction: she keeps finding jobs done before she has written them down, and has to tick things she never gave out. Tenderness (proposal): on the last night she writes 'Jija ji' at the bottom of her list, with a tick and no job beside it, as live text on her card, and shows him; he says 'Hmm'.

MASTERJI ('Masterji' and आप, both ways, Masterji's file): he rewired Masterji's shop for nothing in 2001, and Masterji has stitched his shirts at cost ever since; neither mentions it (cast map). Friction: his shirts came back scorched from live wires for years, which Masterji took personally (Masterji's file), and he will not stand still for a fitting, so they hang loose. Tenderness: the slow talker and the man of two words sit on the shop step together, one talking, one saying 'Hmm' (Masterji's file); after every flood he checks the switchboard on the wall their shops share, Masterji's side first, because it is older. For the wedding he stands still for one fitting in thirty years, and wears the new grey shirt on the last night.

CAPTAIN SAHAB ('Captain sahab' and आप): two men of few words who once watched a whole lane final side by side and said four words between them (cast map). Friction: Captain sahab calls every decision aloud; he thinks most of them need no saying. Tenderness: he rewired the lane ground's floodlights for nothing, and Captain sahab lets him sit at the scorer's table, the only person there who does not score.

YOU (तुम, rarely, and no address word at all; you say 'Mausa ji' and आप and -इए): he keeps the chairs outside the ward so you can sleep and never mentions it; he sets half of every sweet lime he peels down beside you; from the corridor he texts you 'So jao.'. Friction: when you try to thank him he leaves the room, and when you offer to take the night chair he says 'Nahin. So jao.' Tenderness: in December he carries a stack of chairs to where you are, sets it down and steps back, waiting: the first load he has ever left you to share.

HIS OWN TWO GROWN CHILDREN (about 32 and 29, working in other cities; never named, painted or on a card unless the owner wants a speaking person in their thirties, cast map): they ring on Sundays; he says 'Haan. Theek.' and hands the phone to Mausi. Friction: they want their parents in a flat near them, the very thing Mama ji wants for Nani, and his 'Hmm' means no. Tenderness: he knows their train times better than they do.

NANI'S LANE (chapter 2's circle, on the cards): they have known him for thirty years as the son-in-law who fixes things at Nani's house. His card notes on them are verdicts on work he has seen them do there, never on character, looks or temper, and never said aloud in a bubble (rule 36). Their crowd at the ward door is told by his line, never painted as figures who could be card people: the corridor behind him stays empty, as 2.03 already has it.

THE DOCTOR, THE NIGHT NURSE AND WARD STAFF ('Ji.' and आप): he stands when the doctor goes by and stays standing until the round has gone; he stands for the night nurse too. He never argues with staff, never pays anyone for a favour and asks the guard for nothing for himself. He never says 'doctor sahab' or 'sister', so neither the doctor nor the nurse is given a gender (chapter 2 writer note).
cast.year_arc: JANUARY (the opening, present day; he is not on the household screen): his first month with no duty roster after 34 years. Up at five, rewiring Mausi's tuition-room fans from the neighbour's stepladder. When a job can wait he still says 'Kal.' MAY, CHAPTER 1 (Lugdi, the night train in a sleeper coach; Mausi's chapter, so he is silent; proposed cameo, painted small but face-on): he boards at the junction with Mausi and too many bags and climbs to an upper berth without being asked; when the coach is asleep, he and Mausi hold hands. He is in none of the dawn panels 1.37 to 1.40: they are outcome beats, and 1.37 and 1.40 have no people. MAY, CHAPTER 2 (Rukavat, his chapter): he carried Nani to the auto at seven. All night he keeps the row of steel chairs outside the ward door, Papa silent on the next one, since one attendant pass lets only you stay inside. At 2.03 he tells Nani 'Half your lane is outside.', the corridor behind him painted empty. He texts you 'So jao.'. At 2.17 he refuses a cot ('The bench is fine.'), and when you offer to take the night chair, 'Nahin. So jao.': the load he will not share, the first end of his arc. He will not go to sleep when Nani sends him, stands as the doctor goes by, and gives his four work verdicts on the lane's cards. At dawn (a proposed panel) he peels a sweet lime with his thumb, face-on, and sets half of it on the chair beside the ward door for you: 'Lo. Aadha.' Before the taxi he says 'Abhi aaya.' and goes ahead with her spare key, which is why he is not in its seats. One wordless story beat before 2.32, not an outcome (proposal): the back step in morning light, a new bulb lit above it and a black ribbed rubber mat on the stone, no people, and a description that names nobody (a name pulls that person's look into the picture, rules review). He is never in a Rukavat panel with Mummy. JULY, CHAPTER 3 (Station, the flood; Masterji's chapter; proposed silent cameo, one panel): the morning the water goes down he kneels at the switchboard on the wall Mummy's shop shares with Masterji's, mains off, while Mummy and Masterji wait with their hands at their sides; the shutter goes up only after his nod. This is his trade on screen, and the plot needs it. 15 AUGUST, CHAPTER 4 (Cricket, the lane cup; Tinku's chapter; proposed silent cameo): on a plastic chair beside Tinku's scorer's table, forearms on his knees, one nod at each wicket; nothing to fix, and for once he lets himself just sit. DECEMBER, CHAPTER 5 (Jadugar, the wedding at Nani's house; Mami's chapter; proposed silent cameos): first through the blue gate at dawn with two folding steel chairs, last to leave; Mami puts him on no list. On the last night the canopy lights trip and the lane goes dark; seconds later the lights come back and he is on the low wooden stool at the switchboard by the gate, which the Jadugar look can paint as the magic show's lights out, lights on. The other end of his arc: he carries a stack of folding steel chairs to the foot of the picture, sets it down turned towards you, and steps back, hands empty, waiting. Nothing leaves the frame towards you and you are never painted (rule 7). He never carries the cake (a card decision, 5.24). THE ALBUM (present day): back row, in the new grey shirt, the only one looking up at the lights instead of at the camera. FROM JANUARY TO DECEMBER: from the man who carries every load alone and will not share the night ('Nahin. So jao.') to the man who sets half the load down for you; and, in his words, from 'Kal.' to 'Abhi.'

voice.register: Low, slow and plain: the quietest voice in the cast, with long gaps his hands fill. Most bubbles are two to four counted words and none is more than six (names and kin words not counted, as in rule 62; his own cap, well inside rule 62's ten), usually in two short pieces: an opener ('Hmm.', 'Hain?', 'Lo.' or the thing itself), then the state of a thing. His usual sentence is about a thing, not a person: the wire, the bench, the board, the food, the job, given a state or a verdict. Verdicts on things are often bare ('Taar dheela.', 'Board theek.') and sometimes keep their verb ('Bench theek hai.'); comfort and kind lines always keep their 'hai' ('Achha hai.', 'Amma ji mazboot hain.'), so he never talks in telegrams. His own jobs come with the pronoun dropped ('Aata hoon.', 'Garam karta hoon.', 'Ho gaya.'). His orders are small and practical: rest ('So jao.'), hands off live current ('Switch mat chhoona.'), and the next little job as he hands something over ('Lo, Mausi se baat karo.', 'Haath dho lo.'). He answers more than he asks; his few questions are about sleep, water or a drip. Nearly every bubble is followed by something his hands do, and when a beat needs more he speaks again after a deed, so a run is two bubbles with an action between them. He talks most to whoever should be resting (you, at the ward). His few words are kind and busy, never the silent head of the house. Told apart from the other short voices by shape and source, not by owned words: Nani gives people orders and counter proverbs; Captain sahab makes a cricket call, then gives the reason; Tinku gives a score with a tag; Mummy lists jobs; Mami reads things back; you name the listener. He reports on things, names almost nobody, counts nothing and leaves himself out.
voice.mix: Bare, plain Hindi, the plainest in the cast after Nani's, with no proverb or image of his own (that is Nani's and Masterji's ground). The common fillers are his as much as anyone's: achha, haan, chalo, arre and theek hai come in mid-line, sparingly, as they would from any man of 58; so do everyday Urdu-rooted words such as waqt, fikr and zaroor ('Waqt lagega.'). English comes in from his work. First, the lineman's nouns, used as Hindi nouns: current, line, fuse, load, meter, earthing, board, switch, wiring, joint. Second, now and then, the everyday Hinglish English verb with ho or kar, and his is always about what the line or the current did, with the thing as the subject ('Line trip ho gayi.', 'Short hua hai.', 'Wiring check ho gayi.'). That is how a lineman really talks, and it keeps his thing-first shape; Mummy's English verbs are counter jobs she hands to people ('MCB check karo'), his are what the current did. The hospital words everyone uses: BP, drip, ward, X-ray. Where everyday Hindi has its own word he takes it: 'bijli' for power, 'taar' for wire, जोड़ for a joint in Hindi mode. No whole English clause (Mama ji's and Mami's), and no English feeling words such as tension, relax or chill. Never 'main switch' or 'mains' in Hinglish, because 'main' reads as मैं. Hinglish mode is Roman Hindi with those nouns. English mode is plain, natural British English, as short as the Hindi: the thing first and himself left out wherever English allows it ('Board's fine. Open the shutter.', 'Lights on, then.'), with the full everyday phrase wherever a clipped one would sound translated ('Get any sleep?', 'It'll take time.', 'No harm done.'). One English word for each work verdict, so the English sort still hears him: mazboot is 'solid' of work and 'strong' of a person, dheela is 'loose', theek is 'fine'.
tics: The thing first, then its state: 'Taar dheela.' | 'Board theek hai.' | 'Fuse ud gaya.' Most of his sentences have a thing as the subject, and none passes a judgement on a person.

'Hmm.' | 'हम्म।' before an answer, or as the whole answer, in at most one bubble in three and never two running; otherwise one slow nod. In chapter 2's three or four bubbles that is once. When he is moved, the 'Hmm' becomes a cleared throat and a look at the window.
Himself left out: first-person verbs only for plain jobs, with the pronoun dropped ('Abhi aaya.', 'Aata hoon.', 'Dekh liya.'). The only 'my' in any mode is the fixed English sorry, 'My mistake.'.

One-word verdicts: 'Theek.' | 'ठीक।' (fine; the bare one-word line is his, while 'theek hai' mid-line is everyone's), 'Mazboot.' | 'मज़बूत।' (solid, of work; strong, of a person; his highest word), 'Dheela.' | 'ढीला।' (loose, sloppy: of a joint, a wire or a job, never of cloth, which is Masterji's, and never of a person), 'Chalega.' | 'चलेगा।' (it'll do: his kind word for a thing that is not quite right).
'Lo.' | 'लो।' as he sets something down or hands it on (half a sweet lime, his shoulder towel, the phone), sometimes with the one small job that goes with it ('Lo, Mausi se baat karo.').

His orders are small and practical: rest ('So jao.'), live current ('Switch mat chhoona.', 'Board mat chhoona.'), and the next little job ('Haath dho lo.'). In English mode the current order is always 'Leave the ___.'.
His exclamation 'Hain?' | 'हैं?' always stands alone at the start of a bubble, with its own question mark.
When thanked he says only 'Hmm.' | 'हम्म।' as he stands up, and leaves the room.
He leaves before a goodbye is over: from a room when he is thanked, from a platform before the train moves. He never waits out the last coach (that vigil is Papa's).

When cross he goes quiet, picks up the nearest job and does it twice as hard (re-tightening a screw that was already tight). If a word comes, it is one flat order about a thing ('Andar rakho.'), with no address word.
Until May a job that can wait is 'Kal.' | 'कल।'; from May on it is 'Abhi.' | 'अभी।', and he never says 'kal' about a job again.
He drops address words with everyone his own age or younger; the only name he says is 'Tinku'. With an elder he never drops the 'ji' ('Abhi, Amma ji.').
catchphrases: 'Hmm. Ho jayega.' | 'हम्म। हो जाएगा।' | 'Hmm. It'll get done.' (his comfort and his promise; no person in it)
'So jao.' | 'सो जाओ।' | 'Go to sleep.' (to whoever should be resting, you most of all)
'Lo. Aadha.' | 'लो। आधा।' | 'Here. Half.' (the half he sets down beside you; a share, not a count, and the only time 'aadha' is in his mouth)
voice.exclamation: 'Hain?' | 'हैं?' | 'Eh?' A nasal sound of surprise with no word in it and no religious sense (matrix 2.13). Said low, for a good or a bad surprise alike. It always stands alone at the start of the bubble with its own question mark, so the Hinglish 'Hain?' is never read as the verb 'hain' (are). A plain 'arre' mid-line is anyone's, his too, but 'Arre waah' is Captain sahab's cry and never his; never a god-word, never another person's cry.
voice.sorry_thanks_love: SORRY: 'Galti ho gayi.' | 'ग़लती हो गई।' | 'My mistake.' Plain everyday north Indian Hindi, still with no subject, and then his hands put the thing right in front of whoever saw. THANKS, GIVEN: two blunt words and the deed, 'Hmm. Baitho.' | 'हम्म। बैठो।' | 'Hmm. Sit.' as he moves his bag off the chair beside him (a command, so it gives you no gender; 'achha kiya' is left to Mummy's 'Bahut achha kiya.'). His work verdict as thanks ('Silai mazboot hai, Masterji.' | 'That's solid stitching, Masterji.') comes at most once a chapter, so it stays a compliment and never becomes a code. THANKS, RECEIVED: just 'Hmm.' | 'हम्म।' | 'Hmm.' as he stands up, and he leaves the room; the leaving is the rest of his answer. LOVE: never said as a feeling; a deed with his hands, here and now: 'Lo. Aadha.' | 'लो। आधा।' | 'Here. Half.' as he sets half a peeled sweet lime down beside you; the steel chairs kept outside the ward all night; the lit back step that nobody mentions.

Everyone's fillers, used sparingly and mid-line: achha, haan, chalo, arre, theek hai; and everyday Urdu-rooted words: waqt, fikr, zaroor.

His trade, as Hindi nouns: bijli, taar, joint (जोड़ in Hindi mode), current, line, fuse, load, meter, earthing, board, switch, wiring; trade verbs with ho or kar about what the line did: trip ho gayi, short hua, check ho gayi, ud gaya (of a fuse); and the ward's BP, drip, ward, X-ray.
Things in the house he reports on: khana, paani, cheeni, bench, kursi, gate, light, seedhi (the back step).
'Ji.' | 'जी।' to the doctor, the night nurse and ward staff, standing up to say it; 'Amma ji' with आप to Nani.

Card notes stay short work verdicts, how someone does a job as a lineman would judge it (slow, rushed, never checks twice), never temper, looks, dress or character, and never said in a bubble (rule 36). The four proposed chapter 2 notes are unchanged.
never: मैं, 'main', 'I', 'me', मेरा, मुझे, 'mera', 'mujhe'; 'my' only in the fixed English sorry 'My mistake.' (a script can check these).
A judgement on a person as the subject of his sentence. People come into his lines only in small practical orders, an address word, or comfort ('Amma ji mazboot hain.').
More than six counted words in one bubble; two of his bubbles back to back with no deed between them.
Any figure or count in speech: no hours, minutes, prices, head-counts or 'dobara'; 'aadha' only in 'Lo. Aadha.'.

'sorry', 'thank you', 'please', 'dhanyavaad' or 'shukriya' (your word for a stranger who has helped): not because anyone owns them, but because his Hindi is plain and older and his sorry and thanks are 'Galti ho gayi.' and 'Hmm. Baitho.'.

Another person's exclamation as his habitual cry (the word said now and then stays free): 'Baap re' (Nani), 'Had hai' (Mummy), 'Kamaal hai' (Papa), 'Oho' (Mama ji), 'Gazab' (Tinku), 'Haaye' (Mausi), 'Uff' (Masterji), 'Arre waah' (Captain sahab), 'Ish' (Mami), 'Badhiya' (yours).

Another person's phrase (phrases stay owned; the common fillers do not): 'Pehle ___' for someone else first (yours), 'phir se naap' (Masterji's re-measuring), 'Iska bill nahin', 'Theek hai, toh' and 'Isme kya' as a brush-off of thanks (Mummy's), 'Next ball', 'Not out', 'Well fielded' (Captain sahab's), 'Tick' and 'Correct?' (Mami's), 'Reached?', 'Pahunche?' and 'Aakhri dibbe tak' (Papa's), 'Suno, suno, suno!', 'Shabaash' and 'bahut yaad' (Mausi's), 'Bas.' as a closing line and 'Khush raho' (Nani's), 'Jeete raho' (Masterji's), 'haan?' as a tag (Tinku's), 'Don't worry' (Mama ji's).
'Chhote' (Mummy's word for her brother).
A proverb, an idiom or an image of his own (Nani's and Masterji's ground); English feeling words such as tension, relax, chill.
Tea as his way of caring (Nani, Masterji and Mama ji already carry it); at home he pours it without a word.
'kal' about a job, from May on.
Any word on anyone's character, temper or looks in speech; any word on a woman's dress, looks or morals.
Any doubt of a report of harassment or a dowry demand, or calling one a misunderstanding (rule 22); no word about one in a bubble at all.
'beta', 'bhaiya', 'didi', a pet name or any word that gives you a gender (rules 8 and 66; rulebook Q7); 'sister' or 'doctor sahab' for the ward staff.
Any religious word or exclamation (the matrix 2.13 list), any caste word or trade-caste name (so 'mithai ki dukaan', never 'halwai'), any brand (rule 3).
A speech, a lecture or unasked advice; a raised voice, except the one time current is live; a joke at anyone's expense but his own; a feeling word about himself.

MAUSI: no name and no address word; तुम both ways; to you and Tinku she is 'tumhari Mausi' | 'तुम्हारी मौसी', and to a nephew or niece on the phone just 'Mausi' ('Lo, Mausi se baat karo.').

YOU: no address word, and तुम rarely; only rule 66 shapes: commands ('So jao.', 'Switch mat chhoona.') and lines where you are not the doer ('Neend aayi?', 'Ho jayega.', 'Lo. Aadha.'). His thanks to you is a command too ('Hmm. Baitho.'), so no line of his to you is outside the three shapes (RULE 66 NOTES). You say 'Mausa ji' with आप and -इए ('Aap so jaiye, Mausa ji.' | 'आप सो जाइए, मौसा जी।'); your thanks, 'Thank you, Mausa ji.' | 'थैंक यू, मौसा जी।' | 'Thanks, Mausa ji.' (your own file keeps 'shukriya' for a stranger who has helped), gets one 'Hmm.' and sends him out of the room.

RULE 66 NOTES: the checker will flag 'हो जाएगा' and 'वक़्त लगेगा' (futures), 'नींद आई?', 'आधा', 'मत छूना' and 'हाथ लगाना', 'हो गया' and 'कुछ नहीं हुआ' (an ending at a sentence's end), and 'करता हूँ' and 'जलाता हूँ' (an ending before हूँ). Each agrees with a thing (the job, the time, नींद, कुछ), is an infinitive command, or is himself. A native reader clears each. OWNER QUESTION, no longer in this file: his thanks 'अच्छा किया' was a past with ने where you are the doer, which none of rule 66's three shapes names; it is now 'हम्म। बैठो।', a command. The open question (a fourth shape for rule 66, or the native reader's cleared list) stays in Tinku's, Mausi's, Papa's, Mummy's and Mama ji's files.

habits: DEVICE: an old phone in a plain grey cover, in his right shirt pocket on vibrate; it comes out only to answer. Painted, its screen is always blank and his words are live text (rule 30). No font-size trait: six files claimed the largest font, and it is not his.
SCRIPT: Roman Hindi with his few trade nouns. Never English sentences (Papa types English) and never Devanagari (Nani's voice typing); the game shows each language mode's version.

SHAPE: a log-book line, from 34 years of night-shift entries: the thing first, then its state ('Board theek.', 'Kursiyan lag gayin.'), one to five words, a capital at the start and one full stop at the end. Never a question mark, never a figure, never a greeting, a name or a sign-off.
ACKNOWLEDGING: 'Ok.', with its capital and full stop, about an hour late. Papa's is 'Noted.' inside a minute, Tinku's is a lowercase 'ok' inside seconds, Masterji's is 'ok ji'.

HIS TELL: the missed call. For 'reached', 'coming' or 'yes' he rings once and hangs up, a habit from the years when every call cost money (readers confirm it reads true for a man of 58). On screen it is a message card reading 'Missed call: Mausa ji' | 'मिस्ड कॉल: मौसा जी', with no app look.
SPEED: about an hour, because the phone is in his pocket and his hands are busy; inside a minute for anything about current, a board or the lights going.

CALLS: he would rather call than type, and never sends a voice note. His calls last under a minute: 'Haan.' at the start, 'Theek.' at the end, and no goodbye. To a nephew or niece with news: 'Achha hai. Lo, Mausi se baat karo.', and the phone goes to Mausi. To his own two grown children, 'Haan. Sab theek hai.', and the phone goes to their mother.
EMOJI: none, ever; no stickers, no forwards, no good-morning pictures (Papa's). The thumbs-up is Mummy's.
One slow right thumb; never a typo, because there are too few words, and never a short form ('h' for 'hai' is Masterji's).

THE FAMILY GROUP: Mausi added him; he posts once or twice a year and reacts to nothing, and knows what is in it because Mausi reads it out. On screen a group message is one message card on the painted blank phone, never a group chat, with no app look and no 'forwarded' label (owner, 23 Oct; rule 3).

look.build: Height band: SHORT, with Masterji (the four bands: tall, Papa, Mami, Captain sahab; middle, Mausi, Mama ji, Tinku, Mummy; short, Mausa ji, Masterji; smallest, Nani). Exact gaps only for the people he shares panels with: half a head shorter than his wife Mausi (chapter 1, side by side); seated beside Papa on the steel chairs, Papa's head clearly higher (chapter 2); taller than Nani in any frame. Thick-set and square: broad chest, thick neck, thick forearms, big square hands with blunt fingers. Solid, never fat, never a belly gag. Base shape: square, shared only with Mummy, a woman, so square is not sorted by gender; never paint him standing level beside her, and never put the two of them in one Rukavat panel.
look.face: A broad square face with a heavy jaw under the beard; a wide, flat nose; deep creases fanning from the outer corners of the eyes, from thirty years of squinting up at poles in the sun, so he always looks as if he faces bright light; a smooth forehead with no lines between the brows (painted brow lines can come out as a forehead mark, rules review); sparse, low, grey eyebrows (he married in, so he lacks the thick straight brows of Nani's line); ordinary ears. AT STRIP SIZE he is one white mass at the top: the brush cut and the beard together. IN CLOSE-UP, in order: the short white beard joined to the moustache; the level-topped white brush cut; the sun-squint creases. Signs of age, carried in the eyes, mouth and neck: white hair and beard, deep lines at the eyes, loose skin at the throat; he must read 58 to 60, never 40, since painted ages read young. His right hand carries a pale, coin-sized burn scar on its back (close-ups and the hands sheet only).
look.skin: Deep brown skin, weathered from years outdoors, darker on the forearms and the back of the neck. Written every time as the tested phrase first, then the depth: 'South Asian features and warm brown skin, deep brown and weathered from years outdoors' (the tested phrase is the one flux-portrait-biases records fixing whitening in the family-magazine style). Above all in Rukavat, his chapter, whose code style string has no skin words, and in Lugdi's and Jadugar's lamp light, which recolours skin. About as dark as Nani and Papa; darker than Masterji, Mummy, Mausi and Mama ji. Every pick is compared with his master swatch, not with words.
look.hair: Thick white hair cut very short, bristling straight up all over and level across the top like a brush, so the head reads square; no parting; white to the roots, no grey streaks. BEARD: a short, close-trimmed white beard about a finger's width deep, joined to a short white moustache over the upper lip; the only beard in the cast (Masterji's file). Never longer, and never with the upper lip shaved, which the realism notes (as the draft cites them, citing Pew) say leans towards a community.
look.glasses_jewellery: No spectacles: he does not need them for what he reads, and Mausi reads the family group out to him (spectacles belong to Nani and Masterji). No wristwatch (Mummy's anchor); he tells the time by the light and the phone. No ring (a gem ring reads as an astrologer's stone), no chain, no thread, no bangle, no earring. The only metal on him is the clip of a line tester (a slim screwdriver with a clear plastic handle) in his left shirt pocket, worn like a pen: a close-up detail, painted only when a head-and-shoulders insert names it, never a strip anchor.
outfits: EVERYDAY, the fixed look (February to November; chapters 1 to 4): a plain dove-grey half-sleeve cotton shirt with two chest pockets, worn loose outside plain navy trousers (loose because he never stands still for Masterji's fittings); his thin plain dark olive-green cotton shoulder cloth, one even colour edge to edge, the size of a long hand towel, laid round the back of his neck and over both shoulders with its two ends hanging down the front of his shirt to his waist (he wipes his face with it in the heat, as men of his age do, India review); black lace-up shoes with thick rubber soles. Phone in the right pocket.
NIGHT, the sleeper coach and the ward (chapters 1 and 2): exactly the same, the shoulder cloth pulled a little closer round his shoulders; nothing added, so the prompt never changes.
HOME (rarely seen): a plain faded navy round-neck T-shirt with nothing printed on it, plain dark grey track pants with no stripes, grey rubber flip-flops; the shoulder cloth stays.

DECEMBER DAYS (the wedding week, chapter 5): a plain dove-grey full-sleeve shirt out over the navy trousers, and his plain dark olive-green wool shawl wrapped round both shoulders, its ends down the front: the same shape and value as the cotton cloth, heavier cloth. No sweater (Papa's and Masterji's winter).

OCCASION (the wedding's last night, chapter 5; the album): a new dove-grey full-sleeve shirt, the one shirt in thirty years he stood still for Masterji to fit, pressed navy trousers, the olive wool shawl round both shoulders, polished black shoes. The comics rule: the costume stays, in a finer cloth. Never a kurta (Papa's and Mama ji's cut), never a white pyjama, never a Nehru-collar jacket, never a safa or any headwear.
look.colour_key: SIGNATURE, by value first: a square-topped white head (brush cut and beard as one white mass) over a dark olive cloth round the neck and both shoulders, a light plain shirt showing between its two ends, dark trousers. At phone size: white top, dark yoke, light middle, dark legs. Never a diagonal (Mummy's alone). Across every look the cloth is the darker mass and the shirt the lighter; value and plainness hold when the hue changes. NOW (master sheet, face chip, album): dove grey, dark olive, navy, white, in even daylight, without STYLE['now']'s 'cool rainy-evening blues'. RUKAVAT (chapter 2, his chapter; the code string's warm teak browns, faded teal and cream with one signal orange): do not lean on colour. The head is left cream, the cloth and trousers dark teak, the shirt a mid teak-grey: a white head on a dark teak block against the pale cream ward wall that Nani's file asks for. Beside Nani her shawl is light and his cloth dark. The style's 'one signal orange' is not on him: chapter 2 names one fixed plain orange object in every panel (the rules review suggests an orange plastic water jug on the bedside locker) or drops the phrase from the story style. Never in one Rukavat panel with Mummy (two dark squares). LUGDI (chapter 1, cameo; violet, indigo, vermilion, marigold): a dark shape: cloth and trousers deep violet-black, shirt mid violet; only the white head catches the marigold lamp. Papa and Mummy take the coach's bright shapes. STATION (chapter 3, cameo; two inks on cream): head bare paper; cloth solid ink round the neck and over both shoulders, its two ends each a hand's width, so they read as two broad dark bands and never as a thin line (Masterji's tape); shirt bare paper; trousers solid ink. Against Papa (light top) and Masterji (light shirt, thin dark tape) the broad dark yoke tells him apart. Kneeling, never level beside Mummy. CRICKET (chapter 4, cameo; outfield green, chalk white, cherry red): cloth near-black green, shirt chalk grey, trousers near-black; placed against Tinku's table and a pale wall, never against the outfield, where a green cloth sinks; never cherry red (Captain sahab's). JADUGAR (chapter 5, cameos; vermilion, magenta, indigo night, emerald, old gold): the grey shirt silver-grey, lit from the front by old-gold lamps so he does not sink into the indigo night; the wool shawl the darkest mass, a deep brown-black lit at its edges, never emerald (a green shawl on a white-bearded elder near the library's bearded magician face may read as a community elder, rules review) and never magenta (Mausi's); trousers dark navy. PROVISIONAL: the chapter JSON look lines and the code STYLE disagree for Station, Cricket and Jadugar (rules review); this key follows the code STYLE and is re-checked once one string per look is settled.
look.prop: THE HALF HE LEAVES YOU: a sweet lime (mosambi) from the bag of fruit visitors bring to a ward (the India review: in much of the north the May ward fruit is mosambi or bananas, and oranges are a winter fruit; readers confirm). He works his right thumb under the thick peel and takes it off in one piece, which nobody else in the family can do (the usual way is a knife; readers confirm a strong thumb can), splits the fruit, and sets one half down on the chair beside you with 'Lo. Aadha.', then goes back to his own. Its story: on 34 years of night shutdowns the gang shared whatever fruit someone brought, and whoever peeled it handed out the halves; he still cannot eat a whole one. Both hands while peeling, face in the frame whenever his hands are; the half is set down, never held out of the frame towards you (rule 7; the held-out hand is left to Mummy's and Mami's marked beats). Painted from its own reference picture. It has no colour duty: Rukavat's signal orange is a scene object now (see colour key). GLOSSARY ROW (new; key 'sweet lime', used word for word in scene words): 'sweet lime: one round sweet lime the size of a fist, with a thick smooth pale green-yellow peel; peeled, its peel lies beside it in one thick curling piece and the pale fruit is split into two halves'. SECOND, WORN: the line tester clipped in his left shirt pocket (close-ups only; it lives in his LOOKS close-up words, not the glossary). CHAPTER 5: two folding steel chairs, one in each hand, carried in front of him; and the stack of chairs he sets down for you. NEVER IN HIS FIXED LOOK: the sweet lime, the chairs, the phone in his hand. Props go in the scene with the hand named.
look.silhouette: A box on a box: a square-topped white head on a square, thick-set body, with a dark yoke of cloth over both shoulders. SEATED (his signature): sits well back on the chair, never perched on its edge, and bends forward from the hips, forearms on his knees, both hands together between them over a sweet lime. STANDING: square, feet apart, arms hanging loose a little away from his body. Known in black at phone size by the square head, the beard joining it to the chest, and the forward block. FAR SPEC (when he is small and painted from words, not from a reference): a short square figure, a white head, a dark band over both shoulders, dark legs. Told from Nani in one panel (a small seated triangle, her cane upright like a pole) by shape and by value, and from Papa on the next chair (a tall upright line, knees together) by mass.
look.shoes: Black lace-up leather shoes with thick rubber soles, scuffed at the toes, laces double-knotted: a lineman's habit of rubber soles out of doors, so never chappals outside the house. Grey rubber flip-flops at home. Polished black shoes for the wedding's last night. Nothing written on soles or sides.

posture.stance: Square, feet shoulder-width apart, weight even on both, arms hanging loose a little away from his body with the hands half-curled, as if about to pick up a tool; chin level. Never hands in pockets, never arms folded, never a hand on the hip (Captain sahab's) or flat on a counter (Mummy's).
posture.sitting: Sits well back on the whole chair, never perched on its front edge (the cast's commonest sit, comics review), and bends forward from the hips: forearms on his knees, hands together between them, peeling or one hand cupped in the other; feet apart; facing the door. He can hold it for hours. Never leaning back with legs crossed, never at the head of a table or in the best chair; in a row of chairs he takes the end one nearest the door.
posture.walk: Slow, steady and even, feet a little apart, a slight roll from the knees; never hurries and never runs, yet arrives first. Carries everything in front of his chest with both hands, elbows out: two chairs, a bag of fruit, a stack of chairs.
gestures: THE HALF SET DOWN: places half a sweet lime on the chair beside you, lets go, and goes back to his own peel; no word, or only 'Lo.'
THE KNOCK: after he has looked at something (a switch, a bulb holder, a latch, a bag's zip) he gives it one knock with the knuckle of his right forefinger, a lineman's rap, then one nod.
STANDING FOR THE DOCTOR: up in one movement, arms at his sides, one small nod, and he stays standing until the round has gone by.
YES AND NO: one slow dip of the chin for yes, one slow turn of the head for no; never the head bobble, which the realism notes call a stock caricature.
WORRY: his left thumb rubs the back of his right hand, where the old scar is.
expressions: NEUTRAL: still as a post, bent forward, forearms on his knees, mouth a flat line under the beard, eyes on the door.
PLEASED: the creases at his eyes deepen and the beard lifts at the cheeks; he looks down at his hands, not at you, and peels a little faster.
WORRIED: the left thumb on the back of his right hand; he stands and goes to look for himself; his jaw works under the beard.
CROSS: silent, brows down, jaw set; he picks up the nearest job and does it twice as hard; never louder.
LAUGHING (once a year at most): silent; his shoulders shake once or twice, eyes shut, mouth closed, head dipped.
TIRED: head back against the wall, eyes shut, hands still on his knees; he never slumps sideways, and his eyes open at any sound.
MOVED: looks away to the window, clears his throat, and busies his hands, peeling far too carefully.
ALERT (the doctor, a spark, a cry): on his feet before anyone else, arms at his sides, chin up.

across_looks: STRIP ANCHORS, checked on every full-figure pick in this order: (1) a short, square, thick-set block, bent forward with forearms on knees or standing square; (2) one white mass at the top, the square brush cut and the short beard together; (3) the dark olive cloth round the neck and over both shoulders, ends down the chest, never a diagonal; (4) a light plain shirt out over dark trousers; (5) two hands, both his, busy with one thing, his face in frame.

CLOSE-UP DETAILS, checked only on inserts, the face chip and head close-ups: the beard joined to the moustache over the upper lip; the sun-squint creases; a smooth forehead with no lines and no mark; no spectacles, bare wrists and fingers; the scar; the line tester clip; the skin against his master swatch, reading 58 to 60.

NOW (master sheet, face chip, album): the fixed look in clean ink outlines and soft flat colour, in even daylight; STYLE['now']'s line words without its 'cool rainy-evening blues'. The face chip needs a new present-day portrait, because portraits.py has no present-day template.

RUKAVAT (chapter 2, his chapter; two face-on panels today, 2.03 and 2.17, the proposed dawn panel, plus the face chip on his four card notes): his LOOKS entry with 'present-day clothes' and the skin words, painted from his Rukavat reference. Period styles paint period dress (chapter 2 check), so no safari suit, flared trousers or big collars. With Nani in the frame, write both top anchors into the prompt (her: small, seated, white plait, round spectacles, light shawl; him: square, white brush cut, short white beard, dark cloth over both shoulders). With Papa on the chairs: a tall line beside a square block. The chapter writer updates 2.03's and 2.17's painting words, which still give him reading glasses on a cord and a shawl.

LUGDI (chapter 1, proposed cameo, silent): climbing to an upper berth or seated in the lamp-lit coach, painted small but face-on; the pulp style's dramatic angles must keep him short and square, not heroic.

STATION (chapter 3, proposed cameo, silent): two inks, so value carries him: a light top with a broad dark yoke over both shoulders, dark trousers, white head left as bare paper. Kneeling at the switchboard, never standing level beside Mummy.

CRICKET (chapter 4, proposed cameo, silent): use STORY_STYLE['cricket'] (the gouache sports annual), not the covers' wide style, which drew photographs; seated beside Tinku's table against a pale wall while Captain sahab stands side-on; no cherry red on him.

JADUGAR (chapter 5, proposed cameos, silent): the grey shirt lit from the front by old-gold lamps, the wool shawl deep brown-black; check his forehead close up, because the playing-card style painted forehead dots on some men (flux-portrait-biases).
WHERE THE FACE DRIFTS, WORDS CARRY HIM: a name tag and face chip on every bubble, his face chip on every card note, and a voice no one else in the cast has.
cast.painter_prompt: ROLE WORD: 'the bearded man' (add to ROLE; never his name, which the painter letters). TWO TIERS (comics review). MASTER LOOKS ENTRY, used only to paint his masters, word for word: 'a 60-year-old Indian man with South Asian features and warm brown skin, deep brown and weathered from years outdoors, short and thick-set with a broad chest, a thick neck, thick forearms and big square hands, thick white hair cut very short, bristling straight up all over and level across the top like a brush, a short close-trimmed white beard joined to a short white moustache over his upper lip, deep creases at the outer corners of his eyes, sparse low grey eyebrows, in present-day clothes: a plain dove-grey half-sleeve cotton shirt with two chest pockets worn loose outside plain navy trousers, a thin plain dark olive-green cotton shoulder cloth laid round the back of his neck and over both shoulders with its two ends hanging down the front of his shirt to his waist, and black lace-up shoes with thick rubber soles'. It says 60 for a man of 58 because painted ages read young. DECEMBER SWAP, the only change all year: 'half-sleeve' becomes 'full-sleeve', and the shoulder-cloth clause becomes 'a plain dark olive-green wool shawl wrapped round both shoulders with its two ends hanging down the front of his shirt'. PANEL TAG, used in every panel where his reference picture is supplied (35 words): 'the bearded man: short, thick-set, about 60, South Asian features and warm brown skin, square white brush cut, short white beard, dark olive cloth round neck and shoulders, light grey shirt out over navy trousers'. In a panel, name what each hand holds in the scene ('in both hands, a sweet lime he is peeling'). MASTER TURNAROUND PROMPT: 'Character turnaround of one man shown four times side by side at the same size, full length, standing square with his arms loose at his sides and his hands empty: from the front, from three-quarter, from the side and from the back, on plain pale grey, in even daylight. The bearded man is a 60-year-old Indian man with South Asian features and warm brown skin, deep brown and weathered from years outdoors, short and thick-set with a broad chest, a thick neck, thick forearms and big square hands, thick white hair cut very short, bristling straight up all over and level across the top like a brush, a short close-trimmed white beard joined to a short white moustache over his upper lip, deep creases at the outer corners of his eyes, sparse low grey eyebrows, in present-day clothes: a plain dove-grey half-sleeve cotton shirt with two chest pockets worn loose outside plain navy trousers, a thin plain dark olive-green cotton shoulder cloth laid round the back of his neck and over both shoulders with its two ends hanging down the front of his shirt to his waist, and black lace-up shoes with thick rubber soles. Clean confident ink outlines, soft even colour fills, gentle paper grain, calm. No text, no letters, no numbers, no words, no logos, no religious symbols, no writing anywhere.' It writes 'soft even colour fills' where STYLE['now'] says 'flat', because 'flat' fires the old apartment row. The last sentence is STORY_NO without its opening sentence ('One illustration panel, full-bleed edge to edge, no border, no frame, no speech bubbles.'), which fights four views; it is proposed as its own constant for model sheets. WORDS KEPT OUT of every prompt and scene description of his until the old take's glossary rows are retired or re-keyed (rules review; probe-checked on this text): bench, seat, stands, flat, floor, cover, pass or passes, watch or watches, match, board, platform, cap, stool (except as the existing low wooden stool), ground, sheet and room. Write 'row of steel chairs', 'goes by' and 'looks at'. Never write 'lineman', 'electrician', 'uncle', 'aunt', 'orange', 'border', 'towel' (it can paint a terry bath towel), 'gamchha' or 'angocha': the first two invite uniforms with badges and shoulder straps, the next two a second person, and the rest a colour, a frame or the wrong cloth.
painter_avoid: Any forehead mark: dot, bindi, tilak or ash lines. FLUX paints dots on some men, most in the playing-card style; prompts do not stop it. Every face-on panel and the face chip get the close-up check. The panel painter cannot yet fix one: SEED_BUMP and DOTS exist only in portraits.py, so cutscenes.py needs a per-panel seed bump and an eye-confirmed paint-out before his face-on panels are painted (rules review).
Lines between the brows, which can be painted as a tilak.
Lightened, pale or European-looking skin, above all in Rukavat (its style string has no skin words) and in Lugdi's and Jadugar's lamp light.
A face that reads 40 or 45: painted ages read young.
A long beard, or a beard with the upper lip shaved (reads as a community marker, the realism notes as the draft cites them); stubble in place of the beard; a beard on anyone else in the panel.

Spectacles of any kind (Nani's round frames or Masterji's half-moons migrating to him), a wristwatch (Mummy's), a ring, chain, pendant, beads, a thread on the wrist or at the collar, a kara or any metal bangle, an earring.
Any cap, skullcap, turban, safa, helmet or hat.
Letters, numbers or logos anywhere: on the shirt, the pocket clip, shoes, phone, chairs or switchboard.
Uniform cues: badges, shoulder straps, epaulettes, a tool belt, khaki (the library's period faces wear railway uniforms).
1980s or older dress in Rukavat and Jadugar: a safari suit, flared trousers, wide collars.
A kurta, a white pyjama, a Nehru-collar jacket (Papa's and Mama ji's), a sweater (Papa's and Masterji's winter), a lungi or dhoti out of doors.

The shoulder cloth wrong: checked (a checked cloth leans to one region, India review), saffron, red or white; a terry bath towel; a thin strap or line (Masterji's tape); a diagonal band over one shoulder (Mummy's); lighter than the shirt; missing.
Emerald or magenta on him in Jadugar; cherry red in Cricket.
A tucked-in shirt (Papa's), a pattern on the shirt (Papa's stripes, Mama ji's check), the shirt darker than the cloth.
Swaps with Nani: her light shawl painted dark, his dark cloth painted light, her plait or spectacles on him, his beard or brush cut on her.
Swaps with Papa on the chairs: Papa made square or bearded, Mausa ji made tall and thin.
A third hand, or a hand with no owner; anything held out of the frame towards the viewer, or running out of the bottom edge, where the painter adds a hand (rule 7).
A pot belly, a comic face, a cigarette, beedi or paan stain, a knife (he peels with his thumb).
Folded hands (reads as prayer) and touching anyone's feet (realism notes).
Leaning back cross-legged, arms folded, hands in pockets, perched on the front edge of a chair: not his shape.
model_sheet: 1. THE CAST FIRST (comics review's order of work): his black shape in the four-band line-up of all ten at phone width, and in each look's strip of all ten as simple flat figures in that look's inks; collisions are resolved on the strips, and the owner approves the pictured line-up, before his master is painted.

2. TWO-PERSON TEST (rules review): Nani with Mausa ji, the chapter 2 pair, in one test picture, once with both master texts and once with both panel tags plus their references; record the pass rate per strip anchor and the swap rate, before more panel words are written.

3. MASTER TURNAROUND, full figure, standing square, everyday look with the shoulder cloth: front, three-quarter front, side and back, on plain pale grey in even daylight. Not yet tested: whether klein can paint four views in one 1024 x 768 picture; if not, paint each view as its own picture from the same words.
4. SEATED TURNAROUND, front and back, bent forward with forearms on knees, because the ward panels see him seated by the door, sometimes from behind.

5. POSES: seated forward on a row of three joined steel chairs, peeling a sweet lime; setting half of it down on the chair beside him, face in frame; rising in one movement as the doctor goes by; carrying two folding steel chairs, one in each hand; setting a stack of chairs down at the foot of the picture and stepping back, hands empty; kneeling at a switchboard; standing on a low wooden stool at a switchboard; seated on a plastic chair beside a scorer's table, forearms on knees.
6. EXPRESSIONS, head and shoulders, written as what the body does: neutral, pleased, worried, cross, laughing (silent), tired (head back, eyes shut), moved (looking away), alert.

7. HANDS SHEET: big square hands with blunt fingers; the pale coin-sized burn scar on the back of the right hand; the right thumb under a sweet lime's peel; the half being set down; two hands only in every drawing.
8. HEAD CLOSE-UPS, front and three-quarter, at full size for the audit: forehead smooth and clear, the brush cut level-topped, the beard joined to the moustache, the skin against the master.

9. PROPS SHEET: the sweet lime whole, peeled in one piece, and split into halves; the line tester clipped in a shirt pocket; the cotton shoulder cloth round the neck and over both shoulders; the wool shawl wrapped round both shoulders; black rubber-soled shoes; grey flip-flops; a folding steel chair.
10. OUTFIT SHEET: everyday, night (the same), home, December day, wedding night.
11. FAR SPEC: him small at three distances from words alone (silhouette and two value blocks), for crowd panels where only two people come from references (comics review).

12. PER-LOOK REFERENCES from the picked master, made by the edit model (Flux2KleinEdit, as cutscenes.py paint-refs does) so the painter keeps style and face in one step: the shoulder cloth is baked into every reference, and a second reference shows him seated peeling the sweet lime, so in the ward panels person and prop take one slot (comics review). Needed: Rukavat and the present-day face chip; Lugdi, Station, Cricket and Jadugar only if the owner keeps the cameos. At most two people from references in one panel (klein takes four reference pictures in all).

13. SEEDS AND PICKS: 7100, 7203 and 7319 (cutscenes.py SEEDS), three tries each, picked by eye against the strip anchors for full figures and the close-up details for inserts, with hands counted and forehead and skin checked close up; record the seed picked and his pass rate per panel. A repaint takes a new seed.

14. FILES (proposed): art/refs/people/mausa-ji/sheet-now.png (master), front-now.png, seated-now.png, seated-sweet-lime.png, rukavat.png, and only with the cameos lugdi.png, station.png, cricket.png, jadugar.png; the sweet lime at art/refs/sweet-lime.png; the face chip at design-system/assets/now-mausa-ji.webp.

15. CODE NEEDED FIRST (rules review): looks keyed by look, not by year; panels read from the chapter JSONs, not first-take-script.md; person references routed into paint-refs (REFS holds only the trunk today and refs_of() matches object phrases); paint_refs() refusing a fifth reference; a per-panel seed bump and an eye-confirmed dot paint-out in cutscenes.py; the old take's glossary rows retired or re-keyed to phrases nobody says by accident.

16. GLOSSARY ROWS to add to situations.md before any prompt, for shared objects only, under keys nobody else uses (his shoulder cloth, wool shawl and line tester live in his LOOKS entry, rules review), each saying what to paint: 'sweet lime' (see prop); 'row of steel chairs': three joined steel chairs with perforated metal backs on one steel frame along a corridor wall; 'folding steel chair': a plain grey folding steel chair with a solid square back; 'switchboard': a plain wooden panel on a wall with a row of white switches and one round white fuse holder; 'bare bulb': one plain round light bulb in a white holder fixed above a door; 'ribbed rubber mat': a plain black ribbed rubber mat lying on a stone step.

17. PAINTING RULES: nothing is painted until this workflow and any browser checks have stopped; then every run goes through ~/.claude/heavy-queue/heavyq, one heavy job on the Mac at a time, one person's master at a time, and the owner approves the pictured sheet before any panel. Only if he keeps failing: more reference views first, then a one-person LoRA test through heavyq.
best_scenes: The ward corridor at 3 am: the row of steel chairs by the ward door, Papa silent on the next one, the only two awake.
Rising in one movement as the doctor's round goes by, and staying on his feet until it has gone.
Dawn by the ward door: a sweet lime peeled in one piece with his thumb, half of it set on the chair beside you, his face in frame.
'Nahin. So jao.': you offer to take the night chair, and he will not share the load.
The back step in morning light: a new bulb lit above it, a black ribbed rubber mat on the stone, nobody in the picture and nobody saying a word.
Refusing a cot, refusing sleep when Nani sends him, refusing thanks: three no's, all kind.
The night train: climbing to an upper berth without being asked; his hand in Mausi's when the coach is asleep.
The morning after the flood: kneeling at the switchboard on Mummy and Masterji's shared wall, mains off, everyone's hands at their sides until he nods.
The lane cup: on a plastic chair beside Tinku's table, one nod at each wicket, nothing to fix for once.

The wedding: first through the gate at dawn with two chairs; the lights going out on the last night and coming back with him on the stool by the switchboard; a stack of chairs set down at the foot of the picture for you, and him stepping back.
Any scene where Mausi talks and he says 'Hmm', or where someone thanks him and he finds a reason to walk out.
never_does: Never sits on a card and never asks a decision; Nani asks chapter 2.
Never doubts a report of harassment or a dowry demand, never calls one a misunderstanding, and never says a word about one in a bubble (rules 22 and 26).

Never does any job a chapter 2 decision gives out (the bedside chair, the locker key, the doctor's round, the cots, the tea flask, the chemist, Nani's clothes, the purse, the call to Mama ji, the taxi seats), nor the chapter 5 jobs (the envelopes, the keys, the gift table, the cake), so his kindness never competes with the cards or hints who should have been picked.
Never takes the cot, the lower berth, the best chair or the head of the table.
Never says thank you or sorry in so many words, and never stays in a room where he is being thanked.
Never talks about himself or names a feeling.
Never gives a speech, a lecture or unasked advice; never more than five words a bubble; never a figure in a bubble.
Never raises his voice, except the one time current is live, and never in a chapter whose one shout is taken.
Never comments on a woman's dress, looks or morals, or on anyone's character, in speech.
Never jokes at anyone's expense, and is never the punchline: no age jokes, no belly, and no blood-pressure gag beyond his own one line.
Never holds anything out of the frame towards you; he sets things down beside you. Never touches 'your' arm or shoulder (rule 7).
Never appears in an outcome beat as the cause of anything, and Nani's fall is never pinned on him or anyone (rule 46).
Never pays or tips hospital staff for a favour, and never jumps a queue.
Never drinks, smokes or chews paan on screen.
Never wears spectacles, a watch, a ring, a thread or any headwear.
Never says 'kal' about a job after May.
Never in one Rukavat panel with Mummy.

Never the silent patriarch: his few words always lead to an act, at home and at functions he pours the tea himself (never in chapter 2, where the tea flask is a card's job), and he never has the last say on a family decision.
