cast.name: Masterji (मास्टरजी), about 60, the tailor next door; chapter 3's voice
cast.role: Chapter 3's voice (the July flood week, painted in the Station look). Not family: the tailor who has shared Mummy's shop wall on the station road since 1999. Mummy asks the chapter's eight decisions; Masterji is the chapter's second judging voice (a woman and a man, rule 22), opens the chapter from his own flooded doorway and speaks its fixed ending, which hands the cracked drain to chapter 4's lane cup. Never on a card, never the asker. He speaks in chapter 3 only while rulebook question 11 is open; he may stand silent in another chapter's panel, painted small and face-on from his own model sheet (owner answer 6 settles the bible's older 'seen from behind'). Label on first use: 'Masterji, the tailor next door' | 'मास्टरजी, बगल वाले टेलर मास्टर' | 'Masterji, bagal wale tailor master'. टेलर मास्टर, not दर्ज़ी, which is also a community name; in the east मास्टरजी usually means a schoolteacher, so the label stays exactly this and his first panel (3.02) shows the tape round his neck. Flat by design: one strong trait, one habit, one contradiction, held the same way every time; painted face-on from his own model sheet (owner answer 6). Painter's role word: 'the bald stooped man', taken from his look; never his name, and never 'the tailor', since naming the trade draws a shop or a sewing machine into the flood and the drain. The earlier long file, superseded wherever this one differs: /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-priyanshu-Sex-Ed/f50ea7ee-0855-46a2-8572-0aa08df5b855/scratchpad/characters/masterji-about-chapter-voice.json (where he appears, glossary rows, judging-note candidates, rule checks, sources).
cast.essence: The tailor next door who measures everything, cloth, mud, a neighbour's patience, the weather, and has an opinion on every finger's width of it; exact to a hair by feel, since his tape lost its marks long ago, and never once on time. The type in five words: the station road's slow measurer. The player who says 'I know this person' is Sunita, herself a small-town tailor (personas P3), so he is skilled, dignified and never the joke; Ravi, who runs his family's shop, knows the neighbour who shares his wall. What lifts him above the stock slow tailor is pictured, not only told: the new ready-made shop's bright shutter sits small at the far end of his road while he talks about mud.
cast.backstory: Born in the junction town about 1966. At fourteen (1980) he was apprenticed to the station road's old tailor, who gave him the cloth measuring tape he still wears round his neck; its marks had worn off by the mid-1990s and he has measured by feel ever since, in finger widths and hand spans, which is why the tape is plain and why he never speaks in inches. He opened his own one-room shop on the station road in 1988 and cut himself a black jacket and a matching sleeveless waistcoat for the opening. The jacket hangs on the shop's back wall; the waistcoat, in a thin cotton blend, he has worn every working day since, relined twice, and it still fits 'because I measured right'. In 1999 the empty room next door became Mummy's electrical shop: one wall, one concrete step and every monsoon shared since. He married in 1990; his wife does the hand-finishing at home (buttons, buttonholes, hand hems) and keeps his measurement register. Their son, about 32, cuts shirts in a city garment factory, one pattern four hundred times a day, which Masterji calls 'not tailoring' and is quietly proud of. He lives in the lane behind the station road on the far side of the drain from the family's lane, which is why the drain is his thirty-year argument with Captain sahab. He works at a plain black treadle machine he fitted with a small motor, owns no wristwatch, tells the time by the trains, opens at ten, and dates everything by what was on his machine that year ('the year of Bhai sahab's wedding jacket'), never by a number. In January a ready-made clothes shop opened at the far end of the station road, with a bright new shutter; he gave it one monsoon, and in July it is still there.
cast.want_fear_contradiction: WANTS THIS YEAR: the drain behind the station road mended before another monsoon ruins a bolt of cloth (in July the flood soaks two bolts on his bottom shelf). WANTS FROM YOU: a listener who does not walk off; he has forty-six years of stories and the station road has stopped stopping. FEARS: that the station road forgets him: the new ready-made shop with its bright shutter, a son who chose the factory, and a drain that floods his cloth every July. The fear is in the frame, not only in the backstory: the new shop's shutter sits small at the far end of the road in 3.02 while he talks about mud. CONTRADICTION ('X, but Y'): exact to a hair's breadth, but never on time for anything, his own shutter included. It shows the same way every time: every verdict is a measure by feel ('a finger's width out', 'a hair uneven') and every time is 'bas abhi' (right away), which means an hour; he opens at ten, calls Mummy's nine 'showing off', and blames the trains. Under it: he measures twice and talks three times, so the clock always loses. WHAT HE GETS RIGHT ON SCREEN (the plot uses it, so the men's competence is seen, not only the women's): his forecasts from the feel of cloth are right, and Mummy dries her stock by them (proposed 3.11 and 3.21); his reading of the crack at 3.28 is the one both lanes mend by in chapter 4. THE TURN: on the Saturday after the flood his shutter goes up when hers does, the one time in 27 years, and nobody says a word about it. In December he has Mama ji's wedding kurta ready three days early, the first deadline he has met in thirty years.
relationships: NANI (नानी). History: in 1999, when Mummy's shop opened beside his, Nani came from her town to inspect the street and haggled with him for an hour over the price of one hem; he lost, and has respected her since. Friction: she still says his hems are a hair uneven, and after 44 years behind a grocery counter she may be right, so he re-measures every hem she touches. Tenderness: he edges her shawls free when she visits and asks after her by name every week; when the family comes back in May his first words to Mummy are 'Nani ji theek hain?' He calls her 'Nani ji' (the lane uses the children's word) and says आप; she calls him 'Master', one of only two people who drop the ji.

MUMMY (मम्मी). History: 27 years sharing one wall, one step and every monsoon. Friction: his ten against her nine ('Showing off, Bhabhi ji'); his bolts of cloth lean on the shared wall and she says the damp comes through to her fan boxes. Tenderness: every monsoon they lift each other's shutters; in May, while the family is at Nani's, he lifts her shutter a foot every morning to air the stock and says nothing, and she knows only from the chalk stroke he leaves on it each day (a story fact, never painted: his one object stand-in is the tape). In the flood week his own bottom shelf is under water and he still stands in her doorway first. He calls her 'Bhabhi ji' and says आप; she calls him 'Masterji' and says आप (equal respect between neighbours). They are chapter 3's two judging voices, and their tells never match: she gets more polite when cross, he drops his wander.

PAPA (पापा). History: he stitched Papa's one good jacket, the charcoal stand-collar one, for the 1997 wedding, and lets it out a little every few years without a word; to him that wedding is 'the year of Bhai sahab's jacket'. Friction: Papa arrives at every fitting to the minute, which Masterji finds suspicious ('A man who comes on time wants something'), and he says Papa stands like a timetable and spoils the jacket's line. Tenderness: they share the station road's mornings from either side of the platform, Papa's parcel office and his shutter, and Papa is the one man who waits for him without complaint. He calls him 'Bhai sahab', आप; Papa says 'Masterji', आप.

MAMA JI (मामा जी). History: in the summer of 1999 he measured twenty-year-old Mama ji for his first interview shirt and stitched it free 'for luck'; Mama ji got the job and still says it was the shirt. Friction: now Mama ji orders from the city by phone, sends photographs of cloth, wants it 'by Friday' and haggles like a city man; Masterji says city cloth photographs better than it wears. Tenderness: he still keeps the 1999 slip in his register, and he cuts the December wedding kurta himself, early. He calls him 'Mama ji' (the lane's word) and says आप, now that Mama ji is a grown man and a customer (a ji with तुम read as a mismatch); Mama ji says 'Masterji', आप. The readers' one address table confirms it.

TINKU (टिंकू). History: he stitched her first school uniform. Friction: he says she never stands still long enough to be measured; she scores his lateness out loud on Saturdays ('10:40, Masterji. Fourth late this month.'). Tenderness: she brings his eleven o'clock tea from Mummy's counter every Saturday, and he is the one grown-up who asks to see her scorebook and checks that her columns are straight: 'Barabar.' He calls her 'Tinku', तुम; she says 'Masterji', आप.

MAUSI (मौसी). History: his customer for thirty years. Friction: she complains about every fitting, talks through every measurement so that he loses count ('Mausi ji, the measure goes when you talk'), and comes back every time. Tenderness: he is the one person who lets her finish a sentence, because he talks slower than she does. He calls her 'Mausi ji' (the lane's word), आप; she says 'Masterji', आप. They never share a chapter.

MAUSA JI (मौसा जी). History: the lineman rewired Masterji's shop for nothing in 2001; Masterji has stitched his shirts at cost ever since, and neither has mentioned it once. Friction: Mausa ji's shirts come back scorched from live wires, which Masterji takes personally. Tenderness: the slow talker and the man of two words sit on the shop step together, one talking, one saying 'Hmm', both content. 'Mausa ji' and आप both ways.

CAPTAIN SAHAB (कप्तान साहब). History: the two old men of the drain. They live on the two lanes the drain divides (proposed: Masterji on the far lane, Captain sahab on the family's), and since 1994 have argued every monsoon about whose lane's drain floods the station road. Friction: thirty monsoons of 'that drain sits low'. Tenderness: neither has ever missed the other's monsoon complaint, and 'Let the lane cup decide' hands thirty years of argument to a cricket match, as close as either will come to giving in. He calls him 'Captain', dropping the sahab, and says आप; Captain sahab calls him 'Master', आप. The clipped titles are thirty years of familiarity, not rudeness.

MAMI (मामी). History: they have never met. She sends Mama ji's measurements by message, numbered, with inch marks, and he says she is the only customer in thirty years who measures correctly (he reads inches on a slip; he never says them). Friction: she asks for a delivery date and he gives one, which for him is a risk. Tenderness: two precise people; her numbered list is why the wedding kurta is ready three days early. He calls her 'Mami ji', आप.

YOU (the player). History: he has known you since you could walk; he mended your school bag strap for nothing and still asks after it. You are the listener who stays: he talks cloth and weather while you hold his tea. Friction: in the flood week his talk costs time nobody has. Tenderness: he tells you the weather first, before Mummy; on the step he holds out the tea before he holds out an opinion; at the drain he sends you for the brick that holds his tape down. He says तुम to you with no address word, only in commands, 'who should' asks and lines where you are not the doer (rule 66); once, teasing, he says 'अब तो आप इंचार्ज हैं।' You say 'Masterji' and आप with -इए (the realism notes: आप and ji to every chapter voice).

HIS OWN FAMILY (off screen; never painted unless the owner asks). His wife, married 1990, does the hand-finishing at home and keeps the register; their son, about 32, is a pattern cutter in a city garment factory. Each is named only if they ever come on screen, and then tagged under rule 21.

CHAPTER 3'S CIRCLE (the hired hands). He speaks of them only in his judging notes on their cards, never in a bubble (rule 36), and never about the bullying complaint (rules 22 and 28). He is never painted in a panel beside figures who could be card people (rule 32).
cast.year_arc: JANUARY (present-day opening): off screen. The ready-made shop opens at the far end of the station road; he gives it one monsoon. No line, no painting. MAY (chapter 1, Lugdi; chapter 2, Rukavat): off screen in the junction town. With the family at Nani's, he lifts Mummy's shutter a foot each morning to air the stock and leaves one chalk stroke a day; a story fact, never painted (one object stand-in per person, and his is the tape). JULY (chapter 3, Station; the chapter that turns his year): the flood. He opens sceptical in his own flooded doorway ('All this mud, by Saturday?', then his wander, 'And the sky's still sulking.'), his bottom shelf soaked, and at the far end of the road, small, the new shop's bright plain shutter with no sign. Through the week he dries his bolts of cloth on the next roof and forecasts from the feel of them, and he is right: Mummy's stock is dried by his forecast (proposed lines at 3.11 and 3.21); on a Tuesday evening he holds out tea to you on the step (proposed beat). On Saturday his shutter goes up when hers does, whatever the band (proposed: painted silently at 3.26). He closes the chapter crouched at the cracked drain, his tape lying slack across the crack with a brick on its far end, handing thirty years of argument to the lane cup. 15 AUGUST (chapter 4, Cricket): no lines. Proposed silent presence, small and face-on (owner answer 6): at 4.27, while Captain sahab says 'Both lanes. One drain. Mended.', Masterji is crouched beside the mended drain with his tape lying across it, in place of the tape alone (an object stand-in for one beat at most; Captain sahab's file decides where Captain sahab is). Optionally, before the toss, on the far side of the empty lane ground opposite Captain sahab, hands behind his back, but only in a panel with no players in it (rule 32). DECEMBER (chapter 5, Jadugar): off screen. Mama ji's wedding kurta, cut from Mami's numbered measurements, is ready three days early; Papa's jacket is let out, unmentioned. The family wears his work in Nani's town; no line, no painting. THE CHANGE ACROSS THE YEAR: from a man who fears the road has forgotten him, whose drain floods and whose shutter is always late, to a man whose drain both lanes mend by his reading, whose shutter went up with his neighbour's once, and whose stitching the whole family wears in December. WHERE HE APPEARS: chapter 3 as drafted, 3.02 face-on in the right third in his doorway with Mummy from behind in the left third (now a verdict-and-wander pair) and 3.28 face-on in the right third at the drain (2 lines, the fixed ending), plus his judging notes on decisions 1 and 5 with his face chip. Proposed: 3.11 and 3.21 as a matched pair (rule 37 wants twin C's lead-ins with the same figures and mood, so both or neither), 1 line each, each itself a wander to the weather; a Tuesday tea scene between 3.10 and 3.11, 1 line plus one fixed player line (chapter 3 then has three player lines, the cap); 3.26 silent in his doorway, the same picture for every band. WORD BUDGET (comics review; rule 62's caps wait on question 14): his lines are budgeted as verdict-and-wander pairs from the start, each bubble at most 10 words and each beat at most 20 counted words. His share is about 46 counted words of the chapter's 120 (3.02 10, tea 7, 3.11 7, 3.21 7, 3.28 15); the cut comes from narration and other chapter 3 words, not from his wander; if the chapter still cannot spare it, the tea beat goes before the wander does. Chapter 4: silent presence only. Asker in no chapter; the voice in chapter 3. One present-day portrait as his face chip on every tag and note (rule 22).

voice.register: Slow, warm and unhurried: the station road's slow measurer, one of the cast's four long runners (Papa speaks in exact whole sentences, Mausi fast and tripled, Mama ji in one run-on). SHAPE: a verdict first, short and sure, said as a whole sentence with its verb and its 'hai' (he is the house's slow full-sentence speaker, never one more clipped voice); then, in about one run in two, a turn to cloth or weather, often hinged on 'Waise'. The other runs stop at the verdict, so the turn stays a habit and never a stamp. What tells him apart is this shape and where his words come from (cloth, weather, the garment calendar), not any word he owns: 'waise', 'dekhiye', 'achha', 'arre', 'chalo', 'bas' and 'theek hai' are everyone's. A run is two or three bubbles, budgeted as pairs so a turn is never the line that gets cut; in a single bubble the verdict shows, and the turn too when that line has one. Full stops throughout, even after 'Uff.'; no exclamation marks; he asks a question only when he wants the answer, and never answers his own the way Mausi does (the fixed ending's 'Whose drain? Let the lane cup decide.' hands the question on to the cup). NUMBERS: none in speech. Time is only 'bas abhi' (right away, which means an hour), and he blames the trains; the past is dated by what was on his machine ('the year of Bhai sahab's jacket'), never a year or a count of years. A measure by feel ('ungli bhar', 'baal bhar', 'baalisht') comes at most once in a run. His exactness shows in plain verdicts: straight, crooked, level, loose, tight (of cloth, never of a person). FEELING: said sideways, in cloth and weather pictures a Hindi-first reader follows at once ('Geela kapda sookh jaata hai. Fikr phate ki hoti hai.'), with plain warmth in his thanks ('Sukhi raho.', 'Ehsaan raha.'); never the plain feeling words Mausi and Mama ji own. HUMOUR: kind and whimsical, and rationed: at most one picture a run that gives the sky, the clouds, the mud or the drain a mood (the sky sulks, the clouds sit 'munh phulaaye', the mud sleeps late, the drain is stubborn), and none in a cross line. The joke is at the road, the sky, his own trade or himself, never at a person's body or a woman's clothes, and he is never its butt. WHEN CROSS (at things only: the drain, the sky, cheap cloth): the turn stops. One short verdict, silence, and he straightens out of his stoop. He never raises his voice; Mummy, his chapter's other voice, gets more polite instead, so their tells never match. TALKS MOST TO whoever stands still long enough (you, most of all), Mummy over the wall, and Captain sahab across the drain.
voice.mix: Ordinary station-road Hindustani: a Hindi frame with the everyday words any old bazaar in the Hindi belt shares (fikr, farq, mausam, mizaaj, waqt, zaroor, khair, afwaah, astar). These are the town's words, not his badge: others in the cast say fikr, waqt and zaroor too, so his speech marks the town and never a community, and he is never played for comedy. Tailoring English comes as Hindi nouns (fitting, trial, size, finish, pattern, shutter, and 'ready-made', said with a sniff). His working verbs are the Hindi ones the old master taught him at fourteen (naapna, kaatna, silna, kholna for let out, kasna for take in), and at the counter, as at any tailor's counter, the shop pattern of an English word with ho or kar comes out too ('kandhe ka alter ho jaayega', 'trial ho gaya'); never a whole English clause, which is Mama ji's and Mami's shape. No markedly formal courtesy forms from either side, Urdu or Sanskritised Hindi (the list is in 'never'), so the register reads as an old bazaar; a Hindi-first and an Urdu-speaking reader confirm that both sides are treated alike (rule 65, India verdict 3). In Hinglish mode his lines are Roman Hindi with those nouns. In English mode he speaks unhurried, slightly old-fashioned Indian English: 'Look,' for 'Dekhiye'; 'By the way,' or 'Then again,' for 'Waise', alternating, at most once a run, chosen by sense (a side remark or a counterweight); 'Uff.' kept as it is, since Indian English speakers say it; 'right away' for 'bas abhi'; 'Spot on.' for 'Barabar.'; 'Please don't mind.' for 'Bura mat maaniye.'; and the cloth and weather pictures intact. Never 'Mind you,' or 'Ugh.' (the first read as translated, the second is a teenager's disgust). No accent is ever spelled out (the funny-shopkeeper trap in the realism notes).
tics: Verdict first, as a whole sentence with its verb; then, in about one run in two, a turn to cloth or weather, often on 'Waise' (English 'By the way,' or 'Then again,'). The other runs end at the verdict. 'Waise' itself is anyone's word; the shape is his.

Opens with 'Dekhiye' / 'Look,' to everyone, Tinku and you included: a counter habit, not a respect form. At most one line in three, so it stays a habit. A plain 'dekho' is as free to him as to anyone.

Gives the sky, the clouds, the mud and the drain a mood, at most once a run and never when cross: 'Aasmaan rootha hai', 'Baadal din bhar munh phulaaye the', 'Keechad abhi so raha hai', 'Naali ziddi hai'. Only pictures a Hindi-first reader follows without help.
Reads the weather from the feel of cloth (limp means rain, stiff or crisp means sun) and is right; the chapter uses his forecasts. Asked how he knew: 'Kapde se pata chalta hai.'
Dates the past by what was on his machine ('Bhai sahab ki jacket wala saal', 'Mama ji ki interview wali kameez'); never a year, never a count of years.
Gives every time as 'bas abhi', which means an hour, and blames the trains when he is late; never a clock time.
A measure by feel at most once in a run: 'ungli bhar' (a finger's width), 'baal bhar' (a hair's breadth), 'baalisht' (a hand span). Never a figure, because his tape lost its marks.

Tailoring pictures for whatever he cannot say straight: a person is an old garment relined, the stitching stays home wherever the cloth goes, a city kurta only looks good in photos. Never a picture of anyone's body.

A real idiom from his own trade or weather when one fits, at most one a run, never a coined line dressed as a saying: 'paani sir se upar' at the drain, 'bakhiya udhedna' when he is caught out, 'baal ki khaal nikaalna' of Nani's checking, 'afwaah udna', 'munh phulaana' of the clouds. Proverbs stay Nani's register.

Thanks plainly and warmly: the young get an elder's good wish and the reason ('Sukhi raho. Us chai ne bachaa liya.'), a neighbour gets 'Ehsaan raha.'; sorry is plain too ('Bura mat maaniye.', 'Aap sahi hain.'), and his re-measuring comes at most once a chapter.
Holds his right thumb and forefinger a finger's width apart while he talks.
'Uff.' with a full stop is his only exclamation, at things, never at a person.
When cross, the turn stops: one short verdict, silence, and he straightens out of the stoop.
catchphrases: 'Bas abhi.' | 'बस अभी।' | 'Right away.' His only way of giving a time; it means an hour. (No figure.) Every player has a tailor who says it.

'Barabar.' | 'बराबर।' | 'Spot on.' His one-word praise of work, then a tug of the tape ends. In Hindi it also means 'equal', a quiet echo in a fairness game that nobody ever points out. (English mode was 'Level.', which no English speaker says as praise.)

'Kapde se pata chalta hai.' | 'कपड़े से पता चलता है।' | 'The cloth tells you.' His plain answer when anyone asks how he knew the weather would turn: a remark, not a saying. (It replaces 'Kapde ka bhi mizaaj hota hai.', which read as a coined saying.)
voice.exclamation: 'Uff.' | 'उफ़्फ़।' | English mode 'Uff.' as well, since Indian English speakers say it ('Ugh.' is struck: it is a teenager's disgust, not an old tailor's sigh). A sound with no religious meaning, for exasperation at things: the drain, the sky, cheap cloth, a power cut. Always a full stop, never an exclamation mark; it is his alone among the cast's exclamations, and it fills the place where an elder might reach for a religious word (rule 3). For joy he has no cry: he says 'Achha?' and claims the good news was in the cloth all along.
voice.sorry_thanks_love: SORRY, in plain words first: 'Bura mat maaniye, Bhabhi ji.' | 'बुरा मत मानिए, भाभी जी।' | 'Please don't mind, Bhabhi ji.' (to Tinku or you, 'Bura mat maanna.', a command that marks no gender). When he is shown wrong in front of people he says so, then makes the joke at himself: 'Aap sahi hain. Feeta purana hai, main bhi.' | 'आप सही हैं। फ़ीता पुराना है, मैं भी।' | 'You're right. My tape's old, and so am I.' His trade sorry, at most once a chapter, is to re-measure out loud: 'Bura mat maaniye. Chaliye, phir se naap lete hain.' He never says 'I'm late' (the trains were). THANKS, plain and warm: to the young, an elder's good wish and the reason: 'Sukhi raho. Us chai ne bachaa liya.' | 'सुखी रहो। उस चाय ने बचा लिया।' | 'You're a gem. That tea saved me.' To Tinku 'Jeeti raho, Tinku.', and to a young man such as his son 'Jeete raho.'; never जीते रहो or जीती रहो to you, because the form fixes a gender (rule 66's fourth flag), so you get 'Sukhi raho.', where सुखी never changes. To a neighbour or an elder: 'Bhabhi ji, aapki chhat ne bachaa liya. Ehsaan raha.' | 'भाभी जी, आपकी छत ने बचा लिया। एहसान रहा।' | 'Bhabhi ji, your roof saved my cloth. I owe you.' When he is thanked, he makes the favour small: 'Kinari hi toh thi. Isme kaunsi badi baat hai.' | 'Only an edge. Think nothing of it.' Never a 'no charge' thanks (Mummy's 'Iska bill nahin.'). The owner and the Hindi-first readers confirm that 'Jeete raho' and 'Sukhi raho' pass rule 3 (good wishes with no religious word in them). LOVE: his time, said out loud: the tumbler set down beside you, 'Chai yahin rakh di hai. Abhi garam hai.', then a story offered, 'Bhai sahab ki jacket wali baat sunaaoon?' At a parting it is said sideways in cloth: 'Kapda kahin bhi jaaye, silai yahin ki rehti hai.' | 'कपड़ा कहीं भी जाए, सिलाई यहीं की रहती है।' | 'Wherever the cloth goes, the stitching's from here.' Never 'yaad aayi', 'I missed you' or 'love' (Mausi's and Mama ji's plain words).

JUDGING NOTES (chapter 3's cards only, with his face chip; unchanged by this pass): his idiom is how people are as customers (fidgets through every fitting, never collects the stitching, has every seam redone, wants everything by tomorrow), landing on women and men equally; punctuality stays off his notes (rule 20).
never: Any figure in speech: no inches, minutes, hours, prices, scores, ordinals, years or counts of years (rule 2); no 'sharp', no 'about', 'roughly' or लगभग for a measure. The number leaners are Papa and Tinku.
A measure by feel more than once a run.
A turn to cloth or weather on every run, more than one mood picture a run, or any mood picture in a cross line.

A picture a Hindi-first reader cannot follow ('Barsaat mein ghadi bhi phoolti hai' and 'Ab ye tumhari chai wali barsaat', both struck), or a coined line dressed as a saying ('Kapde ka bhi mizaaj hota hai' and 'Jo waqt par aaye, use kuch chahiye', both struck). Idioms only real ones; proverbs left to Nani.
'Pehle ___' as someone-else-first (yours).
A 'no charge' or bill-free thanks (Mummy's 'Iska bill nahin.').

Another person's phrase or tag, which is not the same as a common word: Captain sahab's 'Arre waah.' and bare cricket calls; Mausa ji's one-word 'Lo.' and 'Theek.'; Nani's closing 'Bas.' and 'Khush raho'; Mausi's 'Suno, suno, suno!', 'Shabaash' and 'bahut yaad'; Papa's 'Kamaal hai' and 'Aakhri dibbe tak'; Mama ji's 'Don't worry'; your 'Badhiya'; the tags 'hai na?' (Mausi), 'haan?' (Tinku) and 'Correct?' (Mami). The common fillers (arre, achha, chalo, suno, dekho, bas, theek hai, haan, waise) are everyone's, and he says them mid-line like anyone.
A whole English clause (Mama ji's and Mami's shape). An English word with ho or kar only in counter talk.
जीते रहो, जीती रहो or any -ते or -ती word before रहो, रहना, रहिए or रहें in a line to you (rule 66's fourth flag); to you it is 'Sukhi raho'.
Hurrying anyone, 'jaldi' about his own work, or 'I'm late'.
Any word on a woman's dress, its length, tightness or modesty (no छोटा or तंग of clothes on a woman, no शर्म, इज़्ज़त, 'decent', 'modern'), or on anyone's body size (no मोटा, पतला).
'Bossy', 'argues', रौब, बहस, or any note about women or men in general.
'Ready-made' as praise.

Markedly formal courtesy forms from either side, Urdu (janaab, aadaab, farmaiye, huzoor, tashreef) or Sanskritised Hindi (dhanyavaad, kripya, shriman, padhariye), and any religious word (khuda hafiz among them): no god's name, blessing, festival word, 'shukr hai', 'tauba', 'Khuda', 'Rab', 'Bhagwan'; in English mode no 'Goodness', 'Heavens', 'Good grief', 'Lord', 'Oh my', 'Bless you' (rule 3).
English mode 'Mind you,' and 'Ugh.' (struck as translated and as a teenager's word).
Beta, beti, bhaiya, didi or any gendered word for you; any future or helper-verb past that changes with your gender in a line to you (rule 66).
A card person's name, or any word from a note on that decision's cards, in a bubble (rule 36).

Any doubt of a report of harassment or bullying, or of a dowry demand, or calling one a misunderstanding (rule 22). His 'Afwaah hai' is for sweet-shop talk only and never sits in a chapter beat near a report twin.
An exclamation mark, a raised voice, or temper at a person.

Mummy: 'Bhabhi ji', आप ('Bura mat maaniye, Bhabhi ji.'). She calls him 'Masterji', आप.
Papa: 'Bhai sahab', आप. Papa says 'Masterji', आप.
Mama ji: 'Mama ji', आप, now that he is a grown customer. Mama ji says 'Masterji', आप.
Tinku: 'Tinku', तुम; his thanks to her is 'Jeeti raho, Tinku.' She says 'Masterji', आप.
Mausi: 'Behenji', आप, as her own file has it: what a neighbour of 60 says to a schoolteacher of 55, while 'Mausi' stays the household's word. Mausa ji: 'Mausa ji', आप both ways. Mami: 'Mami ji', आप.
Captain sahab: 'Captain' (कप्तान), dropping the sahab, with आप; thirty monsoons of familiarity, not rudeness. Captain sahab calls him 'Master', आप.

YOU (rule 66): no address word at all. तुम only in commands ('वो ईंट लाओ। सिरे पर रख दो।'), 'who should' asks ('थान छत पर कौन ले जाए?'), and lines where you are not the doer ('चाय यहीं रख दी है।', where दी agrees with चाय). His thanks to you is 'सुखी रहो।' (सुखी never changes), never जीते रहो or जीती रहो, which fix a gender. 'Dekhiye' reaches you too, as his counter habit. Once in the year, teasing, आप: 'अब तो आप इंचार्ज हैं।' Never बेटा, भैया, दीदी; never आओगे/आओगी, थके हो, आ गए; any flagged line (such as one ending in a verb that agrees with the mud or the stitching) goes to the native reader.
From you to him: 'Masterji' and आप with -इए ('बैठिए, मास्टरजी।'); your one fixed reply 'Bas abhi, Masterji.' is verbless and gender-free.
This list follows the cast map's one address table where it differs; the Hindi-first and South Indian readers sign it off (rule 65).

habits: Device: his son's old phone with a cracked screen guard, kept in his shirt pocket under the sadri (never painted there; any phone in a scene is painted blank, rule 30). He reads it chin up through the bottom of his spectacles, then drops his chin to look over them at whoever is near, as if they sent it.
Script: Roman Hindi in lowercase, 'h' for है, shop English as nouns; spellings drift as romanised Hindi does ('zaroor', 'jaroor').

No digits at all. Sizes and dates travel in the photo of the measurement slip (painted blank), never in his words; times are written as words ('kal shaam', 'parson subah') and pushed back once before they are kept ('aaj zaroor ji').

Punctuation: thoughts joined with two dots '..'; no full stops, no question marks, no exclamation marks. A card holds 10 words or fewer (rule 62, if the owner rules that a message card counts as a spoken line): a longer message goes as two cards sent one after the other, cut at his own '..', and the first card keeps its '..' at the end, as if he is still typing.
The typed turn: about half his messages end on the weather or the cloth ('.. hawa me nami h', '.. aaj baadal nahi'), the same verdict-then-turn shape he speaks in; the rest stop at the news.
'ji' on nearly everything, even 'ok ji'. No emoji, no stickers, no ticks, no numbered lists, no flowers.
Photo first, words after: a photo of a slip or a bolt of cloth, then one short line.
Voice notes only to customers about a fitting, short, with the machine running behind him; never long ones (that is Mausi).
Timing: types slowly with his right thumb before opening, and answers yesterday's messages the next morning ('kal dekha ji').

One forward a year: each June the weather office's heavy-rain warning to everyone he has ever measured, with 'thaan upar rakhein ji' (real information, never politics or rumour; never shown on screen).
The game shows no group chat and no app look; any message of his on screen is a single message on a painted blank phone or a message card, as live text.
samples: To a customer, the time that slips (no digits): 'trial kal shaam ji.. hawa me nami h' then, the next evening, 'parson subah ji.. kapda abhi geela h' then, the morning after, 'aaj zaroor ji' (Trial tomorrow evening.. damp in the air / The day after, morning.. cloth's still wet / Today, surely.)

To Mummy in May, while the family is at Nani's: 'shutter roz thoda utha ke hawa di h ji..' / 'maal sukha h.. idhar dhoop kam' (two cards, one after the other)

To you: 'tumhare bag ki zip lag gayi h ji..' / 'jab chaho le jana' (rule 66: a subjunctive and a command, and the verb agrees with the zip; the checker flags गई before है and a native reader clears it)
To Mama ji, after a photo of city cloth: 'photo me har kapda achha lagta h ji..' / 'haath me lo tab pata chalega'

Possible chapter 3 opener on your phone, the night before the flood (waits on rulebook question 9): 'kapda dheela h ji.. kal bahut baarish..' / 'bhabhi ji ko bolo maal upar rakhein' (a command to you and a polite subjunctive: no gender)

look.build: Short: in the short band with Mausa ji (the comics review's four bands: tall, middle, short, smallest); in any frame only Nani is smaller. No exact gap is promised: he shares panels only with Mummy, and at 3.02 his shop step lifts him, so there his tell is the curve and the bald dome, not height. Slight and narrow-shouldered, a little soft at the middle (never a pot-belly gag), long thin hands. Forty-six years over a machine carry his head and neck forward and round his shoulders, so his outline is a curve. Base shape: the curve, the only one in the cast.
look.face: An oval face with a long upper lip and ears that lie close to his head (stand-out ears were also written for Papa and Mausa ji; his are flat). Three things to remember, all close-up details rather than strip anchors: (1) small half-moon reading spectacles low on the tip of his nose, and he looks over the top of them; (2) thin grey eyebrows that lift over the rims, eyes narrowed as if judging a hem, and nothing at all between the brows (upright lines there are the shape of a tilak); (3) a dry closed-mouth half-smile pulled to his left. Clean-shaven every day: Mama ji has the only moustache and Mausa ji the only beard. Age lives in the eyes, mouth and neck, never on the forehead: deep lines at the outer corners of the eyes, loose skin at the throat, grey hair at the sides; painted ages read young, so the sheet must read 60, not 45.
look.skin: Medium brown, warm and plainly brown. Every prompt opens his skin with the tested words 'South Asian features and warm brown skin' and adds 'a medium brown' after them (only that phrase has been tested against whitening). Darker than Mama ji, lighter than Papa (dark brown) and Mausa ji (deep brown); the exact order is settled on the cast's painted swatch strip, not in words. In Station's two inks his skin is a flat mid-tone of the blue ink, never the bare cream paper; on his bald head a halftone dot can pass for a painted mark, so a person checks every Station forehead and crown at full size.
look.hair: Bald and smooth on top, with a neat, short, close-trimmed band of grey hair running round the sides and back of his head from ear to ear, like a horseshoe; nothing on top, no tuft anywhere. Cut every Sunday.
look.glasses_jewellery: Small half-moon reading spectacles with narrow lenses and thin dark metal frames, worn low on the nose all day. Always written in full as 'half-moon reading spectacles' in his LOOKS entry and in panel words: never 'spectacles' alone (a generic glossary row, if one is made for Nani, would paste her big round frames onto him) and never 'glasses', which the painter's glossary uses for glasses of tea. No cord. Spectacles on Nani (big round) and on him (half-moon) wait on the owner's spectacles question; they never share a chapter. No jewellery at all: no ring (a gem ring reads as an astrologer's stone), no chain, no wristwatch (he owns none, which is his joke), nothing on either wrist. The words 'watch' and 'watches' never appear in a panel of him, since the old take's glossary row pastes a steel wristwatch onto any description that uses them.
outfits: EVERYDAY, the fixed look in every panel unless the scene says otherwise: a plain lavender cotton half-sleeve shirt, pressed and tucked; over it a plain black sleeveless V-neck waistcoat with no collar and a row of plain black buttons, in a thin cotton blend (no wool in the hot months), cut in 1988 with his opening jacket; plain black trousers with a sharp crease; the tape round his neck, lying over the waistcoat; plain black leather sandals with a heel strap. His own clothes are the one thing he finishes on time: they fit perfectly.

FLOOD WEEK (chapter 3): the same shirt, waistcoat and trousers, the trouser legs turned up in neat even folds to mid-calf, both exactly the same height; plain rubber flip-flops. The waistcoat stays on: it is what he is at work. Even in the mud his turn-ups are measured.
AT HOME (off screen; only if ever needed): a plain pale grey cotton kurta and loose white pyjama, barefoot. Never a sleeveless vest, which invites the painter to add a thread across the chest.

WINTER (December, off screen in the take): a full-sleeve lavender shirt under the same waistcoat, nothing more, so the dark V never changes (the sleeveless sweater is gone; it was a three-way duplicate with Papa and Mausa ji).

OCCASION (any function; none planned in the take): the same costume in his best, a new lavender shirt and the waistcoat pressed. The 1988 black jacket hangs on a hanger in his shop and is never worn on screen, so his occasion dress keeps his signature.
look.colour_key: SIGNATURE: a value stack nobody else has: light plain arms and a light V at the throat (the lavender shirt) against a dark body (the black waistcoat and black trousers), with two light lines down the front (the tape lying on the waistcoat). It is a value plan, not a hue, so it holds whichever style string each look ends up with (the code's STYLE or the chapter JSON look lines, still to be settled). Nobody else in the cast wears lavender, and nobody else wears a dark V-neck waistcoat over a light shirt (Papa's and Mausa ji's winter sleeveless sweaters are to go; Papa's and Mama ji's wedding jackets have stand-up collars and appear only in chapter 5, where he does not). NOW (present day): lavender shirt, black waistcoat and trousers, faded ochre tape, black sandals, warm brown skin. STATION (his chapter; deep enamel blue and black ink on cream): shirt left as the cream paper; waistcoat and trousers solid black; tape two thin cream lines on the black, both ends level; half-moon reading spectacles a fine black line; skin a flat mid-tone of the blue ink, never the bare cream paper and, if the style string can say so, never halftone on the face. He is no longer a third cream-over-dark man beside Papa and Mausa ji: he is light arms on a black body. Beside Mummy (from behind at 3.02) she is the dark block with one light diagonal and a bun, he the black body with light arms, a light V and two light lines under a pale bald head. CRICKET (outfield green, chalk white, cherry red): shirt pale lavender kept off pure chalk white (Captain sahab's trousers are chalk white), waistcoat and trousers black, tape ochre; beside Captain sahab's dark red top over white trousers he is light arms over a black body and black legs. JADUGAR (vermilion, magenta, indigo, emerald, old gold): shirt pale lamp-lit magenta-lavender, waistcoat and trousers indigo-black, tape old gold. LUGDI (violet, indigo, vermilion, marigold): shirt pale violet catching marigold lamplight, waistcoat and trousers deep indigo, tape marigold. RUKAVAT (teak brown, faded teal, cream, one signal orange): shirt cream with a grey-lavender cast, waistcoat and trousers dark teak, tape faded ochre; never the signal orange, which is Mausa ji's.
look.prop: SIGNATURE: the tailor's cloth measuring tape, worn round the back of his neck with both ends hanging level down the front of his black waistcoat to the waist, so it reads as two light lines on dark in every look (on the lavender alone it vanished). Story: given to him at fourteen by the station road's old tailor who trained him; its marks wore off by the mid-1990s and he measures by feel, so it is a plain faded ochre band (which keeps numbers out of the paintings, and is why he never speaks in inches). Hands: worn, never held, so it adds no hand. On the one day it comes off his neck (3.28, and 4.27 if allowed) it lies slack across the crack with its far end held down by a brick inside the frame, and he reads it crouching, with his fingers; nothing runs off any edge of the frame, so no hand is implied (rule 7), and the panel's look drops 'round his neck' (the three-hands lesson). It has its own reference picture, and every panel is audited for painted numbers. HIS WORN THINGS LIVE IN HIS LOOKS ENTRY ONLY: the tape as worn, the half-moon reading spectacles, the waistcoat, the sandals, the flip-flops, the turned-up trousers; no glossary row for any of them. GLOSSARY ROWS NEEDED (scene objects, under keys nobody else uses; each says what to paint): tailor's tape (a long narrow band of faded ochre cloth, smooth and plain, with no marks; 3.21's carton tape is written 'packing tape' and gets its own row or none); tailor's chalk (a small white triangle of chalk, unlike chapter 4's chalk lines); tailor's shears (long black-handled shears); steel tumbler (a plain steel tumbler of tea); sewing machine (a plain matte black treadle sewing machine on an iron stand with a wooden top and a small electric motor bolted beside it, no lettering, no gold decoration); bolt of cloth (cloth wound round a long core, stood on end); measurement slip (a small blank paper slip, unruled, unlike the applicants' slips); tailoring shop (a half-raised shutter, a cutting table, bolts of cloth on wooden shelves, a sewing machine by the door, nothing written anywhere); shop step (one long concrete step in front of two shutters); ready-made shop (a new small shop at the far end of the road: a brightly painted plain shutter, raised, plain shirts on hangers inside, no sign, no letters); brick (one plain red brick). None of these rows uses an old row's word (watch, stands, flat, floor, seat, bench, cover, match, wheel, pass, platform). SCENE OBJECTS (in the scene with the hand named, never in the fixed look): tailor's chalk (right hand); tailor's shears (right hand); a steel tumbler of tea (right hand, or held out towards the viewer with his face in the frame); the sewing machine; his blank measurement register; bolts of cloth on his shelves.
look.silhouette: The question-mark curve with a dark body: short, head and neck leaning forward, shoulders rounded, the smooth bald dome on top, light arms against the black waistcoat, two light lines of tape down the front, and his hands clasped behind his back. Readable as a black shape at phone size; in a line-up nobody else is short, bald and curved. FAR SPEC (when he is small and painted from words, not from his reference): a short forward-curved figure with a pale bald head and light arms on a black body; nothing more is needed.
look.shoes: Everyday: plain black leather sandals with a heel strap, polished. At the machine he slips them off and works the treadle barefoot, the sandals left side by side under the machine, toes level. Flood week: plain rubber flip-flops with a white sole and blue straps.

posture.stance: Heels together, toes turned out, weight even on both feet, head and neck forward, shoulders rounded, chin a little down so he looks over his half-moon reading spectacles. In a doorway he is on the step with one shoulder against the doorpost and his hands clasped behind his back. At the cutting table he leans on both fists. He straightens out of the stoop only when he is cross. (Stance goes in the scene words, never in the fixed look.)
posture.sitting: At the machine on a low wooden stool, his back curved over the needle, his right foot on the treadle, his left foot tucked back. On the shared shop step he sits sideways with one leg stretched out, a steel tumbler of tea in his right hand and his left hand resting open on his knee (never forearms on knees: that is Mausa ji's).
posture.walk: Slow, short steps with his hands clasped behind his back, stopping every few steps to look at a hem, a shutter or the sky. He never hurries, even when late. In floodwater he walks carefully on his heels, turn-ups level.
gestures: Tugs the two ends of his tape level with both hands before he gives a view: the tell that an opinion is coming.
Looks over the top of his half-moon reading spectacles, chin down, eyebrows up; reads through them chin up.
Holds up his right thumb and forefinger a finger's width apart to show how far out something is.
Presses his right hand to his lower back as he gets up (the sewing-machine operator's back, realism notes [36]).
Hands clasped behind his back whenever he looks on or walks.
expressions: NEUTRAL: heels together, hands behind his back, head forward, eyes over the half-moon reading spectacles, mouth a level line pulled a little to his left.
SCEPTICAL (his face at 3.02): one eyebrow up over the spectacle rim, chin tucked, head tilted a fraction, lips pressed; hands still behind his back.
PLEASED: one slow nod, both hands tugging the tape ends level, a small closed-mouth smile.
WORRIED: rubs the tape between the thumb and forefinger of his right hand, looks up at the sky, shoulders rise a little.

CROSS: pushes the half-moon reading spectacles up his nose with one forefinger and straightens out of the stoop, chin up, lips thin, and says one short thing with no wander; always aimed at a thing (the drain, the sky), never a person.
LAUGHING: silent; shoulders shake, eyes shut behind the spectacles, head tips further forward, his right hand goes to his lower back.
TIRED: right hand pressed to his lower back, eyes shut, head dropped forward, the tape ends hanging uneven (the one time they are).
MOVED: takes off his half-moon reading spectacles and polishes them slowly on the edge of his waistcoat, looking down, so nobody sees his eyes.

across_looks: STRIP ANCHORS (must survive in every full-figure pick, strongest first): (1) the curve: short, head and neck forward, shoulders rounded; (2) the bald dome with the neat grey horseshoe; (3) the dark V-neck waistcoat with light arms, a clearly dark value against a light one, which holds better than mid tones; (4) the tape as two light lines down the dark front. CLOSE-UP DETAILS (checked only in face-on panels, inserts and the face chip): half-moon reading spectacles low on the nose; clean-shaven; ears close to the head; thin grey eyebrows and nothing between them; a bare forehead and crown; warm brown skin against his swatch. Hue and exact face shape may drift (the drift sheet: hair shape and spectacles held across all five worlds; face, age and skin did not). Never allowed: a straightened back, hair on top, round or full spectacles, a beard or moustache, any mark or line on the forehead or between the brows, pale skin, a stand-up collar in place of his V.

PRESENT DAY (master sheet and face chip): the full fixed look in lavender and black. Every other look is derived from this master by reference editing, so the painter is never asked to change style and keep a face in one step.

STATION (chapter 3, his chapter): two inks on cream. Cream arms and V, a solid black waistcoat and trousers, two cream tape lines: no longer one of three cream-over-dark men beside Papa and Mausa ji. Skin a flat mid-tone of the blue; every forehead and crown checked at full size, since coarse halftone dots can pass for a painted mark. Use cutscenes.py STYLE['station'] for his reference until the owner fixes one style string per look (the chapter JSON look line and portraits.py WORLDS describe Station differently).

CRICKET (chapter 4, silent presence only if allowed): pale lavender arms, black waistcoat and trousers, ochre tape against the green; small and face-on at the mended drain, never the same shape as Captain sahab. Check apparent age (painted ages read young).

JADUGAR (chapter 5): not planned. If ever painted, the playing-card style has painted forehead dots on men in the library, and his bald forehead is a large target: check the forehead and the crown close up.
LUGDI (chapter 1): not planned. Lamplit gouache: marigold tape, pale violet shirt, deep indigo waistcoat; the stoop must survive the pulp style's heroic poses.
RUKAVAT (chapter 2): not planned. The panel style (wides 'sunday') lacks the skin words, so add 'South Asian features and warm brown skin, a medium brown'.
cast.painter_prompt: MASTER TIER (paints the model sheet only; never his name; role word 'the bald stooped man'): the bald stooped man, a short, slight Indian man of about 60, South Asian features and warm brown skin, a medium brown; an oval face with a long upper lip and ears close to his head, deep lines at the outer corners of his eyes and loose skin at the throat, thin grey eyebrows; bald and smooth on top with a neat, short band of grey hair round the sides and back of his head from ear to ear; clean-shaven; small half-moon reading spectacles with narrow lenses and thin dark metal frames, low on his nose; a pronounced forward stoop, head and neck pushed forward, shoulders rounded; a plain lavender half-sleeve cotton shirt; over it a plain black sleeveless V-neck waistcoat with no collar and a row of plain black buttons; plain black trousers with a sharp crease; a long narrow band of faded ochre cloth, smooth and plain, worn round the back of his neck with both ends hanging level down the front of the black waistcoat; plain black leather sandals with a heel strap; present-day clothes. PANEL TAG (30 words, used with his reference picture supplied; stance, hands, props and place go in the scene words): the bald stooped man, South Asian features and warm brown skin, grey hair ringing his bald head, black waistcoat over lavender shirt, a plain ochre cloth band round his neck.
painter_avoid: His name, or 'master' or 'masterji', anywhere in a prompt: names are painted as lettering, and 'master' may paint a teacher at a blackboard. Not 'the tailor' either: naming the trade draws a shop or a sewing machine into the flood and the drain. Use 'the bald stooped man'.

A bindi, tilak or any dot or line on the forehead; check the bald forehead and crown close up in every panel (the forehead check found painted dots on six of eight library faces, a man among them). In Station, read every forehead at full size, because a halftone dot looks like a mark.
Any line between the brows or across the forehead in a prompt: two upright lines are a tilak's shape and three across are another sect mark; age goes in the eyes, mouth and throat.
A tuft of hair at the crown, or any cap or skullcap on the bald head: each reads as a religious marker (rule 3).
A thread on either wrist or across the chest, a ring, a gem ring, a chain, a pendant, a wristwatch.
A beard, a moustache, or stubble that reads as a beard.

Lightened or pale skin, especially in the soft looks (now, Rukavat). cutscenes.py has no SEED_BUMP and no DOTS paint-out (those are in portraits.py for card faces only), so until a per-panel seed bump and an eye-confirmed dot paint-out are added, a person reads every pick and the seed is changed by hand.

Numbers, inch marks or lettering on the tape; a brand name, gold decals or lettering on the sewing machine; any lettering on his shop shutter, slips, register or phone, or on the new ready-made shop (rule 30).
Logos or prints on his shirt or waistcoat; lapels, a collar or a stand-up collar on the waistcoat (Papa's and Mama ji's wedding cut).
A straightened, upright posture (the painter likes upright figures); round or full-rim spectacles in place of the half-moon ones.
A third hand: the tape is worn, never also held; count hands in every pick.

Any tape, cloth or line running off an edge of the frame, above all the bottom edge: it implies a hand holding the other end, which would be the player's (rule 7). At the drain the tape's far end lies under a brick inside the frame.
Any hand or sleeve reaching in from the edge of the frame towards him (that would be the player, rule 7).
The bare word 'spectacles' (picks up any other person's spectacles row) and 'glasses' (glasses of tea); write 'half-moon reading spectacles' and 'a steel tumbler of tea'.

Words that fire the old take's glossary rows in any scene words about him: watch or watches (a steel wristwatch), stands (cricket spectator benches), flat (an apartment building), floor (Dadi's Nashik bedroom), seat, bench, cover, match, wheel (a lorry's steering wheel), pass or passes, platform. Write 'looks on', 'is on the step', 'resting open', 'doorpost'.
'Crown' (a crown may appear, above all in Jadugar), 'question mark' (a printed glyph) and 'border' (STORY_NO says no border) in any prompt; those words stay in these notes only.
A place in the fixed look: it ends at 'present-day clothes'; the town, the road and the shop go in each panel's scene words.

Swapped attributes when he shares a panel with Mummy: her bun or dark kameez on him, his lavender, waistcoat or spectacles on her. Each panel lists who is in it, and a panel with nobody in it names nobody ('the shutter next door', not 'Mummy's shutter').
A younger face: he must read about 60.
model_sheet: ORDER OF WORK: his sheet waits for the cast-wide steps first: the line-up (all ten as black shapes at phone width in the four height bands), the six look strips, the one trait table and the one glossary; the owner approves the pictured line-up before any single sheet.

MASTER SHEET in the present-day style, painted with the tape worn and the waistcoat on, so a person and his signature prop take one reference slot (portraits.py has no present-day template yet and STYLE['now'] bakes in a rainy evening, so the sheet needs a plain neutral background entry first): front, three-quarter, profile (the key view for the curve), back (the horseshoe and the tape across the nape over the waistcoat) and full figure, head to sandals.

LINE-UP: his full figure beside plain grey silhouettes of Papa (tall band) and Nani (smallest), and as a black shape at phone size beside Mummy's (his 3.02 partner); a two-ink version of the master to check Station; the far spec painted once small.

POSES: doorway, hands behind his back; tugging the tape ends level; at the machine on a low wooden stool, barefoot, right foot on the treadle; at the cutting table with tailor's chalk in his right hand, left hand spread on the cloth; holding a steel tumbler of tea out towards the viewer in his right hand; flood stance, trousers turned up level, flip-flops, ankle-deep in brown water; getting up with his right hand on his lower back; crouched at the drain with the tape off his neck lying slack across a crack, its far end under a brick inside the frame, reading it with his fingers, nothing leaving the frame.
EXPRESSIONS (head, shoulders and hands): neutral, sceptical, pleased, worried, cross, laughing, tired, moved, as written under posture.

PROPS SHEET (each its own reference picture): the tape hanging and the tape coiled; tailor's chalk; tailor's shears; a steel tumbler of tea; the plain black sewing machine; a bolt of cloth; a blank measurement slip.

TWO TIERS: the long master text paints the sheet only; panels with his reference picture use the 30-word panel tag. Test both first on the 3.02 pair (Mummy and him), and record the swap rate per anchor before more panels are written.

PROCESS: only after this workflow and any browser checks have stopped, one person's master at a time, three seeds per view through ~/.claude/heavy-queue/heavyq only, never beside a browser or another FLUX job. Pick by eye against the audit list (strip anchors first, then the close-ups of forehead, crown and skin, hand count, stray lettering, apparent age). Then derive the Station reference (and the Cricket one if the owner allows the silent presence) from the picked master with paint-refs (Flux2KleinEdit). Chapter voices need two references; he needs three at most.

PIPELINE GAPS TO FIX FIRST (rules review): cutscenes.py keys looks by year and reads the old script, REFS holds objects only, and paint_refs() never checks klein's limit of four reference pictures; person references and a four-reference refusal come before his panels.

PANELS: at most two people from references in a panel (klein takes four reference pictures: two people, one prop, one place); in 3.02 that is Mummy, Masterji, the key ring and the shop front, and the new ready-made shop far down the road is painted from words. The owner approves the pictured parts sheet before any panel is painted.

FILES (proposed): art/refs/tailor-now.png, art/refs/tailor-station.png, art/refs/tailor-cricket.png, art/refs/tailor-tape.png, with the seeds tried and the seed picked written beside each (file names never reach a prompt).

AUDIT CHECKLIST FOR EVERY PANEL: curve and stoop; bald dome and grey horseshoe, no tuft, nothing on the head; black V-neck waistcoat with light arms, no collar; tape as two light lines with both ends level and no numbers; half-moon reading spectacles; clean-shaven; bare forehead and crown under full-size close-up (Station halftone included); warm brown skin against his swatch; two hands; nothing on the wrists or fingers; nothing leaving any frame edge; no lettering anywhere; reads about 60; not swapped with Mummy.
best_scenes: 3.02, his own flooded doorway, sceptical, hands behind his back, trousers turned up level, beside Mummy's back at her half-raised shutter, and far down the road, small, the new ready-made shop's bright plain shutter with no sign: 'All this mud, by Saturday?' then 'And the sky's still sulking.' His fear is in the frame while he talks mud.
Measuring the flood line on his own shutter with his hand span and drawing one plain chalk stroke at it (silent, comic but dignified; no numbers).
The Tuesday tea on the shared step: he holds out a steel tumbler towards you, face in the frame. 'Tea first. The mud isn't going anywhere.' The listener who stays.

The next roof, drying his bolts of cloth beside Mummy's wet stock, forecasting from the feel of the cloth (3.11), and at her half-raised shutter on Friday night with the clear-skies forecast (3.21); he is right both times.
Saturday, 3.26: his shutter up beside hers for once, him in his doorway; nobody mentions it, whatever the band.
3.28, the cracked drain: crouched, his tape lying slack across the crack with a brick on its far end inside the frame, reading it with his fingers; thirty years of argument handed to the lane cup.
4.27, if allowed: small and face-on beside the mended drain, the tape lying across it, while Captain sahab's line is spoken; a person, not only his tape.
Off screen in December: the wedding kurta ready three days early; the family wears his stitching in Nani's town.
never_does: Sits on a card, asks a decision, or names anyone on a decision's cards in a bubble (rule 36).
Says a word about a woman's dress, its modesty or her morals, or remarks on anyone's body size.
Doubts a report of harassment or bullying, or a dowry demand, or calls one a misunderstanding (rule 22).
Raises his voice, at a person or at anything; his temper is a dropped wander and a straightened back, aimed at the drain, the sky and cheap cloth.
Haggles for laughs, plays the funny shopkeeper, or speaks in a spelled accent.
Speaks a figure as a verdict or a time, says a year, says 'sharp', or hurries.
Gives up the tape or the waistcoat at work, or wears a ring, a thread, a watch or anything on his head.
Touches the player or reaches into the frame's edge; the player is never painted (rule 7).
Uses a gendered word for the player, or a future that changes with gender in a line to the player (rule 66).
Preaches, about fairness or anything else, even with 'barabar'.
Forwards politics, rumour or a religious image.
Becomes the butt of the joke: he is the one who makes it, dryly.

RULE CHECKS PASSED IN THIS FILE: polite forms (आप to Nani, Mummy, Papa, Mama ji, Mausi, Mausa ji, Captain sahab and Mami; तुम to Tinku and you; you say आप and 'Masterji'); no year in any bubble (rule 2); no rule 3 marker in words or on the sheet; lead-in additions come in matched pairs (rule 37); every sample line at most 10 English words; the painter prompt, panel tag, posture, pose and glossary-row words fire none of the old take's glossary rows except 'stool', whose row (a low wooden stool for sitting on) is the one meant (checked with cutscenes.py's own functions, as the rules review's probe does); British spelling; no em or en dashes (checked by script).

CHANGES FROM THE CAST MAP, with reasons: Tinku's 'too thin for any pattern' becomes 'never stands still long enough to be measured' (a man of 60 remarking on a young woman's body breaks his own rule and the Sunita test); the Hindi label uses टेलर मास्टर, not दर्ज़ी, because Darzi is also a community name; the tape stays worn in the fixed look, made safe by its worn-off marks, plain-band wording and the text check (fallback: move it into each scene); punctuality leaves his chapter 3 notes (target 1 counts days late; rule 20); 'Captain' with आप both ways; he lives across the drain (proposal). In this revision: 'Do inch ka farq' becomes 'Ungli bhar ka farq' (no figures in his speech); 'speaks in measurements' stays, by feel; lavender and black gains a black V-neck waistcoat; the role word becomes 'the bald stooped man'. Every revision change and its reason is in revision_notes.

OWNER QUESTIONS: may he stand silent in chapter 4, small and face-on by the mended drain at 4.27? Take the 3.02 wander, the 3.11 and 3.21 forecasts, the Tuesday tea scene and the 3.26 shutter? His share of chapter 3's words (about 46 of 120)? Spectacles on two people? 'Bhabhi ji' for Mummy though he is older than Papa? टेलर मास्टर as the Hindi label? Keep 'barabar' and keep it quiet? His speech without figures (finger widths for inches, 'bas abhi' for 'five minutes')? A black waistcoat in July on a small-town tailor (an Indian reader confirms)?
