cast.name: Captain sahab (कप्तान साहब), about 65
cast.role: The lane's old club captain and the lane cup's only umpire, about 65, and chapter 4's voice (15 August, the lane cup, painted in the Cricket look). Not family: a neighbour on the household's lane in the junction town, in the house where the two lanes meet, beside the cracked drain. One of chapter 4's two judging voices, with Tinku (rule 22: a man and a woman). He sets the stakes, calls the tosses (the toss is his word alone in the cast; Tinku's file bars her from it) and umpires the final. He never asks a decision (Tinku asks all eight, rule 37), never sits on a card, and is met in chapter 4 only while rulebook Q11 is open (a silent presence in chapter 3 is proposed below; the bible allows silent presences). HIS COMPETENCE ON SCREEN, which the plot needs (India review: every man gets one): he sets the stakes that get the drain mended, umpires the final straight, and spreads a tarpaulin over Masterji's cloth on the flood night. Flat by design, with one contradiction held the same way every time and one turn, painted on the page, on cup day. FIRST-USE LABEL, kept word for word: 'Captain sahab, the lane's old cricketer' | 'कप्तान साहब, गली के पुराने क्रिकेटर' (rule 65). In much of north India 'Captain sahab' first means a retired army man, so the label never shortens and the ball is in his hand in his first panel (India review). Plain 'Captain sahab' after that, with a tag on every bubble. His first name is never said: the lane has called him Captain sahab since his first season as captain in 1990, his wife included. ROLE WORD for the painter: 'the old man in the white sun hat' (comics review: a role word from his look), never the name, which the painter letters, and never 'cricketer' or 'captain', which bring kit, a scoreboard, a peaked cap or epaulettes into the flood and the drain (rules review).
cast.essence: The strictest umpire on the lane, who has given every ball by the book for thirty cups and has still not forgiven one decision given against him at his only state trial. A retired bus-depot mechanic with big knuckled hands, he stands side-on as if waiting for the next ball, tosses an old leather ball a hand above his open palm while he thinks, and answers most questions with an umpire's call: 'Out.' 'Not out.' 'No ball.' 'Wait.' The type in five words: the strict old cricket uncle. What makes him not the type: the specific past he carries in his hand and on every lane bat (the match ball the town side gave him at his last game in 2002; bat handles regripped with strips of bus inner tube from the depot), and a failing he cannot see: his verdicts on balls are exact, but his verdicts on people are old grudges kept like scores (he still says one lane player 'plays to the crowd' because of one innings years ago), the trial's failing turned the other way. On cup day, at dusk, in a painted panel and not off it, he lets a call against himself stand: Tinku's book, which once scored a no-ball against his own lane, holds every ball of ten cups, and he tells her to show it to the district.
cast.backstory: Born in 1961 in the junction town, the son of a state bus driver; grew up in the depot quarters, batting with a taped tennis ball against the bus-yard wall. In 1979, aged 18, he went to his one state under-19 trial and was given out leg before wicket first ball by an umpire he still calls blind; he came home on the night train and never got another trial. From 1979 to 1985 he worked at a scooter repair shop by the station; in 1985 he joined the state bus depot as a mechanic and stayed 36 years, retiring in 2021 at 60. He captained the town's club side from 1990 to 2002; the lane has called him Captain sahab since that first season. In a club game in 1987 a fast ball broke his nose, which still bends a little to one side. His last club game was in 2002, aged 41, and the side gave him the match ball, the old leather ball he has carried every day since. In 1994 the lane road was raised and the drain where his lane meets the next one began to flood every July; he and Masterji (who lives on the far lane) have argued every monsoon since about whose lane's drain floods the station road (Masterji's file). On 15 August 1996 he started the lane cup to give the two lanes one day a year on the same side of something. It has one rule, said once and never explained: 'Live on the lane? Then play.' | 'गली में घर है? तो खेलो।' | 'Gali mein ghar hai? Toh khelo.' (India and rules reviews: the draft's रहते हो is masculine and, said to the lane with you in it, gave you a gender; खेलो is a command and clears rule 66.) He made the rule because two lanes never had twenty-two players otherwise, which is why the cup has always been everyone from 18 to 60, women and men alike; he has never called it a rule about anything but numbers. In 2010 a jack slipped at the depot and caught his right knee; he stopped playing even lane cricket and became the cup's only umpire. In 2017 the old scorer could no longer see the far end of the lane, and he handed the cup's book to twelve-year-old Tinku, who had been keeping her own tally on the wall in chalk (Tinku's file). He regrips every lane bat with strips of old bus inner tube. He lives with his wife in the house by the drain; their daughter teaches at a school in the district town and their son works in the city, and the grandchildren come for the cup every year. He walks with Papa at six every morning (Papa's file) and polishes his black shoes when he gets back. His reading glasses stay in a drawer at home. This year: more scooters park on the lane ground than last year, the July flood has cracked the drain, and his knee tells him the cup needs someone after him.
cast.want_fear_contradiction: WANTS THIS YEAR: one more cup on 15 August as it has been since 1996, both lanes out at nine, and someone to hand the cup's book and the toss to before his knee decides for him. WANTS FROM YOU: a straight bat and a fair pick. On cup day he watches whether you pick a side the way he umpires, by the book; he never says so, and nothing he says before a pick hints at one (rules 36 and 39). FEARS: that the cup dies with him and the lane ground becomes parking; under it, that he will be remembered for one ball at his trial and not for thirty cups. CONTRADICTION, held the same way every time: the strictest umpire on the lane, but still sore about one decision given against him at his only trial. He gives any ball by the book without a flicker, and any talk of umpires, luck or fairness brings him straight back to the trial ('My one trial. Not out. Ask anyone.'; no year on screen, rule 2). His judging notes on lane players are the same failing off the field: one innings remembered for years. HABIT OF SPEECH: he answers with umpire's calls (Out, Not out, No ball, Wait, Over), and when he says more, the call comes first and one short reason after it ('No ball. A rule's a rule.'). THE LINE PEOPLE QUOTE BACK: 'Straight bat. Front foot.' | 'सीधा बैट। फ़्रंट फ़ुट।' | 'Seedha bat. Front foot.' Every child of the lane, you included, heard it at seven and still hears it passing his door. WHO SAYS 'I KNOW THIS PERSON': Ravi (P2), the 26-year-old shopkeeper for whom puzzles set in a cricket team are a reason to come back, knows the uncle who ran the gully team; Mr Natarajan (P5), the 61-year-old rule-keeper who believes he treats everyone the same, is Captain sahab, blind spot included. FLAT BY DESIGN, with one turn, painted at 4.26: he lets a call against himself stand.
relationships: NANI ('Nani ji' | 'नानी जी', आप; she says आप and 'Captain sahab', as her file has it): they met at Mummy's housewarming and argued cricket for an hour (she follows the radio commentary), and each still believes they won (cast map). Friction: she is the only person alive who says the trial's umpire was right ('Pad first, bat after.' | 'पहले पैड, फिर बैट।'), and he has not forgiven her for it either. Tenderness: after her fall in May he asks Papa one word on the six o'clock walk every morning, 'Nani ji?', and Papa answers with a time. Little else between them, and both like it that way.

MUMMY ('Bhabhi ji' | 'भाभी जी', his walking friend's wife, आप, as her file has it; she says 'Captain sahab', आप): a lane neighbour who buys every fuse from her shop and asks for two rupees off every time, for sport (cast map). Friction: she has never once given it and he has never once stopped asking; a game between two people who both like rules, never a joke about her prices (the caricature guard on the trader cliché, realism notes). Tenderness: every July she puts the cup's floodlight bulbs aside at cost before he asks, and every year he leaves the full price on her glass counter and walks off before she can argue. After the flood he is the one who tells her 'Not out, Bhabhi ji. Next ball.' On cup day they never share a pose: his folded arms belong to the umpire's spot, and her palm stays pressed on Tinku's scorer's table (her file; comics review).

PAPA ('Bhai sahab' | 'भाई साहब', आप; Papa says 'Captain sahab', आप): lane neighbours and two clocks. Friction: Captain sahab calls the cup for nine; Papa is out at 8:55 with a steel water bottle for the side, and Captain sahab tells him early is a no-ball too ('Nine means nine, Bhai sahab.'). Papa's tease runs the other way ('Captain sahab, nine o'clock means 8:55.', Papa's file). Tenderness: they walk at six every morning, say nothing for half an hour, and neither has missed a morning (Papa's file). In May, the morning Papa is on the night train, Captain sahab walks the route alone and sends him one character: '6'.

MAMA JI (no name, तुम ever since the catch; Mama ji says 'Captain sahab', आप): little history (cast map). Years ago, in a family game on the lane during a visit, Mama ji dropped a catch off the last ball, and Captain sahab has greeted him with 'Catch?' ever since. Friction: Mama ji has promised the cup a proper trophy every year since and it has never come ('Catch, and the trophy. Both dropped.'). Tenderness: he is the one person in Mama ji's year who never asks him for anything, which Mama ji finds restful; and every visit Captain sahab throws him the old ball without warning, and Mama ji drops it (his file).

TINKU ('Scorer' | 'स्कोरर', the title he gave her at twelve, तुम; she says आप and 'Captain sahab'): he handed her the cup's book when the old scorer could no longer see the far end of the lane, and now says the district should see it; she teases him about his trial ('Your one trial again, Captain sahab?', her file, with no year on screen). She is the successor he has not named. Friction: she once scored a no-ball against his own lane in front of everyone, and he has never said she was right. Tenderness: he gives her his chair in the shade every cup (her file). At dusk on cup day, in a painted panel, he tells her to show the book to the district, which is as near as he will ever come to saying she was right; that night she sends the form (her file). Their voices never cross: he makes the calls, she keeps the score (her file). Their anger never matches: he goes still, she goes fast (her file). In a panel the painter tells them apart at once: he stands, tall and side-on under a brim; she sits knees-up, all angles under a high ponytail; one plain mid-grey plastered wall behind both (comics review; her file).

MAUSI ('Madam ji' | 'मैडम जी', as her old pupils call her, आप; she says 'Captain sahab', आप; her file, which also has her secretly delighted by it): Friction: she once sent him a two-minute voice note about when to send the lane side's lunch, and he replied '9 am' (her file; cast map). Tenderness: he sends her basket back with every box washed, which on the lane counts as a speech. Backstory only: she is not in chapter 4 (her file).

MAUSA JI ('Lineman sahab' | 'लाइनमैन साहब', आप; Mausa ji says 'Captain sahab', आप): two men of few words who once watched a whole lane final side by side and said four words between them ('Hmm.' 'Well left.' 'Hmm.' 'Out.'). Friction: Captain sahab calls every decision aloud; Mausa ji thinks most of them need no saying (his file). Tenderness: Mausa ji rewired the lane ground's floodlights for nothing, and Captain sahab lets him sit at the scorer's table, the only person there who does not score (his file). VOICE CONTRAST for writers: Mausa ji's few words are slow, soft, blunt about work and have no subject; Captain sahab's are crisp calls with English cricket words ('Not out. Next ball.'). Neither takes the other's word: no 'Hmm' for Captain sahab, no cricket call for Mausa ji. HEAD CONTRAST for the painter: Mausa ji's white brush crop is his; Captain sahab's hat never comes off (comics review).

MASTERJI ('Master' | 'मास्टर', आप; Masterji calls him 'Captain', dropping the sahab, आप: thirty years of familiarity, not rudeness, as Masterji's file has it): the two old men of the drain (cast map). Since the road was raised in 1994 they have argued every monsoon about whose lane's drain floods the station road (Masterji on the far lane, Captain sahab on the family's). Friction: Masterji says whoever laid the slope could not read a level; Captain sahab says a tailor measures cloth, not drains. Tenderness: on the July flood night Captain sahab brings the old blue tarpaulin from the bus yard and spreads it over Masterji's bolts of cloth, and neither mentions it; Masterji has stitched every pair of his white trousers since 1990 and says the side-on stance wears out the left knee first. Masterji's 'Whose drain? Let the lane cup decide.' (3.28) hands thirty years of their argument to his cup.

MAMI ('Ji', आप; she says 'Captain sahab', आप): no history; two strangers who would agree on everything and discuss nothing; if they pass at the wedding, they nod (her file). At one remove: each tells Tinku which course to do (Mami an accounts course, at every function; he the district scorers' course), so they argue through her without meeting. When Tinku shows Mami the cup's book, Mami says it is the only properly kept book she has seen outside a hospital billing desk; Tinku tells him, and he says nothing and tosses the ball twice.

YOU (तुम, because he coached you; you say आप and 'Captain sahab'): he taught you, like every child on the lane, to hold the bat straight, and he still says 'Front foot.' when you pass his door (cast map). Friction: you were the child who swung across the line, and he still calls it the one shot he could never cure. Tenderness: when you come home he says your best score on the lane, never your marks, your job or your plans; it is the only number about you he keeps, and it marks no gender. What he wants from you he never says: a straight bat and a fair pick. Lines from you to a group that includes him use the polite plural ('पहले सब पानी पी लें।', the You file).

HIS OWN HOUSE (off screen, never drawn, never named): his wife, who also calls him Captain sahab and calls him in from the lane at one o'clock every cup day (he answers 'Last over.' and comes at two); their daughter, a school teacher in the district town; their son in the city; the grandchildren, who come for the cup every year. He posts the cup's end in his own family group: the one message a year he types in full sentences.
cast.year_arc: OPENING (January, present day): not on screen. The date Mummy rings in red, 15 August, is the one he fixed in 1996, and Tinku's 'August 15. Lane cup. I'm scoring.' (1.04) is about his cup. CHAPTER 1 (May, Lugdi, the night train): off screen. The morning Papa is on the train he walks the six o'clock route alone and sends Papa '6' (backstory; a message card only if the owner allows a voice outside its chapter, Q11). CHAPTER 2 (May, Rukavat, the ward night): off screen. From then on he asks Papa 'Nani ji?' every morning on the walk (backstory). CHAPTER 3 (July, Station, the flood): proposed silent presence, painted small but face-on and never speaking (comics review: wherever the rulebook allows a silent presence, paint the person). On the flood night he carries the folded blue tarpaulin over his shoulder and spreads it over Masterji's bolts of cloth. At 3.28, Saturday, he is upright and side-on at the cracked drain in his most-days clothes, the ball held up in his hand, while Masterji crouches over the crack with his tape and says 'The flood cracked the drain between two lanes.' and 'Whose drain? Let the lane cup decide.' That puts the man who owns the cup in the picture the moment it is handed the drain. If 3.28 is his first panel, his face label there carries the full first-use label. CHAPTER 4 (15 August, Cricket, his chapter): a proposed wordless panel before 4.03 shows his own past without a word (comics review): dawn at his front door, sitting back in a plastic chair, winding a strip of black bus inner tube round the handle of the lane's plastic bat, the ball on his thigh. 4.03: two fingers of one hand point at the crack, the ball in the air above his other palm: 'The losing lane mends this drain.' 4.06 and 4.15: beside Tinku at the scorer's table, one plain mid-grey plastered wall behind both, he calls the tosses, 'Toss in half an hour.' and 'Toss in ten minutes.' (twin lead-ins, same figures and mood, rule 37). His five judging notes sit on the cards in game words. A proposed umpire panel at the final: him alone, waist-up, arms folded, the players out of the frame (rule 32), the same in every band (rule 39). 4.26, at dusk, HIS TURN, ON THE PAGE (comics review): Tinku seated in the left third (she speaks first, rule 31), the book open on her knees for the first time, pages turned away; Captain sahab standing side-on in the right third, the ball held still, looking at the book and not at the viewer. After her warm reaction and your fixed reply, he says 'That book. Show the district.' | 'वो किताब। ज़िले को दिखाओ।' | 'Wo kitaab. Zile ko dikhao.' That is his turn: he lets a call against himself stand, the no-ball she scored against his lane, and names his successor without the word. The beat stays inside rule 62 (three pieces of text, 13 counted words with Tinku's 4 and your 4) and adds no beat to an outcome that already breaks rule 42. That night she sends the form (Tinku's file). 4.27, Sunday: the mended drain stays people-free as the outcome painting (rule 32), with his name kept out of its description, and he speaks from off the panel, recast as a call: 'Over. Both lanes mended it.' | 'ओवर। दोनों गलियों ने मिलकर बनाई।' | 'Over. Dono galiyon ne milkar banayi.' CHAPTER 5 (December, Jadugar, the wedding in Nani's town): off screen. He has written to the district association about Tinku's book (never shown, never said); the letter she opens under the tent lights (Tinku's file) is partly his doing, and nobody in the story says so. If he is ever at the wedding, he and Mami nod (her file). ALBUM: not in it; it is Nani's table. HIS CHANGE ACROSS THE YEAR: from keeping the cup and its book to himself, and keeping score of one ball at his trial, to handing the book on in five words.

voice.register: Crisp and low: an umpire's carrying voice that never needs raising. HIS SHAPE IS TWO BEATS: the verdict first, short, then at most one short reason or instruction, never the reason first, 2 to 8 words in a bubble. At the ground and on any ruling the verdict is an umpire's call ('No ball. Line ke peeche se daalo.', 'Not out, Nani ji. Bat laga tha.'). Everywhere else, at the gate, on the six o'clock walk, across the drain, the verdict is plain lane Hindi and the reason comes from the bus depot ('Zyada meethi hai, Master. Bilkul depot canteen wali.', 'Theek hoon. Bas ghutna servicing mein.'). A call shows up in at most one bubble in two, so cricket is his trade, not his whole tongue: a retired depot mechanic talks cricket at the ground and plain Hindi with depot words at the gate. The calls he keeps: 'Out.', 'Not out.', 'No ball.', 'Over.', 'Next ball.', 'Well played.', 'Well fielded.', 'Front foot.', 'Retired hurt.' for his knee, and 'Ruko' ('Rukiye' when an elder can hear). A second thought is a second bubble after a second toss of the ball, never a longer line, and he never adds a third beat: Masterji's verdict wanders on after 'waise', Captain sahab's stops. Short, but not like the cast's other short voices: Nani closes bare fragments and orders, Mausa ji drops the subject, Tinku gives a score and 'haan?', Mami reads things back with a status, you name the listener. Beside Tinku in chapter 4 he gives rulings and she keeps the score: he never describes play as it happens (her commentary) and never says a score. FEELING: in plain words most of the time, said short and once ('Mujhse chook ho gayi.', 'Badi meherbani.', 'Koi baat nahin, khiladi. Hota hai.'). A cricket code for a feeling ('Next ball' as comfort, 'Well fielded' as thanks, 'Front foot' as love) comes at most once a chapter, beside its plain form. 'Well played.' comes once a year, and then he looks away. HUMOUR: sardonic and bone-dry, about his knee, his age and the game ('Purana model hoon, Scorer. Parts nahin milte.'), never about a person's hard fact; while rulebook Q5 is open his jokes stay out of the chapter outcome (rule 46). NUMBERS: rare and marked, only the toss countdown in the two lead-ins (a story deadline, rule 37) and 'Nau matlab nau' once a year to Papa; everything else in words. When he is not sure he waits ('Ruko.') rather than guess out loud. CROSS: he goes still. A whisper bubble, the words further apart, the verdict finger up and kept up; never a shout, never an exclamation mark. Tinku, his chapter's other voice, goes fast when cross, so their tells never match. TALKS MOST TO the lane's players, and on the page to Tinku at the scorer's table, Papa on the six o'clock walk and Masterji across the drain. He is never the asker (rule 37).
voice.mix: A Hindi frame: plain lane Hindi with a few older everyday words in it (meherbani, zaroor, waqt, chook, mol-bhaav). English comes in for two things only, the topic pulling it in, as the realism notes have the older speakers. Cricket: the calls and coaching words, said the way the lane says them (out, not out, no ball, over, next ball, front foot, straight bat, well played, well fielded, clean catch, catch, toss, pitch, crease). Machines: depot nouns (servicing, jack, clutch, tube, grip, tarpaulin, canteen, depot, model, parts), and for a machine job the everyday English verb with karo ('Grip change karo', 'Brake check karo'), the way every depot mechanic talks. His knee stays 'Retired hurt', a call, never 'retire hua'. He never switches a whole clause into English (Mama ji and Mami do). The common fillers are his as much as anyone's, in the middle of a line (achha, bas, arre, haan, chalo, dekho, theek hai). आप and a title to elders and equals; तुम to anyone he has coached or seen drop a catch. HINDI MODE, written fresh for Hindi-first readers: the cricket words every lane fan knows stay (आउट, नॉट आउट, नो बॉल, कैच, ओवर, टॉस, पिच, फ़्रंट फ़ुट, सीधा बैट), and the rest go into plain Hindi: Next ball अगली गेंद, Well played बढ़िया पारी, Well fielded अच्छा पकड़ा (बढ़िया फ़ील्डिंग when it is said of a job off the field), Clean catch साफ़ कैच, Dead ball ये गेंद नहीं गिनी जाएगी, Retired hurt घुटना छुट्टी पर, Last over आख़िरी ओवर; machine verbs in plain Hindi (ग्रिप बदलो). HINGLISH keeps the English calls. ENGLISH MODE: plain, clipped British English with the calls unchanged; 'Arre waah' stays as it is, the way Mami keeps 'Ish'.
tics: Two beats, the verdict then one reason, never the reason first: at the ground 'No ball. Line ke peeche se daalo.' | 'नो बॉल। लाइन के पीछे से डालो।'; off the ground the same shape in plain Hindi: 'Zyada meethi hai, Master. Bilkul depot canteen wali.' | 'ज़्यादा मीठी है, मास्टर। बिल्कुल डिपो कैंटीन वाली।'

At the ground he answers yes and no with a call: 'Not out.' (yes, fine), 'Out.' (no, finished), 'No ball.' (not allowed), 'Over.' (enough). At the gate he says 'Haan.' and 'Nahin.' like anyone. His typed yes is 'Not out'.

The reason comes from the bus depot when it is not from the ground: servicing, jack, clutch, tube, grip, the depot canteen, an old model with no spare parts ('Theek hoon. Bas ghutna servicing mein.').
'Arre waah.' | 'अरे वाह।' quietly, to nobody, at a clean catch, a shot off the middle of the bat, or good news he can see as one, and never louder.
Brings up his one state trial at any talk of umpires, luck or fairness: 'Ek hi trial tha. Not out. Kisi se poochh lo.' Nobody alive was there; no year on screen (rule 2).

Calls people by trade or title: 'Master' (Masterji), 'Lineman sahab' (Mausa ji), 'Madam ji' (Mausi), 'Scorer' (Tinku), 'khiladi' (any child or lane player, women and men alike). Mama ji gets no name, only 'Catch?'
Says the plain thing once and short, and does not say it again: a sorry, a thanks or a comfort is one bubble, then he tosses the ball or walks off.
Tosses the old leather ball a hand above his open palm while he decides; the catch is the full stop on his sentence. A second thought is a second bubble after a second toss, never a longer line.
Cross, he goes still: a whisper bubble, the words further apart, the verdict finger up and kept up.
catchphrases: 'Straight bat. Front foot.' | 'सीधा बैट। फ़्रंट फ़ुट।' | 'Seedha bat. Front foot.' (the line people quote back, kept word for word; still his hello to every child he coached, you included)
'Koi baat nahin, khiladi. Hota hai.' | 'कोई बात नहीं, खिलाड़ी। होता है।' | 'Never mind, player. It happens.' (what every lane child has heard from him after a dropped catch or a broken glass)
'Ek hi trial tha. Not out. Kisi se poochh lo.' | 'एक ही ट्रायल था। नॉट आउट। किसी से पूछ लो।' | 'One trial. Not out. Ask anyone.' (the grudge; no year)
voice.exclamation: 'Arre waah.' | 'अरे वाह।' | 'Arre waah.' Said quietly, to nobody, at a clean catch, a shot off the middle of the bat, or good news he can see as one ('Arre waah. Bilkul bat ke beech se.'). English mode keeps it as it is, the way Mami keeps 'Ish'; if the English readers find it foreign, the fallback is 'Shot.', said quietly, and only at a stroke. 'Arre' on its own belongs to everyone and he uses it mid-line like anyone; the phrase said under his breath is his. Never at a person's looks, never sarcastic, never loud: it is the one warm sound he makes without words, so a power cut or a late guest gets something else. Religious meaning: none; 'waah' is everyday praise. Guards (rule 3): never run on into 'Waheguru', and 'arre' is never followed by a name from any faith ('Arre Ram' is banned).
voice.sorry_thanks_love: SORRY: plain, at once, in front of whoever saw it, in his two beats: the slip owned, then the fact put right. 'Mujhse chook ho gayi, Bhai sahab. Ghadi dheemi hai.' | 'मुझसे चूक हो गई, भाई साहब। घड़ी धीमी है।' | 'I slipped up, Bhai sahab. The clock is slow.' At the ground, at most once a chapter, he takes back his own wrong call the umpire's way: 'Not out. Mujhse chook hui, khiladi.' The one sorry he cannot say is the one owed to the trial's umpire, or to Nani, who says that umpire was right: his contradiction, kept. THANKS: to an elder or an equal, plain and short: 'Badi meherbani, Lineman sahab.' | 'बड़ी मेहरबानी, लाइनमैन साहब।' | 'Much obliged, Lineman sahab.' With the deed, his two-rupee game with Mummy turned round as the full price goes down on her glass counter: 'Poore paise, Bhabhi ji. Aaj mol-bhaav nahin.' At the ground, once a chapter, the cricket form: 'Well fielded, khiladi.' (Hindi 'अच्छा पकड़ा, खिलाड़ी।'). His old deeds stay, never mentioned: Mausi's boxes washed, the tarpaulin over Masterji's cloth. WHEN HE IS THANKED: 'Kis baat ka?', then the credit sent somewhere else ('Kis baat ka, Scorer? Chhaon kitaab ke liye hai.'). LOVE: 'Front foot.', his hello to every child he coached, you included. For you it also comes as the thing he kept: 'Tumhara purana bat hai mere paas. / Nayi grip ke saath.'; on the platform, 'Front foot. Cup pe zaroor aao.' Never your marks, your job, your plans or a number. 'Well played.' (Hindi 'बढ़िया पारी।') is his highest praise, once a year, and then he looks away. COMFORT: 'Koi baat nahin, khiladi. Hota hai.' to a child or a player; for a real loss, once a chapter, the call: 'Next ball, Bhabhi ji. Shutter kal bhi uthega.' (Hindi 'अगली गेंद, भाभी जी। शटर कल भी उठेगा।'). A bare 'Not out.' stays a ruling, never comfort.
uses: Umpire's calls, at the ground and on a ruling, in at most one bubble in two: out, not out, no ball, over, next ball, dead ball, last over | आउट, नॉट आउट, नो बॉल, ओवर, अगली गेंद, ये गेंद नहीं गिनी जाएगी, आख़िरी ओवर
wait | रुको to the players, रुकिए to an elder or a table with an elder at it | ruko, rukiye

Coaching words: straight bat, front foot, cross bat, crease, line, steady batting | सीधा बैट, फ़्रंट फ़ुट, आड़ा बैट, क्रीज़, लाइन, टिक के खेलना | seedha bat, front foot, cross bat, crease, line, tik ke khelna
Praise: well played (once a year) | बढ़िया पारी; well fielded (once a chapter) | अच्छा पकड़ा; clean catch | साफ़ कैच
toss (his word alone in the cast) | टॉस | toss
Bus-depot words: servicing, jack, clutch, tube, grip, tarpaulin, the depot canteen, an old model, spare parts | सर्विसिंग, जैक, क्लच, ट्यूब, ग्रिप, तिरपाल, डिपो की कैंटीन, पुराना मॉडल, पार्ट्स
An English verb with karo for a machine job only, the depot's way: change karo, check karo, fit karo | Hindi mode: बदलो, देखो, लगाओ
the ground, his word for the lane where the cup is played | मैदान | maidan; the pitch | पिच | pitch
player, for everyone, women, men and children alike | खिलाड़ी | khiladi

Plain feeling words: 'Mujhse chook ho gayi' (sorry), 'Badi meherbani' (thanks), 'Kis baat ka?' (when thanked), 'Koi baat nahin. Hota hai.' (comfort), 'Poore paise' (his thanks to Mummy, with the deed) | मुझसे चूक हो गई, बड़ी मेहरबानी, किस बात का?, कोई बात नहीं। होता है।, पूरे पैसे
Older everyday words, as the town says them: meherbani, zaroor, waqt, mol-bhaav | मेहरबानी, ज़रूर, वक़्त, मोल-भाव
The common fillers, mid-line, like everyone: achha, bas, arre, haan, chalo, dekho, theek hai
'Arre waah' | 'अरे वाह' (his exclamation, said quietly)
rule | नियम | niyam
both lanes | दोनों गलियाँ | dono galiyaan
Address words: with आप, Nani ji, Bhabhi ji, Bhai sahab, Madam ji, Lineman sahab, Master, Ji; with तुम, Scorer, khiladi, and no word at all for you or for Mama ji
never: A figure in speech outside the two toss lead-ins (4.06 and 4.15) and 'Nau matlab nau' once a year to Papa: no minutes or clock times, no scores, totals or tallies, no prices, no head-counts, no ordinals. ('Ek hi trial' means 'only the one trial', not a count.)

'Saboot nahin, toh ungli nahin.' | 'सबूत नहीं, तो उँगली नहीं।' in any chapter or form: it is a coined maxim and a demand for proof, and a one-line clip of it reads as 'the family wants proof' whatever it was said about. He never asks anyone for proof (saboot, likhit, writing, proof, सबूत, लिखित); he turns a rumour down with what he saw ('Not out, Bhabhi ji. Subah bhatti jal rahi thi.'), and the build flags proof words near a report beat (rule 22).
Any doubt of a report of harassment or a dowry demand, or 'misunderstanding' about one (rule 22).
A cricket code for every feeling: a call in more than one bubble in two, or a coded feeling ('Next ball' as comfort, 'Well fielded' as thanks, 'Front foot' as love) more than once a chapter.

Other people's phrases, and their exclamations as his habitual cry (the words inside them, and a cry said now and then, stay free): Papa's 'Kamaal hai', 'Darj hai', 'Kripya dhyan dein', 'Aakhri dibbe tak' and any clock time or 'sharp'; Tinku's commentary ('Aur ye gaya!'), score shapes, 'Gazab' and the 'haan?' tag; Nani's closing 'Bas.', 'Chai piyo' and 'Khush raho'; Masterji's 'Jeete raho', 'Uff', 'Aap sahi hain' and 'Theek hai, maan liya'; Mausi's 'Suno, suno, suno!', 'Haay' and 'Shabaash'; Mausa ji's 'Hain?', 'Lo.' for here and a one-word 'Theek.'; Mama ji's 'Oho', the trailing 'aur haan,' and 'Pakka?'; Mummy's 'Had hai!', 'Haan ji, boliye', 'Isme kya' and 'Badhai ho'; Mami's 'Ish', 'Tick', 'Sahi?' and 'Congratulations'; your 'Badhiya.' as an opener, 'Maaf kijiye', 'Shukriya' and the 'Pehle ___' frame.

Other people's shapes: a comma list of jobs (Mummy), three bare fragments in a row (Nani), a whole English clause (Mama ji, Mami), a readback with a status (Mami), a tripled word (Mausi), a third beat that wanders (Masterji).

In Hindi mode, an English cricket phrase in Devanagari that a lane fan would not know: never नेक्स्ट बॉल, वेल प्लेड, वेल फ़ील्डेड, डेड बॉल, रिटायर्ड हर्ट, क्लीन कैच, लास्ट ओवर (rule 65). 'Timed out' leaves his voice in every mode.
Jargon most Indians would not know: googly, silly point, doosra, Duckworth, timed out (rule 2).
A coined saying or maxim. He has no proverbs (they are Nani's way) and no rulings turned into sayings; 'Saboot nahin, toh ungli nahin' was one and is cut.
'batsman', 'ladies', 'boys', 'girls', 'मर्द', 'औरत', 'लड़कियाँ', 'लड़के' about players: everyone is a player (खिलाड़ी) or a batter.

'show-off', 'drama queen', 'emotional', 'bossy', 'argues with everybody', 'knows best', 'moody', 'too modern': words the measure judge read as sexist on sight. Nothing about women or men in general (rule 22).
'beta', 'beti', 'bhaiya', 'didi', 'bhai', 'bro' or any family word to you (rule 8).

A Hindi line to you that changes with gender (rule 66): -ूँगा/-ूँगी, -ोगे/-ोगी, -ेगा/-ेगी, आ गया/गई, रहते हो/रहती हो, and a participle before रहो or रहना (खाते रहो). His lines to you are commands, verbless calls, or lines where you are not the doer ('Tumhara purana bat hai mere paas.').
'Ruko', तुम or a -ो command to anyone older than him; 'Rukiye' | 'रुकिए' whenever an elder is at the table or in earshot.

A god-word or religious exclamation (rule 3; the list in matrix 2.13), 'arre' followed by a holy name, 'waah' run on into 'Waheguru'; no caste word, no brand: the scooters, the phone and the canteen are never named.
A sarcastic 'Arre waah': it stays the one warm sound he makes without words.
A year on screen, '1979' included (rule 2).
A raised voice: no shout bubble, no exclamation mark, no all-capital word.
A spoken bubble over 10 words (rule 62). His own aim is 2 to 8 counted words (names and titles not counted, as rule 62 counts them). Never a speech.
'water', 'wall', 'chalk' (पानी, दीवार, चॉक) in any line: chapter 4 note words (Hari, Agnes, Manju, rule 36); never a card person's name or note word before or during a decision.
'captain' as a job word for anyone else (rule 36: in Hindi the job and his title are one word).
address: YOU: तुम, because he coached you, only in shapes that show no gender (rule 66): commands ('रुको', 'आओ', 'खेलो'), verbless calls ('Front foot.') and lines where you are not the doer ('Tumhara purana bat hai mere paas.'). No name and no family word; 'Front foot.' is his hello. You say आप and 'Captain sahab'.

habits: The phone: a plain phone in a plain dark case with a cracked top corner, kept in a trouser pocket. Painted with a blank screen; every message is live text on it, or a message card under the panel if the phone is small (rules 30 and 40). No app name, app look or 'forwarded' label (rule 3), and no quirk about his eyes or the font size.

Script: English in Latin letters only, never Devanagari and never a Hinglish sentence (realism notes 2.3). The messages are strings of nouns and calls, not English clauses, so this does not break his speech's no-clause rule.
Shape: a telegram in his speaking shape, the thing first, then the place, then one instruction, 1 to 7 words.
His typed yes is 'Not out', his not-yet 'Wait', his enough 'Over'; the lane knows a message is his by it. When he thanks, he types it plainly: 'thank you'.
Figures: none, except the cup's date and its nine o'clock, as digits and only in cup messages. Never a minute, never a score, never a price.

Punctuation: none at all, not even a question mark. The phone capitalises the first letter, and that is his only capital. Never all capitals, which reads as shouting and is the 'WhatsApp uncle' trap (realism notes 7).
The one exception: once a year, in his own family group (mentioned, never shown), he writes the cup's end in full sentences with full stops. That is the tell that it matters.
Emoji: one only, 🏏, on cup messages. Tinku's 🏏 to him copies his. No faces, no folded hands, no stickers, no good-morning flowers, no forwards, ever.
Voice notes: never sends one. He listens to the first few seconds of anyone else's and answers with the one fact asked, or a call.

He sends the same words one by one to every person rather than to a group: he trusts a message he has sent himself. The lane's group exists and is mentioned, never shown (owner, 23 Oct: no group chat).
Reads and answers twice a day, after the walk and before the toss, and within a minute about cricket or the drain; never late at night (he walks at dawn).
One forefinger, slow and deliberate; no typos, because there are so few words.

look.build: HEIGHT BAND: tall, with Papa and Mami (comics review: four bands, not ten ranks; the painter keeps relative height only within one frame at a level camera). Exact gaps only for the people he shares panels with: about half a head over Tinku when she stands (she is seated in almost every panel they share); a full head over Masterji, who crouches or stoops beside him at 3.28; on the walk Papa is a little taller, and the pair is told apart by brim against bare head and upright against leaning, never by height. Lean and wiry, broad and bony in the shoulder, narrow in the hip, thin legs: an inverted triangle (the cast map's triangle group with Nani and Tinku, so the triangle is held by two women and a man). Long arms; big knuckled mechanic's hands (close-up detail: veins on the backs, an old pale scar across the knuckles). One knee has been stiff since 2010, so he carries his weight on the good leg. Fit for 65 but plainly 65: the skin loose at the neck, the shoulders a little forward when he sits.
look.face: CLOSE-UP ONLY (comics review: at strip size a face is a few pixels, so none of this is a strip anchor; it rides on the reference picture and the face chip). A square-jawed, lean face with wide cheekbones and hollows under them. Three features, strongest first: (1) under the brim, the face reads as brim, nose and jaw, the way the method notes' Shikari Shambu is his hat over his eyes; (2) a short, strong nose with a slight bend to one side, broken by a fast ball in 1987; (3) deep squint lines fanning from the outer corners of both eyes, and two deep lines from the nose to the corners of a wide, thin-lipped mouth. Age is carried by the eyes, the mouth and the neck; no lines between the brows, which paint as a forehead mark (rules review). Sparse white eyebrows, deep-set dark eyes that narrow at whatever he looks at, small ears close to the head. Clean-shaven, with a grey shadow of stubble by evening. Not Papa's face: Papa's is long and narrow with a long straight nose; his is square with a short crooked one.
look.skin: Deep brown, darkened by forty years of bus yards and cricket grounds. PROMPT WORDS, always, with the tested phrase first and the depth after it (rules review; flux-portrait-biases): 'South Asian features and warm brown skin, deep and sun-darkened'. No reddish or ruddy word ever reaches a prompt: in soft styles it drifts towards a pale, ruddy face (rules review). The forehead is the same deep brown as the rest of his face: no paler band where the hat shades it, which a painter could turn into a mark. Soft styles (Rukavat, the present day) and the lamp-lit looks (Lugdi, Jadugar) are checked close up for lightening against his master swatch.
look.hair: Close-cropped white hair, short as felt, seen only as a band of white below the brim at the temples and the nape. THE HAT NEVER COMES OFF ON THE PAGE (comics review): bare, his white crop would read as Mausa ji's white brush without the beard, so no picture shows his head without the hat, and no hat-off reference is painted.
look.glasses_jewellery: None. No spectacles in any picture (spectacles stay with Nani and Masterji); his reading glasses live in a drawer at home, with no quirk attached (comics review: six files had a refuses-reading-glasses habit; his is struck). No wristwatch: he goes by the station clock and his phone, and a watch is Mummy's anchor and, painted as a plain steel band, reads as a kara. No ring, chain, thread, bangle or earring. The only thing on his head is the hat.
outfits: CUP DAY ONLY, 15 August (the fixed look of his master; India review: a retired depot mechanic does not wear whites every day): a soft white cotton sun hat with a wide drooping brim all round and one thin cherry-red stripe round the crown, no badge; a deep cherry-red short-sleeved knitted cotton shirt with a soft fold-down white collar and two buttons, plain on the chest (rules review: never called a polo, a word tied to a brand's chest logo); plain chalk-white cotton trousers, tucked in, with a plain brown leather belt; polished black leather lace-up shoes. He umpires; he does not play, so no kit.

MOST DAYS (chapter 3, any present-day lane morning): the same red knitted shirt, plain pale grey cotton trousers, the brown belt, the black shoes, the hat. The stack keeps a light bottom, so the anchors hold without the whites.

HOME AND THE SIX O'CLOCK WALK: a faded cherry-red round-neck cotton T-shirt with no print, plain pale grey cotton track pants with no stripes, the black shoes for the walk and plain grey rubber slippers at home; the hat whenever he is painted, even at his own door before sunrise.

MONSOON AND THE FLOOD (chapter 3): the most-days look, the hat dark with rain and drooping, the pale grey trousers rolled to mid-calf, grey rubber slippers; the folded blue tarpaulin over his shoulder (a scene object, painted from its own reference).

WINTER (January and December only): a cream full-sleeved cable-knit V-neck sweater with a cherry-red stripe round the neck and no badge, over the red shirt, a plain grey wool muffler, the hat (realism notes: a cricket jumper without a badge).

OCCASION (a lane function or a neighbour's wedding; comics review: the occasion outfit keeps the signature colour at the signature scale in a finer cloth): a pressed deep cherry-red half-sleeved cotton shirt in a finer weave with a plain collar, chalk-white trousers, the brown belt, the black shoes, the hat. Never a safa, never a kurta set with a stole.
look.colour_key: KEY: deep cherry red between a light hat and light trousers. STRIP VALUE STACK, top to bottom: light hat, dark torso, light trousers, dark shoes. That stack survives two inks, and nobody else has a light hat. The white collar and the hat's red stripe are close-up details, not strip anchors (comics review). PATTERN: none; plain fields. HUE RULES: a cool, deep cherry red, never orange, rust or saffron, because on 15 August, with white trousers on a green page, an orange shirt reads as the flag (the chapter's look line bans flags). Nothing green on him. The personas file assumes Ravi (P2) is red-green colour blind, so the red must be darker than any green near it and he must read as a dark shirt between a light hat and light trousers; nothing about him is carried by the red alone. THE LOOK STRING DECIDES (rules review): the code's Cricket STYLE inks cherry red, but chapter-4.json's look line ('flat slate-green and chalk-white grounds, scoreboard plates, warm evening light') has no red, and under it his shirt is simply the darkest shape. 'The only cherry red on the page' holds only if the settled string keeps cherry red; until it is settled, the value stack and the brim's shadow carry him. PER LOOK (the garment keeps its value and takes the look's nearest ink): NOW: deep cherry red, white collar, chalk-white or pale grey trousers, white hat with the red stripe, black shoes, brown belt. CRICKET (ch4, his chapter): in every panel he shares with Tinku, one plain mid-grey plastered wall behind both (comics review; her file agrees), since a whitewashed or chalk-white wall swallows his hat; the brim always throws a shadow over his eyes. Mummy goes near-black in Cricket (her file), so red, if the string keeps it, is his alone. STATION (ch3, silent; enamel blue and black on cream): the shirt a solid dark block, hat and trousers cream paper; the opposite stack to Masterji's light shirt over dark trousers, so the drain pair reads at once in two inks. RUKAVAT (ch2, not planned): the shirt a deep teak red, never the signal orange, which is Mausa ji's orange there; hat and trousers cream. LUGDI (ch1, not planned): the shirt deep crimson going violet in shadow, hat and trousers lit marigold by the lamp. JADUGAR (ch5, not planned): the shirt crimson, never the stage's vermilion or magenta; hat and trousers cream lit old gold.
look.prop: THE OLD LEATHER CRICKET BALL. The match ball from his last game as the town side's captain, in 2002, given him by the side; he has carried it every day since. STRIP ANCHOR (comics review: at about 200 screen pixels a figure, a ball in the hand is a dot and its two halves vanish): the toss itself, the ball in the air a hand's height above an open, upturned palm, is the shape that reads; that is the default in his panels and the front image of his sheet. CLOSE-UP DETAIL: a hard ball the size of a fist in dark red leather with a raised seam of white stitching round its middle, one half worn smooth and pale pink from years in his hand and on his trouser thigh, the other half still dark red; no stamp and no lettering in any painting (real balls carry a gold maker's stamp, rule 30). He tosses it and catches it without looking while he thinks; the catch ends his sentence. HANDS: either hand will do; side is a preference to check, never what tells him apart (comics review: the painter does not keep sides, and layouts get mirrored). What matters: the ball is held away from the red shirt (in the air, at hip height, or up against the wall or sky) so it never sinks into it, and the hands count two. When he points, the other hand holds or tosses the ball; for the shadow stroke it goes into a trouser pocket first. Never a second ball, a bat or a stump in his hands on cup day: the stump stays a scene object (draft 4.03, 4.06 and 4.15 gave him one; they are rewritten with the ball). The one bat he touches is in the wordless regrip panel, at his door at dawn, not in play. The lane plays with tennis balls (the chapter's look line); his ball is never in play and nobody else plays with it, though he throws it to you or Mama ji to see if you catch it (Mama ji drops it, his file). ONE REFERENCE SLOT: his master is painted holding the ball, so person and prop take one of klein's four slots (comics review); a three-angle reference of the ball (seam side, worn pink half, in the air above an open palm) is painted once for close-ups. GLOSSARY ROW (new, before any panel, keyed so nobody else's words fire it): 'old leather cricket ball'.
look.silhouette: Side-on, weight on one leg, the other knee soft; a wide drooping brim on top; broad bony shoulders tapering to thin legs; one elbow out with the hand on the hip; the other hand open and upturned with a small round ball in the air above it. The black-shape test at phone size: the brim and the ball above the open palm belong to nobody else. FAR SPEC (when he is small and painted from words only): a tall lean figure side-on, a white brim, a dark red block, pale legs. Beside Tinku, his chapter's other face: tall, standing and side-on under a brim, against her seated angles and high ponytail, one mid-grey wall behind both. Beside Papa on the walk: an upright inverted triangle under a brim beside a taller, leaning, bare-headed line. Beside Masterji at the drain: upright where Masterji crouches or stoops, and dark over light where Masterji is light over dark. With the hat always on, his head never takes Mausa ji's white-crop shape.
look.shoes: Polished black leather lace-up shoes with thin black rubber soles, polished every morning after the walk, worn with the white trousers on cup day and the pale grey ones on most days. At home and in the monsoon, plain grey rubber slippers. Never white canvas shoes (Tinku's), never sports shoes with stripes or logos.

posture.stance: Side-on to whoever he is talking to, as a batter stands at the crease: weight on the good leg, the other knee soft and a little forward, chin up, looking along his nose from under the brim. One hand on his hip; the other loose with the ball, or tossing it. At the boundary he stays side-on and tossing; his arms fold high across his chest only at the umpire's spot (comics review: Mummy's chapter 4 pose must not match his; her file gives her a palm on Tinku's scorer's table and no folded arms). Standing, he never leans on a wall.
posture.sitting: Well back in a plain plastic chair, never on its front edge (comics review: eight files had the front-edge sit), the stiff leg stretched straight out, the other foot drawn in, the ball on his thigh, his thumb turning it along the seam. Never on the ground, a durrie or a step (the knee). At lunch he eats with the steel plate on his knee.
posture.walk: Brisk, short, even steps, upright, arms swinging from the shoulder, with a small stiffness in one leg that he hides by never slowing down. On the six o'clock walk beside Papa, Papa takes long leaning strides and Captain sahab short upright ones, and they are never in step. He walks round the cracked drain, never over it.
gestures: THE TOSS (his default and his front image): tosses the old ball a hand's height above his open palm and catches it without looking, again and again while he decides; when he has decided, he catches it and closes his fist on it. The catch is his full stop.

THE SHADOW STROKE: when he says 'Front foot.' he slips the ball into a trouser pocket and plays a straight-bat forward stroke with empty hands, front elbow high, front foot forward, even at 65, even in a doorway.

THE VERDICT FINGER: when something is final he lifts his forefinger slowly to shoulder height, as an umpire gives a batter out, and holds it there. He uses it for 'no' at home as well as 'out' on the lane, and it is his anger tell. In a painting the finger points up, never at the viewer.
THE TWO-FINGER POINT: he marks a place (the crack, the crease, where someone should stand) with two fingers of one hand pointing down, the ball staying in the other.
expressions: NEUTRAL: side-on, chin up, eyes narrowed under the brim, the ball going up and down a hand's height, mouth a straight line.

PLEASED: one short nod; the ball caught and held still; one corner of his mouth goes up; he says 'Arre waah.' at a shot, or 'Well played.' once a year, and looks away along the lane as if he had said nothing.
WORRIED: looks up at the sky over the depot end and pushes the brim up with one knuckle; the ball held still in his palm; his weight shifts off the good leg and back.

CROSS: goes very still and quiet; the verdict finger rises and stays up; lips pressed thin; eyes fixed on the thing (a scooter on the pitch); his calls come further apart. He never shouts and never waves his arms. Tinku, beside him in chapter 4, goes fast instead (her file), so the two never share an anger tell.
LAUGHING: a short bark of a laugh, head back, and one slap of his palm on his thigh; deep creases everywhere. The hat stays on (comics review).
TIRED: slumped back in a plastic chair, the stiff leg straight out, rubbing the knee with the heel of his hand, the ball in his lap, the hat tipped forward over his eyes.
MOVED: turns side-on away from whoever moved him and looks along the lane; presses the ball hard between both hands; clears his throat once. No tears on screen. Then 'Next ball.'

WORDS KEPT OUT OF EVERY DESCRIPTION OF HIM, because the old take's glossary rows fire on them, plurals and verbs included (rules review probe of terms() and unclear()): stands, match, cover, watch, depot, flat, floor, seat, bench, pass, cap, board, box, card, sheet, stool, room, and the undefined ground, pitch and run until their rows exist. Clothes and the hat live only in his LOOKS entry, never as glossary rows (rules review). CODE ENTRIES: ROLE 'Captain sahab': 'the old man in the white sun hat' (ROLE holds no identical role, so clash() passes; Bauji's 'the old man' belongs to the old take). LOOKS 'Captain sahab': the master text, keyed by look once the pipeline is keyed by look and reads the chapter JSONs, not by year and first-take-script.md (rules review). Never write his name in a people-free panel's description (4.27), because looks() adds his whole look wherever the name appears, possessives included (rules review). painter_avoid: A forehead dot, tilak or any mark on the forehead or the hairline. Men got forehead dots in the playing-card style, and six of eight reused library faces checked close up carried a painted dot, a man among them (method notes). Close-up check on every pick by a person, not a dot finder (Station's halftone fools one). DOTS and SEED_BUMP exist only in portraits.py; cutscenes.py needs a per-panel seed bump and an eye-confirmed paint-out before any face-on panel of him (rules review).
Lines between the brows, which paint as a tilak (rules review).
Lightened skin, a ruddy or reddish face, or a paler band across the forehead where the hat would shade it.
The hat off, at any time, in any picture: bare, his white crop reads as Mausa ji's brush (comics review).
Any cap, and the word 'cap' in the prompt. A white brimless cap on an older man on 15 August reads as a political or religious cap (rule 3); the brim must run all the way round and droop.
A turban, a skullcap, a thread on the wrist, a plain steel bangle (it reads as a kara), a ring, a chain, a thread under the collar, beads.

Any logo, emblem, number or lettering: on the shirt's chest (the painter's favourite place for a logo, and the reason 'polo' never reaches a prompt, rules review), on the hat, on the shoes, and on the ball, since real balls carry a gold maker's stamp (rule 30).
A moustache or a beard: a moustache takes Mama ji's anchor (cast map), a beard Mausa ji's (his file), and a long beard with a shaved upper lip reads as a community marker (realism notes).
The red drifting to orange, rust or saffron: with white trousers on a green-inked page on 15 August it reads as the flag. Reject any pick where the shirt reads orange.
Cricket kit: pads, gloves, a helmet, a bat in his hands on cup day, a 1980s cap, long sideburns. 'Cricketer' and the 1980s sports styles pull it in, which is why neither is his role word.
A ship's or army captain: a peaked cap, braid, epaulettes, a uniform. 'Captain' never reaches the painter.
A famous face: an old man in a drooping sun hat in a 1980s sports-magazine style can drift towards a real cricketer's likeness (rule 3: no famous person). Check by eye.
Looking younger than 65: painted ages read young (the old Dadi read about 60 and was repainted at 78). White hair at the temples, deep lines and the loose skin at the neck must show.
A third hand. Ball, hip and point use two hands only; count the hands in every pick.
The ball painted as a yellow tennis ball, or held against the red shirt where it disappears.
A batter, a bowler or any lane player in his umpire panel or beside him at the final: they are chapter 4's card people (rule 32; rules review).
A whitewashed or chalk-white wall behind him in any panel he shares with Tinku: one plain mid-grey plastered wall (comics review; her file).

Swapping features with Tinku when they share a panel (painters mix up attributes between two people, method notes): the hat, the red shirt and the ball stay on him; the ponytail, headphones and scorebook stay on her.
A stance written into the fixed look: it fights his seated and regrip panels, and 'stands' fires the old spectator-stands row (rules review).
A hand or object reaching out of the frame towards the viewer, which would read as the player's (rule 7). A ball lobbed into the air is fine when no hand of the player shows.
Folded hands, touching feet, a head bobble (rule 3; realism notes on the caricature).
A wooden stump in his hand: draft beats 4.03, 4.06 and 4.15 give him one; they are rewritten with the ball.
Spectacles of any kind.

ORDER OF WORK (comics review): first the cast line-up (all ten as black shapes at phone width in the four height bands) and the six look strips, resolving collisions there; then the trait-table dedupe; only then his master. The owner approves the pictured line-up before any single sheet.

1. MASTER TURNAROUND, present day, cup-day look, full figure, painted holding the ball so person and prop share one reference slot: FRONT (his front image: side-on stance, one hand on his hip, the ball in the air above the other, open palm); three-quarter; profile (the brim, the crooked nose, the side-on stance); back (the hat from behind, the shirt's back and collar, the belt line, the trousers, the shoes; needed for any panel from behind). Three seeds each (7100, 7203, 7319, the seeds cutscenes.py uses), picked by eye against the strip anchors, then a forehead and skin close-up, a hand count and a stray-letter check. Whether klein can paint a multi-view sheet in one picture is untested; if not, one view per picture.

2. LINE-UP STRIP: beside Tinku seated at the scorer's table against a mid-grey plastered wall (his chapter's pair); beside Papa walking (both clean-shaven, so the brim carries him); beside Masterji crouching at the drain (inverted triangle against the curve; dark over light against light over dark, painted once in two inks too); beside Mama ji (round, middle band, with the umbrella). Fixes only the gaps for pairs that share panels.

3. POSES: the toss; the shadow stroke (ball in a pocket, both hands on an imaginary bat); the verdict finger; arms folded at the umpire's spot, alone; the two-finger point down at the crack; sitting well back in a plastic chair, one leg straight out; the regrip at his door; walking briskly; laughing with a palm slap on his thigh, hat on; looking up at the sky; lobbing the ball towards the viewer, his hand open after the throw (no hand of the player, rule 7).

4. EXPRESSIONS, head and shoulders, each with a small full-body thumbnail because faces drift and the body carries the mood: neutral, pleased, worried, cross, laughing, tired, moved, as written in posture. Hat on in every one.

5. OUTFIT VARIANTS in one standing pose, all with the hat on: cup day (the fixed look); most days (pale grey trousers); home; the six o'clock walk; monsoon with rolled trousers and the folded blue tarpaulin; winter sweater and grey muffler; occasion red shirt in a finer weave.

6. PROPS SHEET (their own reference pictures, painted before any panel, glossary rows first): the old leather ball (seam side, worn pink half, in the air above an open palm); the plain plastic chair; the folded blue tarpaulin; the plastic bat with its inner-tube grip.

7. PER-LOOK REFERENCES, made from the picked master with the edit model (Flux2KleinEdit), never asking the painter to change style and keep a face in one step: CRICKET x4 (side-on with the ball in the air; the two-finger point at the crack; seated well back in the chair; standing beside the scorer's table at the mid-grey wall); STATION x1 (upright at the drain, silent, for chapter 3). The present-day master doubles as the face chip's source.

8. FACE CHIP: a 512 x 512 head-and-shoulders portrait from the master, hat on, for every bubble and his five card notes. It needs a present-day template in portraits.py (WORLDS has none today) and the close-up check of forehead, skin and age before use.

9. TWO-TIER TEST before more panels are written (comics and rules reviews: untested whether klein ties long descriptions to the right person): paint 4.06 (him and Tinku) once with both master texts and once with both panel tags plus their references, and record the swap rate for each strip anchor.

10. All painting only after this workflow and any browser checks have stopped (mac-memory-limit), one job at a time through ~/.claude/heavy-queue/heavyq; the owner approves the pictured parts sheet before any panel is painted.

never_does: Shouts, or waves his arms in anger.
Takes his hat off on the page.
Folds his arms anywhere but the umpire's spot.
Doubts a report of harassment or a dowry demand, or calls one a misunderstanding (rule 22).
Says anything about women or men in general, or sorts players into women and men: everyone on the lane is a player.
Moves the cup from 15 August, or lets anyone bat twice.
Says sorry in words.
Gives a time like 8:55, says 'sharp', counts heads or keeps a tally: the toss's countdown is his only figure.
Calls a toss for anyone else to call, or lets anyone else call it.
Wears spectacles, a watch, or anything on his head but the hat.
Fixes the household's wiring or things: that is Mausa ji's way of caring. His is coaching and umpiring.
Preaches or makes a speech: he is never the lane's moral compass (the realism notes' trap of older people as props).
Sits on the ground, a durrie or a step, or plays in the cup since his knee.
Jokes about anyone's hard fact, or names a card person or their note words in a bubble before or during a decision (rule 36).
Forwards anything, sends a voice note, or types in capitals.
Sits on a card or asks a decision (rule 37).
Calls you beta, bhai, bro or any family word (rule 8).
Touches the player, or holds anything out of the frame towards them (rule 7).
Lets anyone else play with his old ball.
Uses a god-word.

Manager of the billing desk at a big city hospital. A chapter voice: met in chapter 5 only while rulebook Q11 is open, never on a card, never the asker (Mama ji asks all eight decisions), never the chapter's shout (that is Mama ji's), painted face-on from her own model sheet (owner answer 6) and tagged on every bubble.
