cast.essence: The city hospital's billing-desk manager who runs her daughter's wedding off the clipboard she was handed on her first day at work in 1999: every envelope, key and plate an item, and every item given a status, done, pending or not known. The type in five words: the organised city sister-in-law. What makes her not the type is on the clipboard itself. Under every list lies one soft, yellowed sheet from her own wedding week in this same house, written the night Nani found her alone in the kitchen and showed her where everything was kept. And at the top of every list since the evening the date was fixed sits one line with no number and no status: her daughter's bag. It is the only item she cannot tick. The one thing that catches her out all week is the one thing never on any list: Nani hands her, the one from outside, the first slice of the cake, and she laughs.
cast.backstory: Born in 1981 in the big city where she still lives (unnamed, rule 3). Her father retired from a clerk's desk in the city's water department; her mother's family is Bengali, settled in the city two generations back, so she grew up in Hindi outside the house and a little Bengali with her mother's sisters. That side is chapter 5's circle (the continuity fix), which gives its three Bengali names a home; nothing on screen marks it. At 18 she joined the billing counter of a big city hospital as a trainee and did her commerce degree in the evenings; it took five years and she is still proud of it. The counter taught her two habits she has never dropped: she says 'Thank you' to every stranger who stands in front of her, and she asks every family at the counter about their children, because families wait there at their worst hour. In 2000 a young man from a small town came to the counter to pay a friend's bill and disputed every line; she made him read it line by line, and he came back the next day with the right change and a box of sweets. That was Mama ji. They married in 2001 at Nani's house, and her family travelled a night by train to a town they had never seen (Mama ji's file). She spent her own wedding week not knowing where anything was kept, which room was whose, or whom to ask. On the last night Nani found her standing alone in the kitchen, and without a word walked her round it, tin by tin and shelf by shelf. Mami wrote it all down on the back of a billing form on her clipboard; that sheet, soft and yellowed now, has lain under every list she has written since. Their one daughter was born in 2002. She has run the billing desk since 2017: a shift of six, every insurance form, every family at the counter at its worst hour, which is why she is calm when others are not. A two-bedroom flat in the city; at the desk by eight, the day's list at eleven at night. Since Nani's fall in May she phones Nani at eight every evening for the BP reading Nani speaks into the phone, and sends the doctor a numbered log each month. This December her daughter marries from Nani's house, the same house, and this time she knows where everything is kept, because she wrote it down in 2001.
cast.want_fear_contradiction: WANTS THIS YEAR: a wedding with no surprises: every envelope, key, room and plate accounted for, and nothing going wrong in her husband's family's house. WANTS FROM YOU: a second pair of hands she need not explain things to twice. She reads your plan back to you once; the day she stops reading it back is her thank-you (her spoken 'Thank you' is for strangers, so it means less). FEARS: something going wrong in Nani's house in front of everyone when she is the one from outside, the city daughter-in-law who did not know where the tins were kept in 2001, and whom Nani, 25 years on, still asks to 'Do sit.' like a guest. Under that, the day the list is finished, because its top line is her daughter going. She never says either aloud. CONTRADICTION, held the same way all week: she plans every minute of the week her daughter leaves, and leaves the leaving itself without a status. The top line of every wedding list, 'Beti ka bag' (her daughter's own suitcase), has no number and no tick, the only line on any of her lists without one; on the wedding evening she stands by the packed suitcase with the pen above that line and does not write, and that is the one time she cries all week, alone. All week her no is 'Not on the list.'; on the last night Nani hands her the first slice, the thing that was never on any list, and she laughs, surprised, and turns her own words round: 'Well. That wasn't on my list.' HABIT OF SPEECH: numbers her items and ends each with its status; reads your plan back before she writes it. THE LINE PEOPLE QUOTE BACK: 'One, keys. Two, envelopes.' | 'पहला, चाबियाँ। दूसरा, लिफ़ाफ़े।' | 'Pehla, chaabiyan. Doosra, lifafe.' WHO SAYS 'I KNOW THIS PERSON': Farida (P6), the staff nurse in a joint family, who meets this woman at her own hospital's billing counter and at her own family's weddings; and Shruti (P1), the analyst who lives by lists and statuses. FLAT BY DESIGN: a chapter voice is made recognisable by one habit and one contradiction (Forster's flat character, in the method notes); the household stays round.
relationships: NANI ('Mummy ji' | 'मम्मी जी', आप; Nani says आप to her, the one in-law she is formal with, as Nani's own file has it): since the fall in May, Mami phones at 8 pm every evening for the BP reading Nani speaks into the phone and logs it; Nani answers on the first ring and says every time 'मेरा BP मुझे पता है।'. Friction: whose kitchen it is in the wedding week, and Nani will not let her medicines go on anyone's list. Tenderness: in 2001, in Mami's own wedding week, Nani found her standing alone in this kitchen and walked her round it; the yellowed sheet under every list is that walk. Nani trusts her lists and pretends not to. Greeting: Mami bends from the hips and takes Nani's hand in both of hers, and Nani pats it (no feet touched, a greeting that marks no community; Nani's palm on the head is kept for Mama ji, as Nani's file has it). Nani's आप reads as coldness unless people see it, so Mami remarks on it once, to you, with Nani in earshot: 'Mummy ji still says "Do sit." Like a guest.' (Nani's file asks for this line). It is paid off by Nani's December first तुम to her three in-laws together (Nani's file: 'All of you too. Sit with us.') and by the first slice of the cake, handed to Mami in Mami's own two-person panel (Nani's file).

MUMMY ('Didi' | 'दीदी', आप; Mummy calls her 'Bhabhi' and says तुम, and to you calls her 'tumhari Mami', as Mummy's file has it): sisters-in-law who both run things, one a shop and one a desk. Mummy trusts her lists and doubts her city prices; Mami prices the caterer at city rates and Mummy re-prices every line (Mummy's file). Friction: Mummy prices everything, Mami gives everything a status, and neither will use the other's word. Tenderness: in July's flood Mami sent a numbered list for the shop's claim (photos before cleaning, stock with bills, the form signed); Mummy said she did not need it and used every line. At the wedding they split the house without a word (Mummy's file), and at one in the morning they count plates side by side; it is the one place Mami says no thank-you, because family is not a counter. Which sister takes the kitchen is for the cast table: Mummy's file gives it to Mummy, Mausi's to Mausi.

PAPA ('Jija ji' | 'जीजा जी', आप; he says आप to her and no name, his formality): the other list-keeper. Friction, mild: she numbers, he times; she asks 'What is item 3?' and he answers with a time, and their lists never match column for column. Tenderness: he sends her every guest's train times and she replies with a numbered list, the happiest exchange of his year; item 1 on every wedding list reads 'Papa: trains' (Papa's file), the one item she never has to chase. She is the only one who answers his 6:10 good-morning flower, every morning, with one tick. In chapter 5 he is painted alone at the platform (his file), so they share no panel there.

MAMA JI (no name; तुम both ways, so the game's own couple carries no honorific-to-husband pattern, as the realism notes ask; he calls her 'Boss' | 'बॉस' in front of the family, his file, pending the owner; to the young ones she calls him 'your Mama ji' | 'तुम्हारे मामा जी'): married in 2001, a year after he disputed a hospital bill at her counter. He promises, she plans; he says seventy, she counts sixty; they bicker in front of everyone and decide everything in private. She is the calm one and he is the worrier: the script the game measures, turned over without making him the one who is managed, because each is right once (his file): she about the plates, he about the people. She says so on screen at 5.13, beside him at the steaming kettle: 'Every cook was booked. Yours came.' (his file offers the line; she owns the credit). Friction: every number he says grows, and she writes down the smaller one. Tenderness: he is the only person allowed to write on her list, in his own hand, and she always ticks his item first; on Friday night he brings her tea on the gate step ('Boss, chai. List kal.', the writers' ear only, since that panel stays wordless). She is half a head taller than him and has never once stood so as to hide it. In chapter 5 his phone stays in his pocket (his file), and nobody comforts her at the cake, so he puts no arm round her there.

TINKU ('Tinku', तुम; Tinku says 'Mami' and आप): two list-keepers, one who scores and one who ticks. Friction: at every function Mami tells Tinku to do a proper accounts course, because she fought five years of evenings for her own commerce degree, and Tinku keeps a tally of how often ('That's four, Mami.'); in the wedding week Mami asks her to take the headphones off, and she does not (Tinku's file). Tenderness: the two of them end the wedding checking each other's counts, and they match (Tinku's file). Proposed for Tinku's writer, as Mami's release (comics review): when the counts match, Mami hands Tinku her pen and lets her write the total, the only time anyone but Mama ji writes on her list, and she never mentions the accounts course again.

MAUSI ('Badi Didi' | 'बड़ी दीदी', आप; Mausi calls her 'Bhabhi' and says तुम, as both files have it): Mausi thinks city people waste money; Mami thinks Mausi feeds people too much. Mausi sends three-minute voice notes; Mami replies to each with a numbered summary ending 'Correct?', and Mausi says yes to all of it without reading. Mausi teases her for saying 'Thank you' to the tent man 'like a bill'. At the wedding Mausi's basket bag feeds Mami's list and they are allies, never two women set against each other (realism, caricature traps). Mausi is silent in chapter 5 while rulebook Q11 is open.

MAUSA JI ('Bade Jija ji' | 'बड़े जीजा जी', आप, the word her husband uses for him, so she never says 'Jija ji' to two men in one week; Mausa ji's file lists plain 'Jija ji', so the cast map's address table settles it): first through the blue gate at dawn with two folding steel chairs and last to leave (his file). She puts him on no list, because he does everything that is not on it; he is the only job she trusts without writing it down.

MASTERJI ('Masterji', आप; they have never met): she sends Mama ji's measurements for the wedding kurta by message, numbered and to the quarter inch, and he says she is the only customer in thirty years who measures correctly. She means to meet him in December and does not find the time.
CAPTAIN SAHAB ('Captain sahab', आप): no history; two strangers who would agree on everything and discuss nothing. If they pass at the wedding, they nod.

YOU (she says तुम, only in commands, 'who should' asks and lines where you are not the doer; no name, no family word; you say 'Mami' and आप: 'Mami, dikhaiye.' | 'मामी, दिखाइए।' | 'Let's see, Mami.', as your file has it): she has watched you at every family function doing the job nobody gave you. On Thursday she stands at the blue gate with Mama ji, her eyes on you: 'Your Mama ji says seventy. You run my list.' (5.03), then unclips the day's job list card and holds it out to you in both hands, her face in the frame (5.04). She reads your plan back once ('So. Keys with you, from tonight. Correct?'); from Friday she stops reading it back, which is the nearest she comes to thanks. She never asks how you are; she puts a tick beside your line. You are the one she tells about Nani's आप.

HER DAUGHTER, THE BRIDE (24; never drawn, named, on a card, or spoken of in a bubble beyond 'my daughter'): the reason for the list. Mami started 'Wedding list 1' the evening Mama ji sent 'December. My daughter's wedding. Everyone comes.' (1.04), and its top line that evening was 'Beti ka bag'. The daughter's own grey suitcase, packed by the daughter, is the one object that stands in for her, in one wordless panel (the comics review allows one object stand-in, one beat). Its contents are never listed or shown, and nothing in it is a gift or goods for the groom's side (rule 22).

HER OWN SIDE (chapter 5's circle, per the continuity read: her mother's Bengali family and her father's people, come for the wedding): she has known each of them all her life; her judging notes about them are a desk manager's log of queues, receipts and forms; her bubbles never name, point at or describe them (rule 36), and her notes land as often on men as on women (rule 22). This is the cast's only strand from the east, so a Bengali reader and the measure judge read chapter 5's notes for one thing alone: no Bengali stock joke (fish, sweets, 'babu', bossy mothers) anywhere (India review).
cast.year_arc: On screen she is chapter 5 only (rulebook Q11). The rest of her year happens off screen, in the city, and is written down so writers know what she brings into December. JANUARY (the opening, present day): not on screen. The evening Mama ji sends 'December. My daughter's wedding. Everyone comes.' (1.04), she starts 'Wedding list 1' on her clipboard, over the 2001 sheet, and writes 'Beti ka bag' at its top with no number. MAY (chapters 1 and 2, the night train and the ward): at her desk in the city. The morning after Nani's fall she phones the district hospital's billing counter at seven and has the papers in order before Mama ji has finished worrying; from that evening she phones Nani at eight for the BP and logs it. She decides the wedding needs a second pair of hands in Nani's town, someone who does not need things explained twice. JULY (chapter 3, the flood): sends Mummy a numbered list for the shop's flood claim; Mummy uses every line. AUGUST (chapter 4, the lane cup): nothing; the list reaches the teens. DECEMBER (chapter 5, Jadugar, her chapter), panel by panel: THURSDAY at the blue gate she arrives with 'Wedding list 23', hears Mama ji's 'Sixty guests? Make it seventy!' and says to you 'Your Mama ji says seventy. You run my list.' (5.03); she unclips the day's job list card and holds it out to you, keeping the clipboard (5.04): the woman who never lets go of a list hands you the day's on day one, because she trusts you. THURSDAY NIGHT in Nani's kitchen (proposed, the same for every pick, away from any decision about guests or seats): 'Mummy ji still says "Do sit." Like a guest.' FRIDAY MORNING (5.13, with Mama ji's file): beside him at the steaming kettle, the tent up, she ticks the day's first line and gives him the credit: 'Every cook was booked. Yours came.' FRIDAY, ELEVEN AT NIGHT (proposed, wordless, between 5.19 and 5.20): on the low step of the blue gate, one sandal off, she lifts list 24 and smooths the yellowed sheet beneath it once before she writes (the comics review's one wordless panel of her own past). SATURDAY, the wedding day, in the cream sari with the indigo squares, among empty chairs before the guests come: 'Today, nothing new goes on the list.' (5.20, revised, no guest figures). SATURDAY EVENING (proposed, wordless, after the last decision and before the outcomes): her daughter's grey suitcase stands packed and shut by the gate; Mami beside it lowers the clipboard to her waist, holds the pen above its top line, and does not write; her eyes shut. The one time she cries all week, and nobody sees. THE LAST NIGHT (proposed, her own two-person panel after 5.28, which stays Nani's): the clipboard lies face down on the table; Nani holds out the first slice on a steel plate; Mami bends from the hips to take it and laughs, surprised: 'Well. That wasn't on my list.' She does not sit back (that is Mummy's December beat). Her change across the week: from the one who holds every list, to the one who hands you the day's list on day one, to the one who puts the clipboard face down, and, if Tinku's writer takes it, hands Tinku her pen. WHERE SHE APPEARS: chapter 5 only, in the Jadugar look, plus her present-day face chip on every bubble and judging note; panels 5.03, 5.04, 5.13 and 5.20 now, and four proposed (Thursday kitchen, Friday gate step, the suitcase, the first slice), two of them wordless; five spoken lines (one revised, four new or moved), 37 counted English words, each line within the 10-word cap; the Thursday kitchen line (9 words) can move to the writers' ear if the chapter's word budget is short. A voice, never the asker, never on a card. THE NEXT TAKE: if rulebook Q11 lets the household speak in every chapter, she is the chapter voice most worth keeping.

voice.register: Medium and even, in two voices, and the switch between them is her tell. THE DESK VOICE is for jobs, the list, vendors and strangers. Its lead shape is the readback: 'So.' | 'तो।' | 'Toh.', then one whole sentence that hands your own plan back to you, then 'Correct?' | 'सही?' | 'Sahi?', and she waits for the answer. Its second shape is the status pair: a thing, its status, a full stop, then the next pair ('Keys, pending. Envelopes, done.'; in Hindi mode with no comma, 'टेंट लग गया। रसोइया अभी बाक़ी।'). The item is named, never numbered: no ordinals, no counts, no prices, no clock times. THE HOME VOICE takes over the moment a family feeling arrives (a goodbye, a cousin's news, her husband worried, a report): the statuses stop, and she speaks short whole sentences of plain, warm Hindi with their hai or hoon ('Fikr mat karo. Mummy ji ka BP normal hai.', 'Mujhe yakeen hai.', 'Ab kya karna hai?'). A city manager talks in statuses at the desk and stops at home, and so does she, which is why the desk voice is funny when she turns it on her husband and used in no tender moment. A bubble runs 4 to 10 words, most often 6 to 9; usually one bubble, at most two. Crisp, unhurried and never raised: no exclamation mark in any bubble, 'Congratulations.' and 'Ish.' included, and never the shout (the chapter's shout is Mama ji's). The same pace in a crisis as at tea, which is why people calm down near her. Firm with vendors, polite with elders, sly with her husband. Talked over, she raises the pen, point up, says nothing, and finishes when the room is quiet. When cross she goes slower, turns the clipboard round to face the person, reads the line aloud from it ('Yahan likha hai.') and closes with an icy 'Thank you' to a vendor, or a flat 'Correct?' to family. Apart from the cast: not Mummy's comma lists of jobs and people with no status ('Aur kuch?') or her home things in counter English; not Mausa ji's subjectless verdicts on things; not Captain sahab's call then reason; not Papa's whole sentences with a time in them; not Nani's jobs handed to 'koi'; not Mama ji's run-ons and 'Oho!'. A script can count it: about half her lines carry a status word or end on 'Correct?', and every one of those is about a job, a list or a vendor; her family feeling lines carry none, and most of them have hai or hoon; no line carries an ordinal, a figure or '!'.
voice.mix: City whole-clause switching, the younger urban pattern in the realism notes (the Dehradun code-switching study): she switches at the full stop, a whole Hindi clause and then a whole English one, or the other way round ('Meri shaadi ki bhi list thi. Still on file.'). Inside a Hindi clause the desk crosses over in two ways: its nouns (list, item, form, file, claim, receipt, balance, payment) and, as with most city people under fifty, an office English verb with kar or ho ('List ab tum handle karo.', 'Claim main file karti hoon.', 'Receipt pe sign kar dijiye.', 'Bahut help ho gayi.'). Her English verbs come from the office (file, sign, check, handle, note), never from the home: Mummy turns home things into counter English ('MCB check karo', 'mains off karo'), and Mama ji talks logistics. Her English statuses in Hinglish: done, pending, not known, safe, approved, in progress, closed, still on file, all clear, correct. In Hindi mode a status becomes the everyday Hindi a city office speaks (हो गया, लग गया, बाक़ी, पता नहीं, मंज़ूर, चालू, बंद, ठीक, फ़ाइल में), with पेंडिंग and स्टेटस kept only for her two dry jokes, and with no comma between a Hindi subject and its verb, because spoken Hindi does not pause there; a colon comes only before a label with no verb ('स्टेटस: मेहमान।', 'तुम्हारे मामा जी: अब भी पेंडिंग।'). The commas stay in Hinglish and English pairs. Her Hindi carries people, food, rooms and elders, and the town's everyday Urdu-rooted words sit in it as they do in anyone's (fikr, zaroor, yakeen). 'Thank you' and 'Sorry' are the counter's words, English in every mode (थैंक यू, सॉरी), for vendors and strangers only; with family her sorry is Hindi ('मुझसे छूट गया') and her thanks is plain ('बहुत मदद हो गई'). Polite Hindi to every elder and every vendor (आप, -इए). One Bengali word, her mother's: the exclamation 'Ish.' Nothing else from Bengali, and never a spelled accent. Apart from Mama ji, who leads with fast English and runs his clauses together on 'aur haan', she is clause by clause, each one closed, and her English is the desk's, never logistics talk, slang or 'Don't worry'.
tics: THE READBACK, her lead tic, for jobs and plans: 'So.', your plan in one whole sentence, 'Correct?', and she waits: 'So. Keys with you, from tonight. Correct?' | 'तो। चाबियाँ आज रात से तुम्हारे पास। सही?' | 'Toh. Chaabiyan tumhare paas, aaj raat se. Sahi?'. From Friday she stops reading your plan back to you, and that is her deepest thank-you, the one she never says.

THE STATUS PAIR, for the list and for vendors: thing, comma, status, full stop: 'Tent, done. Cook, pending. Keys, not known.' In Hindi mode the comma goes and the status is everyday Hindi: 'टेंट लग गया। रसोइया अभी बाक़ी।' She names the item, never its place on the list.

THE SWITCH HOME: when a family feeling arrives, the desk finishes its line and plain Hindi, most often with hai or hoon, says the thing that matters: 'Ticket, tiffin, done. Agli baar kab?'; 'Congratulations. Joining kab se? Somvaar? Bahut achha.' No status, file, tick or 'Correct?' in a goodbye, a congratulation, comfort or a report.
She files herself as a joke, never as a feeling. Asked how she is: 'Main? Sab clear hai.' | 'मैं? सब ठीक है।' | 'Me? All clear.' Hurt, said once and dry: 'Status: mehmaan.'

Asks every vendor and helper about their children, the counter's habit and her one interest on the page that is not a list: 'Bhaiya ji, beti ka paper kaisa gaya?'. It is also, quietly, about her own daughter.

'Thank you' and 'Sorry' out loud, in English, to every vendor and stranger, even when cross: the counter's words. Never to family (Mausi teases her for saying it 'like a bill'); thanked at home, she says 'Ghar mein thank you nahin chalta.'
Thanks family in plain words, 'Bahut help ho gayi.', and her husband the everyday way, 'Maan gayi.'; at most once a chapter the pen comes down on a spoken 'Tick.'.

Sly about her husband, said as a status and to the young ones, as if he were not standing there: 'Your Mama ji: still pending.' Once a chapter at most, so it stays a joke and is not her only one: his count, his dinner and the rest get the plain line.

The house's common fillers, like anyone in it: achha, suno, arre, theek hai, chalo, chaliye, to open a line or in the middle of one ('Achha, suno. List ab tum handle karo.'). She owns none of them; her shape is what marks her.
Talked over: raises the pen, point up, says nothing, and finishes when the room is quiet. ('Ek minute' is yours, so she never says it.)
Never a rhetorical or a stacked question (those are Mausi's); every question she asks has one answer, and she waits for it.
Days of the week, never a clock time and never 'soon' as a promise: 'by Saturday', 'Thursday evening'. (At a parting she asks 'Agli baar kab?' and waits for a day.)
No exclamation mark anywhere, spoken or typed, not even for 'Ish.' or 'Congratulations.'

HER NO: 'Not on the list.' | 'लिस्ट में नहीं है।' | 'List mein nahin hai.' Turned round once, at the first slice, laughing and with no exclamation: 'That wasn't on my list.' | 'ये मेरी लिस्ट में नहीं था।' | 'Ye meri list mein nahin tha.' (None of the three carries a number.)
HER HOUSE RULE: 'Ghar mein thank you nahin chalta.' | 'घर में थैंक यू नहीं चलता।' | 'No thank-yous at home.'
voice.exclamation: 'Ish.' | 'इश्श।' | 'Ish.' (kept as 'Ish.' in English mode too, as her own sound). Her mother's Bengali word, for dismay and sympathy only ('oh no', 'oh dear'): the power cut, a child's fever, a spilt glass, a dropped tray. Never for good news, a laugh or a happy surprise: Hindi-mode players know the coy 'इश्श' of old Hindi films, and on a laugh it would read as that, so at the first slice she just laughs and says the line, and good news gets her home voice. Said flat and low, closed with a full stop, never with '!', never with a giggle or a hand to the mouth. No religious meaning. At most once a scene. Nobody else in the cast uses it, and it leans to one region on purpose, her mother's. Two reader checks: a Bengali reader confirms the sense; a Hindi-first reader confirms it is not heard as ईश ('lord', a word rule 3 bans; ईश has a long ई and one श, इश्श a short इ and a doubled श) and that, kept to dismay, it does not read as the filmi coy sound. Many Hindi-first players may hear the coy 'इश्श' whatever the context, so the fallback for Hindi mode is written and ready, and Hindi mode keeps 'इश्श' only if the Hindi-first reader clears it. 'Ish' stays in Hinglish and English, where the Bengali sense survives. In Hindi mode 'अजीब।' takes its place where the dismay is at a thing ('अजीब। बत्ती चली गई।'); where it is sympathy for a person, Hindi mode drops the sound and opens on the care ('बच्चे का बुख़ार उतरा, भैया जी?', 'आस्तीन गीली हुई? कागज़ मैं उठा लेती हूँ।'), since 'अजीब' said to a sick or upset child sounds like a judgement. If the Bengali reader fails it too, 'Ajeeb.' | 'Odd.' goes into the other two modes the same way. Nobody else in the cast uses 'Ajeeb'.
voice.sorry_thanks_love: SORRY, TO FAMILY: plain everyday Hindi, then the right entry at once, aloud: 'Mujhse chhoot gaya, Didi. Shanivaar likhiye.' | 'मुझसे छूट गया, दीदी। शनिवार लिखिए।' | 'I missed that, Didi. Please write Saturday.' SORRY, TO VENDORS AND STRANGERS: the counter's English word, then the fact put right: 'Sorry, Bhaiya ji, mujhse galat likh gaya. Payment Shanivaar ko.' | 'सॉरी, भैया जी, मुझसे ग़लत लिख गया। पेमेंट शनिवार को।' | 'Sorry, Bhaiya ji, I wrote it down wrong. Payment's on Saturday.' Hers is told apart from Mausi's doubled 'Sorry, sorry!' with food and Mama ji's 'Sorry, Didi, poora kasoor mera!' by its size: one plain sentence and the correction, the blame never made bigger. THANKS, GIVEN: to family, plain words, 'Bahut help ho gayi.' | 'बहुत मदद हो गई।' | 'That was a big help.' ('Badi Didi, aapke aane se bahut help ho gayi.'); to her husband, when he turns out right, the everyday 'Maan gayi.' | 'मान गई।' | 'I'll give you that.'; at most once a chapter, the pen comes down on a spoken 'Tick.'; to vendors and strangers, 'Thank you, Bhaiya ji.', English in every mode; to you, besides the words, from Friday she stops reading your plan back, and her typed lists to you lose their 'Correct?' line. THANKS, RECEIVED: from family, the real brush-off of an Indian house, where a thank-you between relatives sounds too formal: 'Ghar mein thank you nahin chalta.' | 'घर में थैंक यू नहीं चलता।' | 'No thank-yous at home.'; from a vendor, 'Thank you, Bhaiya ji.' back. CONGRATULATIONS: 'Congratulations.' in Hinglish and English, 'बधाई हो।' in Hindi mode, with a full stop, then the one practical question she cannot help ('Joining kab se?'). LOVE: plain and short at a parting, once the desk has finished its line: 'Ticket, tiffin, done. Agli baar kab?' | 'टिकट, टिफ़िन, सब रख दिया। अगली बार कब?' | 'Ticket, tiffin, done. When will you come next?', the one question she cannot help, and she waits for a day. Otherwise never in feeling words, and left open: the one line she never ticks, 'Beti ka bag', at the top of every wedding list, and the pen held over it on the wedding evening; Mama ji's item, which she always ticks first, and his hand, the only one allowed to write on her list.

Never a past or a future with you as the doer. No name, no beta, no family word; she often starts with the item, not with 'you'. habits: DEVICE: a large-screen smartphone in a plain navy-blue case, text at the normal size, kept in her bag and out only for a call (at her right ear, the pen slid into the clipboard's clip) or for the night's list. Two quick thumbs. A plain power bank for everyone else's phones. In chapter 5 her phone stays off screen, like Mama ji's.

SCRIPT: Roman letters only, in the city's Hinglish: English items and statuses, Hindi people and verbs, and the office verbs with kar ('Rooms done. Chaabiyan kiske paas?', 'Envelopes Tinku ko handover karo'). Never Devanagari, which is too slow for her. Devanagari versions are given in case the owner applies rule 65 to typed messages; they drop the comma between a thing and its status, as her spoken Hindi does. Her lines to you mark no gender ('You take over Thu evening').

FORMAT: one item per line, a capitalised noun and its status symbol, with a comma before any detail ('Keys, yours ✅'). No line numbers and no digits in any message on screen: that is the typing half of the number cap. No full stops at line ends, no whole words in capitals (capitals read as shouting, realism), no exclamation mark. The first line names the list and the day ('Wedding list, Thu'). On every wedding list the second line is 'Beti ka bag', with no symbol, the only line she never gives a status; then 'Papa, trains ✅', the one item she never has to chase. Family lists end on 'Correct?'; vendor lists end on 'Thank you'.

APART FROM THE OTHERS: Papa types single facts with full stops and times, Mummy lowercase one-liners that end on a figure, Tinku lowercase stretched letters and scores, and you the lowercase colon form ('keys: sorted'), which is why her detail takes a comma, not a colon.
STATUS SYMBOLS, her only emoji: ✅ done, ⏳ pending, ❓ not known. No faces and no hands (👍 is Mummy's; the folded hands wait on the owner), no stickers.
VERSIONS: she never sends a correction; she resends the whole list with 'revised' after the day ('Wedding list, Thu, revised'), so the header carries no figure. On screen, one message card at a time.

THE THANK-YOU IN TYPE: from Friday her lists to you drop the closing 'Correct?' line. Nobody else's list ever does. To family she types no thank-you, as she says none; every vendor list ends on 'Thank you'.
TIMING: lists go out at eleven at night, after her shift and dinner; in the day she replies within the minute; if 'Correct?' has no answer, she rings.
VOICE NOTES: never sends one ('you cannot tick a voice note'); when one comes, such as Mausi's long ones, she replies with a summary list of it ending on 'Correct?'.
FORWARDS: none, ever. Her one reply to a forward: a single ✅ under Papa's good-morning flower, every morning, the only reply he gets.
CALLS: Nani is rung, never texted, every evening since May for the BP; vendors are rung first and then sent a list of what was agreed, ending 'Thank you'.
FIGURES: the monthly BP log she sends Nani's doctor is the one thing she types with figures in it, and it stays off screen.
TYPOS: none; she rereads every list before sending; autocorrect on.

ON SCREEN: single messages only, as live text on a painted blank phone or a message card (rules 30 and 40); no app look, no 'forwarded' or 'edited' label, no group chat on screen (owner, 23 Oct). The Sunday list to you is the one worth showing, early in chapter 5 if the writers have room, because it is where the player first sees the line with no status.

look.build: Tall band, with Papa and Captain sahab, and a little below Papa (the comics review's four bands replace the ten ranks, which the painter cannot keep). Slim, straight-backed, narrow-shouldered and long-waisted. The one exact gap: half a head taller than Mama ji in every panel they share, and never painted shorter. Where Papa leans forward like a man walking into a wind, she has no lean at all, a plumb line. Never frail, never broad. Shares the tall 'line' base shape with Papa, a man, so shapes are not sorted by gender (cast map).
look.face: Three features chosen to be redrawn: a long face with a firm square jaw; thin, high-arched eyebrows that rise when she reads a line she does not like (she lacks the thick straight brows of Nani's line, as the three who married in do); a wide straight mouth that presses into a line while she counts. Also high, wide cheekbones, a narrow straight nose and fine lines at the outer corners of the eyes; no lines between the brows, which the painter can turn into a forehead mark (rules review), so her age sits in the eyes, the mouth and the neck. She should read 45: not 30 and not 60 (painted ages drift young).
look.skin: South Asian features and warm brown skin, medium in tone: the tested words first, the depth word after them (rules review; flux-portrait-biases records light-brown wording coming out pale in the soft styles). Medium, the same depth as Mummy's and Mama ji's, so neither city in-law is the lightest adult in the cast and lightness never lines up with the city, money or the bride's mother (all three reviews). The family's tones are settled once on a painted swatch strip, not in words (comics review, Mama ji's file), and every pick of her is compared with her master's swatch.
look.hair: Straight black hair cut in a jaw-length bob, parted on her left side and tucked behind both ears so the ears show, with a few grey strands at the front. A side parting, so the centre of her head shows only hair. The bob is her strongest anchor after her height: a dark, square-cut mass at jaw level that no one else in the cast has.
look.glasses_jewellery: EVERY DAY: small plain round gold earrings set close on each earlobe, and nothing else. No spectacles (the cast map keeps them to Nani and Masterji; the draft's habit of holding the list at arm's length is gone, since six files shared it). No wristwatch (Mummy's anchor; Mami reads the time off her phone). No bangles, chain or pendant in the everyday look: on a married woman the painter may turn a chain into a black-bead necklace, and her stand-up collar covers the neck. No rings, no nose stud. THE WEDDING DAY AND THE LAST NIGHT (India review, the owner's call): at her own daughter's wedding a bride's mother wears her best gold, and bare she reads as in mourning, so she wears a short necklace of plain gold links lying on her collarbone, matching plain gold drop earrings, and two plain thin gold bangles on each wrist: gold that marks neither marriage nor faith. Every neck and wrist is checked close up for black beads, glass, red or white shell. If the owner allows plain thin gold bangles every day for the married women (the question Mausi's file also asks), she wears one on each wrist all week.
outfits: EVERYDAY (the signature, every working day of the wedding week, in every look): a calf-length cream cotton kurta, straight cut, with three-quarter sleeves and a short stand-up collar buttoned at the throat, hand-printed all over with spaced deep indigo squares turned on their corners, each about two fingers wide, five or six across her front (call it 'the indigo print' in writing; never 'diamond' in a prompt); ankle-length deep indigo straight cotton trousers, showing only as a dark band between the kurta's hem and her sandals; no dupatta, which would add a second chest diagonal (Mummy's alone); a small stone-grey canvas bag on a short strap over one shoulder, hanging under her arm at her side, a short vertical line (comics review; the right shoulder is a preference to check, never what tells her apart); plain black leather sandals with a strap round the heel and no raised heel.

WINTER NIGHTS (December in Nani's town): a plain cream long-sleeved thermal top under the kurta, its cuffs showing at the wrists below the three-quarter sleeves. No jacket, cardigan or shawl: a dark layer would darken her top again at night, an open dark jacket over a light shirt is Papa's Jadugar look, a cream cardigan is Mausi's, and the shawls are Nani's and Mausa ji's.

HOME (her city flat, and Nani's house after eleven at night): an older kurta of the same cut and print, faded and soft, sleeves pushed to the elbow, loose deep indigo cotton drawstring trousers, plain grey rubber slippers; the bag off, the only time it is.

OCCASION (Saturday, the wedding day, and the last night): the costume kept, as comics keep it: a cream silk-look sari printed all over, closely, with the same deep indigo squares at the same scale, with a broad deep indigo edge along its hem and its end, so the cloth reads indigo-and-cream and never plain white; Nivi drape, the end pinned on her left shoulder and never over her head; a deep indigo blouse with elbow sleeves and a high round neck; the wedding gold (see jewellery); no bag, only the clipboard; the same black sandals, because she is on her feet sixteen hours. No red, which is the unseen bride's, and no gold edge, which on a cream sari reads as a regional festival sari. A Hindi-first reader and the owner confirm a cream-ground sari suits a bride's mother (owner question).
WORK (the city hospital's desk; never on screen in the First take): the same kind of kurta; if ever painted, no lanyard, badge or name tag, which carry letters.
look.colour_key: Key: cream with spaced deep indigo squares over deep indigo; value A LIGHT COLUMN FROM COLLAR TO CALF OVER A DARK BAND AT THE ANKLE, under a dark square-cut bob; pattern SPACED GEOMETRIC PRINT, bold enough to read as a texture at strip size; plus the clipboard tipped out at her chest. The draft's dark indigo top is turned round (comics review): it sank into Jadugar's indigo night, and under the chapter JSON's look line it would print black on black. A light column reads against either. The calf length is what keeps her apart from the other light tops, whose light block stops at the waist or hip. Nobody else wears indigo or a geometric print (Papa's are broad vertical stripes, Mama ji's a big gingham, Mausi's and Nani's flowers and leaves). PER LOOK (PROVISIONAL: chapter-5.json's look line says 'flat crimson, gold and black', the code's Jadugar STYLE says vermilion, magenta, indigo, emerald and old gold, and every colour key waits on one string per look; her value stack holds under both). NOW (master, face chip, album): cream, deep indigo squares, deep indigo trousers, a stone-grey bag. JADUGAR, chapter 5, her chapter: under the code's inks, lamplight warms the cream to warm white (never as far as old gold), the squares and trousers stay deep indigo, and she reads against the night by value; under the JSON line, cream with black squares and black trousers. Against the cream stripes of the canopy, her dark bob, her dark trousers and the brown clipboard carry her, so the strip check puts her against both the night and the canopy. The cast collision to settle on the Jadugar strip: four light tops in chapter 5 (Mama ji's cream-and-brown gingham, which reads mid-tone at strip size; Mausi's cream sari with big magenta flowers; Papa's lamp-lit cream shirt under an open charcoal jacket, though he is painted alone at the platform; and hers). Her calf length, bob and height carry her among them, and the strip proves it or the colour changes. LUGDI (no appearance planned): cream lit marigold on its lit side, squares and trousers violet-black. STATION (none planned): a light top in dark lozenges, dark trousers, the same stack as Papa's and Masterji's chapter 3 looks, told apart by the calf length. RUKAVAT (none planned): cream with teal-navy squares, teal-navy trousers. CRICKET (none planned): chalk-cream with slate-blue squares, slate-blue trousers; never cherry red, which is Captain sahab's.
look.prop: THE CLIPBOARD, carried in the writing position (comics review): braced along her left forearm, its top edge tipped out from her chest at about forty-five degrees, the pen in her right hand at it, as a ward sister carries a chart on a round. At phone size it reads as a slanted plane at the chest, not the draft's flat rectangle, which matched Papa's old list (his folder now hangs at his side, his file). Glossary row (new, in Saal Bhar's own glossary section, key 'clipboard'): 'clipboard: a plain brown hardboard writing board about the size of a page of office paper, its corners a little worn, a plain steel spring clip at the top'. Its story: handed to her on her first day at the hospital's billing counter in 1999; when the desk went over to computers she took it home, and every family job since has run off it; the clip has a little rust and she will not replace it. Rigid, brown and showing a clip, it is never confused with Papa's pale-blue folder or Tinku's thick scorebook. Painted from one reference picture (paint-refs), always blank (rule 30). ON IT, two things, each with its own row: the JOB LIST CARD on top (key 'job list card', never 'card' alone, which the need list refuses, or 'wedding card', whose old row paints a red invitation with a gold paisley edge): 'job list card: one plain cream card with a thin crimson edge and nothing printed on it, no lines and no writing'; the chapter's targets and ticks are laid on it as live text (rules review), and it is the same reference at 5.04 and 5.26. Under it, THE YELLOWED SHEET (key 'yellowed sheet'): 'yellowed sheet: one old page of soft, yellowed paper, once folded in four, its creases worn, blank'; it shows only as a pale edge under the card, and once, in the Friday night panel, when she lifts the card and smooths it. SECOND OBJECT: her pen (key 'click pen'): 'click pen: one plain steel ballpoint pen with a click top'; one only, in her right hand or slid into the clip when she stops to listen; never behind her ear (the owner caught three hands on Vikram when a pencil sat behind his ear in the fixed look and in his hand in the scene), never red (the red pen is your object). WORN, NOT HELD: the small stone-grey canvas bag on its short strap, holding the envelopes, keys and receipts (key 'canvas shoulder bag'): 'canvas shoulder bag: a small rectangular bag of plain stone-grey canvas with no markings, on a short strap over one shoulder, hanging under the arm'; never 'sling' in a prompt (an arm sling). A close-up detail, not a strip anchor. THE ONE OBJECT THAT STANDS IN FOR HER DAUGHTER, one beat only: the grey suitcase (key 'grey suitcase'): 'grey suitcase: a plain dark grey hard suitcase with no markings, shut, standing upright'. Her phone, in a plain navy-blue case, stays in the bag in chapter 5.
look.silhouette: STRIP: a tall plumb line with a dark square-cut bob on top, a light column from collar to calf over a dark band at the ankle, and a slanted plane held out at the chest with a short pen stroke at it: a woman writing on a board as she walks. In four strokes: a tall vertical, a dark square at the head, a light column to the calf, a slant at the chest. The bag is a short vertical line at her side, a detail rather than an anchor. On the wedding night the sari's end over her left shoulder gives her one diagonal, as every sari does. Beside Mama ji, round and mid-stride, she is the straight line beside the circle; beside Papa, plumb against his lean, a calf-length column against his short shirt, a board at the chest against a folder at the side. FAR SPEC (for when she is small and painted from words, comics review): 'a tall upright woman with a dark jaw-length bob, a long light kurta to the calf over dark trousers, a board held out at her chest'; checked only for the shape and the two value blocks.
look.shoes: Plain black leather sandals with a strap round the heel and no raised heel, every day of the wedding week and on the wedding night too: she is on her feet sixteen hours and has never worn a heel to a family function. Plain grey rubber slippers at home. No logos or lettering on either.

posture.stance: Bolt upright, weight even on both feet, feet a hand apart and parallel, chin level, shoulders down. The clipboard braced along her left forearm and tipped out from her chest, her right hand at it with the pen, as if mid-line on a round; when she is only listening, the pen goes into the clip and her right hand drops to her side. She never leans on a wall, a pole or a person, and never puts a hand on her hip. Half a head taller than her husband, she does not stoop to hide it.
posture.sitting: She does not take a chair while there are guests to come: chairs are on the list, and they are for guests. She perches on the nearest hard thing that is not a guest's chair, the gate step, the edge of a table, a stack of plastic chairs, one knee crossed over the other, the clipboard on her top knee and the pen moving. (The draft's front-edge perch is gone: eight files shared it, comics review.) On Friday at eleven at night, on the low step of the blue gate with one sandal off, still writing. At the first slice she does not sit at all: she bends from the hips to Nani seated, the clipboard face down on the table beside her. Sitting back in a chair at last is Mummy's December beat, not hers.
posture.walk: Quick, short, even steps in a straight line down the middle of the lane, her head turning left and right as she passes things on the list, the way a ward round moves; she stops dead, writes one line and walks on. She never runs and never hurries (Mama ji hurries). The clipboard stays tipped out on her forearm; the bag stays still at her side.
gestures: THE CLICK: before she speaks, her right thumb clicks the top of her pen once. (Tinku taps her pencil twice and Papa taps twice, so Mami never taps.)
THE TICK: one short, hard downward stroke of the pen on the list, her chin dipping with it; it is her 'Tick.' with or without the word.
THE CLIP: when she stops to listen or takes a call, she slides the pen into the clipboard's steel clip, so there is only ever one pen in the picture and one hand free.
THE RAISED PEN: pen held up, point to the sky, at shoulder height, when someone talks over her; she says only the item's place ('Three.') and waits.
DOWN THE LIST: she counts by running the pen's point down the card, line by line, never on her fingers (Nani counts with one finger, Tinku shows totals with an open hand).
THE TURN: when cross, she turns the clipboard round to face the other person and reads from it.
THE TOP LINE: before she writes anything new, the pen's point rests a moment on the top line, the one with no status, then moves down. Nobody notices but the player.
IDLE HANDS: the left forearm stays under the clipboard; the right hand turns the pen end over end once, then stops.
expressions: NEUTRAL: level gaze, the mouth a straight line, the clipboard tipped out on her forearm, the pen at it, weight even.
PLEASED: one short nod and the tick; the corners of her mouth press in rather than up; no grin.
WORRIED: the arched eyebrows lift, she reads the list again from the top, the pen's point moving faster down the lines; her feet do not move.

CROSS: very still; the pen stops; she turns the clipboard round to face the other person and reads from it in a slow even voice ('It's written here.'); her eyebrows go level. Never a raised voice, never hands on hips.

LAUGHING (rare, at your Mama ji, at herself, and once at the first slice): a short surprised laugh with her head tipped back, the clipboard lowered to her waist for one beat, then back to her forearm.
TIRED (Friday, eleven at night): on the gate step, one sandal off, her shoulders down for once, the clipboard on her knee, smoothing the yellowed sheet before she writes.

GRIEF (the suitcase, Saturday evening): the clipboard lowered to her waist in her left hand, the pen held still above its top line in her right, her eyes shut and her mouth pressed into a line. Alone; nobody comforts her; over in one panel; never played as a joke or as weakness.

test_lines.moment: 1. The lights go out in the middle of dinner. (To you, at the table, while Mama ji goes on eating in the dark; the joke is the picture's, so she says only the plain line. Tests her exclamation at its right size, dismay, and her crisis pace, the same as at tea: the quietest line at the table, and no torch, which five others reach for. In Hindi no comma sits between a subject and its verb. Hindi fallback, ready: 'अजीब। बत्ती चली गई।')
test_lines.en: Ish. The power's gone.
test_lines.hinglish: Ish. Light chali gayi.
test_lines.hi: इश्श। बत्ती चली गई।

test_lines.moment: 2. Someone everyone was waiting for arrives two hours late. (To the cook, the clipboard turned round to face him. Her anger: slower, read from the list, polite to a vendor to the end and closed with her icy counter thanks. No figure: the lateness is told by the meal, not the hours.)
test_lines.en: It's written here, Bhaiya ji: lunch. It's teatime. Thank you.
test_lines.hinglish: Bhaiya ji, yahan likha hai: lunch. Ab chai. Thank you.
test_lines.hi: भैया जी, यहाँ लिखा है: लंच। अब चाय। थैंक यू।

test_lines.moment: 3. A cousin phones to say they have got their first job. (To the cousin, on the line. The home voice: a plain congratulation, the one practical question she cannot help, the answer said back, and a warm word. The cousin's gender stays open: the joining carries the grammar.)
test_lines.en: Congratulations. When's the joining? Monday? Very good.
test_lines.hinglish: Congratulations. Joining kab se? Somvaar? Bahut achha.
test_lines.hi: बधाई हो। जॉइनिंग कब से? सोमवार? बहुत अच्छा।

test_lines.moment: 4. The tea someone has just made has far too much sugar in it. (To Mama ji, who made it, as she hands the cup back. A polite no in her own words, and his favourite word, extra, handed back to him.)
test_lines.en: Sugar, extra. Like your guest list. Not on mine.
test_lines.hinglish: Cheeni, extra. Tumhari guest list jaisi. Meri list mein nahin.
test_lines.hi: चीनी, एक्स्ट्रा। तुम्हारी गेस्ट लिस्ट जैसी। मेरी लिस्ट में नहीं।

test_lines.moment: 5. In front of the family, someone shows that they had a fact wrong. (She is the one who had it wrong: the cook moved to Saturday, she missed it and told everyone Friday. To Mummy, in front of the family. Her sorry in plain everyday Hindi, then the right entry at once.)
test_lines.en: I missed that, Didi. Please write Saturday.
test_lines.hinglish: Mujhse chhoot gaya, Didi. Shanivaar likhiye.
test_lines.hi: मुझसे छूट गया, दीदी। शनिवार लिखिए।

test_lines.moment: 6. Someone they love is leaving, and they say goodbye on a railway platform. (To the one leaving, at the coach door. The desk finishes its line, then the home voice asks the one question she cannot help, and she waits for a day as the train moves. No status in the goodbye. Tinku's line at the same door opens 'Jaldi aana, yaar.', so hers shares none of its words. The question has no verb, so it holds if the one leaving is you.)
test_lines.en: Ticket, tiffin, done. When will you come next?
test_lines.hinglish: Ticket, tiffin, done. Agli baar kab?
test_lines.hi: टिकट, टिफ़िन, सब रख दिया। अगली बार कब?

test_lines.moment: 7. Someone thanks them for something they did. (To anyone in the family who thanks her, you included. Thanks received: the everyday brush-off of an Indian house, where a thank-you between relatives sounds too formal, and the pen goes back to the list.)
test_lines.en: No thank-yous at home.
test_lines.hinglish: Ghar mein thank you nahin chalta.
test_lines.hi: घर में थैंक यू नहीं चलता।

test_lines.moment: 8. A neighbour passes on a rumour that the corner sweet shop is closing. (To the neighbour who brought it. She judges the talk, never the shop or the person, and checks at the source the way the desk does, a notice on the shop, never proof from the teller. Rule 22 guard: never used in a chapter that holds a report twin. She does not open on Closing?, which three others do.)
test_lines.en: Is it? Status not known. Any notice on the shop?
test_lines.hinglish: Achha? Status not known. Dukaan pe koi notice hai?
test_lines.hi: अच्छा? अभी पता नहीं। दुकान पर कोई नोटिस लगा है?

test_lines.moment: 9. Heavy rain floods the lane outside the house. (To Mummy. Her worry comes out as the insurance claim, her own desk's work and the July list Mummy used line by line, with an office verb on kar.)
test_lines.en: Didi, bills in plastic. Photos, definitely. I'll file the claim.
test_lines.hinglish: Didi, bill plastic mein, photo zaroor. Claim main file karti hoon.
test_lines.hi: दीदी, बिल प्लास्टिक में, फ़ोटो ज़रूर। क्लेम मैं भरती हूँ।

test_lines.moment: 10. Someone asks them how they are. (Asked by the tent man. She files herself as a joke, with no figure, and turns at once to his child, which is quietly about her own.)
test_lines.en: Me? All clear. Did your daughter's result come out, Bhaiya ji?
test_lines.hinglish: Main? Sab clear hai. Aapki beti ka result aaya, Bhaiya ji?
test_lines.hi: मैं? सब ठीक है। आपकी बेटी का रिज़ल्ट आया, भैया जी?

test_lines.moment: 11. A child knocks a glass of water across the table. (To the child, at the same pace as tea. A home moment, so no status pair: the child first, her dismay at its gentlest and the sleeve asked about, then the papers, which she picks up herself, said with its hoon. Hindi fallback, ready: 'आस्तीन गीली हुई? कागज़ मैं उठा लेती हूँ।', with no sound, since 'अजीब' to a child would sound like a scolding.)
test_lines.en: Ish. Did your sleeve get wet? I'll get the papers.
test_lines.hinglish: Ish. Aasteen geeli hui? Papers main utha leti hoon.
test_lines.hi: इश्श। आस्तीन गीली हुई? कागज़ मैं उठा लेती हूँ।

test_lines.moment: 12. A phone call brings good news. (To the room, after the call. Joy in the home voice, with no exclamation, since hers is kept for dismay, and her list turned to joy: the good news goes in at the very top.)
test_lines.en: That's wonderful news. It goes right at the top.
test_lines.hinglish: Bahut achhi baat hai. Isko sabse upar likhti hoon.
test_lines.hi: बहुत अच्छी बात है। इसे सबसे ऊपर लिखती हूँ।

The desk shapes (status pair, readback, 'Correct?', 'Tick') are for jobs, lists and vendors; a family feeling gets plain warm Hindi. Test 3 is the reader's line, 'Congratulations. Joining kab se? Somvaar? Bahut achha.' | 'बधाई हो। जॉइनिंग कब से? सोमवार? बहुत अच्छा।' | 'Congratulations. When's the joining? Monday? Very good.' (English 'Joining when?' made natural). Test 6 keeps the desk's 'Ticket, tiffin, done.' and its Hindi 'टिकट, टिफ़िन, सब रख दिया।', so no comma sits before the verb; its home half is now 'Agli baar kab?' (final polish, below). 'Your file: open. Always.' and 'Naukri, done. Tick.' are struck, and the never list now bars the desk voice from goodbyes, congratulations, comfort and reports.

HINDI COMMAS (real-India note and Hindi note 4): no comma between a Hindi subject and its verb anywhere ('बत्ती चली गई', 'टेंट लग गया', 'रसोइया अभी बाक़ी', 'लिफ़ाफ़े अब भी बाक़ी', 'चाबियाँ तुम्हारे पास' in type too). The two notes differed (a colon, or nothing); both are met: nothing before a verb, as spoken Hindi says it, and her colon only before a label with no verb ('स्टेटस: मेहमान', 'तुम्हारे मामा जी: अब भी पेंडिंग'). Commas stay in Hinglish and English, as the note asked.

RULE 66 ON LINES TO YOU: every Hindi line to you is a command, a subjunctive ask, a verbless status or a line whose ending agrees with a thing. The checker will flag some, and a native reader clears each: 'बत्ती चली गई' and 'Light chali gayi' (बत्ती), 'टेंट लग गया', 'काम हो गया', 'कहती हैं' (Nani), 'रखी है' (लिस्ट), 'नया नहीं' (कुछ), 'सब रख दिया' (ने past, agrees with सब), 'अगली बार कब?' Test 12 is to the room, and 'likhti hoon' is her own verb.

ALL THREE MODES WITHIN THE CAP: every bubble is at most 10 counted words (names and kinship names not counted, rule 62), checked with voice_check.py on a copy of the voice folder; the longer runs (the temper line and the comfort line) are two bubbles each; 5.03 is one bubble since the final polish. No religious word, no caste word (रसोइया, never हलवाई), no brand, British spelling, no em or en dashes, no exclamation mark in any of her lines.

FINAL POLISH, THE REPORT LINE (Hindi and rules note, rule 22 across files): 'Mujhe yakeen hai. Bolo, kya likhoon?' raised a pen straight after a report, which can read as wanting it on paper, and the player's file fences writing and proof words from a report beat as Tinku's bans 'Kitaab mein.'. The belief stays first and the list habit turns to action: 'Mujhe yakeen hai. Bolo, ab kya karna hai?' | 'मुझे यक़ीन है। बोलो, अब क्या करना है?' | 'I believe you. Tell me, what do we do now?' FINAL POLISH, TEST 11 (real-India note): 'Papers, safe. Glass, safe. Tumhari aasteen geeli hai?' put the desk voice into a home moment and checked the child after the papers, which read cold on the page. The child comes first now: 'Ish. Aasteen geeli hui? Papers main utha leti hoon.' | 'इश्श। आस्तीन गीली हुई? कागज़ मैं उठा लेती हूँ।' | 'Ish. Did your sleeve get wet? I'll get the papers.' (9, 9 and 10 counted).

FINAL POLISH, 'ISH' IN HINDI MODE (real-India note): many Hindi-first players may hear the coy filmi 'इश्श' whatever the context, so the fallback is written out and ready in the exclamation field and in tests 1 and 11: Hindi mode keeps 'इश्श' only if the Hindi-first reader clears it; otherwise 'अजीब।' where the dismay is at a thing (the power cut), and no sound at all where it is sympathy for a person (the cook's child's fever, the wet sleeve), since 'अजीब' to an upset child reads as a judgement. Her essence, want, fear and contradiction are unchanged.

cast.name: You (the player, a voice only)
cast.role: The protagonist of Saal Bhar, Retake's story mode: the grown-up child of the house, aged 22 to 30, whom the whole family phones. A voice only: never painted, never named, no gender, caste or religion (rules 7 and 8; owner answer 2 of 25 Oct). Never an asker, never on a card, never a judging voice; the one each chapter's asker hands the work to. Label 'You' | 'आप'; the screen reader hears 'You:' | 'आप:' (bubble spec). Round in the story's sense (your year changes, and it pays off with you), but open by design: rich in relationships and nearly empty of self-description, and with no clock of your own (when you sleep, when you reply, where you are at nine), so any of the six players can stand in your place, Shruti on her 9 am bus and Farida on night shifts included (the India review). Who would say 'I know this person': all six (the review: being the grown-up child everyone phones works for every player, the 61-year-old included).
