cast.essence: The family's switchboard. Every call comes to you, and you answer each person in their own language: railway words to Papa, shop words to Mummy, cricket words to Tinku, 'sorted' to Mama ji, plain Hindi to Nani. You ask to see before anything, you put someone else first, and you close each job with one word. You are on everyone's list as the one who does it, and nobody asks how you are, until Nani counts heads in the album and counts you last.
cast.backstory: You grew up in the household's home in the junction town, in a lane off the station road, where Mummy's shutter and Papa's parcel office face each other across one platform. As a child you spent summers in Nani's front-room grocery in her own town, reading her bills and letters aloud, which is how you became her plain-truth person. At eight Mummy taught you to count change at her counter, and you are still the only one besides her who counts the drawer at closing (Mummy's file). On every trip Papa let you hold the tickets, and you never lost one (Papa's file). You did your Class 1 to 5 sums in Mausi's front-room tuition class, and she still calls you her pupil (Mausi's file). Masterji mended your school bag strap for nothing and still asks after it (Masterji's file). Captain sahab taught you, like every child in the lane, to hold the bat straight; you were the child who swung across the line, the one shot he says he never cured, and he still says 'Front foot.' when you pass (Captain sahab's file). Somewhere along the way, because you always picked up, you became the number the family rings first: Mama ji rings you, not his sister; Mausi rings you for the train times; and Tinku keeps a secret tally of how many times the family called you this year (Tinku's file). What fills your working day, where you studied, whether you sleep under the household's roof every night of the year, when you go to bed and when you answer, what you earn and whom you love are never said on screen or in any line, so each player brings their own. When a chapter needs you home for days, one plain line brings you ('Two days off. Saturday's shutter.'), never a job title. Nobody in the story asks when you will marry, comments on your looks, or tells you what to wear.
cast.want_fear_contradiction: WANTS THIS YEAR (the story's want for you; what the player wants for themselves stays their own): everyone to Nani's eightieth in May and through the year, with nobody left off a list. WHAT EACH OF THEM WANTS FROM YOU (the method notes: the protagonist is never drawn, so each person is partly defined by what they want from you): Nani, the plain truth and someone to hold her work when she cannot; Mummy, half the phone calls, asked for with a pen laid down and never in words; Papa, to be the one who never needs reminding; Mama ji, to hear 'Sorted, Mama ji'; Tinku, to be treated as an equal; Mausi, your news first-hand, not through Mummy; Mausa ji, that you sleep while he sits up; Masterji, a listener who does not walk off; Captain sahab, a straight bat and a fair pick; Mami, a second pair of hands she need not explain things to twice. WANTS UNDERNEATH (never said; shown once, in the album): to be counted, once, as one of 'everyone' rather than as the one doing the counting. FEARS: the one person left off the list. Every decision in the year leaves someone out, so this fear is the year's own question, and the game never answers it for you. CONTRADICTION: everyone calls you, but nobody asks how you are, or waits for the answer when they do. This is something the family does to you, not a habit of yours: you do not dodge the question (that was the draft's tic, and it doubled Tinku's, who answers questions about herself with somebody else's score; comics review), so the stand-in stays open for each player. It shows the same way every time: every call to you is about someone else. Mama ji's worry list names everyone and never you, Mummy assigns, Papa checks, Mami puts a tick beside your line, and Mausi, the one who does ask, asks three things at once and talks over your one-word answer. No line of yours says how you are, because nobody stops to hear it. It turns once, in the album, when Nani counts heads round the table and counts you last ('Aur tum.' | 'और तुम।' | 'And you.'), the first time anyone asks and waits, and you say the only line of the year about yourself ('Nani, main bhi.', a proposal).
relationships: NANI (you say 'Nani' and आप with -इए, in plain everyday Hindi; you call her or send a voice note, never a text, because she speaks to her phone rather than typing). History: summers in her front-room grocery, reading her bills and letters aloud; you are her plain-truth person, the one she wants holding her work. Friction: she hands you the job and then tells you how to run it (Nani's file), and she wants the plain truth from you but will not give it about her own pain; on the ward night you ask it back ('Nani, the pain? The plain truth.'). Tenderness: at her door in May she counts the household with one finger and stops, because you are never painted and so never counted; in the album she counts you last (Nani's file). She says तुम to you only in rule 66 shapes and uses no family word for you (rulebook Q7: 'beta' stays out). Her idiom you hand back: 'sab' (everyone). Her ward-night hand-over: her folder's back page lies on the bed tray, turned towards you. Her file's line is 'Meri gali, tumhari list.'; this file proposes her own weighing words instead, 'Meri gali. Taraazu tumhara.' | 'मेरी गली। तराज़ू तुम्हारा।' | 'My lane. The scales are yours.', so that 'list' stays Mami's word (comics review) and Nani keeps her grocer's scale (her file owns तराज़ू). Rule 66: गली and तुम्हारा end sentences and are caught by check 3; one is a noun and the other agrees with तराज़ू, so a native reader clears both. Greeting: you greet her by name; her palm on the head (the India review's greeting for an elder of eighty) is for painted people only, Mama ji in December, never reaching towards you.

MUMMY (you say 'Mummy' and आप with -इए, exactly as to Papa, so the household does not carry the pattern of honorific speech to the father and familiar speech to the mother, realism notes [6]). History: she taught you to count change at eight, and you count the drawer with her at closing; when you count it right she says 'Ek rupaya kam nahin.', the most she praises anyone (Mummy's file). Friction: she never asks, she assigns, and she answers 'How are you?' with a price. Tenderness: in January you ask for the shop's red 'paid' pen ('Mummy, pen dijiye.') and she lays it down by the calendar, turned towards you, her way of asking you to take half the calls; in the album she lays the spare shop key on the table, turned towards you, and says nothing (Mummy's file). She says तुम to you, and आप and 'ji' only when she is cross (Mummy's file). Typing: you text 'Done' and send her own thumbs-up back to her. Her idiom you hand back: the shutter ('Next monsoon, sandbags first.'). Her flood hand-over (3.03) is her file's 'Hands for the week. The list is yours.'; this file proposes 'Pen tumhara. Shanivaar bhi.' | 'पेन तुम्हारा। शनिवार भी।' | 'The pen's yours. Saturday too.', which ties July to January, keeps 'list' Mami's (comics review) and fits your two days home (India review). Rule 66: तुम्हारा agrees with पेन and भी is a particle; both are caught by check 3 and cleared.

PAPA (you say 'Ji Papa' and आप). History: you held the tickets on every trip as a child and never lost one (Papa's file). Friction: he checks twice what you have already done (your PNR, your platform). Tenderness: he books you the lower berth; in May, his phone dead, he lays his list on the lower berth, turned to face you, and takes his hand away ('My battery has died. Tonight, you are in charge.'), the first list he has ever let go of; from then on he buys folders in pairs and leaves the second copy where you will find it (Papa's file). He texts 'Reached?' after every journey you make without him and means 'I missed you'; you copy his full stops back, so he never reads you as cross, and you answer his good-morning flower every morning. His idiom you hand back: keeping time, without a figure, since the figures are his ('Even the battery kept time, Papa.').

MAMA JI (you say 'Mama ji' and आप). History: he rings you, not his sister, when something has to be done in Nani's town; you are his eyes there. Friction: he makes every number bigger and leaves the how to you; his worry lists name everyone and never ask how you are, because you are the one he is asking (Mama ji's file). Tenderness: in May, when he is the son who is not there, your answer at eight is how he is there, and 'Mama ji, sorted.' | 'मामा जी, सब सेट है।' is the sentence he most wants to hear. He hands you the wedding week through Mami, whose hands may reach towards you, because household hands never do (his file; bible section 4). In December he introduces you to guests by your job: 'In-charge se milo!' | 'इंचार्ज से मिलो!' | 'Meet the in-charge!' (his file). Typing: one message back, in English, where he sends five.

TINKU (you say 'Tinku' or 'scorer', Nani's word for her, and तुम with -ओ commands; never तू, which sounds rude in much of the north, realism notes [5]). History: your younger sister, one to nine years younger, and your rival for being the one everyone calls. Friction: Mama ji calls you, not her, and she keeps a secret tally of how many times the family called you this year (Tinku's file). Tenderness: you are the only one who names her habit out loud, gently ('Scorer, write your own score too.'); on cup day she lays her open scorebook on the table, turned towards you, and hands you the decisions to see what you do with them ('Two targets. Today, your call.'); that night she sends the course form she has kept since March; in December you are the first person she tells about her letter, before Mummy (Tinku's file). She says तुम to you, only in rule 66 shapes (her file leaves तुम or आप to the Hindi-first readers), and uses no address word for you, or 'oye'; never bhai, bro, didi or bhaiya (rule 8). Typing: lowercase both ways, a drawn-object sticker, 'lol'. Her idiom you hand back: her own one word of praise, 'Not out' (her file), never 'Sau mein sau', which is now Mausi's tease.

MAUSI, chapter 1's voice (you say 'Mausi' and आप with -इए). History: Mummy's elder sister, and your old tuition teacher; she still calls you her pupil. Friction: she hears your news only through Mummy, so she asks for it straight, three questions at once, and talks over your answer (Mausi's file); you give one answer for all three ('Haan ji, Mausi.') and let her run on. Tenderness: she says out loud that she missed you the moment she sees you ('Haaye! Bahut yaad aayi.', her file), remembers word for word what you said a year ago, and keeps the place beside her for you. On the train she holds out the berth chart to you with her face in the frame (bible section 4), one of the year's two held-out beats; her food is set down on the berth, never held out. She never touches you (rule 7). Typing: she sends two-minute voice notes; you answer in one short typed line.

MAUSA JI, chapter 2's voice (you say 'Mausa ji' and आप with -इए). History: the retired lineman who has fixed Nani's wiring for thirty years. Friction: when you try to thank him he leaves the room, and when you offer to take the night chair he says 'Nahin. So jao.' (Mausa ji's file). Tenderness: he keeps the chairs outside the ward so you can sleep and never mentions it, sets half of every sweet lime he peels down beside you, and texts you 'So jao.' from the corridor; you share his silence, the one person you never have to answer. In December he carries a stack of chairs to where you are, sets it down and steps back, waiting (his file); the stack stays inside the panel, never carried out of the bottom edge.

MASTERJI, chapter 3's voice (you say 'Masterji' and आप with -इए). History: he has known you since you could walk, and mended your school bag strap for nothing. Friction: in the flood his talk costs time nobody has. Tenderness: you are the listener who stays: on the Saturday morning he sets a tumbler of tea on the step beside you and talks cloth, mud and weather; he tells you the weather before Mummy. Once, teasing, he says 'अब तो आप इंचार्ज हैं।' (Masterji's file). His idiom you hand back: a measurement ('Masterji, measurements for the mud?'). His file has him hold the tea out; this file asks for the tumbler set down on the step (comics review: one giving gesture each, mostly onto surfaces), and his tape stays round his neck, never running out of the frame.

CAPTAIN SAHAB, chapter 4's voice (you say 'Captain sahab' and आप). History: he taught you, like every child in the lane, to hold the bat straight, and you were the child who swung across the line (Captain sahab's file). Friction: on cup day he watches whether you pick a side the way he would. Tenderness: when you come home he says your best score on the lane to the run, never your marks, your job or your plans (his file). Lines to a group that includes him use the polite plural ('पहले सब पानी पी लें।', the continuity fix for 4.14). His idiom you hand back: a cricket call, once, never mocking. His ball stays in his own hand: never lobbed towards you, since a catch would need your hands.

MAMI, chapter 5's voice (you say 'Mami' and आप with -इए). History: she has watched you at every family function doing the job nobody gave you. Friction: she is the only one who runs things tighter than you; she reads your plan back once ('So. Keys with you, from nine. Correct?') and from Friday stops reading it back, which is the nearest she comes to thanks (Mami's file). Tenderness: at 5.04 she holds her clipboard out to you, her eyes on you and Mama ji behind her ('Your Mama ji says seventy. You run my list.'), the second of the year's two held-out beats; she never asks how you are, she puts a tick beside your line. Your reply puts her name first in Hindi ('मामी, दिखाइए।'), so the sentence does not end on -ी; her file's 'दिखाइए, मामी।' should follow. Typing: her numbered lists with ticks come at eleven at night; you answer in your own colon form ('keys: sorted'), never numbered and never with her ticks.

MINOR VOICES the writers may add now that the cast has no cap (the India review asks for the ward's night nurse, the wedding's cook and tent man, and named neighbours of more than one community in Nani's lane and on the station road): you say आप and their name or job word, with 'ji' in Hinglish, and no word that gives them a gender the story has not shown (the night nurse may be a man or a woman). Never a card person, never a joke.

THE CIRCLES ON THE CARDS (chapter 1's cousins, Nani's lane, the shop's applicants, the lane side, Mami's side): you never name, point at, describe or use the note words of anyone on a decision's cards before or during it (rule 36), and never agree or disagree with a remark about them (rule 38). After a pick, only the fixed template names them, in आप whatever their age so one template fits all: 'Mumtaz, the station run is yours.' | 'मुमताज़, स्टेशन का काम आपके नाम।' | 'Mumtaz, station ka kaam aapke naam.'

THE GAME'S OWN VOICE: the question box and the top bar say आप to you and are not you. Your bubble is the `you` kind only: an accent edge, bottom right, tail off the bottom edge, never yellow (rule 38; bubble spec).
cast.year_arc: JANUARY, THE OPENING (present day): your phone lies face up on the bedside table and lights with Nani's 'My eightieth. May. Everyone comes.' (waits on rulebook Q9; if no, Mummy reads it out from hers). In the kitchen Mummy hangs the calendar and rings three dates in red: 'And the rest? Everyone calls you anyway.' You: 'The pen, Mummy.' | 'मम्मी, पेन दीजिए।', and she lays the red pen down by the calendar, turned towards you. The year begins as a job handed over without a word of asking. CHAPTER 1, MAY, THE NIGHT TRAIN (Lugdi, coach S4, fourteen people and ten berths, bible section 8): Papa's phone dies and he lays his travel list on the lower berth, turned to you, the first he has ever let go of ('Tonight, you are in charge.'). You: 'Let's see, Papa.' | 'पापा, दिखाइए।' Mausi boards at 9:40 pm, says out loud that she missed you, asks you three things at once and talks over your one answer ('Yes, Mausi.'); she holds out the berth chart. You tease Papa once about the battery. Fixed reply at Nani's gate: 'Let's go in.' | 'चलिए, अंदर।' What changes: for the first time someone hands you the whole night. CHAPTER 2, MAY, THE WARD NIGHT (Rukavat): Nani runs the ward from her bed; her folder's back page lies on the bed tray turned to you ('My lane. The scales are yours.', proposed for her file). You: 'Let's see, Nani.' | 'नानी, दिखाइए।' The one night the person you answer to is the one who needs looking after: you ask her for the plain truth about the pain, answer Mama ji at eight ('Mama ji, sorted.'), and Mausa ji refuses your offer of the night chair and sits up so you can sleep, a half sweet lime set down beside you. Fixed reply: 'Now rest, Nani.' | 'नानी, अब आराम कीजिए।' What changes: someone looks after you for the first time, and you never say so. CHAPTER 3, JULY, THE FLOOD (Station): when the flood comes you message Mummy 'do din ki chhutti / shanivaar ka shutter' ('Two days off. Saturday's shutter.'), and your beats run Friday night to the Saturday shutter, so a player who works away from home has lived this too (India review). On Friday night Mummy, who never asks, hands you the hiring ('The pen's yours. Saturday too.', proposed for her file). You: 'The slips, Mummy. Let's see.' | 'मम्मी, पर्चियाँ दिखाइए।' On Saturday morning Masterji sets a tumbler of tea on his step beside you while he measures the mud. Fixed reply when the shutter goes up: 'Next monsoon, sandbags first.' What changes: you plan a year ahead, for a shop that is not yours. CHAPTER 4, 15 AUGUST, THE LANE CUP (Cricket): Tinku, your rival for the phone, lays her open scorebook on the table, turned to you, and hands you the day's decisions to see what you do with them ('Two targets. Today, your call.'). You: 'Let's see, scorer.' | 'स्कोरर, दिखाओ।', the one hand-over where your respect form drops, because she is your sister. You tell her to write her own score too, and when Captain sahab looks at her book you hand her own praise back ('Not out, scorer.'). Fixed reply: 'Sunday, then. Bring bricks.' | 'तो इतवार। ईंटें ले आइए।' What changes: you hand something back, and that night she sends the form she has kept since March (Tinku's file). CHAPTER 5, DECEMBER, THE WEDDING WEEK (Jadugar): Mami holds out her clipboard, eyes on you ('Your Mama ji says seventy. You run my list.'). You: 'Let's see, Mami.' | 'मामी, दिखाइए।' On Thursday night three phones and the band at once make you say 'One at a time! Everyone, one at a time.', the only time all year you raise your voice. Mama ji introduces you to guests as 'the in-charge'; Mausa ji sets a stack of chairs down beside you and steps back; Tinku tells you about her letter before anyone. Fixed replies: 'Now, Nani's cake.' | 'अब, नानी का केक।' and, closing the chapter, 'Next year. Same calendar.' | 'अगले साल। यही कैलेंडर।' THE ALBUM (present day): two lines only (comics review). Nani, face-on at last, counts heads round the table with one finger and counts you last: 'Aur tum.' For the first time all year you say a word about yourself: 'Nani, main bhi.' | 'नानी, मैं भी।' | 'Me too, Nani.' (proposal; owner question 6 on the cast map). The one who counted everyone is counted. The year's refrain is 'Let's see': five chapters, five people hand you the work, each in their own words (Papa 'in charge', Nani 'the scales', Mummy 'the pen', Tinku 'your call', Mami 'my list'), and each time your first line is the same, so the player hears the year as a relay that ends with them.

voice.register: Short, calm and level: the steadiest voice in a loud house, and the one that puts the listener's name on every line, which is how a young person in an Indian home talks to elders (the readers marked it as ringing true). THE SHAPE: one or two short beats (a polite request, an offer, a short closed question, or 'Pehle ___'), with the listener's name on them. In Hinglish and Hindi the name opens the bubble, after it a comma ('Papa, zara dikhaiye.' | 'पापा, ज़रा दिखाइए।'); in English it closes the bubble ('Let me see, Papa.'). Only a small word comes before the name: your exclamation ('Badhiya. Papa, jaldi aaiye.'), a common filler ('Achha, Mummy.', 'Theek hai, Papa.'), or a set English phrase that keeps its own order in every mode ('Thank you, Mausa ji.', 'Good morning, Papa.'). Two to six words a bubble as a rule, eight at most, always inside rule 62's ten; a bigger job never makes a longer bubble, it waits for the next exchange. Your lines carry their verbs: requests end on -iye, offers ask in the subjunctive ('Torch main laaun?'), and comfort lines keep their 'hai' or 'hain' ('Nani, sab yahin hain.'); only questions of fact and the closing 'Sab set.' stay bare. Full stops, not exclamation marks: 'Badhiya.' is said level, and you raise your voice once in the year, at the noise in December ('Ek-ek karke!'). Questions are short and closed and ask for facts, never feelings ('Nani, dard?'). You speak last in an exchange, never open a scene, never speak between a decision's question and its pick, and sit in an outcome beat only as its fixed reply (rules 38 and 42). HOW THIS SHORT VOICE DIFFERS FROM THE OTHER SHORT ONES: Nani's closed fragments carry no name and send 'koi' to do the job; Mausa ji drops the subject and does the job himself; Captain sahab gives the call, then one reason; Tinku ends on a score and 'haan?'; Mami reads your words back and asks 'Correct?'. You name the listener, ask to see, offer rather than announce, and put someone else first. WHEN CROSS: you stay polite (your politeness never rises or falls, unlike Mummy's), but the name stands alone at the front, closed with a full stop, and 'Pehle' names whoever was left waiting or left off ('Mama ji. Pehle Nani se miliye.' | 'Mama ji. Go and see Nani first.'). Your anger is on someone else's behalf, never at a person. BUDGET (proposal, kept from the cast file): three to six `you` bubbles a chapter, at most one a scene, the same whatever the player will pick (rule 38).
voice.mix: You mirror the listener, because being understood by each of them is your job, and that mirror is where most of your words come from. With Nani: plain everyday Hindi with Hindi verbs ('phone kijiye', not 'call kijiye'), and no English beyond her own nouns (doctor, BP, ward, ticket, cake, torch). With Mummy: her shop nouns (shutter, stock, bill, slip) on a Hindi frame, but never her counter verbs for home things ('MCB check karo', 'mains off karo' are hers). With Papa: careful Hindi with his railway English (PNR, coach, berth, confirm) and his 'Reached', which stays in English letters in every mode. With Mama ji: the most English you speak to an elder, and his own words handed back ('sorted', 'Don't worry'). With Tinku: young Hinglish, तुम and -ओ commands, a 'yaar' now and then, her name 'Tinku' (and 'scorer' at most once a chapter, at the moment the scorebook matters), and her scorebook noun 'score'. With Mausi, Mausa ji, Masterji, Captain sahab and Mami: polite Hinglish with -इए, using their own nouns only when you hand one back. YOUR OWN ENGLISH, when nobody sets it: the verbs of the phone and the booking, said with kar or ho the way nearly everyone under fifty says them ('call kijiye', 'video call kar lijiye', 'ticket book kar doon?', 'confirm kar diya', 'score update karo', 'shutter down kar doon?'), always in a shape that marks no gender (a polite command, an offer in the subjunctive, a ने past that agrees with the thing). Mummy turns home things into counter English; you turn family business into phone English, because you are the family's switchboard. YOUR OWN HINDI: everyday Hindustani, with the town's common words ('fikr mat kijiye', 'zaroor', 'waqt') and the fillers everybody says ('achha', 'theek hai', 'arre', 'haan', 'zara', 'bas' inside a line), bent back towards Hindi by a small-town home: the shape of the younger speakers in the Dehradun study (realism notes [1]). In Devanagari 'sorted' and 'set' are both 'सेट', never तय, which means 'decided'. HINDI MODE: lines are rebuilt from shapes that mark no gender (rule 66), never translated word for word, and carry only the English a Hindi-first home already says in Hindi (सॉरी, थैंक यू, सेट, स्टॉक, शटर, टिकट, बर्थ, बुक); a phone verb becomes फ़ोन करो and a congratulation becomes बहुत बढ़िया. Numbers: none in speech in any mode. In a message, digits, and only when the fact is a number (ward 3, bed 12, berth 36, 2 days off).
tics: The name on every line. Hinglish and Hindi: the name first, then a comma ('Nani, sorry.' | 'नानी, सॉरी।'). English: the name last ('Sorry, Nani.'). A set English phrase keeps its own order in every mode ('Thank you, Mausa ji.', 'Good morning, Papa.'). Name first in Hindi also keeps rule 66's third check quiet, since नानी, मौसी, मामी and मौसा जी end in -ी. The only lines without a name are to someone the scene leaves unnamed (a child at the table, a cousin on the phone) and to a group, which you call 'sab' | 'सब' | 'everyone'.

You ask to see before anything, with the 'zara' everyone puts on a polite ask: 'Zara dikhaiye.' In every chapter your first line at the hand-over is 'Let me see' with the giver's name. To Tinku and to children it is 'Zara dikhao', the one place your respect form drops, and readers hear the sibling. Only ever about work handed to you: a list, the slips, a scorebook, a clipboard.

Someone else first: 'Pehle ___'. One thing first, then at most 'phir' and one more ('Tinku, pehle score update karo. Phir chai.'); you never count on to a second or third, so no ordinal ever enters. It is how your fear shows: nobody left waiting, nobody left off.

One phrase for a whole job: 'Sab set.' | 'सब सेट।' | 'All set.', said to the person the job was for ('Nani, sab set.'). Never item by item: Mami itemises ('Keys, pending. Envelopes, done.') and you total.

Asked about yourself, you answer with the same words you close a job with, 'Sab set.', and the asker moves on. The switchboard files itself as a job. It is not a dodge: never turned back on the asker, never a figure, never somebody else's news.

Offers, not announcements: where another voice says what it will do, you ask whether you should, in the subjunctive, which marks no gender in Hindi ('Torch main laaun?', 'Ticket main book kar doon?', 'Shutter down kar doon?'). Nothing about yourself: no line says how you feel or what you want, except the album's one line.

You hand people their own words back, and only to their owner, with the owner's name in the same bubble, at most one line in three: Papa's 'Reached' and his timetable, Mama ji's 'sorted', 'pakka' and 'Don't worry', Tinku's 'score', Masterji's 'naap', Mummy's 'stock' and 'shutter', Captain sahab's 'toss', Nani's 'sach-sach'. Never a figure, never a judging note's words (rules 36 and 38), and never Mami's or Mausi's words, so the two chapters where you work beside them never blur. Typed, you copy each person's way of writing back to them.
Short closed questions for facts, never for feelings: 'Nani, dard?', 'Mausa ji, dawai ka time yaad hai?'. Never two question marks (Mausi's typed '??').
catchphrases: 'Zara dikhaiye.' | 'ज़रा दिखाइए।' | 'Let me see.' (to Tinku and children: 'Zara dikhao.' | 'ज़रा दिखाओ।'). The year's refrain, said to each person who hands you the work: 'Papa, zara dikhaiye.' | 'पापा, ज़रा दिखाइए।' | 'Let me see, Papa.' 'Let me see' is the ordinary English phrase; 'Let's see' sounded like a quiz host (readers). If rulebook Q8 puts it on a button, where 'me' is barred, the English button reads 'Let's have a look, Papa.'. Rule 66: the polite command the rule itself names (लिस्ट दिखाइए). Rule 22: only for work handed over, never in answer to anyone telling of harassment or a dowry demand, where it would sound like asking for proof.
'Pehle ___.' | 'पहले ___।' | '___ first.' Someone else always goes first: 'Chaliye, pehle sab paani pee lein.' | 'चलिए, पहले सब पानी पी लें।' | 'Come on, everyone. Water first.'

'Sab set.' | 'सब सेट।' | 'All set.' The one phrase for a whole job, and your answer when anyone asks how you are. To Mama ji, in his own English: 'Mama ji, sorted.' | 'मामा जी, सब सेट है।' | 'Sorted, Mama ji.', the sentence he most wants to hear (his file). Rule 66: सेट never changes with gender. None of the three carries a number.
voice.exclamation: 'Badhiya.' | 'बढ़िया।' | 'Great.' Said level, with a full stop, never '!'. Straight for good news ('Badhiya. Scorer, khud likho.' | 'Great. Write it yourself, scorer.'), and deadpan when something goes wrong, which is your humour ('Badhiya. Captain sahab, toss andar?' | 'Great. Toss indoors, Captain sahab?'); the readers found both uses real. English mode says 'Great.', which Indian English uses both straight and dry; 'Lovely.' sounded British. For big news it grows by one word ('Bahut badhiya.' | 'बहुत बढ़िया।'). It means 'excellent', an everyday word in every community, and calls on no one; 'Great' carries no hidden god's name either, unlike the mild English exclamations under never. Gender: बढ़िया never changes with gender; rule 66's third check flags it when it ends a sentence (-ा), and a native reader clears it. Nobody else in the cast has 'Badhiya.' or 'Great.' as their exclamation; anyone may still say 'badhiya' inside a line.
voice.sorry_thanks_love: SORRY: the plain English word, as a young person says it at home, with the name, and then the other person put in the right rather than yourself put in the wrong: 'Nani, sorry. Aap hi sahi thin.' | 'नानी, सॉरी। आप ही सही थीं।' | 'Sorry, Nani. You were right.' (थीं agrees with Nani, not you). One sorry, never tripled and never with food (Mausi's "Sorry, sorry, sorry!"); no blame made bigger (Mama ji's "poora kasoor mera"); no count put right (Tinku's "Sorry, meri galti. 14 nahin, 15."). 'Maaf kijiye.' | 'माफ़ कीजिए।' | 'Sorry to bother you.' is for strangers only (the night nurse, someone at a counter), as it is in life. THANKS: 'Thank you' with the name: 'Thank you, Mausa ji.' | 'थैंक यू, मौसा जी।' | 'Thanks, Mausa ji.' (and he leaves the room). English mode says 'Thanks', so it stays apart from Mami's "Thank you, Bhaiya ji." to vendors. 'Shukriya' | 'शुक्रिया' only to a stranger who has helped; to your own uncle it would sound formal or filmy. THANKED YOURSELF: you turn it away from yourself, plainly, the way the young do with an elder, then send it on to whoever would be left out: 'Mami, mujhe nahin. Pehle Mausa ji ko boliye.' | 'मामी, मुझे नहीं। पहले मौसा जी को बोलिए।' | 'Not me, Mami. Thank Mausa ji first.' (मुझे marks no gender). Never 'Kis baat ka?', which Captain sahab says in this moment. The fear of the one left off the list; never Tinku's handing the credit back to the thanker, never Mummy's "Isme kya". CONGRATULATING: the short form your own generation uses, then Nani first: 'Badhiya, congrats. Pehle Nani ko khud call karo.' | 'बहुत बढ़िया। पहले नानी को ख़ुद फ़ोन करो।' | 'Great, congrats. Call Nani yourself, first thing.' ("Badhai ho" is Mummy's and "Congratulations." Mami's, if the owner allows them; "Mubarak ho" is unused for now: it and "Badhai ho" are both everyday congratulations and take one ruling, and an Urdu-speaking reader checks that both sides are treated alike, India verdict 3.) LOVE: never said all year, until the album: Nani counts heads and ends "Aur tum.", and you say the only line of the year about yourself, 'Nani, main bhi.' | 'नानी, मैं भी।' | 'Me too, Nani.' (proposal; cast map owner question 6). All year it shows only as their own love handed back in their own words: Papa's "Reached" asked of Papa ('Papa, pahunchkar "Reached" bhejiye.'), the credit Tinku always gives away given back to her in plain words ('Tinku, ye tumne kiya.'), Nani's plain truth asked of Nani ('Nani, dard? Sach-sach bataiye.'), and Mama ji's own "Don't worry" said back to him at eight in the morning.
uses: Polite requests to every elder, many with 'zara': dikhaiye, dijiye, chaliye, kijiye, baithiye, bataiye, miliye, bhejiye, sunaiye, aaiye, boliye, soiye, so jaiye | दिखाइए, दीजिए, चलिए, कीजिए, बैठिए, बताइए, मिलिए, भेजिए, सुनाइए, आइए, बोलिए, सोइए, सो जाइए
Commands to Tinku, to a cousin your own age and to children: dikhao, batao, likho, rakho, le aao, call karo, update karo | दिखाओ, बताओ, लिखो, रखो, ले आओ, फ़ोन करो

Offers in the subjunctive, the main place 'main' appears: 'Torch main laaun?', 'Ticket main book kar doon?', 'Shutter down kar doon?', 'Kal jama kar doon?', 'Shaam ko call karoon?' | टॉर्च मैं लाऊँ?, टिकट मैं बुक कर दूँ?, शटर मैं गिरा दूँ?, कल जमा कर दूँ?, शाम को फ़ोन करूँ?
English phone and booking verbs with kar or ho, in shapes that mark no gender: call, video call, book, confirm, update, down (a shutter) | Hindi mode keeps बुक and कन्फ़र्म and turns call into फ़ोन

Everyday fillers and Hindustani, free for everyone: achha, theek hai, arre, haan, haan ji, zara, bas (inside a line), fikr mat kijiye, zaroor, waqt, kya pata | अच्छा, ठीक है, अरे, हाँ, ज़रा, बस, फ़िक्र मत कीजिए, ज़रूर, वक़्त, क्या पता
pehle | पहले, phir | फिर, ab | अब, abhi | अभी, khud | ख़ुद (news first-hand: 'Pehle Nani ko khud call karo.')
'Sab set' | 'सब सेट' | 'All set'; 'sorted' to Mama ji only, his word
'Badhiya.' | 'बढ़िया।' | 'Great.'; 'Bahut badhiya' for big news; 'congrats' to someone your own age
'Sorry' | 'सॉरी' | 'Sorry' and 'Thank you' | 'थैंक यू' | 'Thanks' to family and friends; 'Maaf kijiye' and 'Shukriya' to strangers
'Ji Papa' | 'जी पापा' (your yes to Papa); 'Zaroor' | 'ज़रूर' (your yes to an elder who asks you to stay or sit)
sab | सब (everyone: Nani's word, and your way to speak to a group)
sach-sach | सच-सच (the plain truth: what Nani wants from you, asked back of her about her own pain, once)
ek-ek karke | एक-एक करके (one at a time: an idiom, not a count; your one raised voice of the year)
'yaar' to Tinku or a cousin now and then, never to an elder; with an elder the name does that work

The family's working nouns, as each owner says them: ticket, PNR, coach, berth, bill, slip (parchi), keys (chaabi), cot, shutter, torch, score | टिकट, पीएनआर, कोच, बर्थ, बिल, पर्ची, चाबी, कॉट, शटर, टॉर्च, स्कोर

Handed back, to their owners only: 'Reached' and the timetable (Papa), 'sorted', 'pakka' and 'Don't worry' (Mama ji), 'score' (Tinku), 'naap' (Masterji), 'stock' and 'shutter' (Mummy), 'toss' (Captain sahab), 'sach-sach' (Nani)
never: Any Hindi form that marks your gender (rule 66): futures in -ूँगा/-ूँगी, -ोगे/-ोगी, -ेगा/-ेगी, -ेंगे/-ेंगी; मैं आ गया/गई, पहुँच गया/गई, थक गया/गई; कर रहा/रही हूँ; थका/थकी हूँ; अकेला/अकेली; a participle before रहो or रहना (cast note on rule 66's fourth flag); 'Main ready hoon'; 'Call karti hoon' and every English verb with a gendered Hindi tail.
A word that fixes your gender, said by you or accepted from others: beta, beti, bhaiya, didi, bhai, bro (rule 8); no 'bro', 'dude' or 'champ' to anyone, and no 'yaar' to an elder.
How you feel or what you want ('I'm tired', 'I'm fine', 'I'm worried', 'I want'), except the album's one line. Each also invites a gendered Hindi ending.
Turning a question about yourself back on the asker ('You first, Mausi.'), a figure, or somebody else's news in its place.
Any figure in speech: no counts, clock times, prices, scores or ordinals (the cast's two number leaners are Papa and Tinku). 'Ek-ek karke' is an idiom, not a count.
An exclamation mark, except the year's one 'Ek-ek karke!'.

Someone else's set phrase, or their exclamation as your habitual cry (the common words inside them, and a cry said now and then, stay free for you): Nani's 'Bas.' as the closer of an argument, 'Baap re', 'Chai piyo', 'Ab ye bhi', 'Khush raho', jobs sent to 'koi'; Mummy's 'Haan ji, boliye', a bare typed 'haan ji' as a whole reply, 'Had hai', 'Aur kuch?', 'mere khaate mein', 'Isme kya', 'Badhai ho' and her counter verbs for home things; Papa's 'Kamaal hai', 'Darj hai', 'Noted', and 'Reached?' as your own question; Mama ji's 'Oho', 'Pakka?' closing a worry, 'Ek kaam karo', 'Full'; Tinku's 'Gazab', 'haan?' as a tag, 'Kitaab mein', 'Faisla tumhara', 'Seriously? Phir se?'; Mausi's 'Haaye', 'Suno, suno, suno!', 'Sorry, sorry, sorry!', 'hai na?', '??'; Mausa ji's one-word 'Theek.' and 'Lo.', 'Hain?', 'Galti ho gayi'; Masterji's 'Uff', 'Chalo, phir se', 'Jeete raho'; Captain sahab's 'Arre waah' and his calls ('Not out', 'Next ball', 'Well played', 'Front foot'), except one call handed back to him, once, never mocking; Mami's 'Ish', 'Correct?' or 'Sahi?' as a tag, 'Tick', 'done', 'pending', 'Congratulations.', ordinals, numbered or ticked items and the 'thing, status' line.
A blessing to anyone ('Khush raho', 'Jeete raho'): the old bless the young, never the other way round.
तुम to any elder, Mummy and Papa included; तू to anyone.
A card person's name, relation, job, looks, pronoun or note word before or during their decision (rule 36); after a pick, only the fixed template line (rule 38).

You always pick up and never leave a message unanswered; that is why everyone calls you. The story never says when, from where or how fast you answer, so a player on night shifts or an early bus fits (India review). You never write first about yourself.

You mirror each recipient's script and punctuation, which the readers marked as ringing true: a voice note to Nani; Mummy's own lowercase with commas and no full stops; Papa's full stops and one fact a line, so he never reads you as cross; English to Mama ji, one message where he sends five; Tinku's lowercase; sentence case to the chapter voices.

English verbs do your messages' work, as they do in your speech: bare participles that mark no gender ('Reached' to Papa only, his word, in English letters in every mode; 'Booked'; 'Sorted' to Mama ji only), and phone verbs with kar in a ने past or an offer ('confirm kar diya', 'call karoon?'). In Hindi mode the rest is rebuilt from ने pasts that agree with the thing (बिल भेज दिया, छुट्टी ले ली) or no verb, never पहुँच गया/गई.
Sorry and thanks type the way you say them, plain and with the name, in the recipient's own case ('sorry mummy', 'Thank you, Mausa ji.').
Digits only when the fact is a number (ward, bed, berth, days off, the head-count of 14); no prices, no scores, no clock times except when Papa asks for one.
Voice notes: you send them only to Nani, who speaks to her phone rather than typing. Mausi's long voice notes get one typed line back.
Forwards: never. Papa's good-morning picture gets 'Good morning, Papa.' back every morning, with no clock time attached.
No typos. The family group can be mentioned, never shown (owner, 23 Oct; rule 47); if the story needs your post there, it is a single message card.

across_looks: 1. Nothing of you is painted in any look, the present day included: no hand, wrist, sleeve, knee, foot, shadow or reflection (rule 7).

2. The eyeline: in a panel where a painted person speaks to you, they turn face-on and look straight out at a grown-up's eye level, in every look now that the household is drawn from its own model sheets (owner answer 6 of 26 Oct). Panels with no painted speaker get no eyeline sentence, so it never adds a figure to a people-free panel (1.37, 1.40, the 2.24 window; rules review).

3. Hand-overs: one giving gesture per person, mostly onto surfaces (comics review), and household hands never reach towards you (bible line 78). Laid down, turned to face the viewer: Mummy's red pen by the calendar (1.05) and her spare shop key in the album; Papa's list on the lower berth (1.10); Nani's folder page on the bed tray (2.04); Tinku's open scorebook on the table (4.04); Mausa ji's half sweet lime beside you and his stack of chairs in December; Masterji's tumbler of tea on his step. Held out, at arm's length in the giver's own two hands with the giver's face in the frame, only at the two chapter-voice beats the bible marks: Mausi's berth chart (chapter 1) and Mami's clipboard (5.04). Nothing thrown or lobbed towards you (Captain sahab's ball stays in his hand), and nothing taut or carried leaves the bottom edge (Masterji's tape, a strap, a string, a stack), because that is where the painter adds a hand.
4. The `you` bubble is the same in every look because the app draws it: accent edge, bottom right, tail off the bottom edge, tag 'You' | 'आप', at most 10 words, never yellow (rule 38; bubble spec).
5. The voice is the same in every chapter: name each listener, 'Let's see' at the hand-over, 'sorted' to close, आप and -इए to every elder, nothing about yourself.

6. Your objects: the red pen and the calendar's rings in the present-day pages; the bedside phone in the present day only; your messages as a plain message card under the panel in a world chapter. Each is one beat, never a stand-in for a painted person (comics review: object stand-ins as the default rebuild the empty rooms).

7. Each look's own trap for a viewer's body. Every look: light from one side, never from behind the people (it throws their shadows towards you and loses their faces) and never from behind the viewer (it would cast your shadow into the picture; rules review). Lugdi: the coach windows curtained, because black glass at night mirrors the bay; and the story panels need a Lugdi style string without 'dramatic angle' (cutscenes.py STYLE['lugdi'] ends with it, and prompt() puts the scene words before the style, so no scene line can overrule it; Cricket's STORY_STYLE already lacks it, the wide 'cricket' style in wides.py does not). Rukavat: the ward's steel tumbler, steel bed rail and any screen painted matte. Station: with two inks a dark mass at the bottom edge reads as a figure, so the bottom edge stays cream paper or the counter's plain top, and the glass counter seen from the customer's side (3.03, exactly where you stand) is matte with soft highlights. Cricket: the table edge plain, with no bat handle or pad rising from the bottom. Jadugar: no stage mirror facing the viewer; brass trays and sweet tins in matte old gold.

Any part of a body at the frame's edge that belongs to no painted person: a hand, wrist, sleeve, knee, lap, foot, shoe tip, or a shadow falling into the picture from the viewer's side (rule 7). Check all four edges of every pick and count every painted person's hands (the three-hands lesson).

Anything taut or carried that runs out of the bottom edge (a tape, a strap, a string, a stack of chairs, a tray), and anything thrown or reaching towards the viewer outside the two held-out beats: that is where the painter adds the viewer's hand (comics review).

never_does: Is painted, in any look or any part: no face, hand, sleeve, shadow, reflection or belonging that marks a gender (rule 7).

Says how they feel or what they want, before the album.
Turns a question about themselves back on the asker; they answer in one word and nobody waits for more.
Speaks to an elder with तुम, or to anyone with तू.
Names, points at or describes a card person before or during their decision (rule 36), or agrees or disagrees with a judging note (rule 38).
Says a line that changes with the pick, or gives a rule for choosing (rule 38).
Doubts a report of harassment or a dowry demand, or calls one a misunderstanding (rule 22).
Jokes, praises, says sorry or says 'well done' in an outcome beat (rules 46 and 64).
Is the comic one; the one dry joke waits on rulebook Q5 and sits in a story beat.
Shouts, thinks in a thought bubble, or narrates in the first person (rule 35).

Teases anyone about their age, weight, phone skills or community; teasing is only ever about a person's own habit, in their own words (realism notes on the 'WhatsApp uncle' and older-people-as-props traps).
Is asked when they will marry, what they will wear, or how much they earn.
Has a clock on screen: when they sleep, wake or reply, or what their work is.
Uses a religious exclamation, a community-leaning greeting or kin word, a brand, or film dialogue (rule 3).
Borrows another person's tic: Mami's 'Ek minute', Mausi's 'Sau mein sau' and '??', Mummy's and Mausa ji's thumbs-up as their own emoji, Mausi's and Mummy's 'suno'.
Opens a scene, or speaks between a decision's question and its pick.

Touches anyone or is touched in a painting; the household lays things down for you, and only Mausi and Mami hold things out (bible section 4; Mausi's and Mami's files).
Sits on a card, asks a decision, or carries a judging note (rules 10, 22, 37).
